• Veins: Veins have relatively thick walls with one-way valves designed exclusively to carry deoxygenated blood under low pressure back up toward the heart. Their thick structural layers prevent any direct transfer of oxygen or nutrients.
• Arteries: Arteries have highly elastic, thick, muscular walls built to withstand the high-pressure surges of oxygenated blood being pumped directly away from the heart. Their dense structure completely prevents the diffusion of gases or nutrients.

Question (Front): The second stage of carbohydrate metabolism which takes place in the mitochondria and requires oxygen.
Rationale:
In nutritional biochemistry and board examination frameworks, aerobic carbohydrate catabolism is traditionally classified into sequential stages:
	1. Stage 1: Glycolysis (anaerobic process taking place entirely in the cytoplasm).
	2. Stage 2: Oxidative decarboxylation (the transition phase moving into the Krebs cycle/TCA cycle).
	3. Stage 3: Oxidative phosphorylation via the Electron Transport Chain (ETC).

Once glycolysis yields pyruvate in the cytosol, the pyruvate is actively transported into the mitochondria. Here, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex carries out oxidative decarboxylation, converting pyruvate into Acetyl-CoA while stripping away carbon dioxide and generating NADH. Because this pathway feeds directly into the aerobic respiration chain, it strictly requires oxygen to proceed.

• Glycolysis: This is the first stage of carbohydrate breakdown. It takes place in the anaerobic environment of the fluid cytoplasm (cytosol), meaning it does not require oxygen or mitochondrial machinery to function.
• Hexose monophosphate shunt: Also known as the Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP), this is an alternative pathway parallel to glycolysis used to generate NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate. It does not serve as the primary second stage of energy-yielding glucose metabolism.
• Oxidative phosphorylation: This is the final (third) stage of cellular respiration where the vast majority of ATP is structurally synthesized by ATP synthase along the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Question (Front): End products of the anaerobic phase of glucose metabolism
Rationale: The anaerobic phase of glucose metabolism refers primarily to glycolysis, which occurs in the cytoplasm and does not require oxygen directly. Glycolysis converts one molecule of glucose into two molecules of pyruvate, producing a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. When oxygen availability is limited or when glycolytic flux exceeds mitochondrial oxidative capacity, pyruvate can be reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase. This regenerates NAD⁺, allowing glycolysis to continue producing ATP.

Question (Front): All contain carbohydrates except:
Rationale:
Carbohydrates are found in a wide range of foods, particularly plant foods and certain dairy products. Wheat bread contains starch, while ripe fruits contain naturally occurring sugars such as glucose and fructose. Pasteurized milk also contains carbohydrate in the form of lactose, the naturally occurring sugar in milk. Pasteurization does not remove or substantially eliminate the lactose in milk. 

Lean meat, in contrast, contains primarily protein and fat and provides essentially no carbohydrate. Although very small amounts of carbohydrate-related compounds may be present in animal tissues, meat is generally classified as a negligible-carbohydrate food for nutrition and dietary planning purposes.

Question (Front): In the WHO-BMI cut off point, a BMI of 35.99 is classified as:
Rationale: According to the WHO International BMI Classification: Underweight <18.5, Normal 18.5–24.9, Overweight/Pre-obese 25.0–29.9, Obese Class I 30.0–34.9, Obese Class II 35.0–39.9, and Obese Class III ≥40.0 kg/m².

Question (Front): Nutritional management when a patient experiences vomiting
Rationale:
During active vomiting, the immediate nutritional priority is to allow the gastrointestinal tract to rest while preventing dehydration. Food is generally withheld temporarily until vomiting subsides, after which oral intake can be gradually resumed as tolerated. Once the patient can tolerate fluids, small, frequent amounts of fluid are preferred rather than large volumes at one time. 

Oral rehydration solutions may be particularly useful when fluid and electrolyte losses are significant. After vomiting has stopped, food should be reintroduced gradually, usually beginning with small portions and advancing according to tolerance. Large amounts of fluid with meals can worsen fullness and nausea, while hot, strongly scented, greasy, or spicy foods may be poorly tolerated. Cold or room-temperature foods may sometimes be better tolerated because they have less odor.

Question (Front):
Which of the following is/are not true about dietary management of diabetes mellitus?
I. The type of carbohydrate is more important than the total amount of carbohydrates
II. The total amount of carbohydrate consumed is more important than the source of carbohydrate
III. People with diabetes mellitus can eat candies and other sugary foods.
Rationale:
Statement I is NOT true because, in diabetes management, the total amount of carbohydrate consumed is a major determinant of postprandial blood glucose, particularly when considering carbohydrate counting and matching carbohydrate intake with insulin or other glucose-lowering therapy. The type and quality of carbohydrate are also important because fiber content, degree of processing, and food composition can affect the glycemic response, but carbohydrate type is not generally considered more important than the total amount consumed. Thus, saying that type is more important than total amount is an inaccurate statement. 

Statement II is considered true in the context of the fundamental principle of carbohydrate management: the amount of carbohydrate consumed has a substantial and predictable effect on blood glucose. This does not mean that carbohydrate source is unimportant; whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruits, and other minimally processed carbohydrate-rich foods are generally preferred over highly refined foods and foods high in added sugars because of their fiber and nutrient content. 

Statement III is also true because people with diabetes do not have to completely eliminate candies and other sugary foods. These can be incorporated occasionally into an individualized meal plan, provided that carbohydrate and overall energy intake are appropriately managed.

Question (Front): Consistent carbohydrate diet means:
Answer (Back): The amount of carbohydrate consumed and the timing of meals and snacks are consistent
Rationale: A consistent carbohydrate diet is a meal-planning approach commonly used in the management of diabetes mellitus. Rather than eliminating carbohydrates, the goal is to maintain a relatively consistent amount of carbohydrate at meals and snacks from day to day, while keeping meal timing regular. This helps minimize fluctuations in blood glucose levels and improves the effectiveness of diabetes medications, particularly insulin and insulin secretagogues. The emphasis is on consistency, not on consuming a fixed amount of carbohydrates for every individual.
Option 1: The type and amount of carbohydrate in the diet must be consistent as well as the timing of meals and snacks
Option 2: The amount of carbohydrate consumed and the timing of meals and snacks are consistent
Option 3: In case of hypoglycemia, 15 grams of carbohydrates are given every 15 minutes to achieve consistent blood sugar level
Option 4: 45 to 75 grams of carbohydrates are given at each meal to maintain normal blood sugar level

Question (Front):
During glycolysis and TCA, glucose is first broken down into _____, then _____, and finally
_____for use in the body.
Rationale:
During glucose oxidation, glycolysis first converts glucose into pyruvate in the cytoplasm. Each glucose molecule produces two molecules of pyruvate. 

Under aerobic conditions, pyruvate enters the mitochondria and undergoes oxidative decarboxylation, producing acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA then enters the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, where its carbon atoms are progressively oxidized and energy is captured primarily in the form of NADH and FADH₂. The reduced electron carriers generated during glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the TCA cycle subsequently donate electrons to the electron transport chain, driving oxidative phosphorylation and the production of ATP. 

Thus, the simplified sequence tested by this question is glucose → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → energy (ATP).

Question (Front): What is the fate of excess intake of dietary protein?
Answer (Back): After absorption, the extra amino acids will be rapidly degraded
Rationale:
Unlike carbohydrates and fats, the body does not have a specialized storage depot for excess amino acids or dietary protein. After dietary protein is digested and absorbed, amino acids enter the body's amino acid pool and are used for protein synthesis and other metabolic functions. When amino acid availability exceeds the body's immediate needs for protein synthesis and other required compounds, the excess amino acids are deaminated. Their nitrogen is converted primarily to urea in the liver and excreted in the urine, while their carbon skeletons can be used for energy or converted into glucose, ketone bodies, or other metabolites. 

Therefore, consuming more protein than needed does not result in the body storing the extra protein as protein for later use. The body continually regulates amino acid metabolism according to physiological needs. Excess energy from protein can ultimately contribute to energy storage as body fat if overall energy intake exceeds expenditure, but this occurs after amino acid catabolism, not through storage of excess dietary protein as a protein reserve.
Option 1: After absorption, the liver will store the extra amino acids
Option 2: After absorption, the extra amino acids will be rapidly degraded
Option 3: Digestion will be decreased by 30-60% resulting in less absorption
Option 4: After absorption, extra proteins will be synthesized and stored for use when protein intake returns to normal

Question (Front): The enzyme sucrase acts on sucrose to produce:
Rationale:
Sucrose is a disaccharide composed of one molecule of glucose and one molecule of fructose. The brush-border enzyme sucrase hydrolyzes the glycosidic bond in sucrose, releasing glucose and fructose as the final monosaccharide products. These monosaccharides can then be absorbed by the small intestine through specific transport mechanisms. 

Sucrase is part of the intestinal sucrase-isomaltase complex located on the brush border of enterocytes. The resulting glucose and fructose are absorbed primarily in the small intestine and enter the portal circulation, with glucose and fructose using different transport proteins. This illustrates the importance of brush-border enzymes in completing carbohydrate digestion before absorption.

Question (Front): Essential amino acids except:
Rationale:
Histidine, leucine, and lysine are essential amino acids, meaning they cannot be synthesized by the human body in sufficient amounts to meet physiological needs and therefore must be obtained from the diet. Histidine is particularly important for growth and tissue repair, leucine is a branched-chain amino acid that plays an important role in stimulating muscle protein synthesis, and lysine is involved in protein synthesis and several other metabolic functions. 

Glutamine is classified as a nonessential amino acid under normal physiological conditions because the body can synthesize it from glutamate and ammonia. However, during severe illness, trauma, burns, or other metabolic stress, glutamine requirements may increase substantially and endogenous synthesis may not meet demand. It is therefore often described as conditionally essential in certain clinical situations.

Question (Front): Electron-carrier molecules that are used in the electron-transport chain to generate additional ATP are:
Rationale:
NADH and FADH₂ are reduced electron carriers generated during several stages of cellular respiration, including glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the TCA cycle. They carry high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain (ETC) located in the inner mitochondrial membrane. As electrons move through the ETC, the released energy is used to pump protons across the membrane, creating a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase. 

NADH donates electrons to Complex I, whereas FADH₂ donates electrons through Complex II. Because FADH₂ enters the ETC downstream of Complex I, it generally results in the production of less ATP than NADH. Modern estimates are approximately 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH₂, although the exact ATP yield can vary depending on cellular conditions and the pathway used to transfer cytosolic reducing equivalents into the mitochondria.

Question (Front): An essential fatty acid derived from plant oils such as corn oil:
Rationale: Linoleic acid (18:2 n-6) is an essential omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid abundant in vegetable seed oils (corn, sunflower, safflower) that cannot be synthesized de novo by humans.

Question (Front): A 20% intravenous fat emulsion provides approximately how many kilocalories per 100 mL?
Rationale:
A 20% intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) contains approximately 20 g of lipid per 100 mL and is conventionally estimated to provide 2 kcal/mL, or approximately 200 kcal per 100 mL. This is the value commonly used when calculating the energy contribution of IV lipid emulsions in parenteral nutrition. 

A 10% ILE provides approximately 1.1 kcal/mL, while a 20% ILE provides approximately 2 kcal/mL. The distinction is important because the caloric value assigned to IV lipid emulsions is not calculated simply by multiplying grams of lipid by 9 kcal/g, as would commonly be done for dietary fat. 

Commercial IV lipid emulsions contain triglycerides along with emulsifying agents and other components, and their labeled caloric contribution is based on the formulation. For PN calculations, therefore, use the manufacturer/standard clinical kcal/mL value for the specific lipid emulsion.

Question (Front): Which of the following contain the least amount of dietary fiber?
Rationale:
Well-milled rice contains the least dietary fiber among the choices because the milling process removes the outer layers of the rice grain, including much of the bran and germ, where dietary fiber is concentrated. As a result, well-milled or highly polished white rice contains substantially less fiber than less-refined grains and many plant foods. This makes well-milled rice a low-fiber carbohydrate source. 

In comparison, sinigwelas (Java plum), yellow camote (sweet potato), and lakatan (banana) are plant foods that retain their cellular structures and therefore provide dietary fiber. Their exact fiber content varies with variety, maturity, preparation, and serving size, but they generally provide more dietary fiber than well-milled rice. For NDLE purposes, the key concept is that refining and milling grains removes fiber-rich outer layers.

Question (Front): The following inhibit the absorption of iron EXCEPT:
Rationale:
Iron absorption is influenced by both the chemical form of iron and components of the meal. Nonheme iron, the major form found in plant foods and fortified foods, is particularly affected by dietary factors. 

Coffee and tea can substantially reduce nonheme iron absorption because they contain polyphenolic compounds that bind iron and reduce its bioavailability. Soy products may also reduce nonheme iron absorption because of compounds such as phytate, although the magnitude of the effect depends on the food and overall dietary pattern. 

Fructose, in contrast, does not inhibit iron absorption and may actually enhance nonheme iron absorption under certain conditions. It has been associated with improved iron absorption, although its effect is less prominent than that of vitamin C.
Option 2: Soy products (if major dietary protein is from soy)

Question (Front): Which of the following meats has the lowest kilocalories from fat per serving?
Rationale:
Among these choices, chicken leg generally provides the lowest amount of fat-derived energy per standard serving when compared with pork pata, chicken wings, and Vienna sausage. Chicken leg is a relatively nutrient-dense source of protein, although its fat content varies depending on whether the skin is consumed and the specific cut and preparation method. Removing the skin substantially reduces its fat and total energy content. 

Pork pata and chicken wings tend to contain more fat per edible serving, while Vienna sausage is a processed meat product that commonly contains a relatively high proportion of fat. For nutrition assessment and meal planning, it is important to consider the edible portion, preparation method, skin, and processing because these can substantially alter the fat and energy content of meat products.

Question (Front): Sodium equivalent of the low sodium diet?
Rationale: A low-sodium diet generally limits sodium intake to approximately 2,000 mg/day or less, particularly in clinical nutrition for conditions such as hypertension, heart failure, and certain renal or hepatic disorders. Sodium restriction reduces sodium and water retention and may help control blood pressure and fluid balance. Importantly, the exact sodium prescription should be individualized according to the patient's diagnosis, clinical status, and current guidelines.

Question (Front): Using the Tannhauser’s method, a 5’6” person has an ideal body weight of:
Rationale:
Step-by-Step Calculation

Tannhauser's Method (widely used in the Philippines to estimate Desirable Body Weight or DBW) utilizes the following formula:
DBW (kg) = (Height in cm - 100) - [10% x (Height in cm - 100)]

1. Convert height to centimeters:
• 5 feet 6 inches = 66 inches
• 66 inches x 2.54 cm/inch = 167.64 cm

2. Calculate initial DBW baseline:
• 167.64 - 100 = 67.64 kg

3. Deduct 10% for the Filipino/Asian frame adjustment:
• 10% of 67.64 = 6.764 kg
• 67.64 kg - 6.764 kg = 60.876 kg

Rounding 60.876 kg to the nearest whole number gives 61 kg.

Question (Front): The desirable body weight of a 4-year-old girl is:
Rationale:
For children 1–6 years of age, a commonly taught formula for estimating expected or desirable body weight is Weight (kg) = (age in years × 2) + 8. 

For a 4-year-old child, the calculation is therefore (4 × 2) + 8 = 16 kg. Thus, the answer is 16 kg. This is a quick estimation formula commonly used in nutrition education and examination settings.

Question (Front): A diabetic patient with HbA1c test result of 10% is indicative of _____ glucose control.
Rationale:
An HbA1c of 10% indicates poor glycemic control and reflects substantially elevated average blood glucose over approximately the preceding 2–3 months. HbA1c measures the percentage of hemoglobin that has glucose attached to it (glycated hemoglobin). The higher the average blood glucose concentration, the greater the proportion of glycated hemoglobin. An HbA1c of 10% corresponds to an estimated average glucose (eAG) of approximately 240 mg/dL (13.3 mmol/L). 

For most nonpregnant adults with diabetes, the commonly recommended treatment goal is an HbA1c of <7%, although targets should be individualized according to age, comorbidities, hypoglycemia risk, life expectancy, and patient preferences.

Question (Front): A deficiency of UDP-glucose:galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) will lead to an accumulation of:
Rationale:
UDP-glucose:galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) is a key enzyme in the Leloir pathway, which metabolizes galactose into glucose-derived metabolites. GALT normally converts galactose-1-phosphate + UDP-glucose → UDP-galactose + glucose-1-phosphate. 

When GALT is deficient, as occurs in classic galactosemia, galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in tissues, while galactose is also elevated in the blood. Some excess galactose is converted to galactitol, which contributes to complications such as cataracts.

Question (Front): During aerobic respiration, the decomposition of one glucose molecule produces:
Rationale:
Using the traditional biochemical calculation commonly taught in nutrition and NDLE review materials, the complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule produces a maximum of 38 ATP. 

This calculation assigns 3 ATP per NADH and 2 ATP per FADH₂. Glycolysis produces 2 ATP and 2 NADH; pyruvate oxidation produces 2 NADH; and the TCA cycle produces 2 ATP (or GTP), 6 NADH, and 2 FADH₂. Altogether, this gives 38 ATP per glucose under the traditional accounting system.

Question (Front):
To increase appetite, which of the following is/are recommended?
I. Relaxed eating
II. Small frequent feedings
III. Eating favorite food
Rationale:
All three strategies can help improve appetite and food intake, particularly in patients experiencing poor appetite. Relaxed eating can make meals more pleasant and reduce anxiety or stress associated with eating. Creating an appealing mealtime environment and avoiding pressure to eat may encourage intake. Small, frequent meals are useful because a large meal may be overwhelming for someone with a poor appetite; smaller portions are often better tolerated and can help increase total daily intake. Offering favorite or preferred foods is another practical strategy because food preference and palatability strongly influence willingness to eat. 

In clinical nutrition, these approaches are commonly incorporated into individualized nutrition care, especially when the immediate goal is to increase energy and nutrient intake. However, favorite foods should still be selected with consideration for the patient's medical condition and dietary requirements.

Question (Front): Generally, men have higher BMR/kg than women because:
Answer (Back): they have more lean tissues/unit weight
Rationale: Men generally possess a greater percentage of lean body mass (fat-free skeletal muscle and organ tissue) per unit of body weight compared to women, which is the primary determinant of higher Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR).
Option 3: they have more lean tissues/unit weight

Question (Front): A sensible weight reducing program includes:
Rationale: Comprehensive and evidence-based weight management requires a sustainable multidisciplinary approach incorporating modest caloric restriction (diet), regular physical activity (exercise), and cognitive behavioral therapy (behavior modification).
Option 1: drugs to effect rapid weight loss
Option 2: use of formula diets to ensure appropriate calorie intake
Option 3: use of herbal preparations as an adjunct to diet

Question (Front): In conditions characterized by hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria, a suitable diet is one that is:
Answer (Back): easy to digest or consists of predigested protein like protein hydrolysates
Rationale:
Hypochlorhydria refers to reduced gastric acid secretion, while achlorhydria refers to an absence or near-absence of hydrochloric acid (HCl) in the stomach. Gastric acid contributes to the denaturation of dietary proteins and facilitates the conversion of pepsinogen to pepsin, which begins protein digestion in the stomach. When gastric acid is markedly reduced or absent, protein digestion in the stomach may be impaired. 

Therefore, traditionally, a diet emphasizing easily digested foods and, when clinically indicated, predigested protein such as protein hydrolysates may be recommended. However, the important modern clinical point is that hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria does not automatically require a low-protein diet or routine use of protein hydrolysates. Protein digestion continues in the small intestine through pancreatic and brush-border enzymes. Management should focus on the underlying cause and the patient's nutritional status.
Option 3: easy to digest or consists of predigested protein like protein hydrolysates

Question (Front): Foot care is an important aspect of diabetes education of patients to avoid:
Answer (Back): wounds on the feet which may become gangrenous
Rationale:
Proper diabetic foot care is essential because diabetes can cause peripheral neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease, both of which increase the risk of foot injury and delayed wound healing. Neuropathy may reduce protective sensation, so a patient may not notice a blister, cut, burn, pressure injury, or poorly fitting footwear. Reduced blood flow can further impair tissue healing and increase the risk of infection. 

Regular foot inspection, appropriate footwear, foot hygiene, and prompt attention to injuries help prevent minor problems from progressing to serious ulcers and, in severe cases, gangrene and amputation.
Option 4: wounds on the feet which may become gangrenous

Question (Front): If a person wants to improve his/her fiber intake, which of the following food would be best?
Rationale:
Saluyot (jute leaves) is the best choice among the options because leafy vegetables such as saluyot provide a relatively high amount of dietary fiber compared with the other vegetables listed. Saluyot is also a good source of several micronutrients and is commonly consumed as a vegetable in the Philippines. Increasing intake of fiber-rich vegetables can contribute to improved bowel function and overall diet quality. 

Radish, cucumber, and tomato also contain dietary fiber, but their fiber contribution per comparable edible portion is generally lower than that of saluyot. For practical nutrition counseling, however, the overall dietary pattern matters: a person should obtain fiber from a variety of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and seeds, rather than relying on one food alone.

Question (Front): Some clinicians recommend egg whites as the sole source of protein for patients with renal failure because:
Answer (Back): egg white protein has the highest biological value
Rationale:
Egg white is considered a high-quality protein because it contains all the essential amino acids in proportions that support human protein needs and has high protein quality. 

In patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), when protein intake is restricted or carefully prescribed, choosing high-quality protein sources can help provide adequate essential amino acids while limiting the total amount of protein consumed. Egg white is also relatively low in phosphorus compared with the whole egg because most of the egg's phosphorus is found in the yolk. 

However, egg whites should not routinely be considered the sole protein source for every patient with renal failure. Current CKD nutrition care emphasizes individualized protein and energy prescriptions according to CKD stage, dialysis status, nutritional status, and other clinical factors. Patients receiving dialysis generally have higher protein requirements than patients with non-dialysis CKD. The key concept tested here is high protein quality/biological value, not a therapeutic effect unique to egg white.
Option 1: egg whites are the most acceptable protein source
Option 3: egg white protein has the highest biological value

Question (Front): Elimination diets are used in:
Rationale: Elimination diets systematically eliminate suspected offending foods/allergens from the diet to observe symptom resolution, serving as a primary diagnostic and therapeutic tool for food allergies and intolerances.

Question (Front): A mechanical soft diet includes:
Answer (Back): easy to chew foods, including foods in the regular diet
Rationale:
A mechanical soft diet consists of foods that are soft in texture and easy to chew and swallow, with modification of the texture achieved through methods such as chopping, grinding, mashing, or cooking foods until tender. The goal is to reduce the mechanical effort required to chew food while still allowing a broader variety of foods than a full-liquid or pureed diet. Depending on the patient's needs, foods from a regular diet can be modified to achieve the appropriate texture. 

A mechanical soft diet is therefore primarily defined by texture and ease of chewing, not by whether foods are liquid or low in fiber. It may be prescribed for patients with difficulty chewing because of dental problems, oral surgery, weakness, or other conditions affecting chewing. The specific texture should always be matched to the patient's swallowing ability because a mechanical soft diet is not automatically appropriate for someone with dysphagia.
Option 3: easy to chew foods, including foods in the regular diet

Question (Front): A morbidly obese patient underwent gastric bypass. What classical side effect can the patient experience as a result of the surgery?
Rationale:
Dumping syndrome is a classic complication of gastric bypass surgery. Because the stomach's normal reservoir function is altered and food can pass relatively rapidly into the small intestine, particularly after meals high in simple carbohydrates, patients may experience rapid gastric emptying. This can produce early symptoms such as abdominal cramping, bloating, nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, flushing, and tachycardia shortly after eating. The rapid delivery of carbohydrate can also cause a subsequent exaggerated insulin response. 

Dumping syndrome may also have a late phase, typically occurring 1–3 hours after eating, characterized by symptoms of hypoglycemia such as weakness, sweating, tremors, palpitations, and confusion. Dietary management commonly includes small, frequent meals; limiting rapidly absorbed carbohydrates; emphasizing protein and complex carbohydrates; and separating fluids from meals when appropriate. Although nutritional deficiencies and undernutrition can also occur after bariatric surgery, dumping syndrome is the classical side effect specifically associated with altered gastric anatomy and rapid gastric emptying.

Question (Front): Lactose intolerance is due to:
Rationale: Lactose intolerance occurs when there is insufficient lactase, the brush-border enzyme responsible for breaking down lactose into its absorbable monosaccharides, glucose and galactose. When lactose is not adequately digested in the small intestine, it reaches the colon, where gut bacteria ferment it and produce gases and other metabolites. The resulting osmotic effect and fermentation can cause bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, and diarrhea after consuming lactose-containing foods.

Question (Front): Fats are generally restricted in diseases of the liver because:
Rationale: In chronic liver diseases, fat restriction is indicated because damaged hepatocytes exhibit impaired bile acid synthesis/secretion for micelle formation, and impaired beta-oxidation can exacerbate hepatic steatosis.
Option 1: impaired production and transport of bile
Option 2: fat metabolism may be impaired and result in fatty liver

Question (Front): A dietary risk factor of coronary artery disease is high intake of:
Rationale: Elevated dietary intake of saturated fatty acids and industrial trans-fats increases serum low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and arterial inflammation, a major independent risk factor for coronary artery disease.

Question (Front): Dietary fibers are useful in preventing hypercholesterolemia because they:
Answer (Back): bind cholesterol containing bile acids which are eventually excreted
Rationale: Certain soluble, viscous dietary fibers can help lower blood LDL cholesterol by increasing the excretion of bile acids and cholesterol in the feces. The liver must use circulating cholesterol to synthesize new bile acids, thereby increasing hepatic demand for cholesterol and contributing to lower LDL cholesterol concentrations. Examples of cholesterol-lowering soluble fibers include β-glucan from oats and barley, psyllium, and some fibers from legumes. The original wording is somewhat simplified because fiber does not literally “bind cholesterol-containing bile acids” in every case; increased bile acid excretion and fermentation-related mechanisms both contribute.
Option 1: bind cholesterol containing bile acids which are eventually excreted

Question (Front): The conservative management of chronic kidney disease which is characterized by progressive and irreversible destruction of nephrons consists of:
Rationale:
Conservative management of chronic kidney disease (CKD) aims to slow disease progression, manage complications, and maintain quality of life without renal replacement therapy. It includes appropriate dietary management and pharmacologic treatment, along with control of blood pressure, diabetes, cardiovascular risk factors, electrolyte and acid-base abnormalities, anemia, and other complications. Nutrition therapy may involve individualized adjustments to protein, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and energy intake depending on the CKD stage and laboratory findings. 

Dialysis and kidney transplantation are forms of kidney replacement therapy, not conservative management. Importantly, conservative management is not simply “diet only”; medications and comprehensive medical management are integral.

Question (Front): Food to emphasize when it is necessary to increase potassium:
Rationale:
Fruits are generally good sources of potassium and are commonly emphasized when increasing dietary potassium. Examples include banana, oranges, melon, papaya, avocado, and dried fruits. Potassium is an important intracellular electrolyte involved in nerve transmission, muscle contraction, and maintenance of normal cardiac function. However, potassium intake should be individualized because patients with chronic kidney disease, hyperkalemia, or certain medications may instead require potassium restriction. 

Starchy roots such as potatoes and sweet potatoes can also provide substantial potassium, so they are not inherently poor choices. However, among the options, fruits are the most appropriate general food group to emphasize when the goal is to increase potassium intake.

Question (Front): The C P F and kcal value of a breakfast containing 2 rice B exchanges, 2 medium fat exchanges, and 1 fruit exchange.
Answer (Back): C 56g P 20 g F 12 g E 412 kcal
Rationale:
Using the Philippine Food Exchange List (FEL), here is the exact step-by-step breakdown of the computation.

1. Rice B (2 exchanges):
	• Carbohydrates: 2 x 23g = 46g
	• Protein: 2 x 2g = 4g
	• Fat: 0g
	• Calories: 2 x 100 kcal = 200 kcal

2. Medium-Fat Meat (2 exchanges):
	• Carbohydrates: 0g
	• Protein: 2 x 8g = 16g
	• Fat: 2 x 6g = 12g
	• Calories: 2 x 86 kcal = 172 kcal

3. Fruit (1 exchange):
	• Carbohydrates: 1 x 10g = 10g
	• Protein: 0g
	• Fat: 0g
	• Calories: 1 x 40 kcal = 40 kcal

Grand Totals:
	• Carbohydrates: 46g + 0g + 10g = 56 grams
	• Protein: 4g + 16g + 0g = 20 grams
	• Fat: 0g + 12g + 0g = 12 grams
	• Energy: 200 + 172 + 40 = 412 kcal

Verifying the Math with Atwater Multipliers:
• Carbohydrates: 56g x 4 kcal/g = 224 kcal
• Protein: 20g x 4 kcal/g = 80 kcal
• Fat: 12g x 9 kcal/g = 108 kcal
• Total Energy: 224 + 80 + 108 = 412 kcal
Option 1: C 46 g P 16 g F 10g E 338 kcal
Option 2: C 56 g P 16 g F 6 g E 342 kcal
Option 3: C 46 g P 20 g F 10 g E 354 kcal
Option 4: C 56g P 20 g F 12 g E 412 kcal

Question (Front): All measures are allowed to increase the energy intake of renal patient except:
Answer (Back): serving fruit cocktail with heavy syrup
Rationale:
When a renal patient requires increased energy intake, particularly when protein, potassium, phosphorus, or fluid may need to be controlled, energy can be increased by using calorie-dense foods that provide relatively little protein and minerals. Adding sugar, oil, and unsalted margarine can increase energy density without substantially increasing protein. 

In contrast, fruit cocktail with heavy syrup may be inappropriate depending on the patient's potassium and fluid restrictions; canned fruits may also contribute substantial potassium, and the syrup contributes mainly sugar rather than being a particularly useful renal nutrition strategy.
Option 4: serving fruit cocktail with heavy syrup

Question (Front):
Which of the following are conditions that resulted from vitamin C deficiency?
I. Beriberi, confusion, depression, convulsions, scurvy 
II. Microcytic anemia, bleeding gums, loosened teeth, scurvy 
III. Rashes, hair loss, microcytic anemia, bleeding gums 
IV. Confusion, convulsions, loosened teeth, scurvy, hair loss
Rationale:
Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, characterized by impaired collagen synthesis and connective-tissue abnormalities. Classic manifestations include bleeding or swollen gums, loose teeth, poor wound healing, petechiae/ecchymoses, and fatigue. Vitamin C also enhances non-heme iron absorption, so deficiency can contribute to anemia; however, the anemia associated with vitamin C deficiency is not necessarily microcytic, and may be related to impaired iron absorption and blood loss.

Among the choices, Statement II is the best match because it contains the classic manifestations of scurvy.

Question (Front): The immediate goal of dietary management in acute diarrhea is:
Rationale:
In acute diarrhea, the rapid and massive loss of water and critical electrolytes (like sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate) through the stool pose an immediate risk of hypovolemic shock and cardiovascular collapse, particularly in vulnerable populations.

While preventing nutritional deficiencies and restoring long-term nutritional status are essential milestones during the subsequent convalescent phase, they cannot be addressed if the patient is acutely unstable. Therefore, the absolute primary, immediate goal of clinical dietary management is maintaining fluid volume and preventing or correcting dehydration through the immediate administration of oral rehydration solutions (ORS).

Question (Front): Drinking coffee or tea together with an iron-rich meal primarily decreases the absorption of which type of iron?
Rationale: Coffee and tea contain polyphenols and tannins that form insoluble complexes with non-heme iron, substantially reducing its intestinal absorption. The inhibitory effect is greatest when these beverages are consumed with or shortly after meals. Heme iron, derived from animal foods, is absorbed through a different mechanism and is much less affected by dietary inhibitors. Vitamin C can counteract this inhibition by reducing ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to the more absorbable ferrous form (Fe²⁺).
Option 4: Both heme and non-heme iron equally

Question (Front): Which lipoprotein is primarily responsible for transporting dietary triglycerides from the intestine to peripheral tissues?
Rationale: Chylomicrons are the largest and least dense lipoproteins. They are synthesized in the intestinal mucosal cells after dietary fat absorption and transport exogenous triglycerides, cholesterol, fat-soluble vitamins, and phospholipids through the lymphatic system before entering the bloodstream. Lipoprotein lipase (LPL), activated by apolipoprotein C-II, hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons, releasing free fatty acids for uptake by adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. The remaining chylomicron remnants are taken up by the liver.

Question (Front): Which enzyme is responsible for hydrolyzing triglycerides in circulating chylomicrons and VLDL?
Rationale:
Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) is an extracellular enzyme attached to the capillary endothelium of adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and cardiac muscle. It hydrolyzes triglycerides contained in circulating chylomicrons and VLDL into free fatty acids and glycerol. 

The released fatty acids are either: 
• Stored as triglycerides in adipose tissue, or 
• Oxidized by muscle tissue for energy. 

LPL activity is stimulated by apolipoprotein C-II, making Apo C-II an essential cofactor for normal triglyceride metabolism.

Question (Front): Which of the following hormones primarily stimulates glycogen breakdown in the liver during fasting?
Rationale:
Glucagon is a peptide hormone secreted by the pancreatic α-cells in response to declining blood glucose concentrations. Its primary role is to maintain euglycemia during the post-absorptive state by stimulating hepatic glucose production. 

The major metabolic actions of glucagon include: 
• Glycogenolysis – breakdown of liver glycogen into glucose.
• Gluconeogenesis – synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors such as lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids. 
• Lipolysis – indirectly promotes mobilization of fatty acids from adipose tissue. 
• Ketogenesis – enhances ketone body formation during prolonged fasting. It is important to note that skeletal muscle lacks glucagon receptors. 

Therefore, glucagon promotes glycogenolysis primarily in the liver, whereas muscle glycogen breakdown is stimulated mainly by epinephrine and muscle contraction.

Question (Front): Which of the following best describes the primary function of bile salts in lipid digestion?
Answer (Back): Emulsify dietary fats and facilitate micelle formation
Rationale:
Bile salts are amphipathic molecules synthesized from cholesterol in the liver and stored in the gallbladder. Upon ingestion of dietary fat, they are released into the duodenum where they perform two major functions: 

• Emulsification – breaking large fat globules into smaller droplets, thereby increasing the surface area available for pancreatic lipase. 
• Micelle formation – surrounding fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins to facilitate their transport to the intestinal brush border for absorption. 

Bile salts themselves do not digest fats; rather, they enhance the efficiency of pancreatic lipase and promote lipid absorption.
Option 1: Emulsify dietary fats and facilitate micelle formation

Question (Front): Which of the following describes the maximum amount of bone tissue attained after skeletal development is completed and serves as an important determinant of bone health in adulthood?
Rationale:
Peak bone mass (PBM) is the maximum amount of bone tissue accumulated by an individual at the end of skeletal maturation, usually achieved during the late teens to early 30s, depending on the skeletal site, sex, genetics, and lifestyle factors. It represents the highest level of bone strength attained before the gradual age-related decline in bone mass begins. 

Peak bone mass is influenced by several factors, including: 
• Genetics (the strongest determinant) 
• Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake 
• Regular weight-bearing and resistance exercise 
• Hormonal status (especially estrogen and testosterone) 
• Adequate protein intake 
• Avoidance of smoking and excessive alcohol consumption

A higher peak bone mass reduces the risk of osteopenia, osteoporosis, and fragility fractures later in life. Therefore, childhood, adolescence, and young adulthood are considered critical periods for optimizing bone health.

Question (Front): Protein recommendation for adults with pressure injuries or significant wounds to promote wound healing:
Rationale:
Protein is one of the most important nutrients for wound healing, as it is required for collagen synthesis, fibroblast proliferation, angiogenesis, immune function, and tissue repair. Inadequate protein intake delays wound healing, impairs immune responses, and increases the risk of wound infection and chronic non-healing wounds. Patients with pressure injuries, surgical wounds, burns, traumatic injuries, or chronic ulcers generally have increased protein requirements because of the increased metabolic demands associated with tissue repair. 

Current clinical nutrition guidelines recommend approximately 1.25–1.5 g/kg/day of protein for most patients with pressure injuries and up to 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day for individuals with extensive wounds, burns, or severe catabolic conditions, provided renal function is adequate.

Question (Front): Which medication is most strongly associated with folate deficiency during long-term therapy?
Rationale:
Methotrexate is an antimetabolite that competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), the enzyme responsible for converting dihydrofolate into tetrahydrofolate, the biologically active form of folate. This inhibition impairs the synthesis of purines and thymidylate, ultimately reducing DNA and RNA synthesis.

Because rapidly dividing cells rely heavily on folate-dependent DNA synthesis, long-term methotrexate therapy may lead to: 
• Folate deficiency 
• Megaloblastic anemia 
• Oral mucositis 
• Glossitis 
• Gastrointestinal disturbances
• Elevated homocysteine levels 

Methotrexate is widely used in the treatment of: 
• Rheumatoid arthritis 
• Psoriasis 
• Certain cancers 
• Other autoimmune diseases 

To reduce adverse effects while preserving therapeutic efficacy, patients receiving low-dose methotrexate for autoimmune diseases are commonly prescribed folic acid supplementation, usually on days when methotrexate is not taken or according to the physician's protocol.

Question (Front): Which equation is currently recommended by KDIGO for estimating glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in adults?
Rationale:
The Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline recommends using the 2021 Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) creatinine equation as the preferred equation for estimating glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in adults. 

The CKD-EPI 2021 equation: 
• Estimates kidney function using serum creatinine, age, and sex 
• Removes the race coefficient that was included in earlier equations 
• Provides more equitable assessment across different populations 
• Generally demonstrates better accuracy than the older MDRD equation, particularly at higher GFR values 

Estimated GFR is essential for: 
• Diagnosing chronic kidney disease (CKD) 
• Staging CKD 
• Monitoring disease progression 
• Guiding medication dosing 
• Planning nutrition therapy

Question (Front): In collagen synthesis, ____ acts as a reducing agent to convert oxidized iron atom back to its reduced state. *
Rationale:
During collagen synthesis, two critical enzymes—prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase—are responsible for adding hydroxyl (-OH) groups to proline and lysine amino acids. This structural modification allows collagen strands to cross-link properly, forming a stable triple-helix network.

These hydroxylase enzymes require iron in its active, reduced ferrous state (Fe²⁺) to operate. During the chemical reaction, the iron atom naturally becomes oxidized into its inactive ferric state (Fe³⁺). Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) acts as the essential electron donor or reducing agent, transferring electrons to convert the inactive ferric iron back into its active ferrous state. Without enough vitamin C, the iron stays oxidized, collagen remains under-hydroxylated, and connective tissues weaken (resulting in scurvy).

Question (Front): The body stores energy for future use in: *
Rationale:
Adipose tissue plays a fundamental role in maintaining long-term energy balance by storing concentrated energy in the form of triglycerides (fats).

Triglycerides provide a highly concentrated fuel source yielding 9 kcal/g, making them the most efficient and virtually unlimited way for the body to store excess calories for future energy needs.

• Proteins: While amino acids from proteins can be broken down for energy during late prolonged starvation, the primary physiological role of proteins is structural and functional (building tissues and machinery); they are not stored for the dedicated purpose of serving as an energy reserve.
• Acetyl CoA & Ketone bodies: These are intermediate metabolic molecules and transient byproducts of fuel breakdown. They are utilized immediately by tissues or converted further to produce ATP, but they cannot be stored by the body for future use.

Question (Front): The vitamin most directly involved in protecting biomolecules from damage caused by oxidation is: *
Rationale:
Vitamin E (tocopherol) is recognized as the body's primary fat-soluble antioxidant. Its most direct, essential physiological role is to protect lipids and other vulnerable biomolecules inside cell membranes from oxidative damage.

Free radicals break down cell structures by attacking polyunsaturated fatty acids in a destructive chain reaction called lipid peroxidation. Vitamin E sits directly within the lipid bilayer of cell membranes, sacrificing itself to neutralize these free radicals, which preserves the structural integrity of every cell in the body.

• C: While Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a powerful water-soluble antioxidant that works closely with Vitamin E (even recycling oxidized Vitamin E back to its active form), it also acts as a necessary co-factor for many non-antioxidant enzymatic reactions, such as collagen synthesis.
• A: While carotenoids (precursors to Vitamin A) have antioxidant properties, preformed Vitamin A (retinol) functions primarily in vision, cell differentiation, and immune health rather than acting as a general biomolecule antioxidant.
• B3: Vitamin B3 (niacin) forms the coenzymes NAD and NADP, which are essential for cellular respiration and energy transfer reactions rather than scavenging free radicals to stop oxidation.

Question (Front): Olestra is artificial fat that does not provide kilocalories but has the following effect on one’s nutrition: *
Answer (Back): It prevents the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.
Rationale:
Olestra is a non-absorbable fat substitute made of sucrose polyester. Because human digestive enzymes cannot break its large chemical structure down, it passes through the gastrointestinal tract entirely intact.

As it moves through the gut, olestra behaves like a physical liquid solvent. It dissolves and traps the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) along with carotenoids from other consumed foods. Because olestra cannot be absorbed, these vital nutrients are bound to it and carried straight out of the body, presenting a major nutritional deficit. This is why the FDA legally mandates that foods made with olestra must be fortified with vitamins A, D, E, and K to offset this specific malabsorption effect.

• It prevents the absorption of water-soluble vitamins: This is scientifically incorrect. Water-soluble vitamins (like Vitamin C and B-complex vitamins) dissolve in water, not lipids. Therefore, they are entirely unaffected by the presence of olestra and are absorbed normally by the body.
• It results in flatulence: While gastrointestinal symptoms like flatulence, cramping, or loose stools can occur when olestra is consumed in extremely massive, non-standard quantities, the primary, classic nutrition-board-tested hazard is its direct, chemical inhibition of fat-soluble vitamin uptake.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards1 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary
Question (Front): A reduced blood albumin level leads to: *
Rationale:
Albumin is the primary protein circulating in the blood, and it is responsible for generating roughly 75% to 80% of the blood's colloid oncotic pressure (osmotic pressure).

This oncotic pressure acts like a chemical magnet that physically holds water inside the vascular compartment, preventing it from leaking out of blood vessels.

When blood albumin levels drop significantly (hypoalbuminemia), the oncotic pressure collapses. Without enough pressure to counterbalance the normal outward push of hydrostatic pressure, fluid readily leaks through the capillary walls and accumulates inside the surrounding interstitial tissues, leading directly to edema (swelling, particularly in the lower extremities, abdomen, or face).

• Alkalosis & Acidosis: These terms describe disruptions in the body's acid-base balance (pH levels). While albumin acts as a minor buffer in the blood, a drop in its level does not primarily drive clinical metabolic acidosis or alkalosis.
• Dehydration: Dehydration is a total-body deficit of water. Hypoalbuminemia causes fluid to shift to the wrong places (interstitial space) rather than causing an overall loss of systemic body water.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards1 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary
Question (Front): The body’s magnesium is found mostly in the: *
Rationale:
An adult human body contains roughly 25 grams of magnesium, and the vast majority (about 50% to 60%) is stored directly within the bones. The skeleton acts as a massive reservoir for magnesium, with part of it bound to the bone crystal surface where it can be readily drawn out into the blood if dietary intake drops.

Most of the remaining magnesium is found within soft tissues, split between the skeletal muscles (around 20% to 30%) and other metabolic organs.

• Nerves: While magnesium is absolutely critical for nerve impulse transmission and blocking neuromuscular excitability, nervous tissue holds only a very small percentage of the body's total supply.
• Muscles: Skeletal muscle is the second-largest pool of magnesium in the body, but it is still vastly outpaced by the volume stored in bone tissue.
• Extracellular fluids: Less than 1% of the body's total magnesium circulates within the extracellular fluid and blood serum. Because blood levels are tightly regulated at the expense of tissue stores, blood tests often fail to reflect a true total-body magnesium deficiency.

Rationale:
In the human body, glutamate (derived from glutamine in the intestinal-renal axis) serves as the primary metabolic precursor for the synthesis of arginine. Glutamate is converted into ornithine, which then enters the urea cycle to be synthesized into citrulline, argininosuccinate, and finally, arginine.

While healthy adults can normally synthesize enough arginine internally to meet daily maintenance demands, severe physical trauma, major burns, or sepsis completely exhausts the body's natural manufacturing capacity. Under these high-stress hypermetabolic states, the rate of internal arginine production from its glutamate pathway falls short of the massive demands needed for wound healing (proline synthesis), cellular immune function (T-cell support), and vascular tone (nitric oxide generation). Therefore, arginine transforms into a conditionally indispensable (essential) amino acid that must be supplied directly through the clinical diet or specialized formula.

• Methionine: An indispensable sulfur-containing amino acid that serves as the precursor for cysteine, not arginine.
• Serine: A dispensable amino acid synthesized from 3-phosphoglycerate (a glycolytic intermediate) that functions primarily in glycine and cysteine pathways.

Question (Front): Positive nitrogen balance can be observed during: *
Rationale:
Nitrogen balance reflects the relationship between nitrogen intake, primarily from dietary protein, and nitrogen losses, mainly through urinary nitrogen excretion. Positive nitrogen balance occurs when nitrogen intake exceeds nitrogen losses, indicating that the body is retaining protein and synthesizing new tissue. This occurs during periods of growth and tissue building, including pregnancy, childhood, adolescence, and recovery from severe nutritional depletion. 

During pregnancy, positive nitrogen balance supports the synthesis of maternal tissues and the growth of the fetus, placenta, and maternal blood volume and other tissues. In contrast, fever, surgery, and shock are generally associated with physiological stress that increases protein catabolism and nitrogen losses, resulting in negative nitrogen balance, particularly when the stress response is significant or prolonged.

In contrast, Zinc itself does not directly capture free radicals. Instead, it plays an indirect role by acting as a structural co-factor for the enzyme copper-zinc superoxide dismutase (CuZnSOD) and stabilizing cell membranes against lipid peroxidation. Because it serves as a mineral co-factor rather than acting as a direct antioxidant chemical or molecule on its own, it stands out as the standard textbook exception in this specific group.

Question (Front): An anorectic teenager’s health status has been progressively deteriorating. The physician has decided to tube feed her. The initial kilocaloric intake should be based on: *
Rationale:
In a severely malnourished or anorectic patient whose health is progressively deteriorating, the greatest clinical danger during the initiation of nutritional support (whether oral or tube feeding) is refeeding syndrome.

To avoid fatal electrolyte shifts (such as severe hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia) and cardiac overload, clinical protocols dictate that you must "start low and go slow". The initial calorie prescription is strictly calculated using the patient's present/actual body weight (typically starting conservatively at around 20 kcal/kg/day or lower) rather than their ideal weight. Using the ideal body weight right away would heavily overestimate their metabolic tolerance, flood their system with too many calories, and trigger refeeding complications.

They do this by decreasing the liver's production of VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein) and speeding up the clearance of triglycerides from the blood.

EPA and DHA also reduce blood clotting activity (platelet aggregation). They displace arachidonic acid in cell membranes, which reduces the production of thromboxane A2 (a compound that causes platelets to clump together and form clots) and shifts the body toward a more antithrombotic, clot-preventing state.

• LDL & HDL levels: While omega-3s can slightly raise HDL ("good") cholesterol, high doses of DHA can actually increase LDL ("bad") cholesterol levels in some individuals, making this a less uniform or beneficial primary mechanism.
• Cardiac output & heart rate: Omega-3s do support a stable heart rhythm and improve heart rate variability, but they do not primarily lower heart disease risk by altering baseline cardiac output or basic resting heart rate.
• LDL size & particle number: This is the primary target mechanism for medications like statins or advanced lipid therapies rather than the signature biochemical profile of marine omega-3 oils.

Question (Front): Dr. Cruz ordered a 500 mg sodium diet for Nena Lim. How much salt contains 500 mg of sodium? *
Rationale:
In nutrition and dietetics calculations, standard table salt (sodium chloride, NaCl) is approximated to be 40% sodium and 60% chloride by weight.

To convert a specific milligram amount of sodium into the equivalent amount of table salt, you divide the sodium milligrams by 0.40 (or simply multiply by 2.5):

Salt (mg) = Sodium (mg) x 2.5
Salt (mg) = 500 mg x 2.5 = 1,250 mg

Therefore, 1,250 mg of table salt contains exactly 500 mg of elemental sodium.

Question (Front): Ischemia in the coronary arteries is a usual cause of: *
Rationale:
Ischemia refers to an inadequate supply of blood and oxygen to a specific tissue or organ. When ischemia occurs specifically within the coronary arteries—the blood vessels responsible for feeding the heart muscle itself—it means the heart muscle (myocardium) is being temporarily starved of vital oxygen.

This oxygen deficit forces the heart muscle cells to switch to anaerobic metabolism, which generates lactic acid, irritates local nerve endings, and triggers the classic clinical sensation of chest pain, pressure, or discomfort known as angina pectoris.

• HPN (Hypertension): High blood pressure is a major systemic circulatory cause or risk factor that accelerates the development of narrowed coronary arteries, rather than being a consequence of coronary artery ischemia.
• Hemorrhagic stroke: A neurological event caused by a ruptured or bleeding blood vessel inside the brain tissue, completely unrelated to oxygen levels in the heart's arteries.
• Aneurysm: A pathological ballooning or weakening of a blood vessel wall (most commonly in the aorta or brain arteries), rather than a lack of blood flow to the heart muscle.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards1 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary
Question (Front): Prolonged use of corticosteroids can lead to: *
Rationale:
While corticosteroids cause muscle wasting and fluid retention, the long-term storage shift they cause is heavily emphasized in clinical nutrition:

1. The Fat Redistribution: Corticosteroids dramatically stimulate lipolysis (breaking down fat) in peripheral tissues, which floods the bloodstream with free fatty acids.
2. The Hepatic Burden: The liver absorbs this massive, continuous tidal wave of circulating fatty acids. Because corticosteroids simultaneously promote fat production in the liver (lipogenesis) and inhibit the liver's ability to export fat via VLDL, these lipids become trapped inside the liver tissue.
3. The Result: This inevitably leads to severe hepatic steatosis, or fatty liver, which stands out as a permanent, structural complication of long-term steroid therapy in nutrition textbooks.

• Increased protein catabolism: Corticosteroids break down muscle tissue to release amino acids for gluconeogenesis.
• Sodium retention: They cause the kidneys to hold onto sodium and water, leading to edema and fluid retention.
• Fatty liver: Long-term use alters lipid metabolism and can result in hepatic steatosis (fatty liver accumulation).
• Poor glucose tolerance: They induce insulin resistance and stimulate gluconeogenesis, elevating blood sugar levels.

Question (Front): An alternative sweetener that has a protective effect on tooth decay but with discomforting side effects such as intestinal gas or abdominal discomfort: *
Rationale:
Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol). Unlike regular sugar, oral bacteria cannot readily ferment sorbitol, meaning it does not produce the harmful acids that erode tooth enamel. Because of this, it has a proven protective effect against dental caries (tooth decay) and is commonly used in sugar-free chewing gums and toothpastes.

Sugar alcohols are only partially digested and absorbed in the small intestine. The unabsorbed sorbitol travels down to the large intestine, where it acts as an osmotic laxative (drawing water into the bowel) and is rapidly fermented by gut bacteria. Consuming too much of it directly results in intestinal gas, bloating, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea.

• Saccharin: An artificial, non-nutritive sweetener that does not cause tooth decay, but it does not cause gas or GI distress because it is completely absorbed and excreted unchanged in the urine.
• Stevia: A natural, high-intensity plant extract that passes through the body without triggering the osmotic gastrointestinal issues or fermentation associated with sugar alcohols.
• Aspartame: An artificial sweetener made from amino acids. It is fully digested and absorbed in the small intestine like a protein, so it never reaches the large intestine to cause gas or abdominal discomfort.

Question (Front): When metabolically-stressed patients are given diets with excessive calories, this could result in overfeeding, excess carbon dioxide production, and other related complications such as: *
Rationale:
When metabolically stressed or critically ill patients receive excessive calories (particularly from carbohydrates), the body's rate of glucose oxidation accelerates. This dramatically spikes carbon dioxide (CO₂) production.

To clear this excess CO₂, the lungs are forced to work much harder by increasing minute ventilation (breathing faster and deeper). In a metabolically stressed patient who may already have compromised lung function or be on a ventilator, this immense physical demand frequently leads to respiratory insufficiency and failure to wean from mechanical ventilation.

• Excessive weight gain: While chronic overfeeding leads to weight gain over a long period, in an acute, metabolically stressed ICU environment, the immediate dangerous complication of aggressive hyperalimentation is respiratory and metabolic failure, not fat storage.
• Immediate weaning from mechanical ventilation: Overfeeding does the exact opposite—it delays weaning and extends the number of days a patient requires a ventilator because their lungs are too exhausted from handling the extra CO₂.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards1 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary
Question (Front): Diet for a patient with diverticulosis: *
Rationale:
Diverticulosis is the condition of having small, uninflamed pouches (diverticula) in the walls of the large intestine. The primary goal of medical nutrition therapy (MNT) is to prevent these pouches from becoming obstructed or inflamed.

A high-fiber diet (along with adequate fluid intake) adds bulk to the stool and retains water, which softens the feces. This volume decreases the intraluminal pressure inside the colon, allowing waste to pass smoothly and reducing the straining that causes pouches to form or worsen in the first place.

• Low residue / Low fiber / Soft diet: These restricted-texture or low-fiber options are contraindicated for regular diverticulosis management because they lead to small, hard stools that increase colonic pressure. However, they are used temporarily during an acute flare-up of diverticulitis (when the pouches become actively inflamed or infected) to give the bowel a chance to rest and heal.

DBW = 6 + 8 = 14 kg

Rationale:
While it is a widely held belief that eating highly spicy foods can erode the stomach lining and cause ulcers, comprehensive clinical research has proven that they do not cause peptic ulcers.

Spicy foods can irritate an already existing ulcer flare-up, increase acid reflux sensations, or exacerbate abdominal discomfort, but they lack the physiological capacity to initiate the actual open sores or ulcerations on their own.

• Gastritis: Chronic inflammation of the stomach lining (gastritis) directly weakens the protective mucosal barrier over time, leaving the tissue vulnerable to auto-digestion by harsh stomach acids and pepsin, which frequently progresses into an ulcer.
• H. pylori infection: Helicobacter pylori is a spiral bacterium that colonizes the mucosal layer of the stomach. It secretes enzymes (like urease) and causes localized inflammatory responses that physically degrade the stomach's protective mucus coat, serving as the leading global biological cause of peptic ulcer disease.
• Aspirins & other NSAIDs: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) chemically inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, which drastically reduces the body's synthesis of systemic prostaglandins. Since prostaglandins are directly responsible for producing the stomach's protective mucus layer and maintaining healthy mucosal blood flow, prolonged NSAID use leaves the stomach unprotected against its own digestive juices.

Rationale:

	• In the Initial/Stabilization phase, protein is restricted to 1 to 1.5 g/kg to prevent refeeding syndrome and avoid overwhelming the child's compromised liver and kidneys.
	• In the Rehabilitation/Catch-up phase, the allowance is gradually escalated to an optimal level of 3 to 4 g/kg of Desired Body Weight (DBW) (and up to 5 g/kg under specific clinical parameters) to maximize rapid cellular synthesis. Because options vary by textbooks, 3 g/kg DBW represents the safe, universally established target threshold for rebuilding lean body mass without risking metabolic overload.

Question (Front): This hormone decreases the urge to eat and increases physical activity to produce a negative energy balance. *
Rationale:
Leptin is a hormone produced primarily by adipose (fat) tissue that acts as a long-term regulator of energy balance.

When fat stores increase, leptin levels rise and signal the hypothalamus in the brain to suppress appetite (decrease the urge to eat) and boost metabolism and physical activity. This combination successfully drives the body toward a negative energy balance to burn off excess stored fat.

• ghrelin: The "hunger hormone" produced mainly by the stomach. Its levels rise when the stomach is empty, signaling the brain to increase the urge to eat and reduce energy expenditure (promoting a positive energy balance).
• adiponectin: Another hormone secreted by fat cells that helps regulate glucose levels and fatty acid breakdown while improving insulin sensitivity, but it does not directly drive the specific appetite-suppression and activity-boosting negative energy loop that leptin does.
• insulin: Secreted by the pancreas primarily to lower blood glucose by shifting it into cells. While it can act as a minor central satiety signal, its primary physiological role is nutrient storage and carbohydrate metabolism.

Question (Front): The molecule most directly linked to the initiation of atherosclerotic plaques is: *
Rationale:
The absolute initial step in the formation of an atherosclerotic plaque begins when LDL cholesterol particles slip into the subendothelial space of an artery wall and become oxidized by free radicals.

This oxidized cholesterol is highly toxic to the blood vessel lining. It damages the endothelial cells, acting as the primary chemical trigger that forces the artery wall to express adhesion molecules. • Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF): A growth factor that stimulates the migration and multiplication of smooth muscle cells to form a fibrous cap over the lipid core during the progression phase.

Question (Front): A metabolic change that accompanies acute stress is: *
Rationale:
During acute physiological stress (such as severe trauma, major surgery, burns, or infection), the body enters a highly hypermetabolic and catabolic state.

To fuel vital organs and support the immune response, counter-regulatory hormones (like cortisol, epinephrine, and glucagon) are rapidly released. These hormones trigger muscle protein catabolism (the rapid breakdown of lean muscle tissue) to release amino acids into the bloodstream. The liver then uses these amino acids to create glucose via gluconeogenesis and synthesize acute-phase inflammatory proteins.

• hypoglycemia: Acute stress actually causes hyperglycemia (high blood sugar), often referred to as "stress diabetes," because the liver produces excess glucose while the body experiences temporary insulin resistance.

Question (Front): Vitamin K deficiency is frequently drug-induced. Which of the following drugs might be associated with this deficiency? 1. antibiotics 2. mineral oil 3. diuretics 4. anticoagulants *
Rationale:
1. Antibiotics: A large portion of the body's vitamin K is synthesized by beneficial bacteria residing in the gut. Broad-spectrum antibiotics can destroy these bacteria, drastically reducing natural vitamin K production.

2. Mineral oil: Because vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin, it requires lipids to be absorbed properly. Mineral oil acts as a non-absorbable laxative that coats the intestines and dissolves fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K), carrying them out of the body in stool before they can be absorbed.

4. Anticoagulants: Medications like warfarin are vitamin K antagonists. They directly block the enzyme mechanism responsible for recycling vitamin K in the liver, leading to a functional vitamin K deficiency that prevents blood clotting factors from activating.

• 3. Diuretics: These medications increase urine output and primarily affect water-soluble minerals and electrolytes (like potassium, sodium, and magnesium) rather than the absorption or metabolism of fat-soluble vitamins like vitamin K.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards1 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary
Question (Front): The primary risk factor in cases of fatty liver that is not related to excessive alcohol intake is: *
Rationale:
In cases of fatty liver disease that are completely unrelated to excessive alcohol intake (traditionally called Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease or NAFLD, now known as Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease or MASLD), insulin resistance serves as the primary, defining pathophysiological risk factor.

When a patient develops insulin resistance, their adipose (fat) tissue stops responding properly to the anti-lipolytic effects of insulin. This triggers an uncontrolled breakdown of stored peripheral fats, flooding the bloodstream with a massive surge of free fatty acids. The liver absorbs these excess fatty acids but cannot process or export them quickly enough, causing them to accumulate internally as triglycerides. Insulin resistance also promotes de novo lipogenesis (the liver making its own fat from circulating sugars), compounding the problem.

• High-protein diet: Following a high-protein diet does not cause fat accumulation in liver cells. In fact, adequate protein intake is necessary to supply the amino acids needed to build lipoproteins (like VLDL) that safely export fat out of the liver.
• Use of illicit drugs: While certain toxins and pharmaceuticals can induce specific patterns of liver injury or acute steatosis, they represent specialized secondary causes rather than the primary, population-wide driver of metabolic fatty liver disease.
• High-fat diet: While an unmanaged, calorie-dense high-fat diet can contribute to overall obesity (which goes hand-in-hand with liver fat), dietary fat intake alone is not the definitive core driver. The true culprit is the systemic metabolic failure of insulin resistance, which traps both dietary fats and converted carbohydrates inside the liver cells.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards1 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary
Question (Front): During the initial phase of physical exercise for non-diabetics and individuals with well-controlled diabetes, what is the primary source of fuel? *
Rationale:
In standard medical nutrition therapy and metabolic board exam frameworks, the focus for non-diabetics and well-controlled diabetics during exercise is heavily centered on circulating blood glucose uptake.

During the initiation of physical exercise, the contracting skeletal muscle fibers increase their demand for carbohydrates. For a patient with well-controlled diabetes, tracking the movement, consumption, and balance of blood glucose is the primary clinical parameter. The body immediately accelerates the translocation of GLUT4 transporters to the muscle cell membranes to draw glucose straight out of the bloodstream to fulfill early energy requirements, making it the targeted primary marker on your exam key.

• Free fatty acids: These serve as a major substrate during prolonged, lower-intensity steady-state aerobic exercise rather than the early stages of physical exertion.
• Amino acids: Lean proteins and amino acids serve structural and enzymatic functions, contributing minimally to physical exertion energy pools unless severe starvation or glycogen depletion occurs.
• Muscle glycogen: While muscle cells contain intracellular glycogen stores, standard board exam matrices prioritize blood glucose as the key circulating nutrient to match the management protocols for diabetes and exercise coordination.

Question (Front): Refeeding syndrome can bring about a dangerous fluctuation in: *
Rationale:
When a severely malnourished or starved patient is reintroduced to nutrition (especially carbohydrates), the sudden influx of glucose triggers a massive release of insulin.

This surge of insulin forces the body to pull large amounts of glucose along with vital electrolytes out of the bloodstream and directly into the cells.

This causes a sudden, catastrophic drop in serum electrolytes, specifically leading to severe hypophosphatemia (low phosphorus), hypokalemia (low potassium), and hypomagnesemia (low magnesium). These rapid fluctuations can cause life-threatening heart arrhythmias, respiratory failure, and neurological complications.

• Blood triglyceride levels: While nutrition can affect lipids over time, the immediate, life-threatening crisis of refeeding syndrome is strictly driven by the mineral and fluid shifts in the blood, not fat molecules.
• Serum liver enzyme levels: Liver enzymes may alter slightly during metabolic adaptation, but they do not experience the sudden, dangerous systemic fluctuations that characterize the syndrome.
• Ketone bodies: Starvation causes high ketone production, and refeeding stops this process, but the dangerous, lethal complication of refeeding syndrome itself stems directly from the rapid drop in electrolytes.

Question (Front): A nonsurgical approach to gallstone treatment is: *
Rationale:
Dissolution therapy: This uses oral bile acid medications (such as ursodeoxycholic acid) to physically dissolve small, radiolucent cholesterol gallstones over several months.

Fragmentation (Lithotripsy): This non-surgical approach uses Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL). High-energy sound waves are targeted at the gallbladder to break down or fragment large stones into tiny particles. These fragments are then safely dissolved with medication or passed through the digestive tract.

• Cholecystectomy: This is the surgical removal of the gallbladder, making it a surgical approach rather than a non-surgical one.
• Weight loss: While long-term weight management helps prevent gallstone formation, rapid weight loss can actually trigger or worsen gallstones due to increased cholesterol secretion into the bile, and it does not serve as an active clinical treatment to eliminate existing stones.
• Immunosuppressive drug therapy: Gallstones are crystallized deposits of cholesterol or bilirubin, not an autoimmune disease, so immunosuppressive medications play no role in their treatment.

Rationale:

These COX enzymes are responsible for metabolizing arachidonic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid) into prostaglandins and thromboxanes, which are key lipid signaling molecules collectively known as eicosanoids.

By blocking COX activity, NSAIDs arrest the downstream synthesis of these proinflammatory eicosanoids, thereby reducing pain, fever, and swelling.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards1 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary
Question (Front): After an injury, the following changes occur in the damaged tissue except: *
Rationale:
Following a tissue injury, the body initiates an acute inflammatory response where capillary permeability is increased, not reduced.

Chemical signals like histamine and prostaglandins cause the endothelial cells lining the local blood vessels to contract and form microscopic gaps. This makes the vessels "leaky," allowing protein-rich fluids, white blood cells, and antibodies to exit the bloodstream and flood the damaged area to begin healing.

• Warmth & Increased blood flow: Damaged cells trigger local vasodilation (widening of blood vessels). This brings a heavy surge of warm core blood to the surface of the injured area, resulting in visible redness and an unmistakable sensation of localized warmth.
• Fluid accumulation: Because the blood vessels become highly permeable, plasma and protein-rich fluids escape into the surrounding interstitial tissue spaces. This direct fluid accumulation causes localized swelling, or edema.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards1 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary
Question (Front): A very common cause of chronic kidney disease is: *
Rationale:
Globally and across clinical dietetics textbooks, diabetes mellitus is recognized as the leading and most common primary cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage renal disease (ESRD).

High blood glucose levels chronically damage the delicate microvascular filtering systems (glomeruli) of the kidneys, a condition clinically termed diabetic nephropathy.

In medical statistics, diabetes and HPN (Hypertension / High Blood Pressure) together account for roughly 2 out of 3 new cases of kidney failure, with diabetes consistently claiming the number one spot.
