The Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition (PPAN) 2023-2028 identifies 34 high-priority provinces across the country. These priority areas are selected by the National Nutrition Council (NNC) based on a high magnitude of child stunting (undernutrition) and severe household food poverty thresholds.

Basilan is officially classified as a high-priority province, ranking 9th overall nationwide on the target list for intensive nutrition interventions and financial support.

The Top 10 highest priority provinces targeted for intensive, multi-sectoral nutrition interventions are:
1. Leyte
2. Sulu
3. Negros Occidental
4. Negros Oriental
5. Samar
6. Lanao del Norte
7. Masbate
8. Palawan
9. Basilan
10. Cebu

Key Broad Facts on the 34 Priority Areas:
• The Rest of the Top 16: Immediately following the top ten are Camarines Sur, Quezon, Zamboanga del Norte, Zamboanga del Sur, Maguindanao, and Bukidnon.
• Convergent Strategy: Government programs like the Tutok Kainan Dietary Supplementation Program prioritize these specific locations to provide nutritional support during the critical First 1,000 Days of child development.

Question (Front): The first Philippine food and nutrition plan was called ___?
Rationale:
In 1971, President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. issued Executive Order No. 285, authorizing the National Food and Agriculture Council (NFAC) to coordinate all nutrition activities.

This integrated nationwide operation was officially known as the Philippine Food and Nutrition Program (PFNP) or simply the Philippine Nutrition Program (PNP).

It served as the structural blueprint for national intervention before the creation of the National Nutrition Council (NNC) in 1974 and the later evolution of the framework into what we now call the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition (PPAN).

• Philippine Food and Nutrition Program (PFNP, 1971–1974): Before the formal creation of the council, the National Food and Agriculture Council (NFAC) coordinated the first four-year Philippine Food and Nutrition Program under Executive Order No. 285.
• Philippine Nutrition Program (PNP, 1974–1983): In 1974, Presidential Decree No. 491 established the National Nutrition Council (NNC), formally consolidating national nutrition activities into the Philippine Nutrition Program (PNP). It covered iterations such as PNP 1974–1977 and PNP 1978–1982.
• Food and Nutrition Plan / Philippine Food and Nutrition Plan (FNP / PFNP, 1984–1992): In the mid-1980s, the blueprint returned to a linked agriculture-and-nutrition scope, adopted as the Food and Nutrition Plan (1984–1987) and later updated under the post-1986 reorganized NNC (via Executive Order No. 234) as the Philippine Food and Nutrition Plan (1987–1992).
• Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition (PPAN, 1993–Present): Following the global 1992 International Conference on Nutrition (ICN) in Rome, the Philippines aligned with international frameworks by adopting the title Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition. 

While sometimes referenced alongside the medium-term planning cycles (e.g., MTPFNP/MTPPAN), the core official name of the plan series became PPAN, which has continued across successive medium-term cycles:
	• PPAN 1993–1998
	• PPAN 1999–2004
	• PPAN 2005–2010
	• PPAN 2011–2016
	• PPAN 2017–2022
	• PPAN 2023–2028
Option 4: Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition

Question (Front): ___ is a cluster of programs that is comprehensive, long-range in time frame, and includes defined goals, strategies, and guidelines for implementation.
Rationale:
According to the official Nutrition Program Management and community planning taxonomy, these structural terms are arranged in a specific hierarchy:

1. Plan: This is the highest level of the hierarchy. It refers to a comprehensive, long-range cluster of programs that contains overarching defined goals, strategies, and broad guidelines for implementation. A prime example is the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition (PPAN).
2. Program: This sits below a plan and is a set of interrelated projects that coordinates personnel, facilities, money, equipment, and supplies to accomplish a specific operational objective.
3. Project: This is a specific, time-bound set of tasks or activities undertaken to achieve a given objective according to a defined budget and timetable.
4. Policy: This serves as the broad, overarching legal or administrative instrument—the system of principles or rules—that guides subsequent development plans.

Question (Front): ___ is a specific and time-bound set of tasks or activities undertaken to achieve a given objective according to a defined budget and timeable.
Rationale:
By standard administrative and project management definitions, a project is a temporary, specific, and time-bound endeavor. It possesses a clearly defined start and end date, sequential activities, and a dedicated budget allocated to produce a unique product, service, or result that fulfills a specific objective.

• Policy: A standing operational plan that serves as a broad, ongoing guideline for decision-making and employee behavior rather than a temporary set of tasks.
• Plan: The overarching blueprint or management process of setting broad organizational goals and mapping out how to achieve them.
• Program: A long-term, continuous framework that aggregates multiple individual projects under a shared theme or broader social goal, usually lacking a singular, short-term definitive timeline.

Question (Front): These are programs that address the immediate determinants of fetal and child nutrition and development.
Rationale:
According to global health frameworks (such as The Lancet Maternal and Child Nutrition Series) and Philippine law (such as Republic Act 11148), interventions are categorized based on what causes of malnutrition they address:

• Nutrition-specific programs directly address the immediate determinants of fetal and child nutrition and development. These include factors like adequate food and nutrient intake, infant feeding and caregiving practices, and reducing the burden of infectious diseases. Examples include micronutrient supplementation, exclusive breastfeeding promotion, and the treatment of severe acute malnutrition.
• Nutrition-sensitive programs address the underlying determinants of malnutrition. These involve systemic sectors like agriculture, food security, social protection, clean water and sanitation (WASH), and female education.

Question (Front): These are development projects that were tweaked to produce nutritional outcomes.
Rationale: Nutrition-sensitive

Question (Front): Who is the chair of Provincial Nutrition Committee?
Rationale:
At every level of the local government unit (LGU) framework in the Philippines, the Local Chief Executive serves as the default chairperson of the local nutrition committee:

• Provincial Level: Chaired by the Governor.
• City / Municipal Level: Chaired by the Mayor.
• Barangay Level: Chaired by the Barangay Captain (Punong Barangay).

The Provincial Nutrition Action Officer (PNAO) operates under the leadership of the Governor to handle the day-to-day operations, implementation, and coordination of the province's nutrition programs.

Question (Front): ___is the country's highest policy-making and coordinating body on nutrition.
Rationale:
The National Nutrition Council (NNC) is officially recognized by law as the Philippines' highest policy-making and coordinating body on nutrition.

It was originally created under Presidential Decree No. 491 (The Nutrition Act of the Philippines) in 1974 and is an attached agency of the Department of Health (DOH). The NNC is responsible for orchestrating multi-sectoral strategies like the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition (PPAN) to eliminate hunger and malnutrition nationwide.

• NEDA (National Economic and Development Authority): The country's premier social and economic development planning and policy coordinating body.
• NFP (Nutrition Foundation of the Philippines): A non-government, non-profit organization dedicated to promoting nutritional wellness.
• NCP (Nutrition Center of the Philippines): A private foundation that develops programmatic interventions and specialized nutritional products.

Question (Front): Which law was enacted to contribute to the elimination of micronutrient malnutrition in the country, particularly iodine deficiency disorder, through the cost-effective preventive measure of salt-iodization?

Which law targets addressing specific micronutrient deficiencies by mandatory fortification of staple food items such as rice with iron, wheat flour with Vit A and iron, refined sugar with Vit A and cooking oil with Vit A and voluntary fortification of other food items?
Rationale:
Republic Act 8976 (The Philippine Food Fortification Act of 2000) mandates the fortification of staple foods to address widespread micronutrient deficiencies (specifically Vitamin A, Iron, and Iodine). It explicitly requires the mandatory fortification of:
	• Rice with Iron
	• Wheat flour with Vitamin A and Iron
	• Refined sugar with Vitamin A
	• Cooking oil with Vitamin A

It also covers the voluntary fortification of processed food items through the National Nutrition Council (NNC)'s "Sangkap Pinoy" seal program.

• RA 8172: The ASIN Law (Act for Salt Iodization Nationwide), which mandates the iodization of all food-grade salt.
• RA 10028: The Expanded Breastfeeding Promotion Act of 2009.
• RA 7600: The Rooming-In and Breastfeeding Act of 1992.

Question (Front): To prepare a potential BNS for deployment in his/her barangay, a BNS should undergo a training and  ___ days of practicum
Rationale:
According to the National Nutrition Council (NNC) implementing guidelines under Presidential Decree No. 1569, a potential Barangay Nutrition Scholar (BNS) must successfully complete a two-part basic training program before full field deployment:

1. Didactic Phase: A classroom-based instruction course (traditionally structured as a 5-day to 10-day basic course) covering core technical inputs on malnutrition, health, the First 1000 Days, and data tools.
2. Practicum Phase: A mandatory 20-day hands-on community practicum.

During the 20 days of field practice, the scholar learns to master community nutrition management tasks under direct supervision. This includes operating anthropometric equipment to weigh and measure preschoolers (Operation Timbang Plus), conducting localized family profiling interviews, building a community nutrition spot map, and formulating a customized Barangay Nutrition Action Plan (BNAP).

Question (Front): In the BNS program guidelines, the direct trainer-supervisor of the BNS is:
Rationale:
According to the official guidelines issued by the National Nutrition Council (NNC), the District/City Nutrition Program Coordinator (D/CNPC) serves as the direct trainer-supervisor of the Barangay Nutrition Scholar (BNS).

• The D/CNPC is explicitly tasked with organizing, conducting, and supervising both the core didactic training and the subsequent 20-day local community practicum for new scholars.
• Guidelines specify that only in the structural or operational absence of an assigned D/CNPC will the local City/Municipal Nutrition Action Officer (NAO) step in to assume these training and supervision responsibilities.

Question (Front): The basic tasks of BNS are the following EXCEPT:
Answer (Back): Leads in the preparation of the local nutrition action plan
Rationale:
According to the official National Nutrition Council (NNC) guidelines and the Barangay Nutrition Scholar (BNS) Handbook, the basic tasks of a BNS are clearly codified as:

1. Caring for the malnourished (identifying and tracking them via Operation Timbang Plus)
2. Mobilizing the community
3. Linkage-building
4. Keeping records (maintaining barangay nutrition profiles and family sheets)

The BNS does not lead the preparation of the Local Nutrition Action Plan (LNAP). Leadership and authorship of the plan fall under the mandate of the Local Nutrition Committee (LNC) and its Chairperson (the Punong Barangay / Barangay Captain). The role of the BNS is strictly to assist and provide data to the committee during the formulation of the Barangay Nutrition Action Plan (BNAP).
Option 4: Leads in the preparation of the local nutrition action plan

Question (Front): A suitable indicator for the evaluation of child feeding programs is change in:
Rationale: Supplementary feeding programs for infants and young children primarily target the eradication of wasting (acute malnutrition) and the restoration of normal body mass. The most sensitive, immediate, and reliable indicator to evaluate whether a short-term feeding program is successfully working is the change in a child's weight-for-length (for infants under 2 years) or weight-for-height (for older children).
Option 4: Decreased incidence of diarrhea among children

Question (Front): A point person in nutrition who is a regular employee of and under the plantilla of NNC.
Rationale:
The Regional Nutrition Program Coordinator (RNPC) is a permanent, regular civil service worker who occupies a formal plantilla item directly under the budget and structural organization of the National Nutrition Council (NNC). They serve as the head of the NNC Regional Secretariat, managing regional policy execution, monitoring local implementations of the PPAN, and coordinating across subnational administrative levels.

• CNAO / CNPC (City Nutrition Action Officer / City Nutrition Program Coordinator) & DNPC (District Nutrition Program Coordinator): These positions operate at the Local Government Unit (LGU) level. They are typically funded by the local city, municipality, or province budgets rather than holding a national NNC secretariat plantilla item, or they are designated from other existing local health department roles.

Question (Front): The Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition is integrated and/or consistent with the following EXCEPT:
Rationale:
The Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition (PPAN) serves as the country’s comprehensive multi-sectoral framework designed to combat all forms of malnutrition. It is systematically aligned with, and anchored into, the following major national development strategies:

• Philippine Development Plan (PDP): It is an integral sub-component of the national Philippine Development Plan framework, directly contributing to social transformation, human development, and poverty reduction goals.
• Health for All Agenda of the DOH: It directly supports the Department of Health’s principal universal healthcare blueprints (such as the National Objectives for Health and its respective action agendas).
• Ambisyon Natin 2040: It explicitly serves as an operational mechanism to meet the long-term vision of Ambisyon Natin 2040 by ensuring a healthy, well-nourished, and highly productive citizenry.
Option 2: Health for All Agenda of DOH

Question (Front): The national dietary supplement program targets the following age groups EXCEPT:
Rationale:
The National Dietary Supplementation Program (NDSP)—including its banner strategy Tutok Kainan—deliberately excludes infants 0 to 5 months old from receiving solid food or dietary supplements. According to global and local healthcare standards, infants in this age bracket must practice strict exclusive breastfeeding; introducing any form of dietary supplementation or complementary food would disrupt this and increase the risk of infection.

Targeted Vulnerable Groups Under the NDSP:
• Pregnant women (especially those classified as nutritionally at-risk, provided food support for 90 days).
• Young children 6 to 59 months old (broken down into infants/toddlers aged 6–23 months for complementary feeding, and children aged 24–59 months).
• School children (specifically severely wasted or wasted kindergarten to Grade 6 students enrolled in public schools).

Question (Front): These are development projects that were tweaked to produce nutritional outcomes by targeting households with undernourished children.
Rationale: Nutrition-sensitive

Question (Front): Mobilization of LGUs; policy development for food and nutrition; and strengthened management support are known as ____. These are necessary for the implementation of PPAN.
Rationale:
Under the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition (PPAN) framework managed by the National Nutrition Council (NNC), these three components are specifically classified as enabling support programs:

1. Mobilization of LGUs for nutritional outcomes
2. Policy development for food and nutrition
3. Strengthened management support

These programs are designated to ensure that both nutrition-specific and nutrition-sensitive interventions are well-coordinated and effectively implemented across all local government levels.

Question (Front): It is known as participatory planning that involves local leaders, implementers and people themselves in planning the program.
Rationale:
In program planning and management (particularly within nutrition and public health frameworks), Joint planning is explicitly defined as a type of participatory planning. It acts as a hybrid approach that combines elements of both top-down and bottom-up planning strategies. This method ensures comprehensive collaboration by actively involving local leaders, the implementers, and the target beneficiaries (the people themselves) directly in the program design.

• Microlevel planning: This refers strictly to planning conducted at the localized, community, or grass-roots level (such as creating a specific barangay or municipal nutrition plan).
• Strategic planning: This is a systematic process of mapping out a long-term vision, transforming that vision into broadly-defined strategic goals, and determining the sequential steps needed to achieve them.
• Food and nutrition planning: This is the overarching thematic discipline focused on formulating national policies, interventions, and guidelines to combat malnutrition and ensure food security.

Question (Front): A principle in planning that refers to desired breadth and depth of the nutrition program.
Rationale:
Comprehensiveness is a core principle in nutrition program planning and management. It explicitly dictates that the desired breadth and depth of whatever has been selected as the overall scope of the program or project must be thoroughly and accurately reflected in the actual plan.

• Balance: Emphasizes that all specific activities, tasks, and resource allocations are properly distributed so that they directly contribute to the achievement of the program's objectives.
• Workability: Mandates that the plan must be operationally practical, meaning the objectives are completely realistic and achievable within the set timeframe and available resources.
• Appropriateness: Refers to how well the designed program fits the localized cultural, environmental, and socio-economic context of the target community.

Question (Front): The following is/are true for problem matrix, causal model, or problem tree EXCEPT:
Answer (Back): Formulated by the BNS and presented to LCE as an advocacy tool
Rationale: Formulating a problem tree, causal model, or problem matrix is not a task done individually by the Barangay Nutrition Scholar (BNS). According to local nutrition planning guidelines, it requires collective brainstorming and data analysis from the entire members of the Local Nutrition Committee (LNC) during their strategic planning meetings. The entire plan (not just the tree) is what is eventually packaged and presented to the Local Chief Executive (LCE) for adoption and funding.
Option 1: Trace the chain of factors that can affect nutrition situation
Option 2: Constructed by asking and answering a series of "whys" to understand better the factors
Option 3: Formulated by the BNS and presented to LCE as an advocacy tool
Option 4: Being updated every year as a result of new data on nutrition situation

Question (Front): It refers to concrete and specific statement of desired achievement. It is more focused and specific time dimension, client population and end results.
Rationale:
In program planning and strategic management, objectives are defined as concrete, precise, and short-term statements of desired achievement. Unlike broad statements, an objective is specifically written to outline:
• A defined client population (who will benefit)
• A strict time dimension (when it will be achieved)
• Explicit, measurable end results (what the exact target is)

• Goals: These are broad, long-range, and general statements of an overall vision (e.g., "To reduce the prevalence of malnutrition in the region"), but they lack the operational and highly focused parameters of an objective.
• Mission: This explains the primary motivation, fundamental beliefs, and the overall reason for the organization's existence.
• Vision: This is an aspirational, long-term description of a desired future state.

Question (Front): Among the criteria in selecting nutrition intervention, the following must not be missed:
Rationale:
In classical program management and nutrition planning frameworks (such as those taught by FAO and the National Nutrition Council), interventions must pass three fundamental, non-negotiable filters during the screening phase:

1. Relevance (Appropriateness): Does the intervention directly solve the specific, prioritized nutrition problem of that population? (e.g., if the problem is Vitamin A deficiency, the intervention must be Vitamin A supplementation or food fortification, not general sanitation).
2. Feasibility (Practicability): Can it actually be done given the available budget, technical expertise, administrative infrastructure, and time constraints?
3. Effectiveness (Impact): Is there proven scientific or empirical evidence that this specific strategy will successfully lower malnutrition rates or improve the target nutritional indicators?
Option 1: Relevance, feasibility, ease in targeting and evaluation
Option 4: Relevance, feasibility, political support, willingness of beneficiaries to participate

Question (Front): Pre-program evaluation carried out prior to implementation but after program formulation. It is necessary to reassess development needs and project feasibility.
Rationale:
Ex-ante evaluation (literally meaning "before the event" in Latin) is a pre-program evaluation conducted after the program has been formulated but before actual implementation begins. Its primary purpose is to critically re-assess the localized development needs and rigorously audit the overall project feasibility and design viability before resources are officially spent.

• Program implementation review / Mid-term evaluation: These are ongoing, formative evaluations conducted during the execution phase of the project to check progress and implement corrective adjustments.
• Ex-post evaluation: This is an summative evaluation conducted at the very end or after the completion of the implementation stage to assess the total impact and outcomes.

Question (Front): Food availability at the national level is not enough to provide food security for all households. Moreover, food security at the national and household level does not automatically result to good nutritional status of an individual.
Rationale:
Statement 1 is true: Food availability at the national level (e.g., high national agricultural yields or food imports) speaks only to supply. It does not ensure food security for all households because of barriers to food access (such as low purchasing power, poverty, or poor market distribution systems).

Statement 2 is true: Even if a household is fully food secure and has plenty of food on the table, it does not guarantee that every individual in that house will achieve an optimal nutritional status. This is because individual nutritional status depends heavily on food utilization (how the body absorbs nutrients, which can be ruined by infections or illness), intra-household food distribution (e.g., gender or age disparities in who eats first), and caregiving practices.
Option 1: Only the first statement is true
Option 2: Only the second statement is true

Question (Front): Understanding the ecology of food and nutrition helps in the identification of the root causes of malnutrition problem. It can also help identifying appropriate solutions.
Rationale:
The first statement is true: The "ecology of food and nutrition" refers to the interaction between humans and the environmental, socio-economic, cultural, and political factors that dictate food availability, access, and biological utilization. Understanding this web helps investigators trace how systemic basic causes (like climate or policy) trickle down to underlying causes (like poor sanitation) and immediate causes (like inadequate dietary intake).

The second statement is true: By mapping out these exact ecological pathways, program planners can easily identify where a system is failing and design appropriate, targeted solutions—such as pairing nutrition-specific medical interventions with long-term, nutrition-sensitive agricultural or water security reforms.
Option 1: Only the first statement is true
Option 2: Only the second statement is true

Question (Front): It is a condition in which people do not get enough food to provide nutrients for the body.
Rationale:
In public health and food security frameworks, hunger is defined as an individual-level physiological condition where a person does not have access to enough food to provide the essential nutrients and dietary energy their body needs to function normally.

• Food and nutrition security: This is a comprehensive, positive state where all people at all times have physical, social, and economic access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food to meet their dietary needs for an active and healthy life.
• Malaise: This is a general, non-specific medical term describing a vague feeling of bodily discomfort, illness, uneasiness, or lack of energy.
• Food security: This focuses primarily on the broad availability, access, and stability of food supplies at the household or community level, rather than the specific physical condition of lacking food nutrients.

Question (Front): All of the following are possible causes of transitory food insecurity except:
Rationale:
Transitory food insecurity is defined as a short-term, temporary, or sudden drop in the ability to produce or access enough food. It is typically triggered by unpredictable external shocks.

Droughts and floods are classic examples of acute environmental shocks that cause immediate, temporary food shortages. The lean season represents a cyclical, temporary phase between planting and harvesting where food supplies naturally drop for a limited period.

A lack of food storage, on the other hand, is a structural and systemic infrastructural deficiency. Because it is a permanent condition deeply embedded in a region's agricultural infrastructure, it serves as a core driver of chronic food insecurity rather than a temporary or passing shock.

Question (Front): It is the focus of the Sustainable Development Goal #2
Rationale:
The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are a blueprint of 17 global goals to build a better future. SDG #2 focuses directly on ending hunger, achieving food security, improving nutrition, and promoting sustainable agriculture.

• Health: This is SDG #3 (Good Health and Well-being).
• Access to clean water and sanitation: This is SDG #6 (Clean Water and Sanitation).
• Responsible production and consumption: This is SDG #12 (Responsible Consumption and Production).
Option 2: Access to clean water and sanitation

Question (Front): Which of the following provides information on annual food production, distribution of food within the country, and imports and exports?
Rationale:
A Food Balance Sheet (FBS) is a comprehensive macro-level statistical report compiled annually (often by national agencies like the Philippine Statistics Authority and globally by the Food and Agriculture Organization) to track a country's total food supply and utilization over a specific timeframe.

It specifically synthesizes three critical dimensions of data:
1. Annual Food Production: The total quantity of food commodities cultivated domestically.
2. Imports and Exports: The flow of food moving into and out of the country's borders to calculate net available supply.
3. Distribution/Utilization: How the total available food is split within the country across human consumption, livestock feed, seed use, manufacturing, and structural waste.

• Commercial market databases: These track private consumer buying trends, brand performance, and retail sales, rather than integrated national agricultural and border trade balances.
• Food records: This is an individual-level dietary assessment method where a single person logs their personal daily intake, which tells you nothing about nationwide trade or agricultural production.

Question (Front): Which of the following statements are true regarding body measurements?
Rationale: All of the above
Option 1: Infants and children under the age of two should be measured in the recumbent position
Option 2: A knee height measurements is useful for people with spinal curvature
Option 3: Head circumference is used as a measure of brain size in infants and young children

Question (Front): Which of the following is not plagiarism?
Answer (Back): Re-drawing the RCT process, it not original or specific
Rationale: Re-drawing a generic, standard Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) flow diagram or process does not constitute plagiarism. The standard components of an RCT process (e.g., enrollment, allocation, intervention, follow-up, and analysis) are considered a universally accepted methodology and common scientific framework rather than a unique, specific text or an individual's proprietary intellectual property.
Option 1: Transcribing or modifying text from any printed material (encylopedias, books, magazines, newspapers)
Option 2: Using another student's work and claiming it as your own
Option 3: Using photographs, video or audio without permission
Option 4: Re-drawing the RCT process, it not original or specific

Question (Front): Based on WHO cut-off points, a BMI of 27 is considered to be which of the following?
Rationale:
WHO Standard Adult BMI Reference Ranges

The international classification breaks down weight status according to these specific metric boundaries:
• Underweight: BMI less than 18.5
• Normal weight: BMI of 18.5 to 24.9
• Overweight: BMI of 25.0 to 29.9 (A BMI of 27 falls directly in this bracket)
• Obese: BMI of 30.0 or higher

Question (Front): Which dietary assessment method determines nutrient intake by asking how often certain foods are consumed?
Rationale:
By definition, a Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ) asks a participant to report how often (the rate or frequency, such as daily, weekly, or monthly) they consume specific items from a pre-defined checklist of foods over a designated timeframe.

• Diet history: This is an in-depth retrospective interview method that focuses on mapping out overall long-term habitual eating patterns, meal frequencies, cooking behaviors, and general food habits, rather than solely ticking off the frequencies of a structured food item checklist.
• 24-hour recall: This method asks the participant to remember and describe all food and beverages consumed over the exact, immediate 24 hours prior to the interview. It looks at a single-day snapshot of consumption rather than the general frequency of specific items over time.

Question (Front): Wasting in children is defined as _________?
Answer (Back): Weight-for-height that is more than 2 Z-scores below the reference
Rationale:
In pediatric anthropometry and public health frameworks managed by the World Health Organization (WHO), childhood malnutrition indicators are divided into distinct categories based on standard deviations (Z-scores) relative to a healthy reference population:

• Wasting (Acute Malnutrition): This measures body mass in relation to body length. It is defined as a weight-for-height (or weight-for-length) value that sits more than 2 standard deviations below (-2 Z-scores) the WHO Child Growth Standards. It signifies rapid, severe weight loss or a failure to gain weight, typically caused by recent starvation, severe illness, or infection.
• Stunting (Chronic Malnutrition): This measures linear growth retardation and is defined as a height-for-age value more than 2 Z-scores below the reference. It reflects long-term, ongoing nutritional deprivation.
• Underweight: This is a composite metric combining acute and chronic factors, defined as a weight-for-age value more than 2 Z-scores below the reference.
Option 1: Weight-for-height that is more than 2 Z-scores below the reference
Option 2: Height-for-age that is more than 2 Z-scores below the reference
Option 3: Weight-for-age that is more than 2 Z-scores below the reference

Question (Front): Abdominal obesity in females is defined as a waist–hip ratio greater than:
Rationale:
According to the World Health Organization (WHO) diagnostic guidelines, abdominal obesity (also known as central or android obesity) is measured using specific cutoff thresholds for the waist–hip ratio (WHR):

• Females: Abdominal obesity is defined as a waist–hip ratio greater than 0.85.
• Males: Abdominal obesity is defined as a waist–hip ratio greater than 0.90.

Any values exceeding these points indicate a high concentration of visceral fat around the abdominal organs, which is heavily associated with an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular diseases.

Question (Front): A function of public health nutritionist which focuses on assisting the community to solve their diet and nutrition related problems.
Rationale:
According to standard professional public health nutrition curriculum tracking guides (like those from UPLB and the FNDRC mock boards), the roles are explicitly partitioned by these exact action fragments:

1. Program Implementer: The core action of this role explicitly states that the nutritionist "guides or assists the people in solving their diet and nutrition-related problems" directly in the field. It is an on-the-ground execution role focused on helping the community change behaviors and overcome immediate barriers.
2. Program Administrator: This function is academically defined as focusing on financial management, budgeting, and organizing the personnel who are involved in the nutrition program implementation.
3. Program Planner: Focuses on organizing program planning activities, assisting the community in identifying and prioritizing their problems, and designing the specific course of action to be taken.
4. Program Organizer / Assessor: Focuses on initiating the development of the organization or community network to clear the path for future interventions.

Question (Front): “Hidden hunger” refers to:
Rationale:
"Hidden hunger" is a specific public health term used to describe a chronic lack of essential vitamins and minerals (micronutrients)—such as iron, iodine, vitamin A, and zinc—in a person's diet.

Unlike classic undernutrition (like marasmus or wasting), where a person visibly looks emaciated due to a severe shortage of total calories or protein, hidden hunger often goes unnoticed. An individual may consume enough food or calories to feel full or maintain a normal body weight, but their body is still suffering from invisible, internal nutrient starvation that damages their immune system, cognitive development, and overall physical health.

Question (Front): With reference to the UNICEF framework on the causes of undernutrition, unhealthy environment is categorized as:
Rationale:
Under the globally recognized UNICEF Conceptual Framework on the Causes of Malnutrition, the factors that lead to undernutrition are structurally categorized into three distinct, hierarchical levels of causation:

1. Immediate Causes (Individual level): These are the direct physical factors that affect the person's body—specifically inadequate dietary intake and diseases.
2. Underlying Causes (Household/Community level): These are the social, economic, and environmental factors that lead to those immediate causes. An unhealthy environment (such as a lack of safe water, poor sanitation, and inadequate hygiene) falls squarely in this category, alongside a lack of household food security and inadequate caregiving practices.
3. Basic Causes (Societal level): These are the systemic or structural root problems within a society, such as political instability, poverty, poor governance, and lack of resources.

Question (Front): Which is true about the physical growth of an infant?
Answer (Back): The infant’s length changes more slowly than the weight
Rationale:
An infant's birth weight typically doubles by about 4 to 6 months, not two months. It does triple by one year, but the first half of the statement is biologically inaccurate for normal infant development.

Weight changes much faster and more dynamically than height (linear growth). During the first year, an infant's weight triples (a 200% increase), whereas their length increases by roughly 50% (from an average of 20 inches at birth to about 30 inches at one year). Linear growth is a more gradual, steady biological process compared to rapid mass accumulation.
Option 1: The infant’s length changes more slowly than the weight
Option 2: Infants’ birth weight doubles by about two months and triples by one year
Option 3: A and B are both TRUE
Option 4: A and B are both FALSE

Question (Front): Babies with low birth weight:
Answer (Back): Have high possibility of neonatal death compared with non-low birth weight infants
Rationale:
To understand why only this option is correct, let's break down the clinical parameters of both statements:

• While it is true that low birth weight (LBW) infants have an increased susceptibility to infection and difficulty regulating their body temperature, they do not have mature kidneys. On the contrary, their organs are highly underdeveloped and immature, often leading to a reduced number of nephrons at birth and an increased risk of chronic kidney disease later in life. Because of the word "mature", Statement A is factually incorrect.
• Epidemiological statistics show that low birth weight is a leading driver of newborn mortality. LBW infants have a significantly higher possibility of neonatal death—ranging from 20 to 24 times more likely to die shortly after birth compared to infants born with a normal weight.
Option 1: Have high possibility of neonatal death compared with non-low birth weight infants
Option 2: Have an increased susceptibility to infection, difficulty regulating body temperature and mature kidneys
Option 3: A and B are both TRUE
Option 4: A and B are both FALSE

Question (Front): What is the recommended ratio of whole milk and water when preparing milk for an infant below three months of age?
Rationale:
When preparing traditional, home-modified animal milk for an infant below three months of age, the standard pediatric and public health recommendation is a 2:1 ratio (2 parts whole cow's milk or carabao's milk to 1 part water), usually paired with a specific amount of sugar (around 5%).

Whole, undiluted animal milk contains an exceptionally high concentration of protein and minerals (such as sodium and phosphorus). A young infant's immature kidneys cannot handle this heavy solute load, which can lead to severe dehydration.

Diluting the milk with 1 part water lowers the renal solute load to a safer level for infants under 3 months. After the child passes 3 months of age, their renal function matures slightly, and the ratio is typically advanced to 3:1 before moving to whole, undiluted milk later in infancy if commercial formula or breast milk is absolutely unavailable.

Question (Front): The effortless expulsion of gastric contents caused by GI reflux in babies
Rationale:
Regurgitation is clinically defined as the effortless, passive expulsion of swallowed food or gastric contents from the stomach back into the esophagus and mouth. In infants, this is primarily driven by an immature lower esophageal sphincter—a common, normal condition known as gastroesophageal reflux (GER) that usually resolves on its own as the baby grows.

• Colic: This refers to periods of intense, frequent, and unexplained crying in an otherwise healthy infant, often thought to be linked to gas or abdominal discomfort, rather than the physical ejection of stomach contents.
• Diarrhea: This describes loose, watery stools passing through the lower gastrointestinal tract, not an upward reflux into the mouth.
• Spitting-up-food: While this is the casual, everyday term parents use for this exact behavior, Regurgitation is the primary scientific and medical terminology used in public health exams to describe the involuntary mechanism itself.

Question (Front): An infant is physiologically ready for solid foods when:
Rationale:
An infant becomes developmentally and physiologically ready to transition to solid foods (complementary feeding) around 6 months of age, marked by several key internal changes:
• Saliva is produced: Around 3 to 6 months, an infant’s salivary glands mature, significantly increasing saliva production. Saliva contains lubricants and enzymes that help moisten and break down solid textures.

• Gastric acidity increases: A newborn's stomach has a relatively high pH (less acidic). As the infant approaches 6 months, gastric acid production increases, lowering the stomach pH to adult-like levels. This is necessary to properly digest complex proteins from solid foods and kill harmful foodborne pathogens.
• Enzymes for starch digestion are produced: During early infancy, levels of pancreatic amylase (the enzyme needed to digest complex starches) are very low. By 6 months of age, the secretion of these digestive enzymes matures significantly, allowing the infant's GI tract to safely process and absorb starches from rice, cereals, and mashed root crops.
Option 4: Enzymes for starch digestion is produced

Question (Front): Which is true about the basal metabolic of the elderly?
Answer (Back): A and B are both FALSE
Rationale:
The basal metabolic rate (BMR) does decline with age, but it happens because of a decrease in the functional capacity of cells and a prominent loss of functioning lean muscle tissue (sarcopenia). It does not decline because cell capacity increases.

The decline in baseline metabolic needs is typically accompanied by an increase in body fat (adipose tissue) and a redistribution of fat toward the abdomen, rather than a decrease in body fat.
Option 1: A and B are both FALSE
Option 2: It declines with age because of the increase in the functional capacity of cells
Option 3: The declined metabolic needs is accompanied by a decrease in body fat
Option 4: A and B are both TRUE

Question (Front): Psychological related factors resulting to malnutrition in elderly except:
Rationale:
Immobility is a physical/biological factor: It refers to the physical inability to move around easily, which causes malnutrition by making it difficult for an elderly person to shop for groceries, lift heavy cooking utensils, or prepare meals independently.

The other options are psychological/social factors: Living alone (which leads to loneliness and isolation), depression, and anxiety are all mental, emotional, or psychological states that directly destroy an elderly person's appetite, interest in food, and motivation to eat (a condition often called the "anorexia of aging").

Question (Front): Hyposmia is also know as:
Rationale:
Hyposmia is the official clinical term for a partially reduced or lowered ability to smell and detect odors. It is very common in older adults due to natural aging, as well as clinical conditions like chronic sinusitis, viral infections, or neurodegenerative changes.

• Decreased taste sensitivity: This is known as hypogeusia (whereas a complete loss of taste is ageusia).
• Loss of appetite: This is known clinically as anorexia (such as the anorexia of aging).
• Lowered thirst sensation: This is known as hypodipsia.

Question (Front): Which is true about menopause among females:
Answer (Back): A and B are both TRUE
Rationale:
Menopause is the permanent cessation of menstrual periods resulting from the natural biological aging of the female reproductive system:

• Statement A is TRUE: As a woman transitions into menopause, her ovaries dramatically reduce their secretion of the key female sex hormones, leading to severely decreased levels of estrogen and progesterone. This sharp hormonal decline is responsible for classic menopausal symptoms like hot flashes and night sweats.
• Statement B is TRUE: The root biological cause of this hormone drop is the natural depletion of the ovarian reserve. A woman is born with a finite number of primordial follicles. Over her reproductive lifespan, as more follicles undergo ovulation or atresia (shrinkage/cell death), the ovaries end up with a significantly lower number of viable ovarian follicles. Consequently, fewer follicles develop completely to ovulate and transform into a corpus luteum (the temporary structure responsible for secreting progesterone).
Option 1: A and B are both TRUE
Option 2: A result of decreased levels of estrogen and progesterone
Option 3: A result of less number of ovarian follicles and corpora lutea
Option 4: A and B are both FALSE

Question (Front): The breast milk that women produce in the first few days after delivery
Rationale:
Colostrum is the distinct, specialized form of breast milk produced by the mammary glands in late pregnancy and the first few days after delivery (typically days 1 to 4). It is a thick, yellowish fluid that is uniquely adapted to a newborn's immediate needs:

It is highly concentrated with leukocytes and protective antibodies—especially Immunoglobulin A (IgA)—acting as the infant's first natural vaccine.

It contains high levels of epidermal growth factors to help mature the infant's gut lining, and acts as a mild laxative to assist the baby in passing meconium (the first stool).

• Mature milk: This thinner, bluish-white milk transitions in around day 10 to 15 postpartum, supplying the stable balance of water, carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins needed for long-term growth.
• Foremilk: This is the milk available at the beginning of a single feeding session, which is watery and high in lactose to satisfy the infant's thirst.
• Hindmilk: This is the creamier milk released toward the end of a single feeding session, which is dense in fat and calories to promote satiety and weight gain.

Question (Front): A multi-level tool for promoting and sustaining risk-reducing behavior change in individuals and communities by distributing tailored specific messages through a variety of channels.
Rationale:
Behavior Change Communication (BCC) is a strategic, multi-level framework designed to foster and maintain healthy, risk-reducing lifestyle habits within populations.

It systematically delivers tailored, highly specific messages designed to resonate with particular audiences. Rather than relying on a single approach, BCC distributes these messages across a variety of communication channels—including interpersonal counseling, group discussions, community media, and mass marketing campaigns.

While Nutrition Education is a component of this process, BCC focuses more broadly on the psychological and social drivers of action to shift actual behavior, moving beyond simply providing raw academic facts.

Question (Front): Which is an example of interpersonal communication?
Rationale: Interpersonal communication refers to a face-to-face, interactive exchange of information between two or more people. In this context, nutrition counseling is the perfect example because it involves a direct, personalized, two-way dialogue between a healthcare professional (or nutrition worker) and an individual client or family. This layout allows for active listening, immediate feedback, and tailored advice.
Option 3: Airing of nutrition messages in TV

Question (Front): Who is the chair of the National Nutrition Council Governing Board?
Rationale:
By law, under Presidential Decree No. 491 (The Nutrition Act of the Philippines) and subsequent executive updates, the Secretary of the Department of Health (DOH) serves as the official Chairperson of the National Nutrition Council (NNC) Governing Board.

The NNC is the country's highest policy-making and coordinating body on nutrition. Its leadership structure consists of:
• Chairperson: Secretary of the Department of Health (DOH)
• Vice-Chairs:
	1. Secretary of the Department of Agriculture (DA)
	2. Secretary of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG)

The board also includes the heads of several other departments (such as DepEd, DSWD, DTI, DOST, and DOLE) alongside representatives from the private sector to ensure a multi-sectoral approach to addressing malnutrition.
Option 4: Department of Interior and Local Government

Question (Front): Which law specifies rules and regulations which contain standard procedures to be followed for rooming-in and breastfeeding in all private and government health institutions?
Which law requires private enterprises as well as government agencies, including government-owned and controlled corporations, to put up lactation stations?
What executive order regulates the marketing of infant milk formula, other milk products, foods and beverages, as well as feeding bottles and teats?

What law strengthens the Barangay Nutrition Program by providing for a Barangay Nutrition Scholar in every barangay to assist in the coordination and implementation of nutrition programs, projects, and activities and the barangay level?
Rationale:
Signed on June 11, 1978, Presidential Decree No. 1569 is titled "Strengthening the Barangay Nutrition Program by providing for a Barangay Nutrition Scholar (BNS) in every barangay, providing funds therefor, and for other purposes."

It officially established the BNS program across the Philippines, mandating that every barangay should have a trained local volunteer (the BNS) responsible for:
• Monitoring the nutritional status of children through routine weighing (Operation Timbang Plus)
• Linking malnourished children and families to health and nutrition services
• Coordinating nutrition programs, projects, and activities directly at the grass-roots barangay level

Question (Front): The tolerable upper intake level (UL) is the largest daily nutrient intake shown to harbor no adverse side effects to ___
Answer (Back): A large majority of individual in a particular age or gender group
Rationale:
The reason the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL), or Upper Tolerable Limit, applies to a large majority (almost all) of individuals in a specific group but not absolutely everyone, is due to the inherent biological variability in the human population and the conservative methodology used to establish the UL.

Estimated Average Requirement (EAR), which is set at the median requirement covering only half of a group, not the UL. The UL is therefore a ceiling for safe habitual intake and not a recommended target intake.
Option 1: Half the individuals in a particular age or gender group
Option 2: A large majority of individual in a particular age or gender group
Option 3: Everyone in a particular age or gender group

Question (Front): Based on the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Ranges (AMDR), energy from fat as a percentage of total energy for adults should be within the range?
Rationale:
The correct range is 15-30% of total energy based on the Philippine Dietary Reference Intakes (PDRI) AMDR for fat in adults.

Carbohydrate: 55-75%
Protein: 10-15%
Fat: 15-30%

Question (Front): Which one of the following statements is incorrect?
Answer (Back): According to Pinggang Pinoy, meat, fish, and alternatives should comprise one-third of the plate
Rationale: Answer should be 1/6 ~ 17%.
Option 1: According to Pinggang Pinoy, half of our plate should be include fruits and vegetable
Option 2: According to Pinggang Pinoy, meat, fish, and alternatives should comprise one-third of the plate
Option 3: The statement "Eat lots of fruits and vegetables" is a food-based dietary guideline
Option 4: The statement "Eat less sodium-no more than 2g/day" is not food-based dietary guideline

Question (Front): Nutritional Deficiency is usually initiated by __?
Answer (Back): Inadequate dietary intake of one or more nutrients
Rationale:
This is the 1st stage, based on schema of the development of nutritional deficiency. This stage precedes any measurable biochemical, functional, or clinical change in the body. Illness and low income are underlying or basic causes that may contribute to inadequate intake but are not themselves the initiating physiological event. 

The sequence generally progresses from dietary inadequacy to depleted tissue stores, then biochemical changes, and finally clinical signs.
Option 1: Inadequate dietary intake of one or more nutrients

Question (Front): Following the stages of developing nutrient deficiency, what is the appropriate method for the first stage?
Rationale:
The correct answer is dietary assessment because the first stage of deficiency is inadequate dietary intake, and only dietary methods (recalls, records, FFQs) can directly capture what and how much a person is eating. 

• Anthropometry reflects later effects on body size and composition, appearing only after prolonged deficiency. 
• Clinical assessment detects obvious signs and symptoms, which appear latest in the sequence. 
• Biochemical assessment detects depleted nutrient stores or altered biomarkers, a stage that occurs after dietary inadequacy but before clinical signs. Matching the assessment method to the stage of deficiency ensures problems are caught as early as possible.

Question (Front): Include factors that influence health: biological, chemical, physical, social, cultural, economic, genetic, and behavioral
Rationale:
Determinants is the standard epidemiological term for factors that influence the frequency and distribution of health-related states. 

• Distribution refers to how disease or health outcomes are spread across person, place, and time, not the causal factors themselves.
• "Health-related states and events" refers to the outcomes being studied, not their causes. 
• "Application" is unrelated to this definition.

Question (Front): The theoretical or conceptual framework for the research defines the boundaries of your problem; and is used to develop a perspective in which the factual and conceptual elements become interconnected into a logical structure of relationships. Which one of the following is false?
Answer (Back): In formulating conceptual framework, you may look at the various theories upon which you can base your study
Rationale:
The false statement is D; in constructing a conceptual framework, the researcher draws upon related studies and existing theories, so the missing element is "related studies,"

• Choice A is true because both frameworks are built from facts and explanations grounded in existing knowledge of the problem. 
• Choice B is true because the theoretical framework specifically presents the theory underpinning the research problem. 
• Choice C is true because the conceptual framework maps out relationships among the specific concepts/variables under study.
Option 1: Both theoretical and conceptual frameworks consist of facts and explanation which proceed from the understanding on the knowledge about a problem
Option 2: Theoretical framework presents the theory from which your research problem was derived
Option 3: In the conceptual framework you present the relationship between the specific concepts for study
Option 4: In formulating conceptual framework, you may look at the various theories upon which you can base your study

Question (Front): Research design should be accurate. This means:
Answer (Back): Strive to be definite, precise, and exact
Rationale:
In research methodology and design, distinct terms specify the standard requirements for a study's framework:

• Accurate: Means that the researcher must strive to be definite, precise, and exact with their parameters, measurements, and data representation to avoid errors.
• Objective: This corresponds to option A (Unbiased, unprejudiced, detached, impersonal). It ensures the findings are guided by empirical data rather than personal opinions or emotions.
• Analytical: This describes option B, focusing on breaking down complex subjects into their individual, fundamental parts to comprehend them comprehensively.
Option 2: There are relatively agreed-upon defined traits or boundaries which specify what kind of things or boundaries you study
Option 3: Strive to be definite, precise, and exact
Option 4: Concerned with the identification and study of the component parts or elements which make up the things which you study

Question (Front): Which type of objective is the most applicable if your study uses methodology research design?
Rationale:
In research methodology textbooks, a methodological research design (sometimes called methodological research) does not focus on investigating a substantive medical or social phenomenon itself. Instead, its primary purpose is the controlled development, testing, and validation of the research tools themselves.

The Goal of Methodological Design is to target the validation or evaluation of a measuring instrument, scale, survey tool, or clinical questionnaire to ensure it possesses high validity and reliability before it is deployed in field studies.

	• To explore relationship: Best fits a correlational or explanatory research design.
	• To make comparison between groups: Best fits an experimental, quasi-experimental, or comparative research design.
	• To describe population or certain phenomena: Best fits a classic descriptive or observational research design.
Option 2: To describe population or certain phenomena

Question (Front): It is the study of assessment of diet and its relationship to disease etiology in the populations.
Rationale:
Nutritional epidemiology specifically studies dietary patterns and nutrient intake in relation to disease occurrence at the population level.

• "Food and nutrition research" is a broader, generic term not specific to disease etiology. 
• "Food and nutrition epidemiology" and "food epidemiology" are not the standard, recognized terms used in the field.

Question (Front): The 3Rs are principle of good science designed by scientist to improve animal welfare and scientific accuracy. Which of the following means finding ways of making animals' lives better in labs, this can include toys for animals or better training for technicians.
Rationale:
Refinement - Minimize animal pain, suffering, and distress.

• Reduction - Use the minimum number of animals necessary.
• Replacement - Use non-animal methods where possible.
• Recognition - random word which start with letter R.

Question (Front): It is the practice of analyzing describing a complex phenomenon in terms of phenomena that are held to represent a single or more fundamental level, especially when this is a said to provide a sufficient explanation
Rationale:
Reductionism is a philosophical and scientific approach that breaks down complex systems or phenomena into their smaller, simpler, or more fundamental components. In research (especially in fields like nutritional biochemistry or physiology), it assumes that understanding these isolated, individual parts provides a sufficient explanation for the behavior of the entire system.

• Scientific Method: The systematic, step-by-step process of observing, forming a hypothesis, experimenting, and drawing conclusions to gather knowledge.
• Research Method: The specific tools, techniques, or procedures used to collect and analyze data (e.g., surveys, randomized controlled trials, or double-blind studies).
• Research Design: The overall structural blueprint or strategy chosen to integrate the different components of a study in a coherent and logical way (e.g., cross-sectional, cohort, or experimental design).

Question (Front): What is the over-all goal of nutritional epidemiology?
Answer (Back): To contribute to the prevention of disease and the improvement of public health
Rationale:
The correct answer is to contribute to the prevention of disease and the improvement of public health, which represents the ultimate purpose (goal). Choices A, B, and D are all legitimate specific aims or objectives that serve this larger goal.

“Goal" (why it exists)
"Objectives" (what it specifically does to get there)
Option 1: To monitor the food consumption, nutrient intake and nutritional status of a population
Option 2: To assess  the strength of diet-disease associations
Option 3: To contribute to the prevention of disease and the improvement of public health
Option 4: To generate new hypothesis about diet and disease

Question (Front): What study design will you use to determine the relation of wealth status (rich, middle class) and fruit intake (in grams) per day.
Rationale:
Cross-sectional is the most applicable for determining the current, simple relationship between an exposure (wealth status) and outcome (fruit intake).

• Cohort - aim to determine the cause-and-effect relationship between an exposure and the development of a disease/outcome over a long period of time
• Case series - aims to provide a detailed description of a small number of patients (case series) or a single patient (case report) with an unusual or novel condition
• Case-control - aims to determine the past exposures that led to a rare disease/outcome

Question (Front):
What statistical test will you use in the study particularly if the data is normally distributed?

Study: to determine the relation of wealth status (rich, middle class) and fruit intake (in grams) per day
Rationale:
T-test - parametric test used to compare the means of exactly two groups. Since there are only two wealth statuses to compare fruit intake then this is the correct answer.

• ANOVA - parametric test used to compare the means of three or more groups.
• Chi-square test - used for categorical data
• Mann-Whitney - is a non-parametric test

Question (Front): Refers to a phenomenon which is thought to occur when people observed during a research study temporarily change their behavior or performance
Rationale:
Hawthorne effect occurs when participants change their behavior simply because they know they are being observed or studied.

• Ecological fallacy - Mistakenly applying conclusions drawn from group-level data (e.g., states, countries) to individuals within those groups.
• Systematic error - Consistent, non-random error that always biases measurements in the same direction (e.g., a poorly calibrated scale).
• Placebo effect - A positive or therapeutic effect that results from a participant's expectation or belief in the treatment, rather than the treatment's actual physiological mechanism.

Question (Front): This means making up data, experiments, or other significant information in proposing, conducting, or reporting research
Rationale:
Fabrication is the act of making up data or results entirely and recording or reporting them as true.

• Falsification involves manipulating research materials, equipment, or processes, or changing/omitting data so that the research record does not accurately represent the actual work.
• Plagiarism is using another person's ideas, processes, results, or words without giving them proper credit.

Question (Front): Which of the following is not a nutritional exposure?
Rationale:
IQ score functions as an outcome (dependent variable) not an exposure (independent variable/risk factor) in most nutrition research contexts. Physical activity, coffee intake, and reading food labels are all behaviors or exposures that can be investigated as potential predictors of a nutrition-related outcome.

Exposure is the cause or predictor (the independent variable or risk factor), which is the factor being investigated for its effect. Outcome is the effect or result (the dependent variable), which is the disease, event, or condition being studied.

Question (Front): Interpret the results of correlation between abdominal circumstances and HDL cholesterol level: r = 0.16, P = 0.002.
Answer (Back): There is no correlation between abdominal circumference and HDL cholesterol level, and it is unlikely that our result is caused by play of chance
Rationale:
The correct interpretation is that there is essentially no meaningful correlation between abdominal circumference and HDL cholesterol, and the small effect that was found is unlikely to be due to chance.

r = 0.16 (Weak Positive Correlation). The value is close to zero, meaning the linear association is minor. The positive sign means that as abdominal circumference increases, HDL cholesterol tends to slightly increase as well.

p= 0.002 (Statistically Significant). Since p<0.05 (the common threshold), we reject the null hypothesis. The observed correlation of 0.16 is highly unlikely to have occurred by random chance.
Option 1: There is a significant correlation between abdominal circumference and HDL cholesterol level
Option 2: There is no correlation between abdominal circumference and HDL cholesterol level, and it is likely that our result is caused by play of chance
Option 3: Abdominal circumference measurement may predict HDL cholesterol level
Option 4: There is no correlation between abdominal circumference and HDL cholesterol level, and it is unlikely that our result is caused by play of chance

Question (Front): Which of the following is false?
Answer (Back): The tests of significance enable the researcher to know for sure that the researcher's analysis correct
Rationale:
In biostatistics and research methodology, statistical tests of significance can never provide absolute certainty or prove that an analysis or hypothesis is "correct" for sure.
• Hypothesis testing operates entirely on probability, measuring the strength of evidence against a null hypothesis.
• A statistically significant result (e.g., p < 0.05) simply means that the observed data or difference is highly unlikely to have occurred by pure random chance under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true. It always leaves open a margin of uncertainty.

• Option A is TRUE: Inferential statistics deal purely with mathematical probability, not certainty. There is always a non-zero risk that your conclusions are false positives or false negatives.
• Option B is TRUE: There is an inverse mathematical trade-off between the two types of errors. If a researcher strictly lowers the significance level (α, the probability of a Type I error) from 0.05 to 0.01, the standard for rejecting the null hypothesis becomes much harder to meet. This automatically increases the probability of committing a Type II error (β, missing a real effect).
• Option C is TRUE: Parametric tests (like the t-test or ANOVA) carry strict assumptions about data structure, requiring variables to be continuous and measured on an interval or ratio scale, alongside approximately normal distributions. Non-parametric tests are used for nominal or ordinal data.
Option 1: The tests of significance deal with probability not certainty
Option 2: The tests of significance enable the researcher to know for sure that the researcher's analysis correct
Option 3: Generally speaking, a parametic test of significance should be used when the data represent interval or ratio scale
Option 4: As a researcher decreases the chances of committing a Type I error, the researcher increases the probability of committing a Type II error

Question (Front): The first president of the Dietetic Association of the Philippines:
Rationale:
Presentation Perez - first president of the Dietetic Association of the Philippines.

Question (Front): A function of public health nutritionist which focuses on assisting the community to assesses the program’s success or failure by evaluating program activities.
Rationale:
Program Evaluator since this function specifically involves to evaluate whether a program met its objectives by systematically assessing its activities and results. 

• Program Assessor focuses on measurement and is a more common term in educational settings. 
• Program Organizer focuses on assembling resources and stakeholders before or during implementation. 
• Program Implementer focuses on carrying out planned activities, not evaluating them afterward.

Question (Front): It refers to a set of processes and conditions by which food is produced, processed, and stored, marketed and distributed, and prepared and consumed for proper nutrition and good.
Rationale:
• Food Security - the state of having reliable access to sufficient, affordable, nutritious food.
• Food Path - the entire set of activities from farm to fork (production, processing, distribution, consumption, and waste).
• Ecology of Food and Nutrition - the complex relationship between humans, food, and the natural, social, and cultural environment.

Question (Front): The lowest level of structural organization of the living human body
Rationale:
To understand the structural hierarchy of the human body, scientists view it in six increasing levels of complexity, from smallest to largest:

1. Chemical Level (Lowest): This includes atoms (such as carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen) and molecules (like water, DNA, and glucose) that combine to form the basic building blocks of life.
2. Cellular Level: Molecules combine to form cells, which are the basic structural and functional units of an organism.
3. Tissue Level: Groups of similar cells join together to perform a highly specific function (e.g., epithelial, connective, muscular, or nervous tissue).
4. Organ Level: Different types of tissues join together to form recognizable structures with specific shapes and functions (e.g., the stomach, heart, or liver).
5. System Level: Related organs connect to form an organ system with a common function (e.g., the digestive or cardiovascular system).
6. Organismal Level (Highest): All structural parts of the human body working together to create a single, living individual.

Question (Front): In the female hormonal system, the source of luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone or LHRH is:
Rationale:

Any hormone that has the phrase "releasing hormone" in its name (such as LHRH/GnRH, TRH, CRH, and GHRH) is manufactured and secreted by the specialized nerve cells of the Hypothalamus.

The hypothalamus secretes LHRH into tiny blood vessels that travel directly to the Anterior Pituitary Gland. There, it triggers the pituitary gland to produce and release Luteinizing Hormone (LH) and Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) into general blood circulation to act on the ovaries.

• Anterior pituitary gland - GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, PRL

• Ovary - estrogen, progesterone, inhibin, androgen

Question (Front): The placenta is formed for different purposes EXCEPT:
Answer (Back): For production of nutrients and vitamins
Rationale:
The placenta serves as the physiological lifeline between the mother and the fetus, acting temporarily as the fetus's lungs, kidneys, gut, and liver.

• Storage: The placenta dynamically stores nutrients like glycogen, iron, and specific fat-soluble vitamins during early pregnancy to ensure a steady, regulated supply is available for the developing fetus.
• Waste Removal: It efficiently clears fetal metabolic waste products (such as carbon dioxide, urea, and uric acid) from the fetal bloodstream and transfers them into the maternal blood for excretion.
• Supply Line: Its paramount baseline function is to transfer oxygen, water, glucose, amino acids, and essential vitamins from the maternal bloodstream into fetal circulation via the umbilical cord.

The placenta cannot synthesize or manufacture nutrients and vitamins from scratch. It relies entirely on drawing these essential substances from the mother's circulation. It does produce hormones (such as hCG, progesterone, and estrogen), but not nutrients or vitamins.
Option 1: To supply the fetus with nutrients and oxygen
Option 2: For production of nutrients and vitamins
Option 3: For storage of nutrients and vitamins
Option 4: For removing of fetal waste products

Question (Front): Possible consequences of iodine deficiency during pregnancy:

Cretinism is an irreversible condition characterized by severe mental retardation, deaf-mutism, short stature (dwarfism), and spastic diplegia. It is uniquely linked to profound maternal and fetal iodine deficiency during critical early periods of brain development.

While options A, B, and D are broader obstetric complications that can result from many different underlying medical and nutritional issues, cretinism stands out as the direct, hallmark clinical manifestation of severe iodine deficiency disorder (IDD) in a developing fetus.

Question (Front): The human milk has a high concentration of the following minerals EXCEPT:
Rationale:
In maternal and child nutrition, human milk is characterized as a poor source of total iron, containing a very low absolute concentration of the mineral (approximately 0.2 to 0.4 mg/L).

Despite its low concentration, healthy full-term infants do not typically require iron supplementation during the first 6 months of exclusive breastfeeding. This is because the iron present in breast milk is exceptionally bound to lactoferrin and paired with high lactose and vitamin C levels, allowing up to 50% of it to be absorbed by the infant's gut (compared to only ~4% absorption from cow's milk or standard infant formula).

Calcium, Potassium, and Phosphorus are major essential macrominerals found in much higher, structural quantities in human milk to directly drive infant bone mineralization, fluid balance, and cellular development.

Question (Front): Which of the following conditions lead to contraindication to breastfeeding?
Rationale:

Because lactose—the primary sugar in human breast milk—breaks down into glucose and galactose, breastfeeding a baby with this condition causes toxic levels of galactose to accumulate in their body.

If breast milk is not immediately replaced with a lactose-free formula, it can rapidly lead to life-threatening complications, including liver failure, severe brain damage, cataracts, and shock.

Question (Front): Based on the general Management of Childhood Illness (IMC) color-coded triage system, what color indicates urgent hospital referral or admission?
Rationale:
In the World Health Organization's (WHO) Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines, a distinct three-color-coded triage system is used to quickly classify a child's illness and guide treatment protocols:

• PINK (Severe Classification): Indicates urgent hospital referral or admission. A pink row or box on the clinical chart indicates that the child exhibits general danger signs or severe symptoms (such as severe pneumonia, severe dehydration, or severe acute malnutrition). Immediate pre-referral treatment (like a first dose of antibiotics) is given before urgent transfer.

• YELLOW (Specific Outpatient Treatment): Indicates that the child needs a specific medical treatment that can be managed at an outpatient health facility. Healthcare workers prescribe oral drugs and counsel the caregiver on how to administer them at home.

• GREEN (Supportive Home Care): Indicates that the child has no signs of severe illness or conditions requiring specific medical treatments. The caregiver is given simple advice on supportive home management, such as continuous feeding and fluids.

Question (Front): Myers-Briggs Type indicator is an example of  ___.
Rationale:
While the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) is fundamentally a psychological tool designed to map personality profiles, it is heavily utilized in public health education, academic counseling, and workforce training to classify distinct learning styles.

The four primary dichotomies directly correlate with how individuals absorb, process, and retain new information:
• Extraversion (E) vs. Introversion (I): Dictates a preference for active, group-oriented learning versus reflective, independent study.
• Sensing (S) vs. Intuition (N): Reflects a preference for concrete facts and sequential learning versus abstract theories and imaginative concepts.
• Thinking (T) vs. Feeling (F): Influences whether a learner evaluates information using logical, objective analysis or personal, value-driven judgments.
• Judging (J) vs. Perceiving (P): Governs structural preferences, distinguishing those who thrive on rigid timelines and planned tasks from those who prefer spontaneous, open-ended environments.

• Behavior change theories - Transtheoretical Model (Stages of Change)
• Learning theories - Social Learning Theory (Bandura)
• Element of learning - Reinforcement

It historically expanded the definition of health by stating that it is not merely the objective of living or the absence of disease, but a positive concept and resource for everyday life emphasizing social, personal, and physical capacities.

The agreement shifted public health focus heavily toward the determinants of health, identifying fundamental prerequisites such as peace, shelter, education, food, income, a stable ecosystem, and sustainable resources.

• Campaign - coordinated, sustained effort to achieve a specific long-term goal.

Question (Front): Why are theories important in nutrition education?

Rationale:

• The other choices each describe legitimate but narrower functions of theory (serving as the basis for behavior change, identifying target audiences, or identifying moderators of change), while the correct answer most comprehensively captures theory's overall guiding role in shaping the full intervention design process.

Question (Front): Which country made the first specific commitment on the UN Decade of Action on Nutrition?
Rationale:
On May 22, 2017, Brazil became the first country to make SMART commitments as part of the United Nations (UN) Decade of Action on Nutrition 2016–2025. Ricardo Barros, Minister of Health of Brazil, made the announcement at the UN in Geneva, on the first day of the Seventieth World Health Assembly.

Brazil’s 3 commitments, to be achieved by 2019, are as follows:
• Stop the growth in the adult obesity rate (which currently stands at 20.8%)
• Reduce by at least 30% consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages among adults
• Increase by at least 17.8% the proportion of adults who regularly eat fruit and vegetables

Brazil outlined specific policy measures it will take to achieve these goals. These include fiscal measures (tax reductions, subsidies) to reduce the price of fresh foods, microcredit loans to family farmers, and cash transfers to poor families so that they can buy fresh produce.

See reference here: https://www.who.int/news/item/22-05-2017-brazil-first-country-to-make-specific-commitments-in-un-decade-of-action-on-nutrition
