Question (Front): In what year was the first International Conference on Nutrition held?
Rationale:
In early 1989, at the fifteenth session of the Subcommittee on Nutrition of the United Nations Administrative Committee on Coordination (ACC/SCN), an international conference on nutrition was proposed. Subsequently the Executive Board, at its eighty-fifth session in January 1990, endorsed the proposal that WHO and FAO should jointly convene such a conference in close collaboration with other United Nations agencies and with concerned multilateral, bilateral and nongovernmental organizations.

The International Conference on Nutrition was held in Rome, from 5 to 11 December 1992. The Conference was not seen as an end in itself but rather as a step in the continuing process to strengthen commitment and the action necessary to prevent and alleviate nutrition problems. Enthusiasm has been generated in many countries for the implementation of plans which must now begin. Through increased awareness of the extent and seriousness of nutrition- and diet-related problems, the process leading to the Conference resulted in the public and private sectors' increased willingness to work together to tackle them.

Question (Front): The 2025 Global Nutrition Targets include reduction in childhood:
Rationale:
Wasting is one of the six original WHO Global Nutrition Targets for 2025. The six original 2025 targets cover stunting, wasting, overweight, anemia, low birth weight, and exclusive breastfeeding.

• Target 1: 40% reduction in the number of children under five years of age who are stunted
• Target 2: 50% reduction in anaemia in women of reproductive age.
• Target 3: 30% reduction in low birth weight
• Target 6: Reduce and maintain wasting in children under five years of age to less than 5%.

Meanwhile, targets 4 and 5, which are close to being met in 2025, have been revised to raise ambition:
• Target 4: Childhood overweight: The ambition of the target has been strengthened from the original target of maintaining the 2012 prevalence to reducing overweight among children under five to below 5% by 2030.
• Target 5: Exclusive breastfeeding: To accelerate progress, the target has been increased from the original up to 50% of infants exclusively breastfed during the first six months of life by 2025 to up to 60% by 2030.

See reference here: https://www.who.int/teams/nutrition-and-food-safety/global-targets-2030

Question (Front): Which of the following conditions accounts for the most non-communicable disease worldwide?
Rationale:
According to official global statistics from the World Health Organization (WHO), Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) are responsible for approximately 74% of all deaths worldwide.

Among these conditions, cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the absolute leading cause of mortality and morbidity globally:
• Cardiovascular Diseases (CVDs): Account for the vast majority of NCD deaths, causing roughly 17.9 to 19 million deaths annually (primarily driven by ischemic heart disease and strokes).
• Cancers: Follow as the second largest group, accounting for around 9 to 10 million deaths each year.
• Chronic Respiratory Diseases: Account for approximately 3.9 to 4 million annual deaths.
• Diabetes: Accounts for roughly 1.6 to 2 million deaths annually.

Together, these four groups make up over 80% of all premature NCD-related mortality worldwide.

Question (Front): What is the WHO recommendation for physical activity among adolescents?
Answer (Back): At least an average of 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous intensity across the week
Rationale:
It is recommended that children and adolescents should do at least an average of 60 minutes per day of moderate-to-vigorous-intensity, mostly aerobic, physical activity, across the week. 

Vigorous-intensity aerobic activities, as well as those that strengthen muscle and bone, should be incorporated at least 3 days a week.

Adults should do at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity; or at least 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity; or an equivalent combination of moderate- and vigorous-intensity activity throughout the week, for substantial health benefits.

See reference here:

WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (2020): https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/faa83413-d89e-4be9-bb01-b24671aef7ca/content
Option 1: At least an average of 30 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous intensity across the week
Option 2: At least an average of 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous intensity across the week
Option 3: At least 75 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous intensity across the week
Option 4: At least 150 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous intensity across the week

Question (Front): The WHO recommends reducing the intake of free sugars to less than ___ in both adults and children

Option 2: less than 10% of total energy intake

Rationale:

in adults (strong recommendation).

Question (Front): Newborns weighing 2000 g or less at birth should be provided with _____ Kangaroo mother care as possible.
Rationale:
The WHO publication Kangaroo Mother Care: A Practical Guide recommends initiation of short KMC sessions when the baby starts to recover, even if the baby still requires medical treatment such as intravenous fluids or oxygen. 

It also recommends that continuous KMC should be initiated only after the baby is stable, meaning that the baby must be breathing spontaneously without additional oxygen. For the routine care of newborns weighing 2.0 kg or less at birth, the “WHO recommendations on interventions to improve preterm birth outcomes” recommend KMC, which should be initiated in health-care facilities as soon as the newborns are clinically stable. 

These babies should be provided with as close to continuous KMC as possible. Currently, there is no recommendation for KMC for unstable neonates weighing less than 2.0 kg at birth.

See references here:

Kangaroo mother care: Implementation strategy for scale-up adaptable to different country contexts (WHO, 2023): https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/71660bad-f029-4d9e-a2a4-63d8c59a8ce1/content

WHO Immediate KMC Study Group (2020). Impact of continuous Kangaroo Mother Care initiated immediately after birth (iKMC) on survival of newborns with birth weight between 1.0 to < 1.8 kg: study protocol for a randomized controlled trial. Trials, 21(1), 280. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13063-020-4101-1

Question (Front): This pertains to a set of tools and procedures to classify the nature and severity of food insecurity.
Rationale:
IPC (Integrated Food Security Phase Classification) is a globally standardized system specifically designed to classify the nature and severity of food insecurity into distinct phases (from minimal to famine). 

• EWS refers to an Early Warning System, which focuses on early detection of deteriorating conditions. 
• OPT, Operation Timbang, is a child weighing activity, unrelated to food insecurity classification. 
• SFP, Supplementary Feeding Program, is an intervention, not a classification tool.

Question (Front): This refers to a city or municipal-based nutrition surveillance system for detecting, at an early stage, an impending deterioration of food security situation based on agreed food and nutrition-related indicators and corresponding cut-offs or trigger levels.
Rationale:
The correct answer is EWS (Early Warning System), which is specifically designed at the LGU level to detect early signs of impending food security deterioration using agreed indicators and trigger levels. 

EWS and IPC work together in practice, but EWS is specifically the local, trigger-based detection mechanism.

Question (Front): The Nutriskwela Community Radio Network partners named their stations with words starting with this letter.
Rationale: The correct answer is the letter K, reflecting the “ka-“ branding convention used across Nutriskwela community radio stations established by the NNC.

Question (Front): Promote Good Nutrition is a component of this program.

Question (Front): ____ aims to improve the nutrition knowledge, attitudes, and practices of families to increase demand for adequate, nutritious, and safe food.
Rationale:
PGN (Promote Good Nutrition) is a key component of the Philippines' Accelerated Hunger-Mitigation Program (AHMP). It is strategically designed to improve the nutrition-related knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors of families to cultivate a sustainable demand for adequate, healthy, and safe food.

• AHMP (Accelerated Hunger-Mitigation Program) is the overarching mother program addressing hunger and food security.
• IYCF (Infant and Young Child Feeding) represents the specific set of optimal guidelines and target behaviors (like exclusive breastfeeding and appropriate complementary feeding) that the PGN promotes to mothers and caregivers.

Question (Front): What is stated in the 5th Nutritional Guidelines for Filipinos
Answer (Back): Consume milk, milk product, and other calcium-rich foods, such as small fish and shellfish, every day for healthy bones and teeth
Rationale:
Formulated by the Food and Nutrition Research Institute (FNRI-DOST), the 10 messages (popularly popularized as the 10 Kumainments) are chronologically ordered as follows:

1. 1st Guideline: Eat a variety of foods everyday to get the nutrients needed by the body.
2. 2nd Guideline: Breastfeed infants exclusively from birth up to 6 months, then give appropriate complementary foods.
3. 3rd Guideline: Eat more vegetables and fruits every day.
4. 4th Guideline: Consume fish, lean meat, poultry, egg, dried beans or nuts daily.
5. 5th Guideline: Consume milk, milk products, and other calcium-rich foods.
6. 6th Guideline: Consume safe foods and water to prevent diarrhea.
7. 7th Guideline: Use iodized salt to prevent Iodine Deficiency Disorders.
8. 8th Guideline: Limit intake of salty, fried, fatty, and sugar-rich foods.
9. 9th Guideline: Attain normal body weight through proper diet and moderate physical activity.
10. 10th Guideline: Be physically active, make healthy food choices, manage stress, avoid alcoholic beverages, and do not smoke.
Option 1: Consume milk, milk product, and other calcium-rich foods, such as small fish and shellfish, every day for healthy bones and teeth
Option 2: Use iodized salt to prevent Iodine Deficiency Disorders
Option 3: Eat more vegetables and fruits every day to get essential vitamins, minerals, and fiber for regulation of body processes.
Option 4: Limit intake of salty, fried, fatty, and sugar-rich foods to prevent cardiovascular disease

Question (Front): What is stated in the 7th Nutritional Guidelines for Filipinos
Answer (Back): Use iodized salt to prevent Iodine Deficiency Disorders
Rationale: Nutritional Guideline for Filipinos (NGF) Rule #7 specifically recommends: "Use iodized salt to prevent Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD)." Iodized salt is mandated under RA 8172 (ASIN Law) to eliminate goiter, cretinism, and mental impairment.
Option 1: Consume milk, milk product, and other calcium-rich foods, such as small fish and shellfish, every day for healthy bones and teeth
Option 2: Use iodized salt to prevent Iodine Deficiency Disorders
Option 3: Eat more vegetables and fruits every day to get essential vitamins, minerals, and fiber for regulation of body processes.

Question (Front): Which age group is the target in Operation Timbang Plus
Rationale:
Operation Timbang (OPT) Plus is the regular child growth assessment of all children 0-59 months old conducted annually in all barangays in the country to identify and locate families with malnourished preschool children and determine the overall nutrition situation in the area. It also involves planning, follow-up, and data quality check.

Question (Front): This program involves the provision of pharmaceutical preparations of vitamins and minerals.
Rationale:
Micronutrient supplementation, defined specifically as providing vitamins and minerals in pharmaceutical form (such as capsules, syrups, or tablets) directly to individuals.

Food fortification instead adds nutrients to commonly consumed foods during processing. Livelihood assistance and food production are indirect, food-security-oriented interventions.

Question (Front): This relates to the process by which the nutritional quality of food crops is improved through agronomic practices, conventional plant breeding, or modern biotechnology.
Rationale:
The correct answer is biofortification, specifically defined by improving the nutrient content of crops themselves through agricultural or breeding methods (such as Golden Rice enriched with vitamin A precursor).

See reference here: https://www.who.int/tools/elena/bbc/biofortification

Question (Front): ____ is an information-sharing type of activity that provides nutrition information to 10-12 participating mothers who are seated in a circular position
Rationale:
Pabasa sa Nutrisyon (PSN) is an information-sharing nutrition education initiative developed by the Nutrition Center of the Philippines (NCP). It is traditionally formatted as a community course where small groups of around 10 to 12 target mothers or caregivers sit in a circular arrangement to comfortably read, learn from standard nutritional guidelines, and share personal child-rearing experiences.

• Nutribus - 1980’s Nutrition Education using a bus.
• TCP - Teacher Child Parent Approach - The Teacher-Child-Parent approach to nutrition is a collaborative strategy where teachers, parents, and other community members work together to promote and improve children's nutrition through consistent education and support
• Kumare - (Kalusugan para Umunlad si Mare) is a maternal health program designed to improve the delivery of much-needed iron supplements to pregnant women. This approach increases the number of prenatal visits, the number of iron tablets consumed, and improved hemoglobin levels. The intervention is anchored on training and re-orientation of health workers by giving them more responsibility for the mothers in their catchment area.

Question (Front): Which is a livelihood assistance program?
Rationale:
Lingap sa Mahirap: A historical, comprehensive poverty alleviation fund introduced during the Estrada administration targeting the 100 poorest families in every province and city to deliver integrated social welfare packages.

• Tindahan Natin Program (TNP): This is a national government initiative implemented by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD). It serves as a livelihood assistance and job generation project alongside working as a targeted food price subsidy. It provides micro-financing and starter capital for low-income individuals, barangay councils, or community groups to set up small grocery stores (tindahan) that sell low-priced, quality food items like NFA rice and noodles.
• Ginintuang Masaganang Ani: An overarching agricultural modernization program run by the Department of Agriculture (DA) focused on boosting crop productivity, farm technology, and national food sufficiency.
• Sustansya para sa Masa: A multi-sectoral national movement launched to combat malnutrition through public food fortification strategies, such as adding Vitamin A to localized products.

Question (Front): What is/are the priority foods source/s during the early emergency period?
Rationale:
Water and calories are the two most immediately life-sustaining priorities in the very early phase of an emergency response. 

• Water alone is insufficient because caloric/energy needs are also urgently critical for survival. 
• Adding protein and further adding fat reflect priorities that become important slightly later, as the emergency response matures beyond the immediate survival phase into more complete dietary support.

Question (Front): Which CMAM component treats children with SAM with poor appetite or medical complications?
Rationale:
Inpatient care, which is specifically designated within the Community-based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) framework for children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) who present with poor appetite (failed appetite test) or medical complications requiring more intensive, facility-based treatment. 

• Outpatient care is instead used for SAM children who pass the appetite test and have no medical complications, allowing home-based management with ready-to-use therapeutic food.
• Home care and community care are not standard, formally defined CMAM components matching this specific clinical criterion.

Question (Front): Characterized mainly by a program already prepared by a group external to a community or environment. It may also mean top-down approach which is characterized mainly by the formulation of a plan at a higher level (e.g. national level), for implementation at a lower level (e.g. municipality or barangay).
Rationale:
Pre-determined planning is defined as a top-down approach where plans are formulated at a higher level (e.g., national) for implementation at a lower level (e.g., barangay), without the community's initial input into design. 

• Self-determined planning instead involves the community itself formulating its own plan. 
• Joint planning involves collaboration between external and community stakeholders together. 
• Strategic planning refers to a broader planning methodology focused on long-term goal-setting.

Question (Front): The following are characteristics of nutrition-oriented development planning EXCEPT:
Answer (Back): Malnutrition is merely a problem of food consumption and availability
Rationale:
Nutrition-oriented development planning explicitly recognizes malnutrition as a complex, multi-causal problem, not one reducible to just food consumption/availability alone. 

Nutrition being included as an objective integrated into development planning, diagnostic analysis used to identify causes, and nutrition actions applied across local/national and sectoral plans are all genuine, defining characteristics of this planning approach.
Option 1: Malnutrition is merely a problem of food consumption and availability
Option 2: Nutrition is included as an objective and integrated into development planning
Option 3: Diagnostic analysis is used in identifying cause of malnutrition
Option 4: Nutrition actions are applied in local and national levels; and in sectoral development plans

Question (Front): Mechanism for planning, implementing, monitoring, evaluating, and coordinating the local plans of action for nutrition at the province, city/municipality, and barangay levels.
Rationale:
Local Nutrition Committees (LNCs) serve as multi-function coordinating role across all local government levels in the Philippines, chaired by the respective local chief executive, and the basic functional unit of the nutrition program implementation and management.

See more here: https://nnc.gov.ph/mindanao-region/lnc-the-basic-functional-unit-of-the-nutrition-program/

Question (Front): Local nutrition committees are chaired by the following local chief executives, EXCEPT:
Rationale:
Congressmen are national legislative officials, not local chief executives, and therefore do not chair Local Nutrition Committees. 

Barangay Captains, Mayors, and Governors are all local chief executives who chair LNCs at their respective barangay, city/municipal, and provincial levels.

Question (Front): Local nutrition action plans (LNAP) serves as the mechanism to achieve nutrition goals at the city/municipal/provincial level. It should be harmonized in the local development system and plans, EXCEPT:
Rationale:
Environmental Impact Assessment is a project-specific environmental review process, not one of the standard local development planning documents that the Local Nutrition Action Plan (LNAP) is meant to be harmonized with. 

The Comprehensive Land Use Plan, Executive Legislative Agenda, and Comprehensive Development Plan are all standard local government planning documents that the LNAP should align with to ensure nutrition is mainstreamed into broader development planning and budgeting processes.

Question (Front): Focal persons for nutrition at the local levels are:
Rationale:
Regional nutrition focal points/officers serve national/sub-national levels.

• BNS, CNAO, MNAO, PNAO, RNAO - national level
• BNS, CNAO, MNAO, PNAO, RNPC - national level
• BNS, CNPC, MNPC, PNPC, RNPC - national level

Question (Front): In preparing for program planning and management, the first step is:
Answer (Back): Identifications/mobilization of LNC or planning core group
Rationale:
Establishing the group responsible for leading the planning process is the necessary first step before any assessment, goal-setting, or plan preparation can occur. 

Assessment or diagnostic analysis, setting goals and objectives, and preparing the plan of operation are all important subsequent steps, but they require an organized planning group to already be in place to carry them out.
Option 3: Identifications/mobilization of LNC or planning core group

Question (Front): Re-planning is a necessary step in nutrition program planning and management. In doing so, the following are revisited:
Rationale: Re-planning revisits the nutrition situation, the goals and objectives, and the strategies for targeting and implementing interventions together. Re-planning is triggered by monitoring and evaluation findings that suggest the current approach needs adjustment, and effective re-planning requires reassessing the full planning cycle.
Option 3: Strategies in targeting for and implementation of nutrition interventions

Question (Front): In nutritional assessment, causes of malnutrition must be classified into immediate, underlying and basic causes. Food insecurity and poor child care are classified as:
Rationale:
Underlying causes – contributing causes; food security, health services, practices

• Immediate causes – direct causes; food and care (individual level)
• Basic causes – societal; political, economic, education etc.
• Cross-cutting causes

Question (Front): Key decisions for implementation of nutrition programs/projects/activities such as continue with or without modification; stop the implementation; replace with new interventiion are done in what phase/step of program management?
Rationale:
Re-planning is a specific decision types (continue, modify, stop, or replace an intervention) made once monitoring and evaluation data reveal how a program is performing. 

• Assessment and plan preparation occurs before implementation and does not involve adjusting an ongoing program. 
• Implementation is the execution phase itself. 
• Monitoring and evaluation generates the data that informs these decisions but is technically the data-gathering step preceding the actual re-planning decision-making.

Question (Front): A method of delivering goods and/or services to a selected group of individuals or households rather than to every individual or household in the population.
Rationale:
Targeting is defined as directing program benefits to a specifically selected subgroup rather than universally to the entire population. 

• Prioritizing of beneficiaries is a related but broader concept describing the ranking of need, not the delivery mechanism. 
• Sampling refers to a research/survey selection method, not a program service delivery approach. 
• Identification and selection of clients is part of the targeting process but does not capture the full definition of the delivery method as precisely as "targeting" does.

Question (Front): Depends on decision-making structures at the community level to allocate program goods or services effectively according to the criteria as defined in the program objectives.
Rationale:
Community-based uses local knowledge and consensus (e.g., councils) to select beneficiaries.

• Administrative - uses official records and pre-determined criteria (e.g., income data, public registries).
• Self-targeting - uses program design (e.g., low-quality food, hard labor requirement) to make the benefit unattractive

Question (Front): It is the regular and periodical follow-up of the implementation of planned activities and progress to determine whether steps in the strategy are followed and whether program objectives by phase or activity are attained as planned.
Rationale:
Monitoring is tracking progress and resource use against plans, usually ongoing and internal.

• Systematic Assessment of Progress (SAP) - structured, periodic check to see if short-term goals are being met and whether the project logic remains sound
• Evaluation - determining relevance, effectiveness, impact, and efficiency of the project, often periodic or end-of-cycle
• Sustainability - ensuring benefits continue after the program's funding or external support ends

Question (Front): Information which is used to measure changes which occur during course of program it allows one to monitor the progress of the program or it is a measure of progress towards meeting a program's objectives
Rationale:
Indicators are specific, measurable values that show the status or progress toward a desired result or goal.

• Data - raw, unorganized facts and figures
• Records - stored, organized sets of data about a specific entity
• Criteria - standards or principles used to judge, classify, or make a decision (e.g., age, income level).

Question (Front): It refers to the changes in the condition of the target population which generally reflect the primary objectives of the project or program, e.g. percent improvement in the prevalence of stunting in the municipality.
Rationale:
Impact indicator - measures long-term, ultimate changes in well-being or the environment (e.g., reduced mortality rates, national poverty reduction)

• Input indicator - measures resources put into a program (e.g., funds spent, staff hired)
• Output indicator - measures direct, tangible results of program activities (e.g., training sessions held, meals served)
• Outcome indicator - measures changes in behavior, knowledge, or condition achieved by the target group (e.g., improved hygiene practices, increased enrollment)

Question (Front): It shows how inputs or resources invested in the project are transformed through a series of sequential processes into outputs; helpful in monitoring ongoing projects or activities.
Rationale:
Process evaluation - assessing how the program was implemented and managed (efficiency, quality).

• Ex-ante evaluation - assessing potential before program starts (feasibility, relevance).
• Ex-post evaluation - assessing actual results/impact after program ends (overall success).
• Result evaluation - assessing what the program achieved (outcomes, effects, and impact).

Question (Front): In process evaluation, the following questions will be addressed, EXCEPT:
Answer (Back): What will be the result of this project?
Rationale: The question "what will be the result of this project?" belongs to result evaluation, which focuses on outcomes and impact, not process evaluation, which focuses on implementation quality and efficiency.
Option 1: Are we doing our job well?
Option 2: What can we be improved upon in the project?
Option 4: What will be the result of this project?

Question (Front): Adoption of Local Nutrition Action Plan by the LGU requires:
Rationale: Formal LNAP adoption by a local government unit requires multiple coordinated steps together: acceptance, approval, and endorsement by the local chief executive to the Sanggunian; sponsorship by a member of the local legislative body; and a resolution filed for adoption and funding.
Option 1: Acceptance, approval and endorsement of LCE to Sangguniang Bayan/Panlalawigan
Option 2: Sponsorship by a member of the local legislative body
Option 3: Resolution filed for adoption and funding of the LNAP

Question (Front): Field visits, meeting, record keeping, reporting, plan implementation reviews and special studies are known approaches for:
Rationale:
The correct answer is monitoring and evaluation combined, since this specific list of activities (field visits, meetings, record keeping, reporting, implementation reviews, special studies) spans both the ongoing, process-tracking functions of monitoring and the more in-depth, periodic assessment functions of evaluation.

• Monitoring alone or evaluation alone would not fully encompass this comprehensive list of approaches, since some (like routine field visits and record keeping) are more monitoring-oriented while others (like special studies) are more evaluation-oriented. 
• "Monitoring or evaluation" incorrectly implies these are separate, alternative approaches and not combined, integrated set of activities.

Question (Front): In the Monitoring and Evaluation of Local Level Plan Implementation (MELLPI) of the National Nutrition Council, which one refers to the highest award given to an LGU?
Rationale:
The National Nutrition Council (NNC) utilizes the MELLPI framework to monitor Local Government Units (LGUs) and recognize them with progressive awards for outstanding performance in implementing the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition (PPAN):

• Nutrition Honor Award (NHA): This is the highest and most prestigious accolade given to an LGU. It is conferred only to LGUs that have maintained excellent nutrition program implementation for six (6) consecutive years, coming with a standard ₱1,000,000 cash prize and trophy.
• Consistent Regional Outstanding Winner in Nutrition (CROWN) Award: Given to an LGU that has been a regional winner for three (3) consecutive years. After achieving the CROWN, an LGU must successfully clear 1st and 2nd Year CROWN Maintenance Evaluations before it can qualify for the final Nutrition Honor Award.
• Green Banner Seal of Compliance: The initial tier of recognition awarded at the regional level to municipalities, cities, or provinces that excel in their annual nutrition performance benchmarks.
Option 2: Consistent Regional Outstanding Winner in Nutrition

Question (Front): Views malnutrition as a disease which has to be cured by therapeutic approaches
Rationale:
• Social Welfare - malnutrition as deprivation of social safety net
• Agriculture - malnutrition due to limited food production
• Education - malnutrition is due to poor nutrition knowledge and skills

Question (Front): In 2014, the National Nutrition Council Governing Board approved and adopted the guidelines on local nutrition planning that direct LGUS to come up with a ______ local nutrition action plan.
Rationale: The 2014 NNC guidelines for LGU-level Local Nutrition Action Plans, aligning with the local government's typical elected term of office. Aligning the LNAP's three-year cycle with local elected officials' terms helps ensure political ownership and continuity of nutrition planning across the term of local leadership.

Question (Front): The LNAP is best prepared on the first semester of an election year to ensure that the nutrition agenda is integrated in the Executive Legislative Agenda which becomes the bases for local development plan and in-turn the annual investment plan. This is essential for:
Rationale:
Local budgeting because timely integration of the nutrition agenda into the Executive Legislative Agenda ensures that nutrition programs are properly reflected and funded in the subsequent Annual Investment Plan and local budget allocations. 

While local planning, implementation, and monitoring/evaluation are all eventually affected by this timing, the question mentioning ELA and AIP points most directly to securing adequate budgeting for nutrition programs.

Question (Front): In planning for a food for work intervention, the following key decision points must be considered, EXCEPT:
Answer (Back): Will the assistance be in cash or kind?
Rationale: By definition, food-for-work is already established as a food (in-kind) assistance modality, so this cash-versus-kind question does not apply as a decision point within a program already defined as food-based.
Option 1: What food commodities will be used?
Option 2: What volume of food will be given for each unit of work?
Option 3: Will the assistance be in cash or kind?
Option 4: What complementary services will be provided?

Question (Front): In planning for a supplementary feeding, the following are key decision points, EXCEPT:
Answer (Back): What technology of production will be promoted?
Rationale: “What technology of production will be promoted?” refers to a food production intervention.
Option 1: Type of commodity to be used to include for formulationss like Nutripak
Option 2: What technology of production will be promoted?
Option 4: Mechanism for community mobilization and particpation of parents

Question (Front): This serves as complementary activity in making the implementation of most of the nutrition interventions effective.
Rationale:
Nutrition Education functions as a cross-cutting, complementary activity that enhances the effectiveness of virtually all other nutrition interventions by ensuring beneficiaries understand and can sustain the benefits of programs like feeding, fortification, or livelihood support. 

Livelihood Assistance, Home/School/Community Food Production, and Supplementary Feeding are specific, standalone interventions.
Option 3: Home, School, and Community Food Production

Question (Front): Interventions that address the immediate causes of malnutrition.
Rationale:
Nutrition-specific interventions address the immediate, direct causes of malnutrition at the individual level (e.g., micronutrient supplementation, breastfeeding promotion, treatment of acute malnutrition).

• Nutrition-sensitive interventions instead address the underlying causes of malnutrition, such as food security, health services access, and caregiving practices, operating at a different causal level. 
• "Nutrition and Development Interventions" and "Nutrition-in-Development Interventions" are not standard, recognized terms in this classification framework.

Question (Front): In 1976, Letter of Instruction 441 directed the Department of Local Government and Community Development (now called DILG) to establish ____ in every region, province, city, municipality to implement nutrition action plans.
Rationale: Functional nutrition committees, which LOI 441 specifically mandated be established at every administrative level to implement nutrition action plans, laying early institutional groundwork for what would later become the Local Nutrition Committees.

Question (Front): A BNS is trained volunteer community worker with the following qualifications EXCEPT:
Rationale: At least high school graduate - the law states ‘elementary’ or ‘primary school’ (see PD 1569)
Option 3: Willingness to serve, part-time or full-time
Option 4: More than 18 years old, but younger than 60 years old

Question (Front): A decision-making process of identifying potential nutrition problems and needs of a specific population group, analyzing possible ways of preventing and controlling malnutrition, allocating resources based on needs and expectations, and taking deliberate action to address nutritional problems, including those related to monitoring and evaluation.
Rationale:
Nutrition Program Management is executing, supervising, and coordinating all activities to achieve program goals.

• Nutrition Program Planning - designing the specific program: defining objectives, strategies, resources, and implementation steps.
• Nutrition Intervention - specific action designed to directly improve nutritional status (e.g., supplementation, education).
• Food and Nutrition Planning - macro-level process to set national/regional policies and strategies for food supply and consumption.

Question (Front): A researcher wants to conduct a study wherein men with coronary artery disease and a comparable group of men without coronary artery disease were asked about their prior use of aspirin. This is an example of which type of study?
Rationale:
This scenario perfectly illustrates the design of a case-control study based on two defining factors:

• Selection by Outcome (Disease Status): The researcher selects participants based on whether they already have the condition of interest. The "cases" are the men with coronary artery disease, and the "controls" are the comparable group of men without the disease.
• Retrospective Assessment: The researcher then looks backward in time ("asked about their prior use of aspirin") to compare how frequently each group was exposed to the factor being studied.

• Ecological study - Comparing the average per capita salt intake across ten different countries to the average national hypertension rate in those same countries.
• Randomized clinical trial - Dividing 500 patients with a specific disease into two groups: one receiving a new drug and one receiving a placebo (or standard treatment), and then following both groups for a year to see which group has a better outcome.
• Case series - A doctor publishing a report detailing the clinical presentation, diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes for three unusual patients presenting with the same rare cluster of symptoms at their clinic over a six-month period.

Question (Front): It refers to the epidemiological approach which explains the occurence, nature, and extent of a disease:
Rationale:
Man-Agent-Environment triad - epidemiological model; analyzing disease causation via host, pathogen, and surroundings.

• Triple A approach - cycle for planning: assessment, analysis, action
• UNICEF framework - three-level causes of malnutrition: basic, underlying, and immediate (food/health).
• Undernutrition infection cycle - vicious spiral where poor nutrition weakens immunity, increasing infection risk, which worsens nutrition.

Question (Front): A good survey sample is one in which:
Rationale: In most social, health, and market research, the goal is to have a representative sample that reflects the heterogeneity (diversity) of the larger population.
Option 1: the entire population to be studied is included
Option 2: all the characteristics of the population are represented proportionately

Question (Front): It describes the adequacy with which any measurement or index reflects the nutritional parameter of interest:
Rationale:
Validity - measuring what you intended to measure (truthfulness)

• Accuracy - how close a measurement is to the true or accepted value (correctness)
• Specificity - a test's ability to correctly identify negative cases (truly non-diseased or non-affected).
• Precision - how close repeated measurements are to each other (consistency/reproducibility)

Question (Front): A measure of years in perfect health lost:
Rationale:
DALY - Disability-Adjusted Life Year (Burden of Disease): Measures the total healthy life years lost (YLL + YLD).

• YLL - Years of Life Lost (Mortality): Measures the number of years lost due to premature death.
• YLD - Years Lived with Disability (Morbidity): Measures the number of years lived in less than full health due to illness or injury.
• QALY - Quality-Adjusted Life Year (Health Economics): Measures the value of a year of life adjusted by its quality or utility.

Question (Front): Which of the following methods can be used to estimate height?
Rationale:
When a patient cannot stand straight due to physical disabilities, bedridden status, or severe skeletal deformities (such as kyphosis or scoliosis), indirect anthropometric measurements are used to estimate stature:

 There is a strong biological correlation between an individual's arm span and their actual height. In a healthy adult, the distance from the tip of the middle finger of one hand to the tip of the middle finger of the other hand (when arms are extended fully at a 90-degree angle from the torso) roughly equals their max height.

Other common clinical measurements used in height-estimation equations include knee height and demispan (half of the arm span).

• Skinfold thickness - fat deposits
• MUAC - muscle mass
• Chest circumference - chest size

Question (Front): Which of the following is a dietary assessment method which uses specific food item list to record intakes over a given period?
Rationale:
Food frequency questionnaire (FFQ), which is defined precisely by its use of a structured, predetermined list of food items that respondents report consuming over a specified recall period (e.g., past month or year). 

• The 24-hour food recall instead captures all foods consumed in the preceding 24 hours without being restricted to a predetermined food list. 
• Diet records involve prospectively recording all foods eaten in real time, also without a fixed food item list. 
• Food weighing involves precisely weighing all food consumed.

Question (Front): Which of the following describes nutrition surveillance?
Answer (Back): Keeping watch over nutrition in order to make decisions that will lead to improvement in nutrition in population
Rationale: This responds to the main goal of nutrition surveillance is to continuously monitor a population's nutritional status so leaders can make informed decisions and policies that improve health and fix nutrition problems.
Option 1: Keeping watch over nutrition in order to make decisions that will lead to improvement in nutrition in population
Option 2: Provides information about dietary intake patterns, specific foods consumed and estimated nutrient intake
Option 3: Mortality and morbidity data to identify groups at high risk and indicate the extent of risk of the community

Question (Front): It is a condition when thiamin is deficient
Rationale:
Beri-beri is a classic, well-established clinical deficiency disease resulting from inadequate thiamine (vitamin B1) intake, presenting with neurological (dry beri-beri) or cardiovascular (wet beri-beri) manifestations. 

• Pellagra - niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency 
• Ariboflavinosis - riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency 
• Tiqui-tiqui is actually a traditional Filipino rice bran extract historically used as a treatment/cure for beri-beri

Question (Front): Multiple replicates of 24-hour food recall is used to measure nutrient intake to meet ___ level of study objectives
Rationale: Second-level study objectives (often referred to as secondary or specific objectives) break down primary research goal into actionable, measurable steps. First-level (primary) objective states WHAT you want to achieve overall, second-level objectives explain HOW you will achieve it by focusing on specific variables, steps, or populations.

Question (Front): Moderate IDD in the population is indicated by median UIE level of:
Rationale:
The severity of Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD) in a population is classified based on the Median Urinary Iodine Excretion (UIE) or Concentration (UIC) levels:
• Severe Iodine Deficiency: Median UIE of <20 µg/L
• Moderate Iodine Deficiency: Median UIE of 20–49 µg/L
• Mild Iodine Deficiency: Median UIE of 50–99 µg/L
• Adequate Iodine Nutrition: Median UIE of 100–199 µg/L (Target public health range for school-age children)

Question (Front): The plasma retinol level of Flora is 25 µg/dL. How do you interpret this value?
Answer (Back): Flora has an acceptable plasma retinol level
Rationale:
In public health and clinical nutrition, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) establish specific reference thresholds for circulating plasma or serum retinol to evaluate Vitamin A status:

• Deficient / Severe Deficiency: Less than 10 µg/dL (< 0.35 µmol/L).
• Low / Subclinical Deficiency: 10 to 20 µg/dL (0.35 to 0.70 µmol/L).
• Acceptable / Adequate: More than 20 µg/dL (≥ 0.70 µmol/L).

Flora's level is 25 µg/dL, which places her comfortably above the 20 µg/dL cutoff, classifying her Vitamin A status as acceptable or adequate.
Option 1: Flora has a deficient plasma retinol level
Option 2: Flora has a low plasma retinol level
Option 3: Flora has an acceptable plasma retinol level
Option 4: Flora has high plasma retinal level

Question (Front): Using the WHO standard, what is the classification of goiter if the thyroid gland is enlarged and easily visible from a distance?
Rationale:
In 1994, the WHO, UNICEF, and the International Council for Control of Iodine Deficiency Disorders simplified the scale down to the standard 3-tier system:

• Grade 0: No goiter (neither palpable nor visible).
• Grade 1: A mass that is palpable but not visible when the neck is in a normal position.
• Grade 2: A swelling that is clearly visible when the neck is in a normal position and is consistent with an enlarged thyroid upon palpation.

Question (Front): Keshan disease is a deficiency in?
Rationale:
The correct answer is selenium, a trace mineral deficiency specifically linked to Keshan disease, an endemic cardiomyopathy first identified in selenium-poor regions of China.

Keshan disease is an endemic, potentially fatal form of dilated cardiomyopathy (weakening and enlargement of the heart muscle).

 It is directly linked to severe dietary selenium deficiency, typically occurring in rural regions where the soil lacks selenium, leaving local agricultural crops deplete of the mineral. It was first documented in Keshan County, China.

Question (Front): A condition characterized as having sand paper feel of the skin:
Rationale:
In clinical nutrition and dermatology, follicular hyperkeratosis (also known as phrynoderma or "toad skin") is classic textbook-defined by a rough, sandpaper-like texture on the skin.

This condition occurs when the body overproduces keratin (a structural protein), which forms hard, scaly plugs that block the openings of hair follicles. This creates tiny, elevated, rough bumps typically found on the back of the upper arms, thighs, and buttocks.

In a board exam context, follicular hyperkeratosis is highly pathognomonic for Vitamin A deficiency or a chronic lack of essential fatty acids (like Omega-3).

• Pellagrous dermatitis - symmetric, dark, scaling rash on sun-exposed skin (the "casal's necklace").
• Petechiae - tiny, non-blanching red or purple dots on the skin due to bleeding under the skin.
• Xerosis - generalized, abnormal dryness of the skin (or mucous membranes).

Question (Front): A condition characterized by vertical fissuring in the lips:
Rationale:
Cheilosis is the vertical cracking/fissuring at the lips, sometimes extending to angular fissures at the mouth corners (angular stomatitis).

• Fluorosis - affects tooth enamel (mottling) from excess fluoride
• Glossitis - inflammation of the tongue
• Dermatitis - general skin inflammation

Question (Front): Schilling test is used to assess the status of this vitamin?
Rationale: The Schilling test is a classic diagnostic procedure specifically designed to assess the body's ability to absorb vitamin B12, including distinguishing whether malabsorption is due to intrinsic factor deficiency (pernicious anemia) or another cause.

Question (Front): A condition when folate and Vitamin B12 are deficient
Rationale:
Megaloblastic anemia - RBCs are large and immature due to impaired DNA synthesis; large (macrocytic) RBCs; caused by folate or vitamin B12 deficiency.

• Microcytic anemia - RBCs are abnormally small.
• Pernicious anemia - megaloblastic anemia caused specifically by lack of intrinsic factor (for B12 absorption).
• Hypochromic anemia - RBCs are pale due to insufficient hemoglobin.

Question (Front): Which among these food items is a good source of preformed Vitamin A?
Rationale:
Egg yolk contains preformed vitamin A (retinol) directly, as animal-source foods provide vitamin A in its ready-to-use, preformed (retinol) state. 

Grains, peanuts, and corn oil are all plant-based foods that, if they contain any vitamin A activity at all, would provide it as provitamin A carotenoids (like beta-carotene) rather than preformed vitamin A, which the body must convert before use.

Question (Front): Laxatives can affect nutrient absorption through ___
Rationale: Laxatives work primarily by speeding up gastrointestinal transit time, which reduces the contact time between food/nutrients and the absorptive intestinal surface, thereby impairing nutrient absorption.

Question (Front): The method used to analyze protein content of foods in the FCT:
Rationale:
Kjeldahl method is the standard, classic laboratory technique for determining protein content by measuring total nitrogen and applying a conversion factor, widely used in food composition analysis.

• Soxhlet - fat/lipid extraction and analysis
• Roes-Gottlieb - specific method for fat analysis in dairy products
• Carr-Price - colorimetric method historically used for vitamin A analysis

Question (Front): Sonia has a fasting blood sugar level of 118 mg/dl. According to the assessment criteria of WHO, this value can be classified as  ____
Rationale:
According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and standard medical assessment guidelines, intermediate states of glucose regulation are formally categorized using the term "impaired".
• Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG): Defined as a fasting blood sugar level between 100 mg/dL and 125 mg/dL (or 6.1 mmol/L to 6.9 mmol/L based on specific WHO thresholds). Since Sonia's value is 118 mg/dl, it falls precisely within this category.
• Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT): Refers to blood sugar levels that are elevated during a 2-hour postprandial or oral glucose tolerance test (140–199 mg/dL).
In a clinical or exam context, these clinical categories represent "prediabetes," flagging that the individual's glucose metabolism is altered but has not yet met the diagnostic cutoff for a diabetes mellitus classification (≥126 mg/dL).

Normal Levels
	• Fasting Blood Sugar: Less than 100 mg/dL (< 5.6 mmol/L)
	• 2-Hour Oral Glucose Tolerance Test: Less than 140 mg/dL (< 7.8 mmol/L)
	• HbA1c: Less than 5.7% (< 39 mmol/mol)

 Impaired Levels (Prediabetes)
	• Fasting Blood Sugar: 100 to 125 mg/dL (5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L) — called Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG)
	• 2-Hour Oral Glucose Tolerance Test: 140 to 199 mg/dL (7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L) — called Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT)
	• HbA1c: 5.7% to 6.4% (39 to 46 mmol/mol)

 Diabetes Mellitus
	• Fasting Blood Sugar: 126 mg/dL or higher (≥ 7.0 mmol/L)
	• 2-Hour Oral Glucose Tolerance Test: 200 mg/dL or higher (≥ 11.1 mmol/L)
	• HbA1c: 6.5% or higher (≥ 48 mmol/mol)
	• Random Blood Sugar: 200 mg/dL or higher when accompanied by severe symptoms like extreme thirst or frequent urination

Question (Front): Diagnostic test to determine the sufficiency of post nutriture to permit cells, tissues, organ systems or the host to optimally perform nutrient dependent biologic function.
Rationale:
Functional test is the measure of actual physiological/biological functions.

• Biochemical test - laboratory test
• Clinical test - physical test
• Static test - single-point-in-time biochemical measurement

Question (Front): An essential trace element for both humans and animals.
Rationale:
Molybdenum is a recognized essential trace element required by both humans and animals for enzymatic cofactor functions (such as in xanthine oxidase). 

Bromine, lithium, and vanadium are elements that have been studied for potential biological roles but are not established as essential trace elements with confirmed dietary requirement status in the same way molybdenum is officially recognized.

Question (Front): It is a condition when Vit B3 is deficient
Rationale:
Pellagra is a niacin deficiency, classically presenting with the "three Ds": dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia (and if untreated, a fourth D - death).

• Ariboflavinosis – riboflavin deficiency
• Beri-beri – thiamin deficiency
• Tiqui-tiqui - extract to cure beri-beri

Question (Front): Which of the following is a functional test used to assess Vitamin A?
Rationale:
In nutritional assessment, diagnostic tools are broadly split into biochemical (static) tests and functional tests:

A functional test measures the actual biological or physiological consequence of a nutrient deficiency on body function. Vitamin A is vital for the formation of rhodopsin (visual purple) in the rod cells of the retina, which allows eyes to see in dim light. The dark adaptation test evaluates the functional impairment of night vision caused by early-stage Vitamin A deficiency.

	• Test for serum albumin: A biochemical test primarily used as a general indicator of visceral protein status or systemic inflammation rather than a vitamin check.
	• Immunological test: Assesses immune system components (like T-cell counts or antibody levels). While Vitamin A impacts immunity, it is not a direct diagnostic test for it.
	• Test for urinary creatinine: Used alongside height measurements to calculate the creatinine-height index (CHI), which estimates skeletal muscle mass or evaluates kidney function.

Question (Front): Which of the followng is NOT a substrate used to assess zinc status?
Rationale:
Nails are not a standard, validated substrate used in clinical or population-level zinc status assessment. 

Hair, saliva, and blood/plasma are all recognized substrates that have been used, with varying degrees of reliability, to assess zinc status in research and clinical settings.

Question (Front): Breastmilk can be used for biochemical assessment of ?
Rationale:
In public health and community nutrition assessments, breast milk retinol concentration is a well-established, non-invasive biomarker used to evaluate the Vitamin A status of both lactating mothers and their breastfed infants.

• Breast milk retinol levels are highly sensitive to maternal Vitamin A intake and liver reserves.
• The World Health Organization (WHO) recognizes breast milk testing as a valuable epidemiological tool. A high prevalence of low breast milk retinol concentrations (e.g., < 1.05 µmol/L or < 30 µg/dL) in a community indicates a subclinical Vitamin A deficiency problem requiring public health interventions like maternal postpartum supplementation or food fortification.

• Vitamin K & Vitamin D: Human breast milk is inherently and universally low in both Vitamin K and Vitamin D, regardless of maternal nutritional status. Because their baseline levels in milk are naturally close to zero, breast milk is not used as a reliable biochemical index to assess systemic status for these vitamins.
• Vitamin E: While present in breast milk (especially colostrum), serum alpha-tocopherol blood tests remain the primary clinical diagnostic tool for Vitamin E, rather than breast milk analysis.

Question (Front): What is the biochemical criterion included in the WHO classification scheme for xerophthalmia?
Rationale:
Plasma vitamin A level is the standard biochemical marker used alongside clinical/ocular signs (like night blindness, Bitot's spots, corneal xerosis) in the WHO classification of xerophthalmia severity.

• Skinfold thickness – measures body fat
• Sensitivity test for Vitamin A deficiency - vague, non-standard term rather than a recognized biochemical criterion
• Urinary Vitamin A concentration - not the standard biochemical measure used for vitamin A status, since vitamin A is fat-soluble and stored/circulated differently than water-soluble vitamins excreted in urine.
Option 2: Sensitivity test for Vitamin A deficiency

Question (Front): Irma weighs 56 kg and stands 5 feet. What is her body mass index?
Rationale:
Body Mass Index (BMI) is calculated using the formula:
BMI = Weight (kg) / [Height (m)]²

1. Convert height from feet to meters:
	• 5 feet = 60 inches
	• 60 inches × 0.0254 meters/inch = 1.524 meters

2. Square the height in meters:
	• 1.524 × 1.524 = 2.3226 m²

3. Divide weight by squared height:
	• 56 kg / 2.3226 m² = 24.11

According to both WHO and Asia-Pacific standards, a BMI of 24.11 places Irma in the "Normal" weight category.

Question (Front): The MUAC of Ivanah Kawali indicates 11.5 cm. What is her nutritional status?
Rationale:
The correct answer is Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM), since a MUAC value in the range of approximately 11.5-12.4 cm in children under five is classified by WHO as indicating moderate acute malnutrition. 

MUAC is a simple, field-friendly screening tool widely used in community and emergency nutrition programs to rapidly identify acute malnutrition in young children.

• Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM): Diagnosed only when the measurement drops strictly below 11.5 cm (<115 mm), or if bilateral pitting edema is present.
• Normal Nutritional Status: Indicated by a MUAC of 12.5 cm or higher (≥125 mm).

Question (Front): According to WHO, if the prevalence rate of anemia in a population is 20% it can be classified as?
Rationale:
The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies the severity of anemia as a public health problem based on its prevalence rate within a given population:

• Normal (No problem): Prevalence of 4.9% or lower
• Mild Public Health Problem: Prevalence of 5.0% to 19.9%
• Moderate Public Health Problem: Prevalence of 20.0% to 39.9% — Since the population prevalence is exactly 20%, it marks the lower boundary of a moderate public health crisis, requiring immediate targeted community interventions (such as massive iron-folic acid supplementation or food fortification programs).
• Severe Public Health Problem: Prevalence of 40.0% or higher

Question (Front): A deficiency in ___ can be seen in the nails
Rationale:
Selenium, whose deficiency can manifest with changes visible in the nails (among other signs), consistent with selenium's role in numerous enzymatic and antioxidant functions. 

• Iodine deficiency instead manifests primarily as goiter and thyroid-related signs. 
• Thiamin deficiency manifests as beri-beri-related neurological/cardiovascular signs. 
• Copper deficiency, while it can affect hair (as in Menkes disease), is not primarily associated with nail changes in the same way selenium is.

Question (Front): Ms. Santos is conducting a research which aims to measure the mean nutrient intake of school children. What dietary assessment method will you recommend?
Rationale:
24-hour food recall is well-suited and commonly used for estimating the mean (average) nutrient intake of a group or population, since individual day-to-day variation tends to average out across a sufficiently large sample even with a single recall per person. 

• Food frequency questionnaires are better suited for ranking individuals by relative intake or assessing habitual/long-term dietary patterns rather than precise mean nutrient quantities. 
• Diet records and food weighing are more resource-intensive, detailed methods typically reserved for smaller studies or when precise individual intake data is needed.

Question (Front): This pertains to the number of deaths per 1000 livebirth of infants under 1 year of age in a calendar year in the same period
Rationale:
IMR (Infant Mortality Rate): The number of deaths of children under 1 year of age (0 to 365 days) per 1,000 live births in a given calendar year. It is a standard public health indicator reflecting the overall socio-economic and healthcare status of a population.

• MMR (Maternal Mortality Ratio/Rate): The number of maternal deaths from any cause related to or aggravated by pregnancy or its management during pregnancy and childbirth (or within 42 days of termination) per 100,000 live births.
• NMR (Neonatal Mortality Rate): The number of deaths during the first 28 days of life (neonatal period) per 1,000 live births.
• SMR (Standardized Mortality Ratio): The ratio of observed deaths in the study group to the expected deaths in the general population, or Senile Mortality Rate depending on the epidemiological context.

Question (Front): Obesity prevalence among adults 20 to 59 years old according to the 2021 ENNS is:
Rationale:
According to the 2021 Expanded National Nutrition Survey (DOST-FNRI), based on the WHO Asia-Pacific BMI Classification,

• 18.3% adults were overweight (BMI: 23.0 to 24.9 kg/m²)
• 30.2% were obese class I (BMI: 25.0 to 29.9 kg/m²)
• 10.0% were obese class II (BMI: ≥30 kg/m²).

Question (Front): Menke's Kinky hair syndrome is a deficiency in ____?
Rationale: Menke's kinky hair syndrome is the genetic disorder of copper metabolism/transport that results in severe copper deficiency, presenting classically with sparse, kinky, brittle hair along with neurodegenerative symptoms in affected infants.

Question (Front): An instrument used to measure skinfold thickness
Rationale:
The Lange caliper is a specific instrument designed and validated for measuring skinfold thickness at standardized body sites to estimate subcutaneous body fat. 

Biceps, subscapular, and midaxillary are names of specific skinfold measurement sites on the body.

Question (Front): Which of the following is a measurement of body composition?
Rationale:
Body composition specifically refers to the relative proportions of fat mass versus fat-free (lean) mass in the body, and body fat measurement directly captures one of these two core components. 

• Weight and height are simple anthropometric dimensions that do not by themselves distinguish fat from lean tissue. 
• Head circumference is a growth/development indicator used mainly in infants to assess brain growth.

Question (Front): Bitot's spot is characterized by ___?
Answer (Back): Dryness of conjunctiva with foamy patch
Rationale:
Dryness of the conjunctiva with foamy patches is the precise clinical description of a Bitot's spot, a foamy, triangular, grayish-white patch on the conjunctiva associated with vitamin A deficiency-related xerophthalmia. 

• Night blindness is an earlier, functional (not physical) sign of vitamin A deficiency, appearing before Bitot's spots develop. 
• Conjunctival xerosis refers to generalized dryness of the conjunctiva without the specific foamy patch appearance that defines a Bitot's spot.
• Corneal xerosis refers to dryness affecting the cornea.
Option 3: Dryness of conjunctiva with foamy patch

Question (Front): Sustainability implies food system practices that respect and protect the ecosystems. It is recognized as an important aspect of ensuring the right to food.
Rationale:
• Statement 1 is true: According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), environmental sustainability in a food system is determined by ensuring that the impacts of production, processing, and distribution on the surrounding natural environment are neutral or positive. It explicitly demands the respect and protection of ecosystems by safeguarding biodiversity, water, soil, and minimizing the carbon footprint.

• Statement 2 is true: The "Right to Food" is a formalized human right, and the United Nations recognizes that this right cannot be realized long-term without sustainable practices. If today's food systems destroy ecosystems, deplete freshwater, and accelerate the climate crisis, they compromise the global capacity to feed future generations, thereby violating the progressive realization of the right to food.
Option 1: Only the first statement is true
Option 2: Only the second statement is true

Question (Front): It underpins all other food security dimensions by emphasizing the capacity of individuals and groups to engage in decision and policy making processes.
Rationale:
Agency is the power to make decisions and act on one's own behalf (e.g., choosing what to eat).

• Accessibility - ability to get or afford the resources (e.g., food, services, markets).
• Utilization - ability to properly use the resources to achieve good health (e.g., hygiene, knowledge).
• Sustainability - ensuring the benefits continue after external support is withdrawn (long-term resilience).

• Availability - physical presence of food
• Nutrition security - consistent access, affordability, and utilization of diverse, safe, and nutritious food to ensure a healthy life.
• Economic security - stable income, resources, and access to work that guarantees a basic standard of living and protects against shocks.

Rationale:
In community nutrition, barriers to food security are classified according to specific stages of the Food Pathway:
• Food Distribution Block: Poor road conditions serve as a barrier during the transport and logistics stage. It prevents food from reaching marketplaces efficiently, affecting availability and accessibility rather than the choices made at the household table.
• Food Consumption Blocks: Religious laws (e.g., halal/kosher), personal food preferences, and a lack of knowledge on nutrition are all localized or individual factors that directly obstruct or alter how families choose to consume available food.

Question (Front): This refers to the physical, economic, socio-cultural, and policy conditions that shape access, affordability, safety and food preferences
Rationale:
The term food environment encompasses the collective physical, economic, policy, and socio-cultural surroundings and opportunities that directly influence a consumer's food choices, purchasing habits, and nutritional status.

It acts as the interface where a person makes a decision about what to eat, driven by specific subdomains:
• Physical & Policy Conditions: The location of grocery stores versus "food deserts," food safety regulations, or marketing and labeling laws.
• Economic & Socio-cultural Conditions: Retail prices, household purchasing power (affordability), and family or community traditions that dictate food preferences.

Question (Front): All of the following often shape food environments except:
Rationale:
The correct answer is consumer behavior because consumer behavior is generally considered an outcome or response shaped BY the food environment (through what foods are available, promoted, and priced), rather than itself being a shaping force of the environment. 

Private companies, industry, and legal frameworks are all recognized as active forces that shape food environments.

Question (Front): Two of the following are possible blocks to food availability except:
Rationale:
Food Availability (Supply Side) refers to the physical presence of food through local agricultural production, storage, or imports.
	• Presence of pests and Typhoons are environmental or biological hazards that physically destroy crops, directly blocking availability.
	• Availability of agricultural inputs (like seeds and fertilizer) directly determines how much food can be produced in the first place.

Food Accessibility/Affordability (Demand Side): Market price does not typically prevent food from physically existing or being available in a market. Instead, high prices act as an economic barrier, blocking a family's accessibility or affordability to buy the food that is already there.

Question (Front): All of the following are the main drivers of changes in the food system except:
Rationale:
According to the High Level Panel of Experts (HLPE) on Food Security and Nutrition and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), a food system is conceptually split into Drivers, Core Components, and Outcomes:

Drivers (External Elements): These are the broad, macro-level forces that push or pull the entire food system into changing. The recognized categories of global drivers include:
	• Political and institutional factors (e.g., policies, trade laws, land rights)
	• Economic and market factors (e.g., income shifts, globalization, prices)
	• Technology and innovation factors (e.g., precision agriculture, storage engineering)
	• Biophysical and climate factors (e.g., weather, soil health)
	• Demographic and socio-cultural factors (e.g., population growth, shifting habits)

Food Supply Chains (Internal Component): Food supply chains (comprising agricultural production, storage, processing, and distribution) are not external drivers of change. Instead, they are the internal mechanisms or structural pillars of the food system that get altered or shaped by the drivers.

Question (Front): What is the main advantage of using randomized controlled trial (RCT) in nutrition research?
Answer (Back): It enables researchers to control for confounding variables

• Choice C is false because RCTs are generally more expensive and time-consuming than observational designs. 
• Choice D overstates the claim; RCTs are the gold standard for causal inference but are not the "only way" to study nutrient-health relationships, since other designs also contribute evidence. The RCT's defining strength is its ability to minimize both measured and unmeasured confounding through random allocation.

• To assess the nutritional status of individuals in a clinical setting - surveillance is population-based, not conducted in individual clinical settings.

• It has a limited scope and only tracks a few indicators – incorrect; comprehensive systems typically track a broad and appropriately scoped set of indicators, not just a limited few.

Question (Front): A community nutritionist is tasked with designing an intervention to reduce childhood obesity in a low-income urban neighborhood. A preliminary needs assessment revealed that the primary barriers are limited access to affordable, fresh produce and a lack of safe, accessible recreational spaces. Rationale:
Advocating for a city policy incentivizing mobile produce vendors while also improving a local playground addresses multiple levels of the socio-ecological model (SEM) simultaneously: policy/environmental level (vendor incentives) and physical/community environment level (playground improvement), matching both identified barriers (limited produce access and lack of safe recreational space). 

• A nutrition education class alone addresses only the individual/interpersonal level, ignoring the structural access barriers identified in the assessment. 
• Partnering with a grocery store addresses food access but does not address the recreational space barrier. 
• A school-based program addresses only the school setting and misses the broader community-level access and environment barriers identified. 

The SEM framework explains how multiple levels of influence: from individual factors to broad social structures interact to determine a health outcome, such as malnutrition.
Option 1: Implementing a weekly nutrition education for parents at a local community center.
Option 2: Partnering with a local grocery store to create a "healthy eating" ailse and offering discount coupons for fruits and vegetables
Option 3: Advocating for a city policy that provides incentives for mobile vendores to sell fresh produce in the neighborhood, while also collaborating with the parks and recreation department to improve a local playground

Answer (Back): Principle Neglected: Cultural competency. Next Step: Conduct focus groups with participants to understand their food preferences and dietary habits, and adjust the food packages accordingly.

The correct answer is that the principle neglected is cultural competency, and the appropriate next step is conducting focus groups to understand participants' food preferences and dietary habits and adjusting food packages accordingly. 

High participation with persistently poor dietary outcomes suggests the food assistance being provided may not align with what participants actually want or will consistently consume, pointing to a cultural/preference mismatch rather than a participation or awareness problem.
Option 1: Principle Neglected: Cultural competency. Next Step: Conduct focus groups with participants to understand their food preferences and dietary habits, and adjust the food packages accordingly.
Option 2: Principle Neglected: Outcome-based evaluation. Next Step: Implement a more rigorous evaluation protocol to measure changes in health indicators like blood pressure and BMI.

Question (Front): In a rural community, a nutritionist identifies a high prevalence of iron-deficiency anemia among women of childbearing age. The community has a strong agricultural tradition and relies heavily on local produce of whole grains and legumes, but the soil lacks bioavailable iron. A pilot program introduces a new iron-fortified flour, but a year later, the anemia rates have not significantly improved. Applying the principles of community nutrition, what is the most plausible reason for the program's failure?

Rationale: The correct answer is that the intervention failed to account for food-food interactions, since the community's diet is high in phytates (found abundantly in whole grains and legumes), which are well-known potent inhibitors of non-heme iron absorption, potentially neutralizing much of the benefit of the iron fortification.
Option 1: The intervention failed to account for potential food-food interactions, as the community's diet is high in phytates, which inhibit iron absorption.
Option 2: The program did not employ a randomized controlled trial, making it impossible to accurately measure its impact on the target population.
Option 3: The nutritionist did not adequately engage local political leaders, resulting in a lack of policy support for the program's long-term sustainability.
Option 4: The intervention was not tailored to the individual health needs of each participant, failing to address unique comorbidities that might interfere with iron absorption.

Question (Front): A public health nutritionist is developing a new community-based infant feeding program. Which of the following quality assurance (QA) procedures is most critical for ensuring the program's long term effectiveness and sustainability, beyond a single evaluation cycle?
Answer (Back): Establishing a continuous improvement (CQI) process that involves regular feedback loops from stakeholders and data-driven adjustments to program activities
Rationale:
The correct answer is establishing a continuous quality improvement (CQI) process involving regular feedback loops from stakeholders and data-driven adjustments to program activities, because CQI is specifically designed as an ongoing, cyclical process that sustains program quality and effectiveness well beyond any single evaluation point.

• A randomized controlled trial is a rigorous but typically one-time comparative research design, not an ongoing quality assurance mechanism.
