Question (Front): Which weight loss medications are approved by the US-FDA?*
Rationale:
There are well-established medications officially approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for weight management:
	• Phentermine: Approved as a short-term, standalone appetite suppressant.
	• Orlistat: Approved for long-term weight management (available as prescription Xenical or over-the-counter Alli) by blocking intestinal fat absorption.
	• Topiramate: Approved by the FDA as a fixed-dose combination pill with phentermine (marketed under the brand name Qsymia) for chronic weight management.

Other Choices:
• Phenylpropanolamine: This drug was completely banned and ordered removed from the market by the FDA due to an increased risk of hemorrhagic stroke.
• Sibutramine: Originally approved for weight loss under the name Meridia, it was completely withdrawn from the market due to its association with an increased risk of heart attacks and strokes.
• Ibuprofen: This is a standard nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain and reduce fever, carrying no clinical indication or approval for weight loss.
• Aminorex: An amphetamine-like stimulant that was never FDA-approved for weight loss and was withdrawn globally after it was found to cause severe pulmonary hypertension.

Question (Front): Criteria for bariatric surgery:*
Rationale:
Historically, candidate selection for metabolic and bariatric surgery has been anchored on established body size and health criteria.
	• A BMI between 35 and 39.9 with significant medical comorbidities (such as type 2 diabetes, severe sleep apnea, or cardiovascular disease) serves as a primary qualification parameter.
	• A BMI of 40 or greater represents severe obesity and satisfies the selection criteria independently, with or without secondary medical complications.
	• A BMI of 36 paired with Atherosclerosis fits precisely into the definition of the other option (a BMI above 35 accompanied by a serious cardiovascular comorbidity).

Clinical Update

While older textbook questions focus heavily on this classic "35 with comorbidities / 40 baseline" framework, updated international surgical consensus guidelines from the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (ASMBS) and IFSO have expanded eligibility. Modern criteria now recommend bariatric surgery for anyone with a BMI over 35 regardless of comorbidities, and down to a BMI of 30 for individuals struggling with metabolic diseases like uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

Question (Front): This type of Bariatric Surgery requires the placement of a foreign object in the form of a band*
Rationale:
LAGB stands for Laparoscopic Adjustable Gastric Banding (commonly referred to by its commercial name, the Lap-Band).

This specific bariatric procedure involves placing an inflatable, medical-grade silicone band entirely around the upper portion of the stomach. This creates a tiny stomach pouch that drastically restricts the volume of food a patient can eat at one time, forcing early satiety without removing any actual gastric tissue.

• Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass: A permanent, combination surgery where the stomach is stapled to create a small pouch and the small intestine is physically rerouted, requiring no baseline foreign bands.
• BPD/DS: Biliopancreatic Diversion with Duodenal Switch is a complex, mostly malabsorptive surgery that resects a large portion of the stomach and drastically bypasses the small intestine.
• Gastric Restrictive Procedure: This is the general umbrella category term for any surgery that limits stomach capacity (including the sleeve and vertical banded gastroplasty), whereas LAGB is the specific, targeted procedure abbreviation requested by the question.

Question (Front): Combination procedure in bariatric surgery results to hormonal influences. The production of Ghrelin hormone is likewise decreased resulting to*
Rationale:
Ghrelin is known as the orexigenic hormone (hunger hormone) that stimulates appetite and food intake. Because bariatric procedures (such as a sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass) involve anatomical resection or exclusion of the gastric fundus—where the vast majority of ghrelin is produced—the circulating levels of this hormone drop sharply post-surgery.

A significant reduction in ghrelin eliminates the biological signal that triggers hunger, thereby inducing satiety (prolonged feelings of fullness and diminished appetite).

Question (Front): Which type of bariatric surgery can possibly exacerbate symptoms of Gastroesophageal Reflux?*
Rationale:
A Sleeve Gastrectomy (or vertical sleeve gastrectomy) involves removing approximately 80% of the stomach, converting the remaining portion into a narrow, tube-like structure. This anatomical change drastically increases internal pressure within the stomach tube.

The high intragastric pressure, paired with changes to the angle where the esophagus meets the stomach (the angle of His) and potential weakening of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), commonly causes de novo (new-onset) acid reflux or severely exacerbates preexisting symptoms of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD).

• Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass: This is considered the gold-standard bariatric procedure for patients with severe GERD. Because it separates the acid-producing cells into a bypassed pouch and creates a low-pressure drainage system, it actively cures or significantly improves reflux symptoms. It is frequently used as a corrective surgery for sleeve patients who develop uncontrollable reflux.

Question (Front): The Biliopancreatic Diversion with Duodenal Switch procedure results to some nutrition-related conditions. Choose one that does not apply.*
Rationale: Indigestion and bloating are general, functional upper-GI symptoms. Since the pyloric valve is fully preserved during a Duodenal Switch procedure, normal gastric emptying and stomach digestion are maintained, making classic upper indigestion an inaccurate description of the operation's hallmark downstream complications.
Option 2: Severe malabsorption of macronutrients and micronutrients
Option 3: Changes in gut hormones to reduce appetite

Question (Front): The following are the criteria for Anorexia Nervosa except*
Answer (Back): Recurrent episodes of binge eating within 2 hours
Rationale: Recurrently consuming large amounts of food in a discrete period of time (e.g., within a 2-hour window) accompanied by a perceived lack of control is the fundamental, defining characteristic of Bulimia Nervosa or Binge Eating Disorder. It does not serve as a baseline criterion for Anorexia Nervosa.
Option 3: Recurrent episodes of binge eating within 2 hours

Question (Front): A patient suffering from Bulimia Nervosa is at risk of colon injury due to*
Rationale:
Individuals with Bulimia Nervosa frequently misuse stimulant laxatives to control weight after a binge eating episode. Chronic laxative abuse directly injures the lining of the large intestine and damages the enteric nerves controlling bowel motility.

This toxic damage can progress to a severe, structurally irreversible clinical condition called cathartic colon syndrome. In cathartic colon, the large intestine loses its neuromuscular tone, becomes massively dilated, and can no longer propel stool on its own, increasing the risk of chronic constipation, fecal impaction, and even colon perforation.

Question (Front): When counseling a patient with Bulimia Nervosa the following must be encouraged except*
Answer (Back): Suggest foods for binge eating episode
Rationale:
In clinical psychological and nutritional counseling for Bulimia Nervosa, a Registered Nutritionist-Dietitian (RND) must never suggest, plan, or provide food options for a binge eating episode. The primary goal of Medical Nutrition Therapy (MNT) is to break the restrict-binge-purge cycle. Actively giving food ideas for a binge would validate and reinforce the disordered behavior.

	• Identify food triggers: Pinpointing which foods, emotions, or social scenarios spark an overwhelming urge to binge helps the patient develop healthy, non-food coping mechanisms.
	• Personalize eating pattern: Establishing a highly structured, individualized meal plan (such as eating 3 regular meals and 2–3 snacks at predictable times) keeps the patient physically satisfied, preventing the extreme biological hunger that drives binging.
	• Embrace all food and achieve comfort: Dietitians work to dismantle the toxic "good food vs. bad food" mentality common in bulimia. Helping a patient comfortably reintroduce former fear foods without guilt reduces the psychological drive to binge on them.
Option 2: Embrace all food and achieve comfort
Option 4: Suggest foods for binge eating episode

Question (Front): A 16 year-old patient with normal weight for height and age verbalizes that she wants to die because she is very fat. She believes that people are always staring at her because she is ugly. What should the RND do?*
Rationale:
The patient has explicitly verbalized an active intent to die ("wants to die"). In any clinical setting, an explicit statement of suicidal ideation is a critical psychiatric emergency that completely overrides standard dietary counseling. The immediate, non-negotiable step is to ensure patient safety by initiating an immediate referral to a psychiatrist or mental health crisis professional.

The patient's severe body image distortion (believing she is "very fat" despite a normal weight-for-height profile) combined with ideas of reference (believing "people are always staring at her") are severe psychological indicators highly consistent with severe eating disorders (such as Anorexia Nervosa) or Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD). These conditions require specialized psychiatric stabilization before any structured nutritional therapy can be effective.
Option 2: Tell the patient that she is not overweight
Option 3: Tell the patient that she is experiencing delusions

Question (Front): A patient manifesting the following symptoms has a diagnosis of Symptoms: Repeated chewing and spitting of food, bingeing and purging once a week for 3 weeks, exercising 3 hours daily*
Rationale:
To meet the strict, formal diagnostic criteria for Bulimia Nervosa, a patient must engage in binge eating and inappropriate compensatory behaviors (purging or excessive exercise) at an average frequency of at least once a week for at least 3 months.

Because this patient's binge/purge episodes have only been occurring for 3 weeks (subthreshold duration), they do not meet the full, standard timeline for Bulimia Nervosa. Under standard board exam terminology, cases that display clinically significant disordered eating patterns but fall short of the exact diagnostic durations or specific criteria are categorized under EDNOS (Eating Disorders Not Otherwise Specified). (Note: In modern clinical DSM-5 manuals, this category is updated as OSFED—Other Specified Feeding and Eating Disorder).

The inclusion of repeated chewing and spitting of food is another classic, textbook hallmark behavior frequently categorized under the EDNOS/OSFED umbrella rather than standing as its own distinct standalone diagnosis.

Question (Front): Muscle Dysmorphia also known as Bigorexia is characterized by the following manifestations except*
Rationale:
Eating at night (or Night Eating Syndrome) is an independent eating pattern specification characterized by evening hyperphagia or waking up to consume food during the night. It is not an established diagnostic hallmark or baseline manifestation of Muscle Dysmorphia.

Classic Manifestations of Bigorexia
	• Constant body checking: Individuals with muscle dysmorphia exhibit severe, repetitive body checking habits. This includes spending hours staring in the mirror, constantly using a tape measure to track muscle symmetry, or weighing themselves multiple times a day.
	• A kind of obsessive-compulsive disorder: Under the official DSM-5 criteria, muscle dysmorphia is classified as a specific subtype of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD), which sits directly under the spectrum of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders. The condition drives unrelenting, obsessive thoughts regarding physical inadequacy.
	• Excessive exercise even when injured: A hallmark behavioral symptom is compulsive exercise. The psychological drive to build lean muscle mass is so extreme that the individual will rigidly lift weights or complete high-intensity training sessions even when suffering from clear physical illnesses, fractures, or severe muscular injuries.

Question (Front): The following are consequences of malnutrition in relation to immune response during infection except*
Rationale:
While poor appetite and fatigue are highly common, classic systemic and metabolic symptoms of malnutrition and active infections, they are general physiological responses rather than specific functional alterations of the immune system itself.

	• Reduced production of antibodies: Protein-energy malnutrition directly causes lymphoid tissue atrophy (such as the thymus and bone marrow), which severely impairs B-cell differentiation and downregulates the production of crucial secretory immunoglobulins (like IgA) and antibodies needed to fight pathogens.
	• Poor wound healing: Proper wound healing is an immune-mediated process reliant on cellular immunity. Malnutrition blunts macrophage activation, slows down granulomatous inflammation, and reduces cytokine orchestration, which prevents efficient tissue repair and barrier defense restoration.
	• Alterations in gut microbiome: The gut microbiome is intimately intertwined with mucosal immunity. Nutrient deficiencies compromise intestinal barrier function and mucosal nutrient-sensing receptors, disrupting the commensal gut microbiota balance and compounding immune dysfunction.

Question (Front): A patient with an oral temperature of 38.8 degrees Celsius needs a proper nutrition intervention to support metabolic changes in the body. What should the RND do?*
Answer (Back): Give additional high biologic value protein and fluids
Rationale:
An oral temperature of 38.8°C indicates an active clinical fever (febrile state).

For every 1°C increase in core body temperature above normal, the Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) spikes by approximately 13%. This rapid metabolic shift accelerates tissue breakdown, causing significant lean muscle mass degradation (hypercatabolism) and high fluid loss via sweating and respiration.

To counteract nitrogen wasting and maintain cellular integrity, the Registered Nutritionist-Dietitian (RND) must increase the patient's intake of high biological value (HBV) proteins (such as eggs, milk, fish, and lean poultry), which are efficiently utilized by the body for tissue repair and immune synthesis. Concurrently, aggressive fluid replenishment is a non-negotiable priority to prevent dehydration and support cellular homeostasis.
Option 2: Increase intake of fats to compensate for decreased adiposity
Option 3: Give additional high biologic value protein and fluids
Option 4: Give salabat because ginger has antimicrobial properties

Question (Front): Diarrhea with occasional constipation, vague abdominal pain and occasional rectal bleeding are symptoms of Amoebiasis. What type of diet must be prescribed by the RND?*
Rationale:
Alternating diarrhea/constipation, vague abdominal pain, and blood in the stool is the classic presentation of intestinal Amoebiasis (caused by Entamoeba histolytica). Dietary mechanisms include:

	• Low Residue (Low Fiber): Minimizes fecal volume and eliminates roughage that could mechanically scratch or irritate the already inflamed, ulcerated colonic mucosa.
	• Bland: Excludes chemical irritants such as harsh spices, gastric stimulants, and heavy seasonings that can exacerbate abdominal cramping.
	• Liquid/Fluid Modification: Helps rest the gastrointestinal tract during the acute phase while actively replenishing vital fluids and electrolytes lost through diarrheal episodes to prevent dehydration.
Option 3: High calorie, raw foods allowed as tolerated

Question (Front): The following micronutrients may be deficient among children with Ascariasis lumbricoides*
Rationale:
Ascaris lumbricoides (giant intestinal roundworms) thrive in the human small intestine, where they actively compete with the host child for nutrients.

	• Iron: Intestinal parasite infections damage the gut mucosa, impair absorption, and cause microscopic blood loss, heavily precipitating iron-deficiency anemia in children.
	• Vitamin C: Intestinal inflammation and a compromised gut lining impair the absorption of water-soluble vitamins like Vitamin C. Because Vitamin C is chemically required to reduce ferric iron to ferrous iron for absorption in the gut, a concurrent drop in Vitamin C worsens the child's iron deficiency.

• Zinc and Vitamin C: While zinc deficiency is common in soil-transmitted helminth infections, it is paired with Vitamin C in option D, whereas Iron and Vitamin C is the specific paired textbook key used for this question format.

Question (Front):
Dietary management for Malaria includes a high protein and high carbohydrate diet by increases total caloric intake by how much?*

10%
25%
30%
50%
Rationale: Plasmodium species infection triggers the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), interleukin-1 (IL-1), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), which upregulate hepatic acute-phase protein synthesis and accelerate whole-body protein degradation. To mitigate this hypercatabolic response, medical nutrition therapy dictates an increase in total resting energy expenditure (REE) by approximately 50%, alongside high carbohydrate provision to spare lean body mass and high protein delivery (1.5 to 2.0 g/kg/day) to support tissue repair and immune cell proliferation.

Question (Front): Cholera is an acute dehydrating disease caused by Vibrio Cholerae. It’s symptoms include profuse rice water-like, mucoid stools with fish odor. The primary nutrition intervention goal is*
Rationale:
In acute Cholera, the sheer volume of profuse, watery stools can deplete a patient's entire blood volume and electrolytes within hours, leading to severe hypovolemic shock and death. Therefore, the immediate, life-saving primary intervention goal is the rapid replenishment of fluid and electrolyte losses, typically achieved via intravenous (IV) fluids for severe cases or Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) for mild-to-moderate dehydration.

While introducing a soft, bland, or high-calorie diet to correct nutrient deficiencies is important for long-term recovery once the gut stabilizes, these nutritional interventions are completely impossible and ineffective during the acute phase until the patient is hemodynamically stable and rehydrated.

Question (Front): A patient presents with the following signs and symptoms of infection: Weakness, anorexia, cough, red tongue, fever and pea green colored stool. What could be the patient’s medical condition?*
Rationale:
The presence of a persistent fever, generalized weakness, anoxia, a cough, and a furred tongue with prominent red edges and tip (traditionally referred to as a "typhoid tongue") are classic clinical presentations of a Salmonella Typhi infection.

A defining, textbook feature of Typhoid fever is the development of a slimy, yellow-green liquid diarrhea. Often referred to in board exam vignettes as pea-green or pea-soup colored stool, it is caused by severe localized inflammation, purulent exudates, and necrosis within the intestinal Peyer's patches mixing with mucosal bile.

• Dengue: Characterized by high fevers, severe muscle/joint aches ("breakbone fever"), headaches, and a distinctive rash, but it does not cause pea-green diarrhea or an inflamed red tongue.
• Meningitis: A neurological infection presenting with a high fever, severe headache, rigid stiff neck (nuchal rigidity), and altered mental status rather than a primary gastrointestinal illness.
• Cholera: While it is a major waterborne disease, cholera produces massive volumes of profuse, painless diarrhea classically described as clear "rice-water" stool with a fishy odor, completely distinct from the thick, greenish-yellow pea-soup diarrhea of typhoid.

Question (Front): A patient diagnosed with Rheumatic Fever was prescribed cortisone. Nutrition intervention must include*
Rationale:
While cortisone actively wastes potassium (making potassium-rich foods clinically necessary), the test creator targets sodium restriction based on the following textbook rationale:

1. Fluid Retention and Edema: Cortisone heavily promotes sodium and fluid retention inside the body. In a patient with Rheumatic Fever, this fluid retention is highly dangerous because the disease can cause inflammation of the heart (rheumatic carditis).
2. Preventing Heart Strain: Introducing a strict sodium restriction helps prevent fluid overload, peripheral edema, and hypertension, which directly protects the heart muscles from being overtaxed during the acute phase of Rheumatic Fever.

Question (Front): Isoniazid, a drug for Tuberculosis treatment, is a Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) antagonist. Patients on this medication must be advised to eat more of the following*
Answer (Back): Egg, carrots, camote, tuna, beef, banana and peas
Rationale:
Isoniazid (INH) actively competes with and inhibits the activation of Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine), which can precipitate severe peripheral neuropathy (manifesting as burning, numbness, or tingling in the extremities).

To naturally optimize B6 levels alongside standard clinical supplementation, patients should prioritize foods dense in Pyridoxine. This option provides an exceptionally rich combination of animal and plant-based Vitamin B6 sources, including tuna, beef, banana, peas, and camote (sweet potato).
Option 1: Egg, carrots, camote, tuna, beef, banana and peas
Option 4: Peanut butter, fish, rice, potato, garlic

Question (Front): A patient diagnosed with Tuberculosis has normal BMI. How much protein should be prescribed per day?*
Rationale:
Active Tuberculosis (TB) places the body in an intense inflammatory and hypercatabolic state, resulting in accelerated muscle tissue breakdown and nitrogen wasting. Even if a patient presents with a normal BMI, they require aggressive nutritional therapy to counter cellular destruction, maintain lean muscle mass, and optimize immune function.

Medical nutrition therapy (MNT) guidelines dictate increasing a TB patient's protein intake above the normal baseline to support tissue healing and recovery. Clinical protocols emphasize incorporating adequate high-biological-value protein into the daily diet to support complete tissue healing.

Question (Front): A patient with Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever must avoid*
Rationale:
Patients diagnosed with Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever (DHF) must strictly avoid dark-colored foods and beverages, such as chocolate drinks, cola, coffee, red/violet juices, and dark berries.

DHF compromises blood capillaries and dramatically reduces blood platelets, placing the patient at a severe risk for internal gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding. If a patient consumes a chocolate drink, it can discolor their vomit or stool, staining it dark brown or black. This masks clinical signs of active GI bleeding (such as hematemesis or melena), confusing the medical team and potentially delaying life-saving emergency care.

• Dark leafy vegetables: While green, they do not dye stool or vomit the distinctive tarry black or dark brown color associated with internal bleeding. In fact, they provide vital Vitamin K to support proper clotting pathways.
• Hard candies & Apple juice: These options are clear or translucent, making them completely safe for hydration and carbohydrate maintenance without interfering with medical observations.

Question (Front): Food safety is essential in managing patients with AIDS. The following are food safety measures to be observed except*
Answer (Back): Keep cold food at 35 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit
Rationale:
In clinical food safety protocols, cold food must strictly be maintained at or below 40°F (4°C) (or 41°F depending on localized sanitary code references like ServSafe or the FDA) to inhibit pathogenic bacterial multiplication.

Stating that cold foods can be kept up to 50°F directly breaches the [Food Temperature Danger Zone (40°F to 140°F)](usda.gov ""Danger Zone" (40°F - 140°F)"). Allowing cold food temperatures to climb to 50°F allows highly dangerous, opportunistic pathogens like Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes, and E. coli to rapidly multiply. For immunocompromised individuals, such as patients with AIDS, this minor temperature elevation can lead to a severe, life-threatening foodborne infection.
Option 1: Keep cold food at 35 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit
Option 3: Avoid serving raw fruits and vegetables

Question (Front): To ensure food safety, keeping food between 45 to 145 degrees Fahrenheit or 7.2 to 62.7 degrees Celsius must not exceed*
Rationale:
Leaving perishable food items within this unsafe span (45°F to 145°F / 7.2°C to 62.7°C) for longer than 4 hours permits rapid, exponential multiplication of pathogenic bacteria (such as Salmonella and Staphylococcus aureus), making the food highly toxic and unsafe for human consumption.

1. The Safe Time Window (Under 2 hours): When potentially hazardous food is kept in the Temperature Danger Zone (45°F to 145°F / 7.2°C to 62.7°C) for less than 2 hours, it is still safe to serve, eat, or securely put back into the refrigerator to use later.
2. The Point of No Return (2 to 4 hours): Once food sits out past the 2-hour mark, it enters a dangerous gray zone. While it is still safe to consume immediately, it can no longer be legally or safely put back in the refrigerator because bacteria have entered their rapid, exponential growth phase.

• Under 2 hours: Safe to consume or re-refrigerate.
• 2 to 4 hours: Safe to eat only if consumed immediately; do not put it back in the fridge.
• Over 4 hours: Absolute mandatory discard.

Question (Front): Stage 1 dietary management of poliomyelitis includes 30 to 200 ml tube feeding alternating with water every*
Rationale:
In older, traditional diet therapy manuals for acute infectious neurological disorders like poliomyelitis (particularly cases affecting the bulbar region, which impairs normal swallowing mechanics), Stage 1 protocols utilize tube feeding to guarantee safe nutrition without aspiration.

The standard textbook framework states that the patient should be given 30 to 200 ml of formula via tube feeding, wait 2 hours, and then alternate with water. Spacing the administration out every 2 hours prevents overwhelming the patient's gastric capacity, minimizes the risk of regurgitation, and keeps the patient safely hydrated while their swallowing reflexes are heavily compromised.

*When you encounter this question on your exam, remember this specific gastrointestinal-pacing formula for acute polio management: Tube feeding, wait 2 hours, then water.

Question (Front): A patient with Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome must wear surgical mask at all times except when*
Rationale:
A patient cannot physically consume food or fluids while wearing a surgical mask. Therefore, eating (and drinking) is the only practical and necessary exception where the mask must be temporarily removed.

During these temporary mask-off periods, strict isolation precautions—such as maintaining negative pressure ventilation, keeping the patient in a private room, and ensuring healthcare workers wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) like N95 respirators—are vital to prevent the transmission of respiratory droplets or aerosols.

Question (Front): Middle East Respiratory Syndrome or MERS-COV can be transmitted through*
Rationale:
Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS-CoV) is a zoonotic viral respiratory illness, meaning it is transmitted from animals to humans. Extensive epidemiological studies by global health bodies have confirmed that dromedary camels serve as the primary animal host reservoir for the virus.

While the virus can also spread through direct physical contact with live animals, humans can contract the infection by consuming contaminated, unpasteurized camel products—specifically raw camel milk and undercooked camel meat. Because the virus is heat-sensitive, global public health authorities strictly advise pasteurizing milk and thoroughly cooking meat to eliminate transmission risks.

Question (Front): Virgin Coconut Oil has antimicrobial properties. How much VCO must be given to a patient weighing 176 lbs during the first day of treatment?*
Rationale:
Virgin coconut oil (VCO) has been studied for its potential antimicrobial and antiviral properties. Research involving VCO often explores its components, such as medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) like lauric acid, which are believed to contribute to these properties. Clinical protocols and studies evaluate various amounts of VCO for supportive care, but determining any specific usage requires professional medical evaluation based on an individual's health status and needs.

A specific weight-based formula was used in clinical trial protocols by the Department of Science and Technology (DOST). These clinical trials (such as the DOST-FNRI studies on the antiviral and antimicrobial properties of VCO) use a strict dosage protocol based on a patient’s body weight in kilograms to allow the gut to safely adjust:
• First 3 days (Initial Dose): 0.6 mL of VCO per kilogram of body weight (0.6 mL/kg BW).
• Day 4 to 28 (Succeeding Dose): 1.2 mL of VCO per kilogram of body weight (1.2 mL/kg BW).

1. Convert the patient's weight from pounds to kilograms:
176 lbs / 2.2 = 80 kg
2. Calculate the first-day dosage (using the initial 0.6 mL/kg factor):
80 kg x 0.6 mL/kg = 48 mL

Question (Front): A food and water borne disease that affects the liver resulting to jaundice, severe anorexia, nausea, vomiting and abdominal tenderness*
Rationale:
Hepatitis A is a highly contagious liver infection caused by the Hepatitis A virus (HAV). It is classically defined as a food- and water-borne disease because it spreads primarily via the fecal-oral route. Transmission happens when a person ingests food or water contaminated with the feces of an infected individual (often due to poor hand hygiene or inadequate sewage treatment).

 The virus multiplies inside the liver cells, sparking acute inflammation. This structural irritation produces a distinct, textbook cluster of gastrointestinal and hepatic symptoms:
	• Jaundice: Yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes caused by a buildup of bilirubin in the blood as the inflamed liver struggles to process it.
	• Severe Anorexia: A profound, sudden loss of appetite.
	• Nausea, Vomiting, and Abdominal Tenderness: Driven by an enlarged, inflamed liver (hepatomegaly) pressing against surrounding tissues in the right upper abdominal quadrant.

• Hepatitis B & Hepatitis C: These viral infections are blood-borne and sexually transmitted pathogens. They spread via contact with infected bodily fluids, blood transfusions, or shared needles, rather than through contaminated food or drinking water.
• Cirrhosis: This is a chronic, late-stage pathological condition characterized by irreversible scarring of the liver tissue. It is the long-term result of prolonged liver disease (like chronic alcoholism or chronic Hep B/C), not an acute foodborne illness.

Question (Front): HIV virus may be transmitted from mother to fetus through pregnancy. The virus is also found in breastmilk in low concentrations. The RND must*
Rationale: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life, combined with maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART) that achieves viral suppression, significantly reduces postnatal mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV while drastically lowering infant mortality from infectious diseases compared to replacement feeding. Breast milk provides optimal immunological factors (such as secretory IgA, lactoferrin, and leukocytes) and complete nutrition, which protect against gastrointestinal and respiratory infections that are fatal in non-breastfed infants in high-mortality contexts.

Question (Front): The normal range of body temperature is*
Rationale:
While 37°C (98.6°F) is universally recognized as the standard average human body temperature, normal physiological baselines safely fluctuate within a broader dynamic range.

The medically accepted range of 97°F to 99°F directly converts to 36.1°C to 37.2°C. Temperatures within this bracket are considered afebrile (normal and without fever).

Question (Front): Metabolic changes occur during surgery. The following nutrition related implications are true except*
Rationale: Surgical stress activates the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), alongside non-osmotic release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the posterior pituitary. Elevated circulating aldosterone acts on the distal convoluted tubules and cortical collecting ducts of the nephrons to increase sodium and water reabsorption while excreting potassium and hydrogen ions, resulting in sodium retention rather than sodium loss.

Question (Front): Prior to surgery, the patient must be put on nil per os or NPO for how many hours?*
Rationale:
In general medical and nursing board exam questions, the standard textbook baseline for a complete nil per os (NPO) order prior to elective surgery involving general anesthesia is 8 hours (often clinically phrased as "NPO after midnight" for a morning procedure).

This fasting period guarantees the stomach is completely empty before anesthesia induction. This drastically minimizes the life-threatening risk of pulmonary aspiration (inhaling stomach content or vomitus into the lungs) and severe post-operative nausea.

Modern Clinical Guidelines (ASA)
While standard multiple-choice questions typically group full NPO status into a general 8-hour window, modern American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) guidelines utilize a tiered approach:
• 8 Hours: Required for heavy, fried, or fatty foods and meats (which delay gastric emptying).
• 6 Hours: Required for light meals (e.g., toast) or non-human milk.
• 2 Hours: Minimum restriction for clear liquids (such as water or pulp-free juices).

Question (Front): Post surgery, the patient must be put on NPO for 24 to 48 hours to prevent what?*
Rationale: General anesthesia, opioid analgesics, and surgical stress profoundly suppress gastrointestinal motility, lower lower esophageal sphincter (LES) tone, and dull protective airway reflexes (such as the gag and cough reflexes). If oral intake is permitted while gastroparesis and neuromuscular depression persist, gastric contents, hydrochloric acid, and digestive enzymes can easily reflux into the pharynx and enter the respiratory tract, leading to aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson's syndrome) or bacterial pneumonia characterized by severe hypoxemia, acute lung injury, and inflammatory destruction of alveolar-capillary membranes.

Question (Front): What type of food must be served on the first day post Tonsillectomy?*
Rationale:
A tonsillectomy leaves open, highly raw, and sensitive surgical wounds in the back of the throat. Introducing very cold foods and fluids (such as ice chips, non-red popsicles, and plain ice cream) induces immediate localized vasoconstriction (narrowing of the blood vessels). This reduces swelling, minimizes the risk of post-operative bleeding, and numbs raw nerve endings to alleviate acute throat pain.

The food must be mildly flavored. Highly seasoned, spicy, salty, or acidic foods (such as citrus or tomato-based items) will cause intense chemical burning and painful irritation at the healing surgical site.

Question (Front): Gastric surgeries result to the following nutrition related conditions except*
Rationale:
Decreased peristalsis (or general sluggish movement of the intestines) is not a primary, direct nutrition-related condition caused by gastric surgeries. Peristalsis is a neuromuscular function of the intestinal tract. While systemic opioid medications or immediate post-operative anesthesia can temporarily slow it down, gastric resections themselves do not inherently induce chronic, baseline decreased peristalsis as a hallmark nutritional consequence.

	• Decreased production of pepsin and HCl: Removing or bypassing large portions of the stomach (such as the fundus and body) drastically reduces the number of parietal and chief cells, cutting down the overall secretion of hydrochloric acid (HCl) and pepsinogen.
	• Macrocytic anemia: A lack of stomach tissue leads to a severe shortage of Intrinsic Factor, which is mandatory for absorbing Vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum. Long-term Vitamin B12 deficiency directly causes pernicious or macrocytic anemia.
	• Impaired fat utilization: The loss of stomach churning capacity, combined with a significant reduction in gastric lipase and altered structural transit, prevents the proper emulsification and breakdown of dietary fats, leading to lipid malabsorption.
Option 1: Decreased production of pepsin and HCL

Question (Front): After 7 days of gastric surgery, the patient can be given the following except*
Rationale:
Gastric surgery, commonly known as bariatric surgery, is a medical procedure designed to help individuals with severe obesity lose weight and improve related health conditions like type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease.

Exactly one week (7 days) post-gastric surgery, a patient is transitioning into a smooth, full-liquid or pureed diet phase. Concentrated high carbohydrate sources—such as refined starches, sugary drinks, sweets, and juices—must be strictly avoided.

Introducing a high-carbohydrate load into a structurally altered or reduced stomach causes rapid gastric emptying into the small intestine. This hyperosmolar food mass pulls fluid into the bowel lumen, triggering acute dumping syndrome (characterized by severe abdominal cramps, nausea, rapid heart rate, sweating, and explosive diarrhea).
Option 3: High protein and high fat diet

Question (Front): The patient is complaining of nausea, cramping, sweating, palpitations 10 minutes after eating. What is she experiencing?*
Rationale:
The symptoms of nausea, abdominal cramping, sweating, and heart palpitations occurring rapidly—within 10 to 30 minutes after eating—are the textbook diagnostic presentation of Early Dumping Syndrome.

This condition occurs frequently in patients who have undergone gastric or bariatric surgeries. Because the stomach's storage capacity or pyloric valve function is altered, a large mass of poorly digested, hyperosmolar food drops rapidly into the small intestine. This hyperosmolar mass causes a massive, sudden shift of fluid out of the bloodstream and into the intestinal lumen, leading to acute intestinal distension (causing cramps and nausea) and systemic volume depletion (causing sweating, dizziness, and palpitations).

• Intermediate dumping syndrome: While some textbook sources split dumping into early and late, others refer to an intermediate phase occurring 30 minutes to 1 hour post-meal, primarily characterized by bloating and gas rather than this immediate cardiovascular and gastrointestinal surge.
• Late Dumping Syndrome: Occurs much later—1 to 3 hours after eating—and is driven by a completely different mechanism: reactive hypoglycemia caused by a rapid spike and subsequent overshoot of insulin production.

Question (Front): What must an RND recommend to prevent rapid dumping of food into jejunum?*
Answer (Back): Small frequent feedings in supine position
Rationale:
To prevent the rapid dumping of food contents from the stomach pouch straight into the jejunum, patients are advised to eat small, frequent meals throughout the day. This prevents overwhelming the stomach's limited volume.

Reclining or lying down in a supine position (flat on the back) or semi-recumbent position for 20 to 30 minutes immediately after eating uses gravity to actively slow down gastric emptying. This delays the rapid transit of food into the small intestine, providing immediate relief from both early and late dumping syndrome symptoms.
Option 1: Small frequent feedings in supine position

Question (Front): A patient who underwent ileostomy must be monitored for signs and symptoms of nutrient deficiencies for the following micronutrients except*
Rationale:
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is a water-soluble vitamin primarily absorbed in the jejunum (the middle section of the small intestine). Because an ileostomy redirects or resects parts of the ileum (the final section of the small intestine) and bypasses the large intestine, the jejunum is left completely intact. This allows Vitamin B6 to be absorbed normally, making routine monitoring for a B6 deficiency unnecessary.

	• Vitamin B12: The terminal ileum is the only site in the entire gastrointestinal tract capable of absorbing Vitamin B12 (via the Intrinsic Factor complex). An ileostomy directly disrupts this area, placing the patient at an incredibly high risk for Vitamin B12 malabsorption and subsequent macrocytic/pernicious anemia.
	• Vitamins A & E: The ileum plays a critical role in the reabsorption of bile salts (enterohepatic circulation). When the ileum is bypassed or resected, the depletion of bile salts leads to the malabsorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K).

Question (Front): The following are gas forming foods that must be avoided by patients with colostomy except*
Rationale:
Squash (along with other well-cooked, skinless, non-cruciferous vegetables like spinach) is generally considered easy to digest and gentle on the digestive system. It does not naturally ferment aggressively or produce large amounts of gas.

	• Onion and garlic: These contain volatile sulfur compounds and fermentable carbohydrates (fructans) that cause high amounts of gas and strong stool odors.
	• Dairy: Milk and dairy products containing lactose are highly gas-producing, especially if a patient has any degree of baseline lactose intolerance.
	• Chewing gum: Chewing gum introduces a non-dietary source of gas by causing patients to continuously swallow excess air (aerophagia), leading to immediate flatus accumulation in the colostomy bag. Additionally, many chewing gums use artificial sweeteners (sugar alcohols), which further ferment into gas in the bowel.

Question (Front): Surgery of the intestines results to changes in*
Answer (Back): Production of waste products, absorption of nutrients, and motility
Rationale:
• Absorption of nutrients: The small and large intestines are the primary sites for macro- and micronutrient, fluid, and electrolyte absorption. Resecting or altering these segments directly reduces the functional absorptive surface area.
	• Motility: Intestinal surgery alters the neuromuscular tissue, disrupting normal peristalsis and transit time.
	• Production of waste products: Because nutrient digestion and fluid reabsorption are disrupted, the consistency, volume, and composition of the fecal waste change dramatically (often resulting in loose stools or stomal output).
Option 1: Production of waste products, absorption of nutrients, and motility
Option 2: Satiation, hormone level, absorption of nutrients, and motility
Option 3: Appetite, weight changes, absorption of nutrients, and motility

Question (Front): A patient has a high risk of developing oxalate stones. The RND must recommend intake of high oxalate foods to be avoided. Choose the food that is not high in oxalate content.*
Rationale:
Bananas are naturally very low in oxalate content (typically containing less than 1–2 mg of oxalate per serving). Because they are completely safe to consume, they are highly recommended as a staple fruit choice for patients managing or preventing calcium oxalate kidney stones.

• Tofu: Made directly from soybeans, tofu and other soy products are notoriously high in oxalates. A standard serving of tofu can easily introduce an unsafe concentration of oxalates into the diet.
• Chocolate: Cocoa powder and chocolate products contain very high levels of oxalic acid. Even small servings can significantly spike urinary oxalate levels.
• Kangkong: Also known as water spinach, this dark green leafy vegetable is rich in oxalates, mirroring the high-oxalate profiles of traditional spinach and beet greens which are known to fuel calcium oxalate stone formation.

Question (Front): Post cholecystectomy, the patient must be advised to go on a low fat diet due to*
Rationale:
A cholecystectomy is the surgical removal of the gallbladder. The gallbladder’s primary job is to store and concentrate bile produced by the liver, releasing a concentrated surge whenever a meal containing fat enters the small intestine.

Without the gallbladder, bile drips continuously and directly from the liver into the small intestine in a much more dilute, un-concentrated stream. If the patient consumes a high-fat meal post-surgery, there will not be enough concentrated bile available to efficiently emulsify and digest that fat load. The undigested fat passes straight into the colon, resulting directly in steatorrhea (fatty, greasy, foul-smelling diarrhea).

Question (Front): 19 years old, pre-burn weight 100lbs, third degree burn on the right hand. Compute for the total energy requirement.*
Rationale:
Even though we know a 19-year-old healing from an injury needs a healthy baseline of calories, the Curreri Formula is the exact equation textbook writers use for burn calculations.

1. Convert weight to kilograms:
100 lbs divided by 2.2 = 45.45 kg

2. Determine the Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) percentage:
According to the medical Palmar Method, a patient's entire palm and fingers equal roughly 1% TBSA. Because only the right hand has a third-degree burn, the TBSA value used is 1%.

3. Apply the adult Curreri Formula:
Daily Caloric Need = (25 kcal x kg body weight) + (40 kcal x % TBSA)
Daily Caloric Need = (25 x 45.45 kg) + (40 x 1)
Daily Caloric Need = 1,136.25 + 40 = 1,176.25 kcal

Rounding 1,176.25 kcal to the closest multiple-choice option yields 1200 kcal.

Question (Front): A patient has suffered second degree burn on his right arm and right leg. How much protein must be recommended?*
Rationale: Severe thermal injury triggers a massive hypermetabolic and catabolic state driven by sustained catecholamine, cortisol, and glucagon elevations, leading to accelerated skeletal muscle proteolysis to supply amino acids for hepatic acute-phase proteins, immune cell proliferation, and granulation tissue synthesis. Providing protein at 20% of total energy expenditure (TER) or approximately 1.5 to 2.0 g/kg/day provides the necessary nitrogen substrate to maintain positive nitrogen balance, mitigate lean body mass wasting, and support fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition.

Question (Front): Stress contributes to cancer development by affecting the*
Rationale: Chronic stress activates the sympathetic nervous system and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, sparking a continuous release of stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline. This hormonal surge suppresses cellular immunity, downregulates natural killer (NK) cells and T-cells, and shifts the body into a chronic low-grade inflammatory state. This directly weakens the immune system's natural surveillance defenses, making it significantly easier for mutant or abnormal tumor cells to evade detection, grow, and multiply.

Question (Front): The following are carcinogenic in nature, except*
Rationale: Roasted chicken consists of muscle tissue, water, lipids, and proteins. While high-temperature cooking methods like open-flame grilling or charring can produce trace amounts of heterocyclic amines (HCAs) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), standard roasted chicken does not inherently possess systemic carcinogenic properties. The food item itself is a standard source of dietary protein and amino acids and is not classified as a Group 1 or Group 2A/2B carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

Question (Front): Soy, green tea, fruits and vegetables contain plant chemicals that can neutralize free radicals and aid in cancer prevention. These substances are also known as*
Rationale:
Phytochemicals (also known as phytonutrients) are bioactive, non-nutritive plant chemicals found in foods like soy, green tea, fruits, vegetables, and grains.

Many phytochemicals—such as isoflavones in soy and catechins in green tea—act as powerful antioxidants. They neutralize highly unstable free radicals, protect cellular structures and DNA from oxidative stress, reduce systemic inflammation, and block biological pathways that trigger cancer development.

Question (Front): Consumption of this food increases the risk for liver cancer*
Rationale:
Poorly stored grains and legumes—most notably peanuts—are highly susceptible to contamination by molds like Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus. These molds produce a potent, heat-stable mycotoxin known as aflatoxin (specifically Aflatoxin B1).

Aflatoxin is classified as a definitive Group 1 human carcinogen. Once ingested, the liver processes this toxin, creating a highly reactive intermediate metabolite that directly binds to DNA, inducing specific mutations in the p53 tumor suppressor gene. This DNA damage impairs the body's natural defense against cellular mutations, directly triggering the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer).

Question (Front): A cancer patient may experience eating problems. Choose one that does not apply*
Rationale:
Polydipsia (excessive or insatiable thirst) is a classic clinical symptom of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus or diabetes insipidus, rather than a primary eating problem characteristically induced by oncological malignancies or cancer treatments.

	• Anorexia: Cancer-induced anorexia (loss of appetite) is incredibly common, driven by metabolic changes from tumor-released cytokines, psychological distress, or side effects of chemotherapy and radiation.
	• Lactose intolerance: Radiation therapy to the abdomen or certain chemotherapy agents can severely damage the mucosal lining of the small intestine. This temporarily destroys the brush border enzymes, leading to acute, treatment-induced secondary lactose intolerance.
	• Thrush: Oral candidiasis (thrush) is a common fungal infection in cancer patients due to therapy-induced immunosuppression or side effects like xerostomia (dry mouth). It causes painful white patches in the mouth that make chewing and swallowing highly difficult.

Question (Front): A patient on chemotherapy is complaining of mouth sores. The RND must recommend*
Rationale: Chemotherapy frequently induces oral mucositis, which causes the mucosal lining of the mouth to become highly inflamed, ulcerated, and painful. Cold beverages (and ice chips, popsicles, or chilled soft foods) help vasoconstrict the blood vessels in the oral cavity, which actively numbs the pain, reduces localized inflammation, and provides immediate soothing comfort.

Question (Front): A patient with brain cancer undergoing radiation therapy may experience the following nutrition related side effects except*
Rationale:
While insomnia (difficulty falling or staying asleep) can certainly affect cancer patients due to general psychological stress, anxiety, or specific medications like high-dose corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone), it is classified primarily as a sleep/psychological disorder. It is not a direct nutrition-related side effect caused by localized radiation tissue damage.

	• Loss of appetite: Extremely common during brain radiation due to treatment-induced nausea, altered metabolism, or increased intracranial pressure.
	• Dry mouth: Radiation delivered to the head region can inadvertently clip or irritate adjacent salivary gland structures, leading to a temporary or persistent decline in saliva production (xerostomia), which directly impairs chewing and swallowing.
	• Anosmia and Dysgeusia: Cranial radiation therapy can directly disrupt olfactory nerve pathways and taste buds, causing anosmia (loss of smell) and dysgeusia (distortion of taste), which severely decreases the palatability of food.

Question (Front): Define immunotherapy or biological therapy for cancer treatment.*
Answer (Back): It uses the body’s immune system to fight cancer cells
Rationale:
Immunotherapy, also known as biological therapy, is a type of cancer treatment designed to boost, direct, or restore the body's natural defenses to recognize and destroy cancer cells.

Rather than targeting the tumor directly (like traditional chemotherapy or radiation), immunotherapy trains or enhances the patient's own immune cells (such as T-cells) to seek out and eliminate the malignancy.
Option 1: It uses supplementation to kill cancer cells
Option 2: It uses botanicals to kill cancer cells
Option 3: It uses the body’s immune system to fight cancer cells
Option 4: It uses food as medicine in fighting cancer cells

Question (Front): What type of dietary management must be recommended to a patient on palliative care for end stage cancer?*
Rationale:
In end-stage cancer and palliative care, the primary focus of Medical Nutrition Therapy (MNT) shifts entirely from medical restoration, weight gain, or nutrient correction to maximizing comfort, dignity, and quality of life.

During end-stage disease, patients often experience severe anorexia, metabolic changes, and a natural decline in the desire to eat or drink. Enforcing a strict, aggressive diet plan can cause physical distress (such as nausea, vomiting, or choking). Therefore, the Registered Nutritionist-Dietitian (RND) must always prioritize and consider the patient’s informed preference, honoring what they wish to eat, when they wish to eat, or their right to decline food entirely.

Question (Front): Post mastectomy, the breast cancer patient is complaining of pain. When is the best time to offer food?*
Answer (Back): Offer food when pain is at the lowest level
Rationale:
Severe or acute pain activates the body's sympathetic nervous system, which naturally suppresses the digestive tract, diminishes appetite, and can trigger nausea. Attempting to feed a patient when their pain is peaking often leads to a refusal to eat or food aversion.

To optimize caloric intake and support wound healing post-mastectomy, the best time to offer food is when the patient's pain is at its lowest level (such as shortly after pain medications have taken effect). When a patient is comfortable and rested, their appetite improves, and they can tolerate eating much more effectively.

• Give small, frequent feedings: While small, frequent meals are an excellent supportive strategy for oncology and post-op patients with low appetites, the question specifically asks for the best time to introduce or offer food to a patient struggling with pain. Maximizing comfort during pain valleys remains the prioritized clinical timing principle.
Option 1: Offer food to distract the patient while in pain
Option 3: Offer food when pain is at the lowest level
Option 4: Give small, frequent feedings throughout the day

Question (Front): A cancer survivor is seeking advice on how to prevent recurrence. Choose the correct answer.*
Answer (Back): Fat consumption must be less than 30% of total energy requirement
Rationale:
The three new guidelines, Saturated fatty acid and trans-fatty acid intake for adults and children, Total fat intake for the prevention of unhealthy weight gain in adults and children, and Carbohydrate intake for adults and children, contain recommendations that aim to reduce the risk of unhealthy weight gain and diet-related noncommunicable diseases, such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and certain types of cancer. 

With its guidance on dietary fat, WHO notes that both quantity and quality are important for good health. WHO reaffirms that adults should limit total fat intake to 30% of total energy intake or less.  Fat consumed by everyone 2 years of age and older should be primarily unsaturated fatty acids, with no more than 10% of total energy intake coming from saturated fatty acids and no more than 1% of total energy intake from trans-fatty acids from both industrially produced and ruminant animal sources.
Option 1: Use supplements to prevent cancer recurrence
Option 2: Consume 35g of fiber from fruits and vegetables daily
Option 3: Fat consumption must be less than 30% of total energy requirement

Question (Front): A female patient’s Food Frequency Questionnaire shows daily intake of fried foods, beef and butter. She is high risk for what type of cancer?*
Rationale:
A diet high in fried foods, red meat (beef), and saturated fats (butter) is significantly associated with an increased risk of breast cancer in women.
	• Frying and cooking red meats at high temperatures produce heterocyclic amines (HCAs) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), which are known carcinogens.
	• High-fat and calorie-dense foods contribute to elevated systemic inflammation, weight gain, and increased circulating estrogen levels, which strongly drive hormone-receptor-positive breast cancers.

x Stomach: While fried foods and high-salt diets are risk factors for gastric cancer, this specific cluster of a high-fat, Western-style pattern (beef, butter, fried foods) is a classic hallmark profile used in clinical vignettes focusing on breast and colorectal cancer risks.
x Liver: Liver cancer is primarily linked to alcohol consumption, chronic hepatitis (B or C) infections, and aflatoxins rather than daily beef and butter intake.
x Endometrium: While obesity and high fat intake do increase endometrial cancer risk, breast cancer remains the predominant epidemiological and textbook association for a female patient presenting with this specific high-saturated-fat and high-heat meat dietary profile.

Question (Front): Nausea and vomiting is a common side effect of cancer therapy. The following nutrition interventions are necessary except*
Rationale: While managing nausea and vomiting during cancer therapies like chemotherapy or radiation, patients are advised to avoid oily, greasy, and high-fat foods. High-fat foods slow down gastric emptying (digestion), which can significantly worsen the feeling of nausea and trigger vomiting.

Question (Front): Cancer patients often experience loss of appetite. The following are ways to stimulate appetite except*
Rationale: Give alcoholic beverages anytime
Option 1: Flavor dishes with citrus fruits and spices
Option 3: Add some salt and sugar to taste

Question (Front): Excessive intake of this polyunsaturated fatty acid increases the risk of colon cancer and pancreatic cancer.*
Rationale:
Omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids (primarily linoleic acid and arachidonic acid, found abundantly in commercial vegetable oils like corn oil, soybean oil, and ultra-processed foods) act as direct precursors to pro-inflammatory eicosanoids.

Excessive intake of Omega-6 lipids alters cell membrane structures, leading to the overproduction of arachidonic acid metabolites like Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) and Leukotriene B4 (LTB4). These specific molecules drive systemic inflammation, trigger cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) pathways, block cellular apoptosis (programmed cell death), and stimulate angiogenesis, which significantly fuels the development and progression of colon and pancreatic tumors.

• Omega-3: Possesses powerful anti-inflammatory properties. High intakes of marine Omega-3 fatty acids (like EPA and DHA found in fish oil) are associated with a reduced risk of colorectal and pancreatic cancers by counteracting Omega-6 pathways and inducing cancer cell apoptosis.
• Omega-9: Primarily monounsaturated fatty acids (like oleic acid in olive oil), which are not classified as polyunsaturated fatty acids.
• Omega-16: This is a structurally non-existent fatty acid classification in standard human nutritional physiology.

Question (Front): After eating shrimps, a woman immediately experienced difficulty of breathing, increased heart beat and lightheadedness. She is experiencing a systemic allergic reaction called*
Rationale:
Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening, and rapid-onset systemic allergic reaction. It involves multiple organ systems simultaneously (the respiratory system via difficulty breathing, the cardiovascular system via an increased heartbeat, and the neurological system via lightheadedness from a sudden drop in blood pressure).

Shrimps are a crustacean shellfish, which is one of the leading triggers for severe IgE-mediated anaphylactic reactions in adults. This requires immediate medical intervention with epinephrine.

Question (Front): This is known as the true allergic reaction to food as a result of immune response*
Rationale: Food hypersensitivity is characterized by an adverse, reproducible immune response to dietary proteins. During sensitization, antigen-presenting cells present food peptides to T-helper 2 (Th2) cells, which stimulate B cells to synthesize allergen-specific IgE antibodies. These IgE molecules bind to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils. Upon subsequent re-exposure, allergen cross-linking of IgE triggers degranulation, releasing preformed mediators like histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins. Non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivities involve T-cell-mediated pathways (such as Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome). In clinical nomenclature, 'food hypersensitivity' is the precise, overarching term for any adverse reaction to food that is mediated by these specific immunological mechanisms.

Question (Front): The following are common causes of foodb allergies except*
Rationale: Buckwheat is not classified as one of the major globally recognized food allergens. While an allergy to buckwheat can occur (and is notably monitored under specialized regulatory frameworks in select countries like Japan), it falls entirely outside the standard "Big 8" or "Big 9" major allergens that are taught in public health nutrition.

Question (Front): A patient who is hypersensitive to shellfish must be monitored for nutrient deficiencies of*
Rationale:
In clinical nutrition, when a patient eliminates an entire food group due to a severe allergy or hypersensitivity, they are at risk of missing out on the primary micronutrients concentrated in those specific foods.

	• Zinc: Shellfish (especially bivalves like oysters and mussels, as well as crustaceans like crabs and lobsters) are among the densest dietary sources of highly bioavailable zinc found in nature.
	• Magnesium: Shellfish varieties are also loaded with essential trace minerals and macrominerals, including a significant amount of magnesium per standard serving size. Total elimination of these foods without proper meal planning directly sets a patient up for micro-gaps in these two elements.

Question (Front): The following are symptoms of anaphylactic shock except*
Rationale:
Anaphylactic shock causes a severe, life-threatening drop in blood pressure (hypotension), not an increase.

During anaphylaxis, a massive systemic release of histamine and other chemical mediators causes widespread, rapid vasodilation (widening of blood vessels) and increased capillary permeability (fluid leaking out of blood vessels). This sudden collapse in vascular resistance leads to a profound drop in blood pressure, which restricts vital blood flow to major organs.

True Symptoms
• Decreased blood pressure: The defining cardiovascular hallmark of anaphylactic shock.
• Skin rashes: Often manifest as hives (urticaria), intense itching, or flushing, which are classic early signs of an IgE-mediated systemic allergic reaction.
• Difficulty of breathing: Driven by severe airway constriction (bronchospasm) and swelling of the throat and tongue (angioedema), which can obstruct the airway.

Question (Front): Diagnosis of food allergy can be determined using the oral challenge through what type of diet?*
Rationale:
When identifying or confirming a suspected food allergy using an oral food challenge (OFC), a patient is first placed on a strictly controlled hypoallergenic diet (or elimination diet) for a couple of weeks to allow all baseline allergic symptoms to completely subside.

Once the patient is symptom-free, individual food allergens are systematically reintroduced (challenged) under close medical supervision to see if a specific food reproduces the allergic reaction.

Question (Front): This diet is adequate but excludes the food triggers.*
Rationale:
An avoidance diet (or exclusion diet) is long-term, nutritionally adequate, and sustainable because it simply removes the specific, already-identified target allergens or food triggers while keeping the rest of the diet varied and complete.

An elimination diet is an intensive, short-term diagnostic tool. It removes a massive array of potential food groups (often leaving a very restricted, non-adequate pool of foods) to clear symptoms before a reintroduction phase. Once the definitive triggers are successfully unmasked, the patient transitions to a long-term avoidance diet.

Question (Front): A patient manifests dry, scaly skin. What possible nutrient deficiency does this patient have?*
Rationale:
A lack of Vitamin A impairs normal skin cell turnover and moisture retention, frequently resulting in dry, rough, or scaly skin (as well as conditions like phrynoderma or follicular hyperkeratosis).

	• Protein deficiency typically leads to changes like muscle wasting, edema, or flaky-paint dermatosis (in kwashiorkor) or dry/loose skin (in marasmus).
	• Omega-3 fatty acid deficiency can cause dry or inflamed skin, though Vitamin A is the classic multiple-choice answer for rough and scaly skin manifestations like phrynoderma.
	• Vitamin C deficiency results in scurvy, featuring petechiae, purpura, and bleeding gums rather than primary scaling.

Question (Front): A patient’s skin has goose flesh-like lesions. What type of food must the RND recommend?*
Answer (Back): Yellow and orange fruits and vegetables
Rationale:
Goose flesh-like lesions (clinically diagnosed as follicular hyperkeratinization or phrynoderma) refer to rough, dry bumps that form around the hair follicles due to an abnormal buildup of keratin.

This skin presentation is a classic textbook hallmark manifestation of Vitamin A deficiency. Vitamin A is structurally mandatory to maintain epithelial cellular differentiation and skin membrane health. When Vitamin A levels drop, skin cells overproduce keratin, plugging the follicles and creating a texture that mirrors goosebumps or sandpaper.

To resolve this deficiency, the Registered Nutritionist-Dietitian (RND) must recommend foods rich in beta-carotene (the plant-derived precursor that the human body converts into active Vitamin A). Yellow and orange fruits and vegetables (such as carrots, squash, sweet potatoes, and mangoes) are the primary dietary sources of beta-carotene.
Option 1: Yellow and orange fruits and vegetables

Question (Front): A teenager is complaining of blackheads all over her T-zone. The RND advises him to avoid*
Rationale:
French fries are an ultra-processed carbohydrate with a high Glycemic Index (GI) and glycemic load. Consuming high-GI foods triggers rapid spikes in blood sugar and circulating insulin levels.

This surge elevations in Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1). Elevated IGF-1 levels directly stimulate the sebaceous glands to produce excess sebum (oil) while promoting abnormal skin cell shedding (follicular hyperkeratinization). In the T-zone, this excess sebum combined with dead skin cells oxidizes upon exposure to air, forming blackheads (open comedones).

Question (Front): Physical fitness enables the body to perform the following activities except*
Rationale:
Sitting still is a sedentary behavior that represents a state of rest or inactivity, requiring minimal to no muscular contraction or elevated energy expenditure. It does not rely on or demonstrate an individual's physical fitness.

	• Carry grocery bags filled to the brim: Directly requires muscular strength and muscular endurance to lift and bear heavy loads continuously.
	• Climb 3 flights of stairs: Relies heavily on cardiovascular endurance and lower-body muscular strength to handle repetitive vertical movement.
	• Run fast when being chased by a stray dog: This represents a classic "extra reserve energy for emergencies" scenario, drawing heavily on speed, reaction time, and immediate cardiovascular power.
Option 1: Run fast when being chased by a stray dog
Option 2: Carry grocery bags filled to the brim

Question (Front): What is produced in the muscles during intense exercise which can lead to painful and sore muscles?*
Rationale:
During intense, anaerobic exercise, your muscles require energy faster than your body can deliver oxygen. To keep up, cells break down glucose via anaerobic glycolysis, which produces lactic acid (lactate).

While multiple-choice questions traditionally cite lactic acid as the cause of immediate muscle burning and fatigue during an intense workout, modern exercise science notes that it actually clears from the muscles within a few hours. The prolonged soreness felt 24 to 72 hours after a workout is known as Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness (DOMS), which is driven by microscopic tears in the muscle fibers and subsequent localized inflammation.

Question (Front): What is the ability of a joint or series of joints to move through unrestricted and painfree range of motion?*
Rationale:
In exercise science and physical education, flexibility is defined exactly as the ability of a joint, or a series of joints, to move smoothly and effortlessly through an unrestricted, pain-free range of motion (ROM). It is heavily influenced by the laxity of the joint capsule and the elasticity of the surrounding muscles, tendons, and ligaments.

• Movement: This is a broad, non-specific macroscopic term for any physical displacement or change in the position of body parts, which does not define a targeted joint boundary or capacity.
• Agility: A skill-related component of physical fitness that describes the body's ability to explosively and efficiently change direction and velocity while maintaining total body control and balance.
• Physical Fitness: The overall umbrella state of physiological well-being that enables an individual to complete daily tasks effectively without undue fatigue. Flexibility is just one health-related component inside the wider physical fitness framework.

Question (Front): The following are components of physical fitness except*
Rationale:
Resilience is a psychological and mental attribute that refers to a person's ability to adapt, cope, and mentally bounce back from stress, adversity, or trauma. While it is highly beneficial for mental health, it is not classified as a physical component of fitness in physical education and sports science curriculum frameworks.

The Standard Components of Physical Fitness

Skill-Related Fitness Components
These components focus on sports performance, motor skills, and technical precision:
• Coordination: The ability to use different body parts together smoothly and efficiently (e.g., hand-eye coordination).
• Speed: The ability to move your body or parts of your body quickly over a short distance.
• Balance: The ability to maintain stability and control your body's center of mass over a base of support.
• Other components: Agility, Power, and Reaction Time

Health-Related Fitness Components
These focus on general physiological functioning, disease prevention, and daily bodily efficiency:
• Cardiovascular Endurance
• Muscular Strength
• Muscular Endurance
• Flexibility
• Body Composition

Question (Front): The muscle action that requires the use of energy in the form of ATP*
Rationale: During muscle contraction, myosin heads bind to actin and execute the power stroke via the utilization of ATP, but the detachment of the cross-bridge and the sliding motion itself are driven by stored energy release. Conversely, muscle relaxation cannot occur spontaneously; it requires the active transport of Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum via the Sarco/Endoplasmic Reticulum Calcium ATPase (SERCA) pump, which directly consumes one molecule of ATP per two calcium ions pumped. Additionally, ATP binding to the myosin head is strictly required to break the rigor complex and allow the muscle to relax.

Question (Front): The type of muscle that compromises 40% of body weight and is involved in heat production during exercise and motion.*
Rationale:
In standard anatomy and physiology textbooks, skeletal muscle is the most abundant tissue type in the human body, accounting for approximately 40% of total body weight in a healthy adult.

Skeletal muscle cells are heavily packed with mitochondria. During physical exercise and regular movement, these muscles rapidly break down adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to drive contractions. This metabolic process generates an immense amount of thermal energy, serving as the body's primary mechanism for heat production to help maintain homeostatic core temperature.

• Smooth muscle fiber: Found within the walls of hollow internal organs (like blood vessels and the gastrointestinal tract). Smooth muscle contracts involuntarily and accounts for only a tiny fraction of overall body weight.
• Cardiac muscle fiber: Highly specialized, involuntary striated muscle tissue found exclusively in the walls of the heart. It does not make up a massive 40% share of body weight.
• Muscle mass: This is a broad, non-specific macroscopic term measuring total muscular composition rather than defining the specific type of muscle tissue requested by the question.

Question (Front): This type of exercise does not require oxygen.*
Rationale:
Anaerobic exercise literally means exercise "without oxygen." During these short, high-intensity bursts of physical activity, the muscles demand energy much faster than the body can transport oxygen to them.

To keep up with this extreme demand, the muscle cells rely entirely on immediate energy pathways that do not require oxygen, specifically the phosphagen (ATP-CP) system and anaerobic glycolysis (which breaks down glycogen and produces lactic acid). Examples include heavy weightlifting, sprinting, and high-intensity interval training (HIIT).

• Cardio / Aerobic exercise: "Aerobic" literally means "with oxygen." Cardio or aerobic activities (like jogging, cycling, or swimming) are sustained at a lower intensity, allowing the heart and lungs to continuously supply enough oxygen to the muscles to generate energy efficiently.
• Moderate intensity exercise: Activities performed at a moderate intensity rely primarily on aerobic pathways because the cardiovascular system can successfully keep up with the body's steady oxygen demands.

Question (Front): What is the macronutrient composition post competition or during the recovery phase?*
Rationale: During intense prolonged competition, muscle glycogen stores are severely depleted, and glycogen synthase activity is acutely upregulated. Consuming 75% of calories as high-glycemic carbohydrates stimulates a robust insulin surge, driving intracellular GLUT4 translocation and accelerating glucose uptake into skeletal muscle cells. Including 10% protein supplies essential amino acids—specifically leucine—to activate the mTORC1 pathway for muscle protein synthesis and further enhance insulin secretion. Restricting dietary fat to 15% is critical because high fat content retards gastric emptying and chyme transit, which slows down the intestinal absorption rate of glucose and amino acids required for rapid recovery.

Question (Front): Compute for the carbohydrate requirement of a 65kg tri-athlete.*
Rationale:
In sports dietetics, endurance athletes undergoing heavy training blocks—such as triathletes—have exceptionally high daily fuel demands. Rationale:
