Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Iron absorption is increased by the following nutrients except: *
Rationale: Zinc acts as a powerful inhibitor of iron absorption, rather than an enhancer. High doses of supplemental zinc compete directly with iron for the same membrane transporter pathways—specifically the DMT1 (Divalent Metal Transporter 1) channel—in the brush border cells of the small intestine. Consuming a large amount of zinc blocks this pathway, significantly reducing the absorption rate of non-heme iron.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Except for ____, these essential branched-chain amino acids are used by skeletal muscles for energy during prolonged endurance exercise: *
Rationale:
The three essential branched-chain amino acids are leucine, isoleucine, and valine. They are unique because unlike most other amino acids that are metabolized primarily in the liver, BCAAs skip the liver and are oxidized directly within skeletal muscle tissue to provide energy during prolonged endurance training.

During prolonged endurance exercise, as muscle glycogen stores deplete, muscle cells increasingly burn leucine, isoleucine, and valine for fuel. This drops blood BCAA levels, allowing more tryptophan to cross the blood-brain barrier, which actually contributes to central nervous system fatigue.

Tryptophan is an aromatic amino acid, not a branched-chain amino acid. While it is essential, it is not metabolized directly by skeletal muscle for energy during exercise.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The side chain attached to the carbon atom of a protein molecule which determines the characteristics and functions of each amino acid is: *
Rationale: All 20 standard amino acids share an identical foundational backbone consisting of a central alpha-carbon, an amino group, an acid (carboxyl) group, and a hydrogen atom. The radical group (R-group) is the only component that changes from one amino acid to the next. Its specific chemical layout determines whether the amino acid behaves as hydrophobic, hydrophilic, acidic, basic, or polar.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Considered semi-essential or conditionally essential amino acids except for: *
Rationale:
Alanine is a strictly non-essential (dispensable) amino acid. The body can always synthesize it in adequate amounts directly from pyruvate via transamination reactions, even during periods of severe stress, illness, or rapid growth. It never crosses into the semi-essential category.

• Tyrosine: This is a classic conditionally essential amino acid. It is synthesized directly from the essential amino acid phenylalanine. In clinical conditions like Phenylketonuria (PKU) where the converting enzyme is deficient, or during severe liver disease, tyrosine cannot be produced by the body and must be supplied exogenously through the diet.
• Cysteine: This is a conditionally essential amino acid. It requires methionine as a sulfur donor for its synthesis. In premature infants or patients with severe metabolic stress or cirrhosis, the enzymatic pathways are immature or impaired, making it an essential dietary requirement.
• Serine: This is recognized under advanced physiological frameworks (such as the MedlinePlus Medical Reference) as a conditionally essential amino acid. Under extreme hypermetabolic states or specific clinical pathologies, its endogenous production cannot completely keep up with cellular demands.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): These are simple proteins that give amino acids when hydrolyzed except for ___: *
Rationale: • Metalloproteins are classified as conjugated (or compound) proteins, not simple proteins. Upon hydrolysis, they yield both amino acids and a non-protein prosthetic group, which in this case is a metal ion (such as iron, zinc, or copper).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Factors that increase iron absorption except: *
Rationale: Non-heme iron requires a highly acidic stomach environment to remain soluble and convert from its ferric (Fe^3+) form into the easily absorbable ferrous (Fe^2+) form. Antacids neutralize stomach acid, which directly impairs and decreases iron absorption.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A calorie-free food contains: *
Rationale:
According to official food labeling laws (such as FDA and international food regulations), a manufacturer can legally label a food item as "calorie-free" or "zero calories" if it contains fewer than 5 calories per reference amount customarily consumed (serving size).

Because the body expends a small amount of energy just to digest food, these negligible amounts are rounded down to zero on nutritional facts panels.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Water-soluble vitamins are absorbed in the small intestine except for ____ which is absorbed in the stomach. *
Rationale: While the final absorption of Vitamin B₁₂ actually occurs in the terminal ileum (small intestine), its entire absorption process begins critically in the stomach. The stomach produces hydrochloric acid to unbind B₁₂ from dietary proteins and secretes Intrinsic Factor (IF), a mandatory transport protein. Because B₁₂ requires this extensive gastric phase, many simplified medical board questions uniquely tie its absorption context to the stomach.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): These form the accessory organs of digestion except for the _____: *
Rationale:
The digestive system is split into two primary divisions: the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and the accessory organs. The small intestine is a fundamental component of the GI tract itself—the continuous muscular tube through which food physically passes, undergoes chemical digestion, and gets absorbed.

• Liver: This is a true accessory organ of digestion. Food does not pass through it, but it facilitates chemical digestion by continuously manufacturing and exporting bile into the duodenum to emulsify fats.
• Gallbladder: This is a true accessory organ of digestion. It serves as a secondary storage and concentration sac for the bile produced by the liver, squeezing it into the small intestine when fats enter the tract.
• Pancreas: This is a true accessory organ of digestion. Its exocrine cells synthesize and secrete pancreatic juice containing essential digestive enzymes and bicarbonate ions straight into the duodenum to neutralize acidity and digest macromolecules.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A secretion of the pancreas that neutralizes the acidic fluid from the stomach: *
Rationale:
The pancreas secretes large amounts of sodium bicarbonate into the duodenum. This alkaline fluid directly neutralizes the highly acidic chyme coming from the stomach. This neutralization process protects the delicate intestinal lining and creates the optimal alkaline environment necessary for digestive enzymes to function.

• Digestive Enzymes: While the pancreas secretes critical digestive enzymes (like amylase, lipase, and trypsin), their function is to chemically break down carbohydrates, fats, and proteins rather than directly buffering or neutralizing stomach acid.
• Mucus: Mucus is secreted by goblet cells along the gastrointestinal tract to lubricate food passage and provide a physical structural coating against acid, but it does not act as a primary chemical neutralizing agent.
• Bile: This fluid is produced and secreted by the liver (and stored in the gallbladder), not the pancreas. Its primary function is the mechanical emulsification of fats.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): As BMR increases, there is an increased need for: *
Rationale:
As Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) increases, the body burns through carbohydrates, fats, and proteins at a much faster rate to produce ATP.

Thiamin (B₁), riboflavin (B₂), and niacin (B₃) function strictly as the essential coenzymes required to break down these macronutrients during cellular respiration:
	• Thiamin is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase to kickstart aerobic metabolism.
	• Riboflavin forms FAD/FADH₂, which acts as an electron carrier in the Krebs cycle and Electron Transport Chain.
	• Niacin forms NAD/NADH, the primary electron carrier across glycolysis and mitochondrial pathways.

Because their metabolic utilization is directly tied to total energy expenditure, your physical requirement for these three specific B vitamins scales upward as your BMR increases.

• Vitamins A, C, D, E, and K perform localized or systemic cellular tasks (such as antioxidant defenses, bone mineral regulation, immune signaling, and blood clotting factors) that operate independently of immediate carbohydrate and lipid calorie-burning metrics.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Glossitis is caused by a deficiency of: *
Rationale:
Glossitis—which is inflammation of the tongue causing it to swell, turn smooth, and lose its tiny bumps (papillae)—is a classic clinical hallmark of B-complex vitamin deficiencies. It is most frequently tied to a lack of Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin), Vitamin B₉ (folate), Vitamin B₆ (pyridoxine), Vitamin B₃ (niacin), and Vitamin B₂ (riboflavin).

Cells lining the mouth and tongue have a very rapid turnover rate. Because B vitamins act as essential coenzymes for cellular energy production and DNA synthesis, a deficiency rapidly impairs the body's ability to regenerate these tongue cells, leading to inflammation and atrophy.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which of the following is not a function of the kidneys? *
Rationale:
The kidneys activate Vitamin D (converting it into calcitriol), not Vitamin A. Vitamin A is primarily stored and metabolized by the liver.

• Waste Elimination: The kidneys filter blood to remove metabolic waste products like urea, uric acid, and creatinine via urine.
• Red Blood Cell Production: The kidneys release a hormone called erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates the bone marrow to produce red blood cells.
• Blood Pressure Regulation: The kidneys regulate blood pressure by managing fluid balance and releasing the enzyme renin as part of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Carbohydrate digestion starts in the ____ and is completed in the _____. *
Rationale:
• Starts in the mouth: Carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth, where mechanical chewing combines with the chemical action of salivary amylase to break down large starches into smaller sugars.

• Completed in the small intestines: The process stops temporarily in the highly acidic stomach but is completed in the small intestine. Here, pancreatic amylase and brush border enzymes finish breaking down carbohydrates into basic sugars like glucose for absorption.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Fatty acids formed by hydrogenation of unsaturated fats, converting them from liquid oils to semisolid fats. *
Rationale:
• Industrially, liquid vegetable oils (which are rich in unsaturated fats) have hydrogen gas bubbled through them in the presence of a catalyst. This is done to make them more solid, spreadable, and shelf-stable.
• If the fat is partially hydrogenated rather than fully saturated, a chemical side reaction occurs. The remaining natural carbon-to-carbon double bonds flip from their native "cis" configuration into an unnatural, straight "trans" configuration. This chemical restructuring creates trans-fatty acids (trans fats).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Fat digestion occurs in the: *
Rationale:
The small intestine is the primary site for both the chemical digestion and absorption of dietary fats. This process relies on two critical substances released into the duodenum:
	• Bile Salts: Secreted by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, bile salts act as a detergent to emulsify large fat globules into tiny droplets. This mechanical action dramatically increases the surface area available for enzymes.
	• Pancreatic Lipase: The principal fat-digesting enzyme, which is secreted by the pancreas, breaks down these small emulsified fat droplets into free fatty acids and monoglycerides for absorption by enterocytes.

• The Stomach: While a small amount of lipid digestion begins here via gastric lipase, it is highly limited because the stomach lacks bile salts to emulsify fats efficiently.
• The Large Intestine: The colon is primarily responsible for absorbing remaining water, synthesizing certain vitamins through gut microbiota, and forming feces. No functional fat digestion takes place here.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The hormone secreted by duodenal cells that stimulates the pancreas to release pancreatic juice. *
Rationale:
Secretin, a hormone, is secreted by the "S cells" of the duodenum in response to the acidic pH of the incoming gastric contents (chyme). It travels through the bloodstream to the pancreas and stimulates the release of a pancreatic juice rich in bicarbonate. The bicarbonate acts as a buffer to neutralize the stomach acid, protecting the intestinal lining and creating the optimal alkaline environment for digestive enzymes.

• Cholecystokinin / CCK: Also secreted by the duodenum (specifically by "I cells"), CCK is triggered by the presence of fats and proteins. While it also acts on the pancreas, its primary role is to stimulate the pancreas to release digestive enzymes (like trypsin and pancreatic lipase) and signal the gallbladder to contract and release bile.
• Gastrin: This hormone is secreted by "G cells" in the stomach (not the duodenum) and functions to stimulate the gastric glands to secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl) and pepsinogen.
• Chyme: This is not a hormone at all. It is the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food expelled by the stomach into the duodenum.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A measure of the nutrients a food provides in relation to the energy it provides. *
Rationale:
This is the literal scientific definition of nutrient density. It measures the concentration of beneficial nutrients (such as vitamins, minerals, complex carbohydrates, lean protein, and healthy fats) in a food relative to the total calories (energy content) it delivers. For example, fresh spinach has high nutrient density because it provides massive amounts of vitamins for very few calories.

• Energy density measures the number of calories (energy) per gram of food weight. High energy-dense foods (like potato chips or butter) provide a high amount of calories in a small, lightweight serving size.
• The glycemic index ranks carbohydrates based on how quickly they raise blood sugar levels,.
• Diet diversity refers to eating a wide variety of different food groups to ensure balanced nutrient intake.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): During the fasting stage, one of the following occurs: *
Rationale: Glycogen breakdown is the very first defense mechanism. Your pancreas secretes glucagon, which signals the liver to smash its stored glycogen chains back into free glucose to maintain normal blood sugar levels.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Inactive precursors of enzymes: *
Rationale:
• A) Zymogens / D) Proenzymes: Inactive proteins that must undergo a chemical change (like clipping off a piece of the protein chain) to become active enzymes.
• B) Apoenzymes: The pure protein part of an enzyme that is currently inactive because it is missing its non-protein helper (cofactor or coenzyme).
• C) Coenzymes: Organic helper molecules (often made from B-vitamins) that bind to enzymes to help them perform chemical reactions.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The mineral needed to keep the heart beat steady and plays a major role in maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance. *
Rationale:
Potassium is the primary intracellular cation (positively charged ion) in the body. It functions closely with the heart's electrical conduction system to stabilize resting membrane potentials. Proper levels are absolutely essential to maintain a regular cardiac rhythm and contractility. Severe deviations (either hypokalemia or hyperkalemia) can trigger lethal cardiac arrhythmias.

Potassium works in tandem with sodium via the cellular sodium-potassium pump. While sodium regulates fluid outside the cells, potassium regulates fluid volumes inside the cells, preserving structural cell integrity and overall fluid homeostasis.

	• Sodium: Primarily acts as the major regulator of extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure. While an imbalance stresses the heart indirectly, it does not directly regulate heartbeat steadiness like potassium does.
	• Calcium: Triggers the physical contraction of muscles (including the heart), but it is not the primary ion responsible for maintaining fluid balance across cellular compartments.
	• Magnesium: Acts as a crucial stabilizer for enzymatic functions and works closely with potassium.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Eating foods containing vitamin C in the same meal can increase the absorption of which mineral? *
Rationale:
Dietary iron exists in two forms: heme iron (from animal tissues) and non-heme iron (from plant foods). Non-heme iron is inherently difficult for the human body to absorb because it is typically found in its oxidized ferric state (Fe³⁺).

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) acts as a powerful reducing agent. When consumed in the same meal, it reduces ferric iron (Fe³⁺) into its highly soluble ferrous state (Fe²⁺). It also binds with the iron to form a stable chelate complex that prevents it from binding to inhibitors like phytates or tannins. This significantly boosts iron absorption across the intestinal lining.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Vitamins that function in normal blood formation except: *
Rationale:
Biotin (Vitamin B₇) serves as a vital coenzyme for carboxylase enzymes involved in lipid synthesis, glucose production (gluconeogenesis), and amino acid catabolism. It does not play a direct, primary role in hematopoiesis (blood cell formation) or hemoglobin synthesis.

• Pyridoxine: This vitamin is essential for normal blood formation. Pyridoxine (Vitamin B₆), in its active form as pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), acts as a mandatory coenzyme for the enzyme ALA synthase. This is the enzyme that initiates the very first step of heme synthesis inside the mitochondria. A deficiency in B₆ directly leads to microcytic, hypochromic sideroblastic anemia.
• Cobalamin: This vitamin is crucial for red blood cell development. Cobalamin (Vitamin B₁₂) is a required cofactor alongside folate for DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing hematopoietic stem cells. Without it, bone marrow cells cannot mature normally, resulting in macrocytic or megaloblastic anemia.
• Folate: This vitamin is foundational for hematopoiesis. Folate (Vitamin B₉) is required for the synthesis of purines and thymidylate, which are essential building blocks for DNA replication. When folate is missing, erythroblasts in the bone marrow cannot divide smoothly, leading to aborted maturation and megaloblastic anemia.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Minerals that are effective antioxidants except: *
Rationale:
Chromium (Cr) is a trace mineral primarily known for its role in carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism by enhancing the action of insulin. It does not function directly or serve as a traditional cofactor for major endogenous antioxidant enzyme systems.

• Selenium: This mineral is a well-established and highly effective antioxidant. It forms an essential structural component of the active site of the enzyme glutathione peroxidase, which neutralizes harmful hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides into harmless water and alcohols.
• Iron: This mineral plays a vital role in antioxidant defense mechanisms. Iron (Fe) serves as an essential cofactor for the enzyme catalase, an incredibly rapid antioxidant enzyme that converts toxic hydrogen peroxide molecules into water and oxygen within cells.
• Copper: This mineral is a critical component of the antioxidant defense loop. Copper (Cu) acts alongside zinc as a mandatory structural cofactor for cytosolic superoxide dismutase (CuZn-SOD). This enzyme acts as the first line of defense by transforming highly reactive superoxide free radicals into less destructive hydrogen peroxide.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Two vitamins whose requirements are based on an individual’s energy intake. *
Rationale:
Thiamine (B₁): Serves as a mandatory coenzyme for carbohydrate metabolism and the processing of pyruvate. Standard guidelines traditionally recommend 0.5 mg of thiamine per 1,000 kcal consumed.

Riboflavin (B₂): Serves as a vital electron carrier (FAD) in mitochondrial biological oxidation and the citric acid cycle. Standard requirements are classically set at 0.5 mg of riboflavin per 1,000 kcal.

Niacin (B₃): Serves as a core electron carrier (NAD/NADH) in glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation. Standard requirements are similarly calculated as 6.6 mg of Niacin Equivalents (NE) per 1,000 kcal.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): All are needed for the conversion of tryptophan to niacin except: *
Rationale:
The synthesis of niacin (Vitamin B₃) from the essential amino acid tryptophan occurs via the kynurenine pathway in the liver. This multi-step conversion is highly nutrient-dependent and strictly requires three cofactors:

• Vitamin B₆ (Pyridoxine): Active pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP) is the direct coenzyme required by kynureninase, an essential enzyme in the pathway.
• Vitamin B₂ (Riboflavin): Active FAD is required as a cofactor for kynurenine 3-monooxygenase, and riboflavin is also needed to synthesize active B₆.
• Iron (Fe): Iron is a critical component of the initial rate-limiting enzyme, tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It competes with calcium for absorption: *
Rationale:
Magnesium (Mg) and calcium (Ca) share a common transport and homeostatic regulatory system within the gastrointestinal tract. When consumed in large or highly concentrated supplemental doses, magnesium and calcium directly compete with each other for absorption pathways across the small intestinal mucosa.

• Sodium & Potassium: These monovalent extracellular and intracellular cations are absorbed through distinct, independent active transport and electrochemical channels that do not interfere with or compete against divalent minerals like calcium.
• Phosphorus: While phosphorus (P) interacts with calcium dynamically, it does not directly compete for the same absorption binding sites. Instead, an excessive amount of phosphorus binds chemically with calcium within the intestinal lumen to form an insoluble complex (calcium phosphate), which physically reduces the overall bioavailability of both minerals rather than competing for transport carriers.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It protects folate from oxidative destruction: *
Rationale:
Folate (Vitamin B9) is a highly unstable water-soluble molecule that is extremely susceptible to degradation via heat, UV light, and environmental oxygen. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) acts as a highly effective water-soluble antioxidant and oxygen-scavenger.

In food matrixes, the digestive tract, and blood plasma, Vitamin C shields folate from breaking down by neutralizing free radicals and reducing the primary products of folate oxidation (such as quinonoid dihydrofolate) back into their active, usable forms. Because of this symbiotic protective relationship, a deficiency in Vitamin C often accelerates the depletion and urinary excretion of oxidized folate derivatives.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which of the following statements about ascorbic acid is incorrect? *
Answer (Back): Its requirement varies with the caloric intake.
Rationale:
Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) functions as a water-soluble antioxidant and an essential enzymatic cofactor (e.g., for collagen synthesis). Its daily physiological requirements do not change based on how many calories you eat. In contrast, the requirements for B-complex vitamins like Thiamine (B1), Riboflavin (B2), and Niacin (B3) are directly tied to caloric and carbohydrate intake because they serve as direct coenzymes in energy metabolism pathways.

• Metabolism to Oxalate: This statement is correct. Ascorbic acid breaks down non-enzymatically in the body to form oxalate. This oxalate can bind with calcium in the urinary tract to form insoluble calcium oxalate salts, which are the main components of the most common type of kidney stones.
• Oxidation by Metal Ions: This statement is correct. Ascorbic acid is a strong reducing agent that is easily degraded and readily oxidized in the presence of heat, light, and divalent metal ions like copper (Cu²⁺) and iron (Fe²⁺).

Rationale:
Leucine and lysine are the only two amino acids in the human body that are strictly purely ketogenic. They are degraded directly into acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate, which are precursors for ketone bodies and fatty acids, and cannot be used to synthesize carbohydrates via gluconeogenesis.

• Cysteine: This is a purely glucogenic amino acid. It is converted into the α-keto acid pyruvate through a multi-step oxidative pathway, making it an effective carbohydrate former.
• Glycine: This is a purely glucogenic amino acid. It enters carbohydrate-forming pathways by being converted into serine, which is then deaminated directly into pyruvate (an α-keto acid).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It is the largest single contributor to the body’s energy needs accounting for 60%-80% of its total need for calories. *
Rationale:
Basal metabolism, or Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR), represents the baseline energy expended by the body at complete rest in a post-absorptive state. It is dedicated purely to maintaining life-sustaining vegetative functions—such as cellular respiration, heartbeat, brain activity, and body temperature regulation. In textbook nutrition frameworks, it serves as the largest single contributor to Total Energy Expenditure (TEE), typically accounting for 60% to 80% of daily calorie needs depending on an individual's lean body mass.

• Thermic Effect of Food: This component represents the temporary increase in energy expenditure associated with digesting, absorbing, and storing nutrients from food. It accounts for only about 5% to 10% of total energy requirements.
• Adaptive Thermogenesis: This is the change in energy expenditure in response to environmental fluctuations (like extreme cold stress) or chronic overfeeding/underfeeding. It represents an auxiliary survival adjustment and constitutes a minor, highly variable percentage of daily needs.
• Physical Activity: This comprises the energy expended during voluntary muscle movement and exercise. While it is the most variable and changeable component of a person's daily energy expenditure, it typically contributes only 15% to 30% of total calories in most normal-living adults.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The Krebs cycle is oxygen-requiring and takes place in the: *
Rationale:
The Krebs cycle (also known as the citric acid cycle or TCA cycle) takes place exclusively within the matrix of the mitochondria. This is because all the specific enzymes, coenzymes, and transport proteins required for the cycle are housed inside the mitochondrial membranes.

Although the chemical steps of the Krebs cycle do not directly use oxygen gas (O₂), the cycle is considered aerobic (oxygen-requiring). It cannot run without oxygen because it relies on the electron transport chain (which requires oxygen as the final electron acceptor) to regenerate its essential starting coenzymes, NAD⁺ and FAD.

Biological Value (BV) measures protein quality by calculating the amount of nitrogen retained for tissue growth and maintenance divided by the total nitrogen absorbed from the diet. The formula is:

	• Protein Efficiency Ratio - PER: This measures the weight gain of a growing subject per gram of protein consumed, typically tested on laboratory rats.

Question (Front): Preferred source of energy in COPD: *
Rationale:
Patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) struggle to exhale carbon dioxide (CO₂). Fats are the preferred energy source because they have a low Respiratory Quotient (around 0.7). This means that when the body metabolizes fats for energy, it produces less CO₂ per molecule of oxygen consumed compared to other macronutrients.

Meanwhile, Carbohydrates have an RQ of 1.0, meaning they produce the highest amount of CO₂ waste when broken down. This places an extra load on already compromised lungs, leading to respiratory distress.

A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet helps reduce the overall burden on a COPD patient's respiratory system while still providing adequate calories to fight tissue wasting.

Rationale:
According to nutritional standards and clinical practice guides for hyperuricemia and gout patients, the recommended daily dietary protein allowance is 1 g per kilogram of body weight (1 g/kg BW).

While a high total volume of protein is not responsible for raising uric acid levels, the source of the protein matters. Gout patients are encouraged to meet their standard protein requirement (1 g/kg BW) by focusing on low-purine or plant-based protein options (such as low-fat dairy, eggs, tofu, and legumes) while strictly limiting high-purine animal proteins like organ meats, red meat, and seafood.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The best prescription for a female secretary with a height of 5 ft. 4 inches, weight of 70kg, and FBS of 7mmol/L: *
Rationale:
Step-by-Step Breakdown Using Standard Clinical Nutrition Formulas

To determine the best caloric prescription, we must calculate the patient's Desirable Body Weight (DBW) and apply the correct activity factor adjusted for her clinical status (Overweight + Diabetic).

1. Find the Desirable Body Weight (DBW) using Tannhauser's Method:
	• Convert height to centimeters: 5 ft. 4 inches = 64 inches * 2.54 = 162.56 cm
	• Deduct 100 from height in cm: 162.56 - 100 = 62.56 kg
	• Deduct 10% for the final DBW: 62.56 - 6.25 = 56.31 kg (rounded to 56 kg)

2. Evaluate her Clinical Status & Activity Level:
	• Current Weight: 70 kg (Since her DBW is 56 kg, she is significantly overweight).
	• FBS (Fasting Blood Sugar): 7.0 mmol/L (This meets the diagnostic threshold for Diabetes Mellitus).
	• Activity Level: As an office secretary, her physical activity is classified as Sedentary.

3. Apply the Weight Reduction/Diabetic Caloric Factor:
	• For a normal weight individual with a sedentary lifestyle, the baseline factor is 30 kcal/kg DBW.
	• However, because she is an overweight diabetic, a low-calorie weight reduction regimen is required to optimize insulin sensitivity. The textbook factor for weight reduction in sedentary individuals is 25 kcal/kg DBW.

4. Compute the Total Energy Requirement (TER):
	• TER = 56.31 kg (DBW) * 25 kcal/kg = 1407.75 kcal/day

Rounding to the nearest multiple of 100 as standard practice in dietetic prescriptions yields exactly 1400 kcal/day.

Question (Front): The nutritionist-dietitian must closely monitor the client with nephrotic syndrome for deficiencies of which vitamin? *
Rationale: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), which leads to the urinary excretion of low-molecular-weight plasma proteins, including the 58-kDa vitamin D-binding protein (DBP). Because the majority of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D [1,25(OH)2D] are bound to DBP, their continuous loss in the urine depletes total body stores. Furthermore, impaired renal parenchyma and chronic inflammation decrease the activity of 1alpha-hydroxylase, reducing the conversion of 25(OH)D to its active hormonal form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, thereby disrupting calcium homeostasis and secondary bone mineralization.

Question (Front): Aside from table salt, a low sodium diet limits the use of: *
Rationale: Aside from table salt, processed and ultra-processed foods are the single largest source of sodium in the modern diet. A low-sodium diet strictly mandates limiting these items.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A ketogenic diet is characterized as: *
Rationale:
A classic ketogenic diet is structured to shift the body's primary metabolic fuel source from glucose to fat. To induce this state of ketosis, the diet must dramatically restrict carbohydrates (CHO) and replace those calories with dietary fat.

The standard ketogenic diet typically derives approximately 70% to 80% of daily calories from fat, 15% to 20% from protein, and only 5% to 10% from carbohydrates.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Characterized by low grade fever, body tissue wasting, and dry cough. *
Rationale:
This infectious disease is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The classic symptoms of pulmonary TB include a lingering low-grade fever (often spiking in the afternoon or evening), dry cough (which may start dry before becoming productive or producing blood), and severe body tissue wasting (traditionally referred to as "consumption" due to profound, unintended weight loss and muscle atrophy).

	• COPD: Characterized primarily by a chronic productive cough (with mucus), wheezing, and progressive shortness of breath, rather than a presenting low-grade fever.
	• AIDS: While it causes wasting and fever, it is a complex systemic syndrome of immune failure that manifests through a wide variety of opportunistic infections rather than a localized dry cough complex.
	• Cholecystitis: This is an acute or chronic inflammation of the gallbladder that presents with sharp upper abdominal pain, nausea, and potentially a high fever, rather than chronic respiratory symptoms or progressive body wasting.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A malabsorption problem brought about by shorter and less number of intestinal villi: *
Rationale: Non-tropical sprue (commonly known as celiac disease or gluten-sensitive enteropathy) is an autoimmune disorder triggered by ingesting gluten. The immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of the small intestine, leading to severe inflammation, crypt hyperplasia, and structural damage characterized by the shortening, flattening, and reduction in the number of intestinal villi (villous atrophy). Since villi are responsible for expanding the surface area of the gut, their damage drastically impairs nutrient absorption.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Considered “neutral foods” when following either an alkaline ash or an acid ash diet: *
Rationale:
Foods that are primarily composed of pure fats, oils, or refined sugars leave behind no mineral residue that can alter urinary pH. Therefore, butter, cooking oils, margarine, plain candies, and table sugar are classified as strictly neutral. 

• Acid Ash Foods: Foods high in protein, phosphorus, and sulfur leave behind an acidic residue. This includes meat, fish, poultry, eggs, and whole grains.
• Alkaline Ash Foods: Foods rich in minerals like magnesium, potassium, and calcium leave behind an alkaline residue. This includes almost all fruits and vegetables (even acidic ones like lemons, because the organic citric acid is fully oxidized into water and CO₂, leaving alkaline minerals behind).

Question (Front): Diet for calcium oxalate urinary calculi. *
Rationale: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type of kidney stones. They tend to form more easily in acidic urine. An alkaline ash diet increases the pH of the urine (making it less acidic), which helps keep calcium oxalate and uric acid crystals dissolved so they can be passed safely. This diet focuses on eating foods like vegetables, fruits, and legumes, while reducing acid-forming foods like meats, cheeses, and grains.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It is given when nutrient requirements are greatly increased and the GIT is not functional. *
Rationale:
When a patient's gastrointestinal tract (GIT) is non-functional, blocked, or requires complete clinical rest, enteral options like a gastrostomy or a nasogastric tube (NGT) cannot be used safely. Bypassing the gut entirely becomes mandatory.

While basic "intravenous feeding" usually refers to peripheral lines giving short-term hydration or dilute nutrients (like PPN), TPN is a highly concentrated, hyperosmolar formula packed with complete macronutrients, vitamins, and minerals. Because it is designed to meet massive metabolic demands (such as in severe burns, sepsis, or major trauma), it must be safely administered through a large central vein.

Question (Front):
Refer to the following information. Based on the FEL, the diet of a burn patient contains the following meal pattern for lunch: 90g fried chicken; 160g rice; 45g sauteed squash; 250g fresh milk; and 103g ripe mango.
How much is the CHO content of the meal? *
Rationale:
According to the Philippine Food Exchange List (FEL), each food item is converted into exchange units to calculate its specific carbohydrate (CHO) content:

1. 160g Rice (2 Rice Exchanges):
• 1 exchange of cooked rice = 80g (contains 23g CHO)
• 160g = 2 exchanges
• CHO content: 2 x 23g = 46g

2. 250g Fresh Milk (1 Whole Milk Exchange):
• 1 exchange of whole milk = 250g (contains 12g CHO)
• CHO content: 1 x 12g = 12g

3. 103g Ripe Mango (1 Fruit Exchange):
• 1 exchange of fruit = approx. 100g (contains 10g CHO)
• CHO content: 1 x 10g = 10g

4. 45g Sauteed Squash (1 Vegetable B Exchange):
• 1 exchange of cooked Vegetable B = 45g (contains 3g CHO)
• CHO content: 1 x 3g = 3g (Note: The fat exchange added for sauteing oil contains 0g CHO).

5. 90g Fried Chicken (3 Medium-Fat Meat Exchanges):
• Meat exchanges contain 0g CHO.

Final CHO Summation:

• Rice: 46g
• Fresh Milk: 12g
• Ripe Mango: 10g
• Sauteed Squash: 3g
• Fried Chicken: 0g

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front):
Refer to the following information. Based on the FEL, the diet of a burn patient contains the following meal pattern for lunch: 90g fried chicken; 160g rice; 45g sauteed squash; 250g fresh milk; and 103g ripe mango.
How many kilocalories does the meal contain? *
Rationale:
Step-by-Step Breakdown using the Food Exchange List (FEL)

To find the total energy value of this meal pattern, we break down each food item into its exact base exchanges and adjust for the preparation methods:

1. 160g Rice (Cooked Rice):
	• Exchange value: 1 exchange of cooked rice is equal to 80g (providing 100 kcal).
	• 160g / 80g = 2 Rice Exchanges.
	• Energy Contribution: 2 * 100 kcal = 200 kcal.

2. 250g Fresh Milk (Whole Milk):
	• Exchange value: 1 glass or 1 cup of whole fresh milk is equal to 250g (providing 170 kcal).
	• 250g / 250g = 1 Whole Milk Exchange.
	• Energy Contribution: 1 * 170 kcal = 170 kcal.

3. 103g Ripe Mango:
	• Exchange value: 1 exchange of ripe mango is equal to 103g gross weight (providing 40 kcal).
	• 103g / 103g = 1 Fruit Exchange.
	• Energy Contribution: 1 * 40 kcal = 40 kcal.

4. 45g Sauteed Squash (Vegetable B + Sauteing Fat):
	• Exchange value: 1 cooked vegetable exchange is equal to 1/2 cup or 45g (providing 16 kcal).
	• Preparation Modifier: Because the squash is sauteed, it adds 1 Fat Exchange (providing 45 kcal) for the cooking oil.
	• Energy Contribution: 16 kcal + 45 kcal = 61 kcal.

5. 90g Fried Chicken (Low-Fat Meat + Frying Fats):
	• Exchange value: Chicken is classified as a Low-Fat Meat, where 1 exchange equals 30g cooked meat (providing 41 kcal). Therefore, 90g / 30g = 3 Low-Fat Meat Exchanges.
	• Preparation Modifier: Because it is fried, each of the 3 meat exchanges absorbs approximately 1 Fat Exchange (3 * 45 kcal = 135 kcal).
	• Energy Contribution: (3 * 41 kcal) + 135 kcal = 258 kcal.

Total Energy Summation
Total Calorie Count = 200 kcal + 170 kcal + 40 kcal + 61 kcal + 258 kcal = 729 kcal

Rounding off to the nearest multiple of five as standard practice in FEL board examination questions, 729 kcal yields exactly 730 kcal.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It can bring about severe malabsorption: *
Rationale:
Chronic overuse or abuse of laxatives directly induces severe malabsorption syndromes. Laxatives unnaturally accelerate intestinal motility (peristalsis) or alter osmotic pressure, which forces food contents to rush through the gastrointestinal tract. This rapid transit time denies the small and large intestines the necessary window to digest and absorb essential macronutrients, fat-soluble vitamins (like Vitamin D), and electrolytes. Over time, this leads to structural steatorrhea, mineral depletion, and severe undernutrition.

• Diuretics: While diuretics heavily interfere with fluid balance and can lead to severe potassium depletion or dehydration through increased urinary excretion, they impact renal function rather than causing global nutrient malabsorption in the gut.
• Paracetamol: This is a standard over-the-counter analgesic and antipyretic. While acute toxicity or overdose causes severe hepatotoxicity (liver damage), standard therapeutic use does not impair the mucosal lining of the intestines or produce malabsorption.
• Cough Syrup: Typically containing antitussives or expectorants, these formulations do not target or compromise the digestive mechanics or metabolic transport systems of the small intestine.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Cholesterol level in food considered safe for daily consumption. *
Rationale:
For many years, traditional clinical nutrition guidelines and board manuals (such as the American Heart Association and national dietary guidelines) established a strict upper limit of 300 mg of dietary cholesterol per day for healthy adults to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.

While modern guidelines have shifted to focusing more broadly on limiting saturated fats, the classic dietary limit taught and tested in academic question banks for a "safe daily consumption level" remains 300 mg.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Diet management for a person with esophageal reflux. *
Rationale: Dietary fat stimulates the release of cholecystokinin (CCK) from the duodenal mucosa. CCK induces relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), increasing transient LES relaxations (TLESRs) and facilitating the retrograde flow of acidic gastric contents into the esophagus. Furthermore, high-fat meals delay gastric emptying, prolonging the period of high gastric volume and pressure that promotes reflux episodes. Restricting dietary fat directly attenuates postprandial CCK surges, preserves basal LES tone, and accelerates gastric transit.
Option 3: regular diet with small frequent meals

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Malnutrition due to esophageal tumor is primarily related to: *
Rationale:
The defining hallmark of an esophageal tumor is dysphagia (progressive difficulty swallowing) caused by the physical growth of the tumor narrowing the lumen of the esophagus.

While cancer cachexia can induce a catabolic state or alter systemic metabolism over time, the immediate and primary driver of severe protein-calorie malnutrition in these patients at the time of diagnosis is the simple, mechanical inability to physically swallow and consume enough food. This results in massive, structural inadequate food and fluid intake.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Patients taking medicines with MAO inhibitors should be advised this diet: *
Rationale:
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) are a class of medications used primarily as antidepressants. They work by blocking the enzyme monoamine oxidase, which normally breaks down neurotransmitters as well as tyramine (an amino acid byproduct found in aged and fermented foods).

If a patient taking an MAOI consumes high-tyramine foods, the excess tyramine cannot be broken down. This causes a massive release of norepinephrine, leading to severe vasoconstriction and a dangerous blood pressure spike known as a hypertensive crisis. Therefore, these patients must strictly follow a tyramine-restricted diet.

Aged cheeses (like cheddar, blue, or swiss), cured or smoked meats (like salami and ham), soy sauce, tofu, fermented items (like sauerkraut), tap beer, and red wine.

Rationale:
After colostomy or ileostomy surgery, the bowel and the newly formed stoma are swollen, inflamed, and healing from surgical trauma. A low-fiber, bland diet minimizes irritation to the intestinal lining, reducing the workload on the gut so it can heal efficiently.

High-fiber foods leave a large amount of indigestible residue (bulk) in the digestive tract. Because the internal lumen of a new stoma is narrowed due to post-operative swelling, a high-fiber intake poses a strict risk of causing a painful mechanical bowel blockage.

Because these patients suffer from severe malabsorption and weight loss, restricting fat overly constricts their caloric intake and worsens malnutrition. Instead, a normal, balanced physiological diet is prescribed in tandem with proper enzyme dosing. Fat restriction is only used as a temporary, short-term measure if painful fatty stools (steatorrhea) cannot be managed by medications.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)

Rationale:
Dumping syndrome is a complication that occurs after gastric surgeries (like a partial or total gastrectomy) where food moves too rapidly from the stomach into the small intestine. It does not directly result from or impact the nutrient needs of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD).

	• Medications: Common IBD drugs like corticosteroids lower calcium and vitamin D absorption, while others like sulfasalazine impair folate absorption, altering daily nutrient requirements.
	• Steatorrhea: Excessive fat in the stool (common in Crohn's disease due to bile acid malabsorption) causes a severe loss of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) and calories, increasing nutritional requirements.
	• Fistulas: These abnormal tissue tunnels can leak digestive fluids, causing high-volume losses of protein, electrolytes, and fluids, which drastically spike a patient's nutrient needs.

Question (Front): Ms. Padilla, 30 years old, has several family members who have had cancer. She asks the nurse how she can reduce her risk of cancer. What would you suggest? *
Answer (Back): Reduce her use of smoked, salt-cured, and nitrate-cured foods.
Rationale: Reduce her use of smoked, salt-cured, and nitrate-cured foods.
Option 1: Limit her saturated fat intake to 30% .
Option 3: Reduce her consumption of unpeeled fruits and vegetables.
Option 4: Reduce her use of smoked, salt-cured, and nitrate-cured foods.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Mr. Santos has lung cancer which has metastasized to his spine. Based on this information, it will be essential for the nutritionist-dietitian to monitor him for: *
Rationale:
When a primary tumor (such as lung cancer) metastasizes to the bone/spine, it initiates osteolytic bone destruction. The invading tumor cells stimulate specialized bone cells (osteoclasts) to break down the surrounding bone tissue.

As the bone structure is aggressively broken down and reabsorbed, massive amounts of calcium are dissolved and released directly into the bloodstream. This rapid influx overwhelms the kidneys' ability to excrete it, leading to a dangerous oncologic emergency known as Hypercalcemia of Malignancy (HCM).

Monitoring calcium levels is critical because hypercalcemia can lead to severe confusion, muscle weakness, kidney stones, and lethal cardiac arrhythmias. While dietary calcium restriction is generally not the primary treatment for HCM (as the excess calcium is coming from the bones, not food), the dietitian must aggressively monitor hydration status, fluid balance, and electrolyte trends to support clinical management.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Diet order for irritable bowel syndrome: *
Rationale:
Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder where dietary management focuses on controlling symptoms like cramping, bloating, gas, diarrhea, and constipation. Standard clinical diet orders traditionally incorporate all three modifications:

• High-fiber: Gradually increasing dietary fiber (specifically soluble fiber like psyllium, oats, and flaxseeds) is a primary recommendation. It adds healthy bulk to stools to relieve constipation (IBS-C) while simultaneously helping to solidify loose stools in diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D).
• Avoid highly seasoned foods: Spicy and heavily seasoned foods contain compounds (like capsaicin) that irritate the gut lining and accelerate GI transit. Eliminating them helps reduce abdominal pain, cramping, and sudden bowel urgency.
• Fat-restricted: High-fat, greasy, and deep-fried foods trigger an exaggerated gastrocolic reflex, which causes rapid, painful colonic contractions. Restricting dietary fat intake stabilizes gut motility and prevents immediate post-meal cramping and diarrhea.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A person who has done well for 3 years following a gastrectomy should be alert to signs of: *
Rationale:
The human liver stores a substantial reserve of Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin), which typically lasts 3 to 5 years. Once these internal stores are fully exhausted, symptoms of deficiency begin to appear.

A gastrectomy removes the parietal cells of the stomach, which are responsible for secreting intrinsic factor. Intrinsic factor is a protein absolutely required for Vitamin B₁₂ absorption in the ileum. Without it, the body cannot absorb dietary Vitamin B₁₂, eventually causing macrocytic/pernicious anemia and neurological issues.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Dietary recommendation for clients with cystic fibrosis except: *
Answer (Back): limit the use of table salt
Rationale:
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is caused by a genetic mutation that disrupts the CFTR protein, preventing cells from properly regulating chloride and sodium. As a result, individuals with CF lose massive amounts of salt through their sweat pores (often referred to as having "salty skin"). To prevent hyponatremia (dangerously low blood sodium), dehydration, and heat exhaustion, clients with CF are actively encouraged to liberalize their use of table salt and consume salty snacks. Limiting salt is contraindicated.

Historically, old test bank items sometimes listed fat restriction as an outdated management strategy because patients cannot digest fats well without enzymes. However, in modern clinical nutrition practice—combined with Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT)—a high-fat diet is heavily promoted alongside high calorie and high protein to help meet their high energy demands.
Option 1: limit the use of table salt

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Diet recommendations for clients suffering from severe stress: *
Rationale: energy-modified, high protein diet

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A type of COPD in which the lungs lose their elasticity and the client has difficulty breathing. *
Rationale:
Emphysema is a major form of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) characterized by the permanent destruction of the alveolar walls and pulmonary capillaries. This architectural destruction leads to a severe loss of lung elasticity. Without elastic recoil, the small airways collapse during exhalation, trapping air inside the lungs (hyperinflation) and making it deeply difficult for the patient to breathe.

• Bronchitis: Chronic bronchitis is characterized by chronic inflammation, swelling, and narrowing of the lining of the bronchial airways. Its primary presentation is a persistent, productive cough driven by severe mucus hypersecretion rather than a structural loss of lung tissue elasticity.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Risk assessment CHD includes measurement of blood lipids such as: *
Rationale:
A comprehensive risk assessment for Coronary Heart Disease (CHD) relies on a full fasting lipid profile. Each of the lipid fractions listed in the other options provides distinct, critical diagnostic data regarding a patient's cardiovascular health profile:

• Total Cholesterol (TC): Reflects the overall amount of cholesterol circulating in the bloodstream and is directly linked to blood vessel plaque buildup and disease risk.
• Triglycerides (TG): High levels of these blood fats serve as an independent risk factor for atherosclerosis and metabolic syndrome, often elevated by a high-fat diet, refined sugars, or alcohol.
• HDL-Cholesterol (HDL-C): Known as the "good cholesterol," it plays a protective role by removing excess cholesterol from peripheral tissues and transporting it back to the liver. High levels actively reduce CHD risk.
• LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C): Designated as the "bad cholesterol" and the primary target of clinical lipid-lowering therapies, elevated circulating LDL leads directly to fatty accumulation and narrowing inside the coronary arteries.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The recommended intake for MUFA in the diet is approximately: *
Rationale: less than 7% of total kcal

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Flatulence, cramps, or diabetes may be some unpleasant side effects upon the initiation of this diet: *
Rationale:
When a person suddenly initiates a high-fiber diet, the digestive tract requires a transition period to adapt. The human body lacks the enzymes to digest dietary fiber, so it passes intact into the large intestine. There, resident gut bacteria ferment the fiber. A sudden influx of fiber causes rapid, aggressive bacterial fermentation, which produces large amounts of gas. This trapped gas directly results in flatulence, abdominal bloating, and painful cramps.

While fiber does not cause diabetes, a high-fiber diet is a primary clinical intervention utilized for the management of Diabetes Mellitus. Soluble fiber creates a gel-like substance in the gut that slows down the absorption of glucose, preventing rapid post-meal blood sugar spikes and improving insulin sensitivity.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Chronic diarrhea may be accompanied by a number of nutritional deficiencies due to losses of: *
Rationale:
Chronic diarrhea severely impairs the small and large intestines' ability to absorb nutrients due to rapid transit time and mucosal damage. This leads to widespread malabsorption and excessive losses of:

• Na & K: Sodium and potassium are critical electrolytes lost in high volumes through watery stools, leading to dehydration and electrolyte imbalances.
• Vitamins & minerals: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), water-soluble vitamins (like B-complex), and minerals (such as iron, zinc, and magnesium) are rapidly depleted.
• Protein: Protein-losing enteropathy often occurs during chronic diarrhea, where plasma proteins leak directly into the gut lumen and are excreted, leading to tissue wasting and hypoalbuminemia.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): This type of supplement has shown good results in reducing encephalopathy and in improving nitrogen and energy balance: *
Rationale: Patients with advanced liver disease or cirrhosis typically present with an altered amino acid profile. Their plasma levels of Branched-Chain Amino Acids (BCAAs: leucine, isoleucine, and valine) drop significantly, while levels of Aromatic Amino Acids (AAAs: phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan) rise. This imbalance allows excessive AAAs to cross the blood-brain barrier, altering neurotransmission and inducing hepatic encephalopathy.

Answer (Back): low purine, 1g protein/kg BW, calorie restricted
Rationale: low purine, 1g protein/kg BW, calorie restricted
Option 1: low purine, adequate protein, 3 liters water
Option 2: low purine, 1.5 g protein/kg BW, low alcohol
Option 3: low purine, high CHO, adequate protein, low fat
Option 4: low purine, 1g protein/kg BW, calorie restricted
