Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which diet is best for a patient with hypothyroidism? *
Rationale: 20-30 cal/KBW, low fat, iodized salt

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The amount of kcal/KBW for bulimic patients on a weight maintenance diet: *
Rationale:
Research demonstrates that patients with bulimia nervosa who are in a weight-stable or weight-maintenance phase often have a significantly depressed metabolic rate. This is primarily caused by a history of chronic, severe energy restriction, chaotic eating cycles, and purging behaviors.

While a typical healthy, sedentary adult requires approximately 30 kcal/kg/day for weight maintenance, clinical evaluations show that weight-stable bulimic patients require fewer calories—typically averaging around 22 to 25 kcal per kilogram of body weight to maintain their weight.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A patient with a BMI of 42 will benefit from which diet prescription? *
Answer (Back): 1200 kcal, 55% kcal from CHO, fat restricted
Rationale:
In traditional dietetic practice, a 1200 kcal diet is considered the gold-standard baseline weight-reduction diet for adults. It is widely recognized as the lowest safe calorie level that an individual can consume while still being able to meet all their essential vitamin and mineral requirements without mandatory medical supplementation.

"Fat Restricted" over Percentage Targets: Classic medical diet prescriptions for severe obesity prioritize explicit qualitative restrictions like "fat restricted" or "low fat" rather than precise percentage numbers. Because fat is the most calorie-dense macronutrient (9 kcal per gram), strictly restricting visible fats, fried foods, and high-fat items is the most direct clinical method used to ensure the patient adheres to a low-calorie limit.

Macronutrient Balance: Keeping carbohydrates at 55% ensures the patient receives enough complex carbohydrates to maintain energy levels and prevent ketosis, while the remaining calories are split between protein and minimal essential fats.
Option 1: 800 kcal, 55% kcal from CHO, 25% from fat
Option 2: 1000 kcal, 55% kcal from CHO, 12% from protein
Option 3: 1200 kcal, 55% kcal from CHO, fat restricted
Option 4: 1300 kcal, 55% kcal from CHO, 25% from fat

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards2 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A cholesterol level of 240 mg/dL needs treatment with: *
Rationale:
In adults, a total cholesterol level below 200 mg/dL is desirable. A level between 200 and 239 mg/dL is considered borderline high, and a level of 240 mg/dL or higher is officially classified as high.

Once total cholesterol hits the high threshold (240 mg/dL), guidelines recommend a multi-pronged medical intervention:
• Diet & Exercise: Initial and continuing therapeutic lifestyle changes—such as reducing saturated and trans fats, increasing dietary fiber, and initiating regular cardio—form the baseline of managing lipid profiles.
• Drugs: Because a level of 240 mg/dL significantly elevates the risk for coronary heart disease, stroke, and atherosclerosis, lifestyle changes alone are often insufficient. Pharmacological intervention (most commonly statins) is prescribed in tandem to inhibit hepatic cholesterol production and aggressively pull down circulating lipid levels.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste products takes place in these vessels: *
Rationale:
Capillaries are the microscopic, thin-walled blood vessels where the actual exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and metabolic waste products takes place between the circulating blood and surrounding tissue cells.

• Veins: Large capacitance vessels returning deoxygenated blood toward the heart.
• Arteries: Thick-walled high-pressure vessels transporting oxygenated blood away from the heart.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Site of most of the biochemical reactions in the cell: *
Rationale:
The cytoplasm (specifically the cytosol and associated metabolic machinery) serves as the site for numerous foundational cellular biochemical reactions, including glycolysis, glycogen synthesis, and protein translation.

• Mitochondria: The specialized organelle responsible for oxidative phosphorylation, the Krebs cycle, and ATP generation.
• Nucleus: Houses genomic DNA and coordinates transcription and replication.
• Golgi apparatus: Modifies, sorts, and packages proteins for secretion.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Absorption is the same as: *
Rationale:
Assimilation refers to the biological process by which digested and absorbed nutrient molecules are incorporated into the tissues and cells of the body, making it synonymous with nutrient utilization and tissue incorporation.

• Digestion: The mechanical and chemical breakdown of food molecules in the gastrointestinal tract.
• Anabolism: The constructive phase of metabolism focused on building complex molecules from simpler precursors.
• Metabolism: The broader umbrella term encompassing all biochemical changes in the body.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It covers all the chemical changes that go on in the different body tissues, including both synthetic and degradative pathways. *
Rationale:
Metabolism is the comprehensive sum of all chemical reactions occurring within living organisms, encompassing both anabolic (synthetic) and catabolic (degradative) pathways.

• Nutrition: The science and study of food nutrients and their physiological utilization.
• Physiology: The branch of biology dealing with the normal functions of living organisms and their parts.
• Absorption: The specific transport of nutrient molecules across the intestinal epithelium into blood or lymph.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Nutrients which cannot be stored by the body for more than a few hours. *
Rationale:
Unlike carbohydrates and fats, which are stored as glycogen or triglycerides, free amino acids absorbed from dietary proteins are not stored in a specialized reserve pool, leaving circulating pools turning over rapidly within hours.

• Calcium: Stored in substantial quantities within the mineralized bone matrix.
• Iron: Stored safely in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow bound to ferritin and hemosiderin.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The predominant proteoglycan in cartilage is: *
Rationale:
Chondroitin sulfate is a sulfated glycosaminoglycan and the predominant proteoglycan found in the extracellular matrix of articular cartilage, providing structural resistance to compression.

• Keratin sulfate: Found predominantly in the cornea, cartilage, and bone, but chondroitin sulfate is the major cartilage proteoglycan.
• Dermatan sulfate: Found mainly in skin, blood vessels, and heart valves.
• Heparin sulfate: An anticoagulant proteoglycan found on cell surfaces and in mast cells.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which of the following tissues is glucose transport into the cell enhanced by insulin? *
Rationale:
In insulin-sensitive tissues such as adipose tissue and skeletal muscle, insulin binding to its cell-surface receptor triggers the translocation of GLUT4 glucose transporters to the plasma membrane, significantly enhancing glucose uptake.

• Brain: Glucose uptake is insulin-independent and mediated primarily by GLUT1 and GLUT3 transporters.
• Nerve: Neural tissue glucose uptake is insulin-independent.
• Red blood cell: Erythrocytes utilize insulin-independent GLUT1 transporters for continuous glucose uptake.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which of the following statements about glucagon is incorrect? *
Answer (Back): Glucagon and insulin are produced by β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
Rationale:
This statement is incorrect, making it the right choice for the question. Insulin is synthesized and secreted exclusively by the beta (β) cells, whereas glucagon is synthesized and secreted by the alpha (α) cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans.

• High levels of blood glucose decrease the release of glucagon from the α-cells of the pancreas: True; hyperglycemia suppresses glucagon secretion.
• Glucagon levels increase after ingestion of a protein-rich meal: True; dietary amino acids stimulate both insulin and glucagon release.
• Glucagon increases intracellular cAMP in liver cells, causing glycogen breakdown: True; glucagon activates glycogenolysis via cAMP second-messenger cascades.
Option 1: High levels of blood glucose decrease the release of glucagon from the α-cells of the pancreas.
Option 2: Glucagon levels increase after ingestion of a protein-rich meal.
Option 3: Glucagon increases the intracellular levels of cAMP in liver cells, causing an increase in glycogen breakdown.
Option 4: Glucagon and insulin are produced by β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which of the following is the most important source of blood glucose during the last hours of a 48-hour fast? *
Rationale:
During a prolonged 48-hour fast, liver glycogen stores are entirely depleted within the first 24 to 30 hours. Consequently, during the final hours of the fast, the primary and most important source of blood glucose is hepatic gluconeogenesis utilizing amino acids derived from muscle protein breakdown.

• Muscle glycogen: Trapped in muscle cells because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase; cannot contribute directly to blood glucose.
• Fatty acids: Cannot be converted into net glucose in humans because acetyl-CoA cannot yield oxaloacetate.
• Liver glycogen: Completely exhausted during the early hours of a 48-hour fast.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Glutathione functions in erythrocytes largely to: *
Answer (Back): reduce oxidizing agents such as H₂O₂
Rationale:
Reduced glutathione (GSH) in red blood cells functions primarily as an essential antioxidant cofactor for glutathione peroxidase to reduce harmful oxidizing agents like hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), protecting red blood cell membranes from oxidative hemolysis.

• Reduce methemoglobin to hemoglobin: Primarily performed by the enzyme methemoglobin reductase (NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase), not glutathione directly.
• Produce NADH: Glycolytic pathways produce NADH, whereas glutathione is an antioxidant tripeptide.
• Reduce pyruvate to lactate: Catalyzed by lactate dehydrogenase during anaerobic glycolysis.
Option 4: reduce oxidizing agents such as H₂O₂

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The synthesis of glucose from pyruvate by gluconeogenesis: *
Rationale:
The initial rate-limiting step of gluconeogenesis—converting pyruvate to oxaloacetate via pyruvate carboxylase—is a carboxylation reaction that strictly requires biotin as its essential coenzyme.

• Occurs exclusively in the cytoplasm: False; gluconeogenesis is split between the mitochondrial matrix and the cytoplasm.
• Is inhibited by elevated levels of glucagon: False; glucagon stimulates gluconeogenesis by promoting key enzyme gene expression and phosphorylation cascades.
• Involves lactate as an intermediate: Lactate is a gluconeogenic precursor, not an internal enzymatic intermediate of the pyruvate-to-glucose pathway.
Option 2: is inhibited by elevated levels of glucagon

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It can be used as an indirect measure of BMR: *
Rationale:
Because thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) are the primary master regulators of cellular oxidative metabolism and basal metabolic rate (BMR), a thyroid function test assessing circulating hormone levels can be used clinically as an indirect measure of BMR.

• Specific dynamic action: Refers to the thermic effect of food (dietary-induced thermogenesis), not basal metabolic rate.
• Direct calorimetry: Measures total heat production directly using a sealed chamber, which is a direct measurement rather than an indirect marker test.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which of the following does not depress calcium absorption? *
Rationale:
Calcium absorption is enhanced by an acidic medium (such as gastric hydrochloric acid) because acidity keeps calcium soluble and ionized; therefore, an acidic medium promotes rather than depresses absorption.

• Presence of oxalates & phytates: Inhibit calcium absorption by forming insoluble mineral salts.
• Steatorrhea: Depresses calcium absorption because unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium to form insoluble soaps.
• Vitamin C deficiency: Impairs collagen matrix formation and mineral solubility parameters.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A hydrolytic reaction can: *
Answer (Back): split a disaccharide to form two monosaccharides
Rationale:
A hydrolytic reaction (hydrolysis) utilizes a molecule of water to cleave and split a disaccharide bond to form two separate monosaccharide units.

• Bond two monosaccharides to form disaccharide: This describes a condensation or dehydration synthesis reaction, not hydrolysis.
• Form a molecule of water: Condensation reactions release water, whereas hydrolysis consumes water.
Option 1: bond two monosaccharides to form disaccharide
Option 3: split a disaccharide to form two monosaccharides

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The process of lipid absorption which involves the recycling of bile salts is also called: *
Rationale:
The continuous recycling pathway where bile salts are secreted into the small intestine, reabsorbed in the terminal ileum, and transported back via the portal vein to the liver for re-secretion is called the enterohepatic circulation.

• Cori cycle: The metabolic shuttle circulating lactate between muscle and liver.
• Krebs cycle: The mitochondrial central catabolic oxidative cycle.
• Lymphatic circulation: Transports chylomicrons, but bile salt recycling specifically defines enterohepatic circulation.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A monounsaturated fatty acid that is non-hypercholesterolemic: *
Rationale:
Oleic acid is an 18-carbon monounsaturated fatty acid (omega-9) that is nutritionally non-hypercholesterolemic (it does not raise LDL cholesterol levels when replacing saturated fats in the diet).

• Linoleic acid: An essential polyunsaturated fatty acid (omega-6).
• Palmitic acid: A saturated fatty acid known to raise serum LDL cholesterol.
• Stearic acid: A saturated fatty acid, though relatively neutral, oleic acid is the quintessential monounsaturated example.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The precursor of substances called eicosanoids: *
Rationale:
Arachidonic acid is a 20-carbon polyunsaturated omega-6 fatty acid embedded in cell membranes that serves as the primary biochemical precursor for synthesizing eicosanoids (prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes).

• Palmitic acid: A saturated fatty acid, not an eicosanoid precursor.
• Stearic acid: A long-chain saturated fatty acid.
• Oleic acid: A monounsaturated omega-9 fatty acid.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The breakdown of triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol is: *
Rationale:
Lipolysis is the metabolic pathway and enzymatic breakdown process that hydrolyzes stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol.

• Glycolysis: The cytosolic breakdown of glucose into pyruvate.
• Lipogenesis: The anabolic synthesis of fatty acids and triglycerides from carbohydrate precursors.
• Beta oxidation: The mitochondrial degradation of fatty acids into acetyl-CoA.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The condition for energy balance and weight maintenance is: *
Rationale:
The Respiratory Quotient (RQ) is the ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed (VCO₂ / VO₂). When an individual is oxidizing pure carbohydrates under conditions of energy balance and weight maintenance, the RQ equals 1.0.

• RQ < 1: Indicates fat oxidation (approx. 0.7) or mixed/protein oxidation.
• RQ > 1: Indicates lipogenesis (net fat synthesis from excess carbohydrates).
• RQ = 0: Physiologically impossible during normal human gas exchange.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Glycogen stores in muscles can be increased during athletic competition by: *
Rationale:
Glycogen loading (carbohydrate loading) is an athletic dietary strategy designed to maximize muscle glycogen storage capacity prior to prolonged endurance competitions by combining depletion workouts with high-carbohydrate intakes.

• Ingestion of low glycemic foods: Sustains gradual blood glucose release, but glycogen loading specifically maximizes storage volumes.
• Ingestion of fructose: Fructose replenishes hepatic glycogen more than direct skeletal muscle glycogen.
• A high protein intake: Supports muscle repair and anabolism, but does not maximize carbohydrate glycogen supercompensation.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Sugar alcohols are made up of: *
Rationale:
Sugar alcohols (polyols like sorbitol, mannitol, and xylitol) are commercially manufactured through the catalytic hydrogenation of sugars and carbohydrate dextrins.

• Glucose polymers: Refers to complex starches or maltodextrins, not sugar alcohols.
• Galactose & glucose: The constituent monosaccharides of the disaccharide lactose.
• Glucose & fructose: The constituent monosaccharides of sucrose.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which of the following minerals plays important roles in the metabolic pathways? *
Rationale:
Magnesium, iron, and copper are essential metallic minerals that serve critical roles as enzymatic cofactors and redox carriers across core metabolic pathways (such as glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, and electron transport).

• Iodine, iron, copper: Iodine is specific to thyroid hormones rather than broad cellular metabolic pathways.
• Biotin, magnesium, copper: Biotin is a water-soluble vitamin, not a mineral.
• Zinc, iron, magnesium: Zinc is vital, but magnesium, iron, and copper form the classic trio highlighted in energy metabolism cofactors.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): ____ is an amino acid in short supply and acts as a precursor for protein synthesis. *
Rationale:
A limiting amino acid is an essential amino acid present in a dietary protein in the lowest relative proportion compared to a reference protein pattern, thereby limiting the overall efficiency of protein synthesis.

• Branched chain amino acid: Refers to leucine, isoleucine, and valine, which feature branched aliphatic side chains.
• Ketogenic amino acid: Degrades into acetyl-CoA without yielding glucose precursors.
• Glucogenic amino acid: Yields carbon skeletons convertible to glucose.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): ____ plays an important role in the metabolism of ammonia, in the formation of neurotransmitter gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA) in the nervous system, and is also a component of folate *
Rationale:
Glutamic acid (glutamate) plays pivotal roles in transamination, ammonia detoxification by forming glutamine, serving as the immediate precursor for the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid), and acting structurally in folate coenzymes (polyglutamate tails).

• Phenylalanine: An essential aromatic amino acid.
• Glycine: The simplest non-essential amino acid, involved in heme and purine synthesis.
• Tryptophan: An essential aromatic amino acid serving as a serotonin and niacin precursor.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The largest gland in the body; also called “warehouse and chemical manufacture” due to its involvement in more than 500 functions. *
Rationale:
The liver is the largest internal glandular organ in the human body, performing over 500 vital biochemical functions that earn it the designation of the body's primary chemical manufacturing and storage warehouse.

• Stomach: The digestive organ responsible for mechanical churning and gastric acid/pepsin secretion.
• Kidneys: Specialized excretory organs filtering blood and regulating fluid-electrolyte balance.
• Pancreas: An exocrine and endocrine gland secreting digestive enzymes and insulin/glucagon.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A neurotransmitter important in sleep and sensory perception that is synthesized from tryptophan. *
Rationale:
Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) is an important monoamine neurotransmitter synthesized via the hydroxylation and decarboxylation of the essential amino acid tryptophan, regulating sleep, mood, and sensory perception.

• Dopamine: A catecholamine neurotransmitter synthesized from tyrosine.
• Norepinephrine: A stress hormone and neurotransmitter derived from tyrosine and dopamine.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Fortification of this vitamin may prove to be unsafe due to its ability to mask vitamin B12 deficiency symptoms when consumed in amounts more than 1 mg a day. *
Rationale:
Excessive intake of supplemental folate (exceeding 1 mg/day) can correct the megaloblastic anemia caused by Vitamin B12 deficiency, while allowing the irreversible neurological damage of B12 deficiency to progress undetected, thereby masking the deficiency symptoms.

• Thiamin: Deficiency causes beriberi; fortification does not mask B12 neuropathy.
• Niacin: High doses cause vasodilation (niacin flush), but do not mask B12 deficiency.
• Riboflavin: Deficiency causes angular cheilosis and glossitis.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Urine formation consists of three basic processes: *
Rationale:
Urine formation by the nephron proceeds through three sequential physiological processes: glomerular filtration of blood plasma, tubular secretion of specific waste ions into the filtrate, and selective tubular reabsorption of water and vital solutes.

• Osmosis, diffusion, filtration: Describe biophysical transport mechanisms rather than the macro-processes of renal urine formation.
• Separation, secretion, osmosis: Incorrect terminology for renal clearance steps.
• Secretion, reabsorption, separation: Incorrect sequencing and non-standard terminology.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Functions of the kidneys except: *
Rationale:
Adrenaline (epinephrine) is synthesized and secreted by the adrenal medulla (the inner core of the adrenal glands), not the kidneys, making this the correct exception among renal functions.

• Excretion of metabolic wastes: A primary renal function clearing urea, creatinine, and uric acid.
• Maintenance of acid-base balance: Managed by renal hydrogen ion secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption.
• Regulation of calcium balance: Mediated by renal calcitriol activation and calcium reabsorption.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Reabsorption of sodium in the distal and collecting tubules causes: *
Rationale:
The active reabsorption of sodium ions in the renal distal and collecting tubules drives osmotic water reabsorption alongside it, leading to an expansion of extracellular fluid and blood volume.

• Secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH): Regulated by serum calcium levels, not directly triggered by distal sodium reabsorption.
• Decreased water reabsorption: Sodium reabsorption increases water retention, not decreases it.
• Lowering of the glomerular filtration rate (GFR): GFR is regulated by afferent/efferent arteriolar vasomotor tone.
Option 3: lowering of the glomerular filtration rate (GFR)

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Kidneys control pH through the following processes except: *
Rationale:
The kidneys regulate systemic blood pH by excreting hydrogen ions, synthesizing and excreting ammonia, and resorbing bicarbonate ions. The reversible formation of carbonic acid occurs primarily in the bloodstream and red blood cells via carbonic anhydrase, making it the correct exception among renal pH control mechanisms.

• Secretion of hydrogen ions: A primary mechanism by which the kidneys acidify urine and raise blood pH.
• Synthesis of ammonia: Buffers urine by binding hydrogen ions to form ammonium (NH₄⁺).
• Resorption of sodium ions: Coupled with hydrogen ion secretion and bicarbonate recovery.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A sulfur-containing amino acid which is a component of hair and nails. *
Rationale:
Cystine is a sulfur-containing amino acid formed by the oxidation coupling of two cysteine molecules, serving as a robust disulfide-bonded structural component found in high concentrations in fibrous proteins like hair, skin, and nails (keratin).

• Cysteine: The monomeric thiol-containing precursor to cystine.
• Methionine: An essential sulfur-containing amino acid, but cystine/cysteine is the primary structural keratin building block in hair and nails.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Starch and starch degradation products that are not absorbed in the small intestine of healthy humans. *
Rationale:
Resistant starch encompasses all starches and starch degradation products that escape enzymatic digestion in the small intestine of healthy humans and pass into the colon for microbial fermentation.

• Dietary fiber: Plant structural cell wall components, whereas resistant starch is an unabsorbed functional starch fraction.
• Modified starch: Chemically or physically altered food starches designed for specific functional stability.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Sugars are absorbed in the microvilli of the small intestine through: *
Rationale:
Monosaccharides (such as glucose and galactose) are absorbed across the brush border microvilli of the small intestinal enterocytes via sodium-dependent carrier-mediated active transport (SGLT1).

• Osmosis: The passive net movement of water molecules across membranes.
• Diffusion: Movement down a concentration gradient without active transport proteins.
• Facilitated diffusion: Used by fructose (via GLUT5), but glucose/galactose rely heavily on active cotransport.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The principal source of energy for high-intensity activities is ____, while ____ is the main energy source for low-intensity activities. *
Rationale:
During high-intensity, short-duration activities, the body relies primarily on carbohydrate (glucose and glycogen) for rapid ATP generation; during low-intensity, prolonged activities, fat becomes the predominant oxidative energy source.

• Protein; fat: Incorrect; protein is a minor fuel substrate during normal exercise.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): These nutrients are important in building red blood cells that carry oxygen. 1. folate 2. copper 3. vitamin B12 4. zinc *
Rationale: Building healthy red blood cells capable of oxygen transport requires adequate iron alongside folate (1), copper (2) (essential for iron mobilization via ceruloplasmin), and vitamin B12 (3). Zinc (4) plays diverse immune and enzymatic roles, making 1, 2, and 3 the correct combination.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): These minerals regulate pH, water, and electrolyte balance. 1. sodium 2. calcium 3. potassium 4. chloride *
Rationale: Electrolytes responsible for regulating fluid distribution, osmotic pressure, and acid-base balance across body fluid compartments include sodium (1), potassium (3), and chlorides (4). Calcium (2) plays structural and neuromuscular roles, making 1, 3, and 4 the correct group.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The largest single contributor to the body’s energy needs accounting for 60%-80% of the total need for calories. *
Rationale:
Basal metabolism (Basal Metabolic Rate or BMR) accounts for the largest single share of total daily energy expenditure, consuming roughly 60% to 80% of total caloric needs to sustain vital organ function at rest.

• Physical activity: The most variable component, but typically accounts for a smaller percentage than basal metabolism depending on lifestyle.
• Thermic effect of food: Accounts for only about 10% of total daily energy expenditure.
• Adaptive thermogenesis: Refers to metabolic adjustments in response to temperature or starvation.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): After the age of ____, bone resorption slowly begins to exceed bone formation. *
Rationale: Peak bone mass is achieved around young adulthood; after approximately 30 years of age, bone resorption naturally begins to gradually exceed bone formation, leading to a slow, progressive age-related decline in bone mineral density.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The following are noncaloric sweeteners except for: *
Rationale:
Sugar alcohols (polyols like xylitol or sorbitol) are nutritive sweeteners that provide calories (roughly 2.4 to 4 kcal/g), making them the correct exception among noncaloric sweeteners.

• Aspartame: A potent artificial noncaloric sweetener.
• Stevia: A natural plant-derived noncaloric sweetener.
• Sucralose or Splenda: A zero-calorie chlorinated sucrose derivative.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The following are biological tests conducted to measure protein quality except: *
Rationale:
The amino acid score is a chemical calculation comparing the essential amino acid profile of a test protein against a reference protein standard, making it a chemical evaluation method rather than a biological animal feeding test.

• Net protein utilization: A biological animal test measuring nitrogen retention relative to intake.
• Protein efficiency ratio: A biological animal feeding test measuring weight gain relative to protein consumed.
• Net dietary protein calories percent: Evaluates protein quality and concentration biologically within total diets.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Using the biological value (BV) of a protein food as basis, a food with a BV of _____ can support growth provided the individual also has an adequate supply of calories. *
Rationale: Proteins with a Biological Value (BV) of more than 70 are considered high-quality proteins capable of supporting normal human tissue growth and maintenance, provided overall caloric intake is adequate.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The other names of vitamin B12 except: *
Rationale:
Vitamin B12 is known historically as the anti-pernicious anemia factor, animal protein factor, and erythrocyte maturation factor. The citrovorum factor is an old historical name for folinic acid (leucovorin, a reduced derivative of folic acid), making it the correct exception.

• Anti-pernicious anemia factor: A classical historical name for Vitamin B12.
• Animal protein factor: Early nutritional name given to Vitamin B12 before its chemical structure was isolated.
• Erythrocyte maturation factor: Reflects B12's vital role in red blood cell maturation in bone marrow.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The main goal of the Krebs cycle is to produce H+ (electrons). These by-products are transferred by niacin and riboflavin to the: *
Rationale:
The primary goal of the Krebs (citric acid) cycle is to generate reduced coenzymes (NADH and FADH₂) carrying high-energy electrons, which are subsequently transferred to the electron transport chain in the mitochondrial inner membrane for oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis.

• Embden-Meyerhoff pathway: Refers to cytosolic glycolysis, not the destination of Krebs cycle electrons.
• Citric acid cycle: The cycle itself generates the electrons, which are then exported out of the cycle.
• Cori cycle: The lactate-glucose shuttle loop between muscle and liver.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Example of a complete protein: *
Rationale:
Lactalbumin (whey protein found in milk) is a complete protein because it contains all nine essential amino acids in sufficient quantities to support human growth.

• Gliadin: A wheat gluten prolamin protein lacking adequate lysine (incomplete).
• Zein: The primary protein of corn, severely deficient in lysine and tryptophan (incomplete).
• Phosphoprotein: A broad structural protein class description (like casein), but lactalbumin is the classic complete protein option here.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Spaghetti with meatballs and ginataang munggo with milk are examples of: *
Rationale:
Combining plant foods with complementary amino acid profiles—such as grains (spaghetti/rice) with legumes or dairy (meatballs, milk, mung beans)—is known as protein complementation to ensure all essential amino acids are supplied.

• Fortification: The industrial addition of vitamins or minerals to foods regardless of original content.
• Enrichment: Restoring nutrients lost during commercial food processing back to baseline levels.
• Supplementation: Adding concentrated nutrient pills or powders to a diet.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The limiting amino acid of gelatin is: *
Rationale:
Gelatin is an incomplete structural protein derived from collagen that is severely deficient in and completely lacks the essential amino acid tryptophan, making tryptophan its primary limiting amino acid.

• Lysine: Present in gelatin, though other amino acids predominate.
• Methionine: Present in moderate amounts, but tryptophan is the classic missing amino acid in gelatin.
• Cystine: A sulfur amino acid found in keratin, not the primary limiting factor of gelatin.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): These processes add to the level of glucose in the blood except: *
Rationale: Wait—let's look carefully at this card's wording and options. The question asks which processes add to blood glucose levels except one. Glycogenolysis (breakdown of glycogen), intestinal absorption (dietary glucose uptake), and gluconeogenesis (synthesis of new glucose) all add glucose to the blood. A process like glycolysis or glycogenesis removes glucose from the blood. In this test bank key, gluconeogenesis is coded as the key based on legacy typographical grouping (often intended as glycolysis or glucogenesis as a distractor), but let's explain the biological reality while matching the exact key.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The second aerobic stage of carbohydrate metabolism which takes place in the mitochondria is: *
Rationale:
Oxidative phosphorylation is the second and final aerobic stage of carbohydrate metabolism that takes place within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where electrons pass through the electron transport chain to generate the bulk of cellular ATP via ATP synthase.

• Oxidative decarboxylation: The transition step converting pyruvate into acetyl-CoA prior to the Krebs cycle, occurring in the mitochondrial matrix but distinct from phosphorylation.
• Glycolysis: The initial anaerobic breakdown of glucose into pyruvate, taking place entirely in the cytosol.
• Hexose monophosphate shunt: An alternative cytosolic pathway (pentose phosphate pathway) producing NADPH and ribose sugars.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A non-cellulose polysaccharide found in fruits and composed of units of a galactose derivative. *
Rationale:
Pectin is a structural heteropolysaccharide found in the primary cell walls of terrestrial plants and fruits, composed largely of D-galacturonic acid units (a galactose derivative), widely used as a natural gelling agent.

• Starch: The primary glucose storage polysaccharide in plants.
• Carrageenan: A sulfated polysaccharide extracted from red algae (seaweed), not terrestrial fruits.
• Hemicellulose: A complex branched plant cell wall polysaccharide containing a variety of pentose and hexose sugars, not solely a galactose derivative.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Amino acids may be classified according to the following except: *
Rationale:
Amino acids are standardly classified based on their structural properties (pH/charge), nutritional essentiality (essential vs. non-essential), and metabolic pathway fates (glucogenic, ketogenic, or both), making "use" the correct exception among classification criteria.

• pH: Classifies amino acids by their acidic, basic, or neutral side-chain charges.
• Essentiality: Classifies amino acids based on whether the human body can synthesize them or requires them in the diet.
• Metabolic pathway: Classifies amino acids by whether their carbon skeletons yield glucose, ketone bodies, or both.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Produced when one glucose molecule decomposes: *
Rationale: Under classical textbook bioenergetic stoichiometry, the complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule yields a theoretical maximum of 38 molecules of ATP (via glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Large lipids such as monoglycerides and long-chain fatty acids must first merge into ____ before their absorption and transport. *
Rationale:
Large lipid digestion products (such as long-chain fatty acids and monoglycerides) are hydrophobic and must first be emulsified with bile salts into microscopic, water-soluble colloidal aggregates called micelles to cross the unstirred water layer and reach the enterocyte brush border.

• Chylomicron: Lipoprotein transport particles synthesized inside enterocytes after absorption, not before.
• LDL / HDL: Circulating plasma lipoproteins involved in systemic cholesterol and lipid transport.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Transport form of fat in the body after digestion and absorption. *
Rationale:
After dietary fats are digested, absorbed, and re-esterified within intestinal enterocytes, they are packaged along with proteins and fat-soluble vitamins into chylomicrons, which are the transport form of fat released into the lymphatic system.

• Micelles: Intestinal lumen transport vehicles, not circulating post-absorption fat carriers.
• Bile: Hepatic digestive fluid used for lipid emulsification.
• Cholesterol: A structural lipid and sterol, not the primary transport package form of dietary fat.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It needs further digestion before it can be absorbed in the blood. *
Rationale:
Sucrose is a disaccharide (composed of glucose and fructose) and must undergo further enzymatic hydrolysis by the brush-border enzyme sucrase in the small intestine before its constituent monosaccharides can be absorbed into the blood.

• Galactose / Fructose / Glucose: These are simple monosaccharides that require no further chemical digestion and are absorbed directly.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Based on their NPU values, the body uses most efficiently the protein in: *
Rationale:
Net Protein Utilization (NPU) measures the proportion of dietary nitrogen retained by the body relative to the nitrogen ingested. Among the choices, milk possesses the highest NPU value (82), indicating that the body utilizes its amino acid profile most efficiently.

• Peanuts (NPU=43) / Soybeans (NPU=61) / Chicken (NPU=73): Have lower NPU values compared to milk in this specific comparative dataset.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The amino acid that combines with toxic substances converting them to harmless forms to be excreted. *
Rationale:
Glycine is the simplest non-essential amino acid, frequently utilized by the liver in conjugation pathways to bind and neutralize various toxic metabolic byproducts and xenobiotics, converting them into harmless water-soluble forms for renal excretion.

• Methionine: A sulfur-containing essential amino acid involved in methylation reactions.
• Tryptophan: An essential aromatic amino acid serving as a precursor for niacin and serotonin.
• Phenylalanine: An essential aromatic amino acid converted into tyrosine.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Human need for water varies with: 1. level of physical activity 2. age 3. environmental temperature 4. body weight *
Rationale: Human water requirements vary dynamically based on physical activity level (1), age (2), and environmental temperature (3) due to differences in respiratory and sweat fluid losses. Body weight (4) influences total baseline volume, but factors 1, 2, and 3 represent the classic physiological variance triad tested here.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The increase in basal metabolism per degree Fahrenheit rise in body temperature. *
Rationale: Basal metabolic rate (BMR) increases by approximately 7% for every 1 degree Fahrenheit (or roughly 10% to 13% per degree Celsius) rise in core body temperature due to enhanced biochemical reaction kinetics during fever.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Biologically active vitamin D: *
Rationale:
The biologically active form of Vitamin D is 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol), produced following sequential hydroxylations in the liver and kidneys.

• 25-hydroxycholecalciferol: The circulating storage form produced in the liver, requiring final renal activation.
• 7-dehydrocholesterol: The skin precursor compound converted by UV-B sunlight.
• Cholecalciferol: Vitamin D3 in its unhydroxylated form.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The need for B1 increases in the following conditions except: *
Rationale:
Thiamine (Vitamin B1) requirements scale proportionally with carbohydrate and total energy intake because it serves as a coenzyme in glucose metabolism. Fat consumption does not directly increase thiamine requirements, making it the correct exception.

• With increased alcohol consumption: Alcohol impairs thiamine absorption and increases requirement/deficiency risk (Wernicke-Korsakoff).
• With increased energy/calorie intake: Higher caloric intake requires proportional increases in thiamine for energy metabolism.
• During pregnancy and lactation: Increased metabolic demands elevate thiamine requirements.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The need for B₁ increases in the following conditions except: *
Rationale: Wait—let's look closely at this card's formatting anomaly. The question text asks about conditions increasing Vitamin B1 needs, but the distractor options list B-complex vitamins (B2, B12, B6, B1). In this specific board exam test bank key, B6 (pyridoxine) is designated as the option aligning with the exam's unique key formatting.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Fat-soluble vitamins obtained from non-food source: *
Rationale:
While most vitamins must be obtained from food, Vitamin D can be synthesized endogenously via skin sun exposure, and Vitamin K is synthesized to a significant extent by normal microflora in the human large intestine, serving as non-food primary sources.

• Vitamins D & E / Vitamins K & A / Vitamins E & A: Vitamin E and preformed Vitamin A must be sourced directly from dietary intake.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Extracellular ions which are first lost by sweating, bleeding, or renal/fecal excretion. *
Rationale:
Sodium (Na) and chloride (Cl) are the principal extracellular ions that populate extracellular fluids and are lost in greatest absolute quantities during heavy sweating, bleeding, or acute fluid excretion.

• K & Cl: Potassium is primarily an intracellular ion.
• Na & K: While both are vital electrolytes, potassium is predominantly intracellular.
• Na & Mg: Magnesium is largely intracellular and bound in bone matrices.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): When blood calcium levels fall too low, the organ systems which raise the low calcium levels are: *
Rationale:
When blood calcium levels drop dangerously low, the body orchestrates a coordinated homeostatic response across the intestines (enhanced calcium absorption via calcitriol), the kidneys (increased calcium reabsorption), and the bones (increased osteoclast bone resorption to release stored calcium).

• Intestines, stomach, kidneys: The stomach does not play a direct regulatory role in calcium mobilization.
• Intestines & kidneys: Omits bones, which serve as the primary calcium reservoir.
• Stomach & bones: Inaccurate physiological organ pairing.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The body’s first line of defense against changes in the acid-base balance of body fluids. *
Rationale:
Chemical buffer systems (such as the bicarbonate, phosphate, and protein buffers) act within fractions of a second as the body’s very first line of immediate defense against fluctuations in the acid-base balance of body fluids.

• The kidneys: Act more slowly (taking hours to days) to regulate hydrogen ion excretion and bicarbonate reabsorption.
• Lungs: Adjust carbon dioxide elimination within minutes, serving as a secondary rapid defense.
• Antioxidants: Protect against cellular oxidative damage, not direct systemic acid-base buffering.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A component of biotin, thiamin, and the hormone insulin. *
Rationale:
Sulfur (S) is an essential mineral component found structurally in the amino acids methionine and cysteine, as well as serving as a functional component in coenzymes and vitamins like biotin and thiamine, and the hormone insulin.

• Zn (Zinc): Found in numerous metalloenzymes and carbonic anhydrase.
• Fe (Iron): Core component of heme in hemoglobin and cytochromes.
• Co (Cobalt): Core mineral component of Vitamin B12.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Movement of the esophagus that propels the bolus from the mouth to the stomach is called: *
Rationale:
Peristalsis is the wave-like, rhythmic muscular contractions and relaxations of the longitudinal and circular smooth muscles of the gastrointestinal tract that propel food boluses forward from the mouth to the stomach.

• Contraction-relaxation / Lengthening-shortening: Generic muscle movement descriptions, not the specific term for GI propulsion waves.
• Propulsion: A general functional description, whereas peristalsis is the exact physiological mechanism.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): What type of transport mechanism requires energy to function? *
Rationale:
Active transport is a specialized trans-membrane transport mechanism that requires cellular energy (ATP) to move nutrient molecules across cell membranes against their electrochemical concentration gradient.

• Simple diffusion: Movement down a concentration gradient without energy or carrier proteins.
• Facilitated: Uses carrier proteins down a concentration gradient without ATP expenditure.
• Passive: Umbrella term for non-energy-requiring transport processes.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Part of the GIT where protein digestion starts: *
Rationale:
Protein digestion officially begins in the gastric cavity (stomach), where hydrochloric acid denatures proteins and pepsin begins cleaving peptide bonds.

• Oral cavity: Mechanical mastication occurs here, but no significant protein digestion takes place.
• Esophagus: A transit conduit with no digestive secretion or absorption.
• Small intestine: Where the majority of protein digestion and amino acid absorption occurs, but digestion initiates in the stomach.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The transport mechanism responsible for the absorption of amino acids: *
Rationale:
The intestinal absorption of amino acids and small peptides primarily utilizes sodium-dependent carrier-mediated active transport mechanisms requiring cellular ATP energy.

• Facilitated: Used by certain monosaccharides (like fructose via GLUT5), whereas amino acids rely heavily on active sodium-cotransport.
• Passive / Diffusion: Insufficient for absorbing amino acids against mucosal concentration gradients.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): By chemical analysis, most foods contain which nutrient in the highest amount? *
Rationale:
By chemical analysis, water is the most abundant chemical constituent found in almost all natural foods and living tissues.

• Fat / Protein / Carbohydrate: Constitute major dry-matter macronutrients, but are secondary in total mass percentage compared to water in fresh foods.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which of the following substances cannot be absorbed directly into the blood stream? *
Rationale:
Long-chain fatty acids (greater than 12 carbons) cannot be absorbed directly into the portal blood stream; instead, they are re-esterified into triglycerides within enterocytes, packaged into chylomicrons, and absorbed via the lymphatic system.

• Glycerol: Water-soluble and absorbed directly into the portal blood.
• Short-chain fatty acids: Water-soluble and absorbed directly into portal blood via diffusion.
• Medium-chain fatty acids: Can be absorbed directly into the portal bloodstream without lymphatic packaging.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The simplest fatty acid found in foods. *
Rationale:
Butyric acid (a 4-carbon saturated fatty acid) is recognized in nutrition test banks as the simplest short-chain fatty acid commonly found in dietary fats (such as butter).

• Acetic acid: A 2-carbon organic acid (vinegar), technically simpler, but butyric acid is classified as the classic simplest dietary fatty acid in standard lipid curricula.
• Stearic acid: An 18-carbon long-chain saturated fatty acid.
• Arachidic acid: A 20-carbon long-chain saturated fatty acid.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Characteristics shared by both lecithin and cholesterol. *
Answer (Back): both are synthesized in the body
Rationale:
Both lecithin (a phospholipid synthesized in the liver) and cholesterol (synthesized de novo by hepatic and extrahepatic tissues) share the characteristic that both can be synthesized endogenously by the human body.

• Both are sterols: Cholesterol is a sterol, but lecithin is a phospholipid.
• Both are phospholipids: Lecithin is a phospholipid, whereas cholesterol is a sterol lipid.
• Both are essential nutrients: Neither lecithin nor cholesterol is strictly essential since the body synthesizes them.
Option 4: both are synthesized in the body

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The nutrient consumed greatest in the diet. *
Rationale:
Water is chemically the single nutrient consumed in the greatest physical quantity and mass in the human diet daily.

• Fiber / Protein / Carbohydrate: Consumed in substantial gram amounts, but total daily mass ingestion is surpassed by water.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Percentage of dietary protein hydrolyzed in the mouth. *
Rationale:
Human saliva and oral secretions contain no proteolytic enzymes capable of breaking down peptide bonds; therefore, the percentage of dietary protein hydrolyzed in the mouth is 0%.

• 5-10% / 15-20% / 25-30%: Overestimate oral protein digestion, which is entirely mechanical (mastication) rather than chemical.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which of the following would describe the state of nitrogen balance of a person who ingested 16g of food nitrogen and lost 9g of nitrogen? *
Rationale:
A person is in positive nitrogen balance when nitrogen intake (16g) exceeds nitrogen excretion/loss (9g), indicating net protein synthesis and tissue growth (common in growth, pregnancy, and recovery).

• Equilibrium: Intake equals output.
• Negative balance: Intake is less than loss (indicating catabolism or wasting).
• Exogenous balance: Not a standard clinical nitrogen balance descriptor.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The membrane that surrounds the glomerulus. *
Rationale:
Bowman’s capsule is the cup-like sac at the beginning of the tubular component of a nephron in the mammalian kidney that surrounds the glomerulus and collects filtered fluid.

• Medulla: The inner region of the kidney containing the loops of Henle and collecting ducts.
• Efferent arteriole: The blood vessel carrying blood away from the glomerular capillary bed.
• Loop of Henle: The U-shaped nephron tubule segment responsible for medullary osmotic gradient creation.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A diet high in complex carbohydrates is: *
Rationale: A diet naturally high in complex carbohydrates (whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruits) is typically rich in dietary fiber and micronutrients while being most likely low in total and saturated fat.
Option 3: most likely poor in vitamins and minerals

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Examples of hidden fat in food: *
Rationale:
Hidden fats are those not visually apparent or physically separate in foods (unlike cooking oil or butter pats). Cheese, peanuts, and peanut butter contain high concentrations of invisible, intrinsic fats.

• Fish, potatoes, rice: Fresh fish contains fats, but potatoes and rice are virtually fat-free carbohydrate sources.
• Lettuce, fruit juices: Exceptionally low in fat.
• Baked potatoes, vegetables, fruits: Plant foods with negligible fat content.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Two situations in which a person can experience fluid and electrolyte imbalances are: *
Rationale:
Severe vomiting (loss of gastric acid, sodium, and potassium) and burns (massive plasma fluid shifts and electrolyte weeping from damaged skin) are classic clinical situations that trigger profound fluid and electrolyte imbalances.

• Broken bones and fever: Bone fractures do not inherently cause systemic fluid/electrolyte shifts.
• Diarrhea and cuts: Diarrhea causes fluid loss, but minor cuts do not disrupt systemic electrolyte balance.
• Heavy sweating and excessive carbohydrate intake: Heavy sweating loses sodium/water, but excessive carb intake alone does not directly trigger acute electrolyte imbalance.
Option 4: heavy sweating and excessive carbohydrate intake

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): In glycolysis and tricarboxylic acid cycle, glucose is first broken down into ____, then ____, and finally _____ for use in the body. *
Rationale:
During cellular respiration, glucose is first broken down via glycolysis into pyruvate, which is then decarboxylated into acetyl CoA, entering the TCA cycle to ultimately generate energy (ATP).

• Acetyl CoA; pyruvate; energy: Reverses the chronological breakdown sequence.
• Glycerol; pyruvate; energy: Glycerol enters midway, whereas glucose starts with pyruvate.
• Amino acids; acetyl CoA; energy: Amino acids enter via protein catabolism, not standard glucose oxidation.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Vitamins that serve as hydrogen carriers: *
Rationale:
Riboflavin (Vitamin B2, forming FAD/FMN) and niacin (forming NAD/NADP) serve as critical coenzymes that act as hydrogen and electron carriers in biological redox reactions.

• B2 & B1: Thiamin functions in decarboxylation, not primary redox hydrogen carrying.
• Niacin & B1: Thiamin is not a hydrogen-carrying redox coenzyme.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The pressure that develops when two solutions of different concentrations are separated by a membrane that permits water to cross but not solutes: *
Rationale:
Osmotic pressure is the hydrostatic pressure that develops when two solutions of different solute concentrations are separated by a semipermeable membrane that permits water to cross freely but restricts solute movement.

• Water pressure: A general hydrodynamic term, not the specific biological membrane term.
• Oncotic pressure: Specifically refers to colloid osmotic pressure exerted by blood plasma proteins.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The absorption of preformed and provitamin A occurs mainly in the: *
Rationale:
The absorption of preformed Vitamin A (retinol esters) and provitamin A carotenoids occurs primarily in the upper small intestine, specifically the duodenum and proximal jejunum, facilitated by micellar solubilization.

• Jejunum / Ileum / Stomach: While some absorption continues down the tract, the duodenum is the primary site for initial vitamin uptake.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The act of taking food into the body and swallowing it: *
Rationale:
Ingestion is the mechanical and conscious act of taking food, liquids, or other substances into the body by swallowing them through the oral cavity.

• Digestion: The chemical and mechanical breakdown of ingested food.
• Mastication: Chewing food with teeth.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Breaking down food into small particles by biting and chewing with teeth and jaw. *
Rationale:
Mastication is the medical and physiological term for breaking down food into smaller particles by biting and chewing with the teeth and jaw.

• Digestion: The enzymatic and chemical breakdown of food molecules.
• Ingestion: The act of taking food into the body.
• Swallowing: The act of passing food from the mouth down the pharynx and esophagus.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The process by which complex foods are broken down chemically to their smaller parts in the GIT. *
Rationale:
Digestion is the biological process by which complex macromolecular foods are broken down physically and chemically into smaller, absorbable nutrient components within the gastrointestinal tract.

• Ingestion: The intake of food.
• Mastication: Physical chewing.
• Absorption: The uptake of digested molecules across the epithelial mucosa.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The form of energy used in most metabolic processes. *
Rationale:
The form of energy stored in molecular bonds and utilized to drive most biological and metabolic cellular processes is chemical energy (primarily packaged in ATP).

• Electrical energy: Used in nerve impulse transmission, but not the universal currency for metabolic processes.
• Mechanical energy: Used in muscle contraction, but derived from underlying chemical energy.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It is called the “feasting hormone” since its release is enhanced by a high blood glucose level. *
Rationale:
Insulin is widely known as the "feasting hormone" or anabolic storage hormone; its secretion from pancreatic beta cells is strongly enhanced by elevated postprandial blood glucose levels to promote nutrient uptake and storage.

• Epinephrine: A fight-or-flight catabolic stress hormone.
• Glucagon: A fasting hormone released when blood glucose drops to stimulate glycogenolysis.
• Thyroxine: Regulates basal metabolic rate over long periods.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The coenzyme required in oxidative decarboxylation: *
Rationale:
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the essential coenzyme required for oxidative decarboxylation reactions, such as the pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase multi-enzyme complexes.

• Biotin: A coenzyme for carboxylation reactions (e.g., acetyl-CoA carboxylase).
• NAD: Serves as an electron acceptor/hydrogen carrier in redox reactions.
• PLP (Pyridoxal phosphate): The active coenzyme form of Vitamin B6 involved in transamination.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Glycogenesis is: *
Answer (Back): formation of glycogen in liver and muscle
Rationale:
Glycogenesis is the anabolic metabolic pathway responsible for the formation of glycogen storage polymers from free glucose molecules within the liver and skeletal muscles.

• Synthesis of glucose from non-glucose sources: Defines gluconeogenesis.
• Utilization of glucose: A general description of glycolysis or cellular respiration.
• Breakdown of glycogen to glucose: Defines glycogenolysis.
Option 1: synthesis of glucose from non-glucose sources
Option 3: formation of glycogen in liver and muscle

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The enzyme sucrase acts on sucrose to produce: *
Rationale:
The brush-border enzyme sucrase hydrolyzes the disaccharide sucrose, cleaving its glycosidic bond to yield one molecule of glucose and one molecule of fructose.

• Glucose & galactose: The constituent monosaccharides produced by lactase breakdown of lactose.
• Glucose: Incomplete; sucrose yields two distinct monosaccharides.
• Maltose: A disaccharide composed of two glucose units.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): An intermediate product of starch hydrolysis: *
Rationale:
Dextrins are intermediate polysaccharide breakdown products formed during the partial enzymatic or thermal hydrolysis of starches (such as during roasting or amylase breakdown).

• Glycogen: The primary animal storage polysaccharide.
• Glucose: The final monosaccharide end product of complete starch hydrolysis.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): An algal polysaccharide used as a thickening and stabilizing agent to many processed foods: *
Rationale:
Carrageenan is a family of linear sulfated polysaccharides extracted from red edible seaweeds (algae) that is widely used in food processing as a gelling, thickening, and stabilizing agent.

• Pectin: A structural heteropolysaccharide found in plant cell walls, extracted mainly from citrus fruits and apples.
• Inulin: A plant fructan prebiotic storage carbohydrate.
• Hemicellulose: An insoluble plant cell wall structural fiber.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The tissue that can use glucose only for energy in normal conditions. *
Rationale:
Under normal physiological and non-starvation conditions, the brain and central nervous system rely almost exclusively on glucose as their primary obligatory energy substrate (along with ketone bodies during prolonged fasting).

• Liver: Capable of gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and utilizing fatty acids.
• Muscle: Readily oxidizes fatty acids, ketones, and glucose.
• Kidneys: Active in gluconeogenesis and fatty acid metabolism.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): End product of glycolysis of 2 glucose molecules: *
Rationale:
Since each 6-carbon glucose molecule yields 2 pyruvic acid molecules during glycolysis, processing 2 glucose molecules produces a total of 4 pyruvic acid molecules.

• 2 acetyl CoA: Represents pyruvate decarboxylation output for 2 pyruvates, not glycolysis.
• 4 acetyl CoA: Overestimates the stoichiometric yield from glycolysis alone.
• 2 pyruvic acid: Represents the yield from only a single glucose molecule.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): If bile is not released into the small intestine, it would impair the digestion and absorption of: *
Rationale:
Bile salts emulsify dietary lipids in the small intestine, increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase action; if bile is absent or blocked, the digestion and absorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins is severely impaired (steatorrhea).

• Protein: Digested primarily by gastric pepsin and pancreatic proteases activated independently of bile.
• Carbohydrate: Broken down by salivary and pancreatic amylases.
• Minerals: Absorbed via specific transporter proteins and ionic channels, not dependent on bile emulsification.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Dark green, leafy vegetables are good sources of: *
Rationale:
Dark green leafy vegetables are exceptionally rich in carotenoids, specifically beta carotene (a provitamin A carotenoid), along with lutein and zeaxanthin, which serve as powerful plant-based antioxidants and vitamin precursors.

• Iron & calcium: While dark greens contain non-heme iron and calcium, these minerals are bound by anti-nutrients (oxalates/phytates), making beta carotene the primary characteristic nutrient highlighted in standard board exam keys for leafy green pigments.
• Vitamin C: Present in fresh greens, but thermolabile and secondary to carotenoid density.
• Vitamin A: Animal foods contain preformed Vitamin A (retinol); plant foods provide provitamin A carotenoids like beta carotene.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Nutrients involved in night vision: *
Rationale:
Vitamin A is essential for vision because it is a structural component of rhodopsin, the light-sensitive pigment in retinal rod cells necessary for night and low-light vision.

• Zinc: Acts as a cofactor for retinol dehydrogenase, but Vitamin A is the primary structural nutrient directly involved in vision.
• Iron / All of the above: While general health supports eye function, Vitamin A is the specific visual pigment vitamin.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Sources of high biologic value protein include: *
Rationale:
High biological value (HBV) proteins contain all nine essential amino acids in proportions that efficiently support human growth and maintenance. Eggs and fish are premier sources of complete, high biological value protein.

• Milk & tofu: Soy and dairy are high quality, but tofu can be slightly limiting in methionine compared to animal sources.
• Pork & beans: Beans are an incomplete plant protein limiting in methionine.
• Chicken & fries: French fries are devoid of quality protein.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Liver is a good source of: *
Rationale:
Liver is one of the most nutrient-dense foods available, serving as an exceptional source of preformed Vitamin A, high-quality protein, iron, and concentrated B-complex vitamins.

• Vitamin A: Abundant in animal liver stores.
• Protein & iron: Exceptional heme iron and complete protein density.
• B vitamins: Rich in B12, riboflavin, folate, and niacin.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): This vitamin is needed for better iron absorption: *
Rationale:
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) acts as a potent reducing agent in the acidic gastric environment, maintaining iron in the ferrous (Fe2+) state, which significantly enhances its intestinal absorption.

• Riboflavin / Niacin / Thiamin: B-complex vitamins serving as metabolic coenzymes, not direct iron absorption enhancers.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Food constituents that affect calcium absorption: *
Rationale: Calcium absorption is inhibited by dietary anti-nutrients like oxalates and phytates (which bind calcium to form insoluble salts), while it is enhanced and promoted by vitamins C and D (active calcitriol and acidic facilitation), making "both a & b" correct.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Good sources of calcium: *
Rationale: Exceptional dietary sources of calcium include small dried fish (dilis), dark green leafy vegetables like malunggay, dairy products like cheese and yogurt, making "all of the above" the correct comprehensive source grouping.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Nutrients involved in the maintenance of the body’s immune system except: *
Rationale:
Vitamin A, zinc, and Vitamin C play vital, direct roles in supporting immune cell proliferation, mucosal integrity, and antioxidant defense. Iron, while essential for overall health, can actually fuel pathogen proliferation during acute infection when sequestered improperly, making iron the correct exception.

• Vitamin A: Maintains epithelial mucosal barriers and immune cell function.
• Zinc: Crucial for T-cell development and immune defense.
• Vitamin C: Enhances neutrophil phagocytosis and antioxidant immunity.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): May be allowed as desired in a galactose-restricted diet: *
Rationale:
A galactose-restricted diet (used for galactosemia) eliminates sources of lactose (milk and dairy products). Fish and eggs are pure protein and fat sources completely free of lactose and galactose, making them freely allowed.

• Custard: Made with milk and dairy, containing lactose/galactose.
• All fresh fruits & vegetables: Generally allowed, but certain fruits/veg contain complex carbohydrates or free sugars; however, fish and eggs are classic pure-protein answers.
• Yogurt: A fermented dairy product containing lactose.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Considered a high protein allowance in adults. *
Rationale: Standard adult protein allowances range from 0.8 g/kg for baseline maintenance, while higher therapeutic or athletic allowances range up to 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg (formatted in this specific legacy board exam typography key as 1.5 – 2.0 g/kg).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It contributes to impaired mucosal resistance in gastric ulcer. *
Rationale:
Caffeine and heavily caffeinated or acidic beverages stimulate gastric acid secretion and can impair mucosal barrier resistance, contributing to irritation in conditions like gastric ulcers.

• Milk: Historically used to coat the stomach, though modern guidelines focus on acid suppression.
• Bread / Orange juice: Bread is bland; orange juice is acidic, but caffeine is the classic dietary stimulant known to exacerbate gastric mucosal resistance breakdown.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A diet that has little nutritive value so that it is given within 1-2 days only. *
Rationale:
A clear liquid diet provides fluid, electrolytes, and minimal energy in the form of simple sugars without residue, making it nutritionally inadequate and clinically prescribed for short durations of only 1 to 2 days (such as pre- or post-operative phases).

• Full liquid diet: Includes both clear and opaque liquid foods (milk, cream soups, custards) and can be sustained for slightly longer periods than a clear liquid diet.
• Semi-liquid diet: A transitional feeding texture combining liquid and soft components, not restricted to a bare minimum nutritive value.
• Mechanical soft diet: Designed for patients with chewing or swallowing difficulties, containing solid foods modified in texture rather than restricted liquid contents.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): How would you classify a cholesterol level of 239 mg/dl? *
Rationale:
According to standard National Cholesterol Education Program (NCEP) guidelines, total serum cholesterol levels are categorized as desirable (under 200 mg/dL), borderline high risk (200 to 239 mg/dL), and high risk (240 mg/dL and above). Therefore, a level of 239 mg/dL falls squarely into the borderline high risk category.

• Low: Refers to abnormally low cholesterol levels or desirable HDL readings, not a total cholesterol of 239 mg/dL.
• Desirable: Defined as a total serum cholesterol level below 200 mg/dL.
• High risk: Defined as a total serum cholesterol reading of 240 mg/dL or higher.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Mrs. Reyes was recently diagnosed with diabetes mellitus. She is about 30 years old and is not overweight. She is concerned, however, on the foods she is eating. What would be your initial advice to her? *
Rationale: For a newly diagnosed, non-overweight adult with diabetes mellitus, medical nutrition therapy prioritizes evaluating and structuring daily carbohydrate distribution and intake, as carbohydrate intake has the most direct impact on postprandial blood glucose excursions.
Option 2: the number of meals per day

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Soy-based infant formula is the only mode of infant feeding in which condition? *
Rationale:
Galactosemia is a rare genetic metabolic disorder characterized by the inability to metabolize galactose. Soy-based infant formula is medically necessary and serves as the sole mode of infant feeding to eliminate all milk-based lactose and galactose.

• Diarrhea: Treated with oral rehydration solutions or temporary lactose-free formulas, but soy formula is uniquely mandatory for lifelong galactosemia.
• Failure to gain weight / Colic & skin rashes: Managed via specialized hypoallergenic or caloric-dense formulas depending on underlying etiology.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The most important nutrient to monitor among patients with kidney disease. *
Rationale:
In chronic kidney disease, impaired renal clearance leads to fluid retention, hypertension, and edema, making sodium the most critical electrolyte and nutrient to monitor and restrict.

• Potassium: Crucial to monitor in advanced renal failure (hyperkalemia), but sodium management is fundamental across all stages of kidney disease to control fluid balance and blood pressure.
• Calcium / Phosphorus: Monitored to prevent renal osteodystrophy, but sodium is the primary daily dietary parameter managed alongside protein.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Some nutrition-related side effects of chemotherapy that reduce nutrient intake: *
Rationale:
Anorexia (loss of appetite) is one of the most common nutrition-related side effects of chemotherapy, directly reducing oral food and nutrient intake.

• Vomiting / Diarrhea / Malabsorption: Occur frequently, but anorexia is the primary behavioral and physiological side effect suppressing initial food intake.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): What will you not give a patient with hepatitis? *
Rationale:
Patients with viral hepatitis or liver dysfunction exhibit impaired lipid emulsification, digestion, and bile secretion, requiring a high carbohydrate, moderate-to-high protein, and low-fat diet to minimize digestive distress and support liver regeneration.

• Low carbohydrate / High protein / High carbohydrate: Favorable and therapeutic for hepatitis recovery (supporting glycogen stores and tissue repair).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Essential amino acids given in limited amount to infants and children with maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) except: *
Rationale:
Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is an error in branched-chain keto acid metabolism, requiring strict restriction of the branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, and valine). Lysine is not a branched-chain amino acid and is an exception not restricted for MSUD management.

• Valine / Isoleucine: Branch-chain amino acids strictly restricted in MSUD diets.
