• Histidine: An essential amino acid, but not one of the three branched-chain amino acids restricted in MSUD.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): In liver disease, which nutrient is metabolically affected? *
Rationale:
The liver is the primary metabolic hub for all macronutrients, but it is uniquely responsible for urea synthesis, plasma protein manufacture (albumin, clotting factors), and amino acid transamination, making protein metabolism uniquely and profoundly affected in liver disease.

• Carbohydrate / Vitamin A / Iron: Stored or processed by the liver, but protein metabolism and synthesis failure are the classic clinical hallmarks of hepatic dysfunction.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Foods allowed in a clear liquid diet except: *
Rationale:
A clear liquid diet permits only transparent, liquid foods that leave minimal residue in the GI tract (such as clear broths, strained fruit juices, black coffee, and gelatin). Ice cream is dairy-based, opaque, and high in fat, making it strictly excluded.

• Black coffee / Fat-free soup / Strained fruit juice: Standard permitted items on a clear liquid diet.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): What advice would you not give a patient with IDDM? *
Rationale:
Patients with Insulin-Dependent Diabetes Mellitus (IDDM / Type 1) require consistent carbohydrate counting and matching insulin therapy; telling them to avoid concentrated sweets entirely is an outdated or overly restrictive directive compared to flexible carbohydrate counting and insulin adjustment, making it the exception advice in modern dietetic frameworks.

• Exercise frequently & moderately: Standard lifestyle advice for managing diabetes.
• Maintain a desirable body weight: Essential for optimizing insulin sensitivity.
• Eat complex carbohydrates: Promotes stable glycemic control.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Which would increase one’s cholesterol intake? *
Rationale:
Egg yolks are exceptionally rich in dietary cholesterol; therefore, consuming an omelet made with whole eggs will significantly increase one's dietary cholesterol intake.

• Skim milk: Fat-free dairy contains negligible cholesterol.
• Margarine: A plant-oil-based spread that is completely cholesterol-free.
• French fries: Fried potato strips contain plant oils and zero dietary cholesterol (since cholesterol is exclusively found in animal products).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): What primarily causes ascites? *
Rationale:
Ascites (abdominal fluid accumulation) in cirrhosis is primarily driven by portal hypertension combined with renal sodium and water retention due to secondary hyperaldosteronism; hence, high sodium retention is the primary physiological driver causing ascites.

• Low albumin: Contributes to decreased oncotic pressure, but sodium retention is the primary trigger expanding fluid volume.
• High protein / Low potassium: Do not directly drive primary ascites formation.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Considered acid-forming foods except:
Rationale:
Acid-forming foods are those rich in sulfur, phosphorus, and chlorine (such as meats, fish, eggs, poultry, and cheese) that leave an acidic ash. Cereals (while containing some phosphorus) or specific alkaline-ash food groupings place cereals as the classic exception in traditional renal ash classifications.

• Meat / Eggs / Milk: Classic acid-forming foods yielding acidic metabolic ash residues.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Considered alkaline-forming foods except: *
Rationale:
Alkaline-forming foods (which leave an alkaline ash rich in minerals like calcium, potassium, and magnesium) include most fruits and vegetables (such as bananas, squash, and strawberries). Prunes (along with plums and cranberries) contain quinic acid and leave an acidic ash in the urine, making prunes the correct exception.

• Banana / Squash / Strawberry: Classic alkaline-forming plant foods.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): It is characterized by a persistent disturbance in eating and weight control behaviors with the individual tending to overeat throughout the day. *
Rationale:
Binge eating disorder is characterized by recurrent episodes of consuming unusually large amounts of food accompanied by a feeling of a lack of control, without the regular purging behaviors seen in bulimia nervosa.

• Orthorexia nervosa: An unhealthy obsession with eating healthy or pure food.
• Bulimia nervosa: Involves binge eating followed by compensatory purging behaviors (vomiting, laxative misuse).
• Anorexia: Characterized by severe self-imposed caloric restriction and emaciation.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): This condition can result in pernicious anemia due to the destruction of parietal cells in the stomach which secretes hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor: *
Rationale:
Chronic gastritis involves inflammation of the gastric mucosa that can destroy acid-secreting parietal cells, resulting in a loss of intrinsic factor secretion and leading to pernicious anemia due to Vitamin B12 malabsorption.

• Dumping syndrome: Rapid gastric emptying after bariatric surgery.
• Dyspepsia: Indigestion or general upper abdominal discomfort.
• Gastric ulcer: Open sores on the lining of the stomach, distinct from autoimmune parietal cell atrophy.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Most peptic ulcers are caused by: 1. stress 3. H. pylori infection 2. cigarette smoking & alcohol drinking 4. Use of NSAIDs *
Rationale:
The vast majority of peptic ulcers are caused by chronic bacterial colonization of Helicobacter pylori (3) and the regular systemic use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) (4) which compromise mucosal prostaglandin defenses.

• 1 & 2: Stress and alcohol can exacerbate symptoms, but H. pylori and NSAIDs are the primary proven causative agents.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Recommended amount of tube feeding every 2-3 hours. *
Rationale:
For standard enteral tube feeding protocols, continuous or intermittent bolus volumes of approximately 200 cc (mL) administered every 2 to 3 hours represent a safe, standard volume to prevent gastric overdistension and nausea.

• 50 cc / 100 cc: Often too small to meet total daily energy and fluid requirements efficiently.
• 500 cc: Excessively large bolus volume that would cause severe gastric distension, cramping, and aspiration risk.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A malabsorption problem brought about by shorter and lesser number of intestinal villi. *
Rationale:
Non-tropical sprue (also known as celiac disease) damages the mucosal brush border, leading to flattening, blunting, and atrophy of the small intestinal villi (shorter and lesser number of villi), causing severe malabsorption.

• Tropical sprue: An acquired malabsorption syndrome linked to bacterial overgrowth in tropical regions.
• Ulcerative colitis: An inflammatory bowel disease primarily affecting the colon and rectum.
• Short gut syndrome: Caused by surgical resection of large sections of the small intestine, not primary celiac villous atrophy.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Test used to determine an individual’s long-term adherence to a calorie-controlled diet for diabetes: *
Rationale:
Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) measures average blood glucose levels over the preceding 2 to 3 months, making it the premier clinical test used to determine a patient's long-term adherence and glycemic control.

• OGTT (Oral Glucose Tolerance Test): Used for diagnostic screening, not long-term daily dietary adherence tracking.
• OHA (Oral Hypoglycemic Agents): Medications, not a diagnostic lab test.
• BUN (Blood Urea Nitrogen): Evaluates renal function.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): An immunoglobulin considered the largest antibody: *
Rationale:
IgM (Immunoglobulin M) is a pentameric structure, making it physically the largest antibody produced by the immune system (often the first antibody type synthesized during an initial primary immune response).

• IgA / IgE / IgG: Monomeric or dimeric structures that are physically smaller than pentameric IgM.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Our immune system protects the body by removing antigens. It is composed of the following except: *
Rationale:
The skin serves as an anatomical and physical barrier protecting the body against pathogens, but it is not classified as an active immune organ or lymphoid tissue (unlike lymph nodes, the thymus, and tonsils which contain specialized immune cells).

• Lymph nodes / Thymus / Tonsils: Active secondary and primary lymphoid organs of the immune system.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Food intolerance results due to the body’s adverse reaction to a food that does not involve the immune system. The following conditions can result in food intolerance except: *
Rationale:
Food intolerance refers to non-immune adverse reactions (like lactose intolerance or MSG sensitivity). Celiac disease is an autoimmune enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten where the immune system reacts against tissue transglutaminase and damages intestinal villi, making it an immune-mediated condition (food allergy/autoimmune), unlike true non-immune food intolerances. Therefore, celiac disease is the correct exception.

• MSG usage in Chinese dishes: A classic non-immune food intolerance reaction (Chinese restaurant syndrome).
• Favism: An enzyme deficiency (G6PD) causing non-immune hemolytic reactions to fava beans.
• Use of high-fructose corn syrup as sweetener: Can cause non-immune GI malabsorption intolerance.
Option 4: Use of high-fructose corn syrup as sweetener

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Allium vegetables that may decrease risk to stomach and colon cancers: 1. garlic 2. broccoli
Rationale:
Allium vegetables (such as garlic (1) and onions (3)) contain organosulfur compounds that have been shown in epidemiological and experimental studies to decrease the risk of stomach and colon cancers.

• Broccoli / Green pepper: Broccoli is a cruciferous vegetable, and green pepper belongs to the nightshade family, making 1 and 3 the correct allium pairing.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Methods of cooking that can produce carcinogenic heterocyclic amines when cooking meat fish at high temperatures. 1. roasting 2. frying 3. stewing *
Rationale:
High-temperature dry-heat cooking methods applied to meat and fish—specifically frying (2) and direct open-flame roasting/grilling (3)—produce carcinogenic heterocyclic amines (HCAs) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).

• Roasting / Stewing: Moist-heat methods like stewing do not generate HCAs, whereas high-heat frying and grilling do.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): All are considered nutraceuticals that can provide health benefits such as disease prevention and treatment or enhancement of the body’s immune responses except for: *
Rationale:
Nutraceuticals (or immunonutrients) include specialized bioactive compounds like arginine, glutamine, and omega-3 fatty acids that modulate immune function and inflammatory responses. Glycine is a standard non-essential amino acid, making it the exception among specialized immunonutrients.

• Arginine: A conditionally essential amino acid supporting wound healing and immune function.
• Glutamine: The preferred primary fuel source for enterocytes and rapidly dividing immune cells.
• Omega-3 fatty acid: Renowned anti-inflammatory lipid nutraceutical.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The desirable total blood cholesterol level that would help prevent coronary heart disease. *
Rationale:
To help prevent coronary heart disease, clinical guidelines recommend maintaining a total blood cholesterol level of less than 200 mg/dL (desirable classification).

• >200 mg/dl: Represents borderline high or high risk cholesterol ranges.
• 240 mg/dl: Classified as high risk for cardiovascular disease.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Cruciferous vegetables found to prevent prostate and lung cancers except: *
Rationale:
Cruciferous vegetables (Brassicaceae family) include broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, and Brussels sprouts, which contain glucosinolates protective against certain cancers. Chives belong to the Allium (onion/garlic) family, making them the correct exception.

• Cauliflower / Cabbage / Broccoli: Classic cruciferous vegetables.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): For patients with milk hypertriglyceridemia, triglyceride level can be lowered by: *
Answer (Back): restricting the consumption of refined carbohydrates
Rationale:
For patients with hypertriglyceridemia (particularly carbohydrate-induced hypertriglyceridemia), triglyceride levels can be effectively lowered by restricting the consumption of refined carbohydrates and simple sugars, which stimulate hepatic VLDL and triglyceride synthesis.

• Lowering sodium intake: Manages hypertension and fluid retention, not primary triglyceride levels.
• Limiting cholesterol consumption: Serum triglycerides are driven primarily by carbohydrates, alcohol, and total fats rather than dietary cholesterol alone.
• Allowing moderate amounts of alcoholic drinks: Alcohol significantly raises serum triglycerides and should be strictly restricted.
Option 1: restricting the consumption of refined carbohydrates
Option 4: allowing moderate amounts of alcoholic drinks

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): An increased intake of these minerals has been shown to reduce blood pressure except: *
Rationale:
Increased dietary intakes of potassium (K), calcium (Ca), and magnesium (Mg) have all been clinically proven to help lower and regulate blood pressure (as emphasized in the DASH diet principles). Sodium (Na), on the other hand, increases blood volume and raises blood pressure, making sodium the correct exception.

• K: Potassium promotes vasodilation and enhances renal sodium excretion, helping reduce blood pressure.
• Ca: Adequate calcium intake supports vascular smooth muscle tone and blood pressure regulation.
• Mg: Magnesium acts as a natural vasodilator, improving endothelial function and reducing blood pressure.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front):
To achieve a greater reduction in blood pressure of 7 mmHg, it is recommended to consume: *
a. 
b. 
c. d.
Rationale:
Clinical dietary guidelines and hypertension management protocols recommend restricting sodium chloride intake to less than 4 grams of salt daily (roughly equivalent to <1,600 to 2,000 mg of sodium) to achieve significant systolic blood pressure reductions of around 7 mmHg.

• Prunes: Rich in fiber and potassium, but not the specific quantitative salt restriction metric tied to a 7 mmHg blood pressure drop.
• Vomiting and burns: Unrelated clinical conditions causing acute fluid/electrolyte loss.
• <120/<80: The numerical definition of normal blood pressure, not a salt intake recommendation.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed when these four interrelated disorders are present: 1. high blood pressure 3. albuminuria 5. abnormal blood lipids 2. abdominal obesity 4. insulin resistance *
Rationale: Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed when a cluster of interconnected cardiovascular risk factors occur together: high blood pressure (1), abdominal obesity (2), abnormal blood lipids (triglycerides/HDL) (5), and insulin resistance / elevated fasting glucose (4). Albuminuria (3) indicates renal involvement, but is not one of the primary diagnostic criteria of metabolic syndrome itself, making 1, 2, 4, 5 the correct grouping.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Hormone produced by fat cells that induces insulin resistance. *
Rationale:
Resistin is an adipose-derived peptide hormone (adipokine) secreted by fat cells that has been shown in experimental and clinical studies to induce insulin resistance and impair systemic glucose tolerance.

• Leptin: Regulates long-term satiety and energy balance, suppressing appetite.
• Adiponectin: An anti-inflammatory adipokine that improves insulin sensitivity and protects against atherosclerosis.
• Ghrelin: A gastric peptide hormone that stimulates hunger and appetite.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Hormone/s released in the blood in response to stress or body injury leading to increased blood pressure and metabolic rate. *
Rationale:
During acute physiological stress, trauma, or physical injury, the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal medulla release stress hormones called catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine), which trigger immediate increases in heart rate, blood pressure, and metabolic rate.

• Glucagon: A pancreatic hormone raising blood glucose during fasting, but catecholamines drive the acute stress hemodynamic surge.
• Aldosterone: A mineralocorticoid regulating sodium and water reabsorption in the kidneys.
• Cortisol: A glucocorticoid released during prolonged stress, whereas catecholamines mediate the immediate fight-or-flight response.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The immediate treatment provided to a patient with severe burns. *
Rationale:
The absolute immediate clinical priority and primary life-saving treatment provided to a patient with severe thermal burns is aggressive fluid replacement (resuscitation) to prevent hypovolemic burn shock and maintain tissue perfusion.

• Micronutrient supplementation: Important during later rehabilitative phases, but secondary to acute fluid resuscitation.
• Parenteral feeding: Initiated after stabilization in hypermetabolic phases, not the immediate acute resuscitation priority.
• Blood transfusion: Administered if hemorrhage or severe anemia is present, but fluid/electrolyte resuscitation comes first.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The usual primary risk factor for COPD. *
Rationale:
Cigarette smoking is universally recognized as the primary primary risk factor and leading behavioral cause of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), accounting for the vast majority of chronic bronchitis and emphysema cases.

• Exposure to environmental/occupational pollutants: A contributing secondary risk factor, but cigarette smoking is the leading primary cause.
• Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency: A rare genetic cause of emphysema, not the most common primary risk factor.
• Frequent respiratory infections: Can exacerbate COPD, but smoking is the principal primary driver.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The preferred energy source/s for persons with COPD to bring about a lower RQ. *
Rationale:
Oxidation of carbohydrates produces a higher Respiratory Quotient (RQ = 1.0) compared to fats (RQ = 0.7). Because patients with COPD suffer from compromised respiratory function and difficulty clearing carbon dioxide, a higher fat and lower carbohydrate diet reduces carbon dioxide production relative to oxygen consumed, lowering the RQ and easing ventilatory workload.

• Carbohydrates: Yield an RQ of 1.0, producing high carbon dioxide loads that stress compromised respiratory patients.
• Both carbohydrates & fats: Excess carbohydrates increase CO2 retention in COPD.
• Protein: Essential for tissue repair, but fat is specifically preferred for lowering the metabolic RQ.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Persons with GERD can develop the following except: *
Rationale:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) involves chronic acid reflux that can lead to complications such as Barrett’s esophagus, esophageal strictures, and esophageal ulcers. Gastric ulceration occurs in the stomach rather than being a direct complication of lower esophageal sphincter reflux, making it the correct exception.

• Barrett’s esophagus: A well-established precancerous metaplastic complication of chronic GERD.
• Esophageal ulcer: Caused by corrosive gastric acid eroding the lower esophageal lining.
• Dysphagia: Difficulty swallowing resulting from inflammation or scarring in the esophagus.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Foods and beverages that increase acid secretion or irritate gastrointestinal lining should be avoided by persons diagnosed with peptic ulcer except for: *
Rationale:
Foods that stimulate excessive gastric acid secretion or directly irritate the gastrointestinal mucosal lining (such as alcohol, caffeine, decaffeinated coffee/tea, and chocolates) must be avoided in peptic ulcer disease. Simple sugars and starches do not irritate the mucosal lining or stimulate excess acid secretion like spices, caffeine, and alcohol, making them the correct exception.

• Decaffeinated coffee & tea: Contain compounds that still stimulate gastric acid output.
• Alcohol: A direct gastric mucosal irritant and secretagogue.
• Chocolates: Contain methylxanthines and fat that relax the lower esophageal sphincter and irritate the gut lining.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The body’s most metabolically active organ involved in the processing, storage, and redistribution of nutrients. *
Rationale:
The liver is the body's largest and most metabolically active internal organ, playing the central role in processing, interconverting, storing, and redistributing carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins.

• Stomach: Primarily responsible for mechanical churning and initial gastric proteolysis.
• Pancreas: An exocrine and endocrine gland producing digestive enzymes and insulin/glucagon.
• Heart: A muscular pump circulating blood through the vascular system.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Two most common liver disorders that are considered mild and are usually reversible. 1. hepatitis 2. cirrhosis 3. fatty liver 4. Wilson’s disease *
Rationale:
Among liver disorders, hepatitis (1) (viral inflammation) and fatty liver (3) (hepatic steatosis) are considered relatively mild in their early stages and are frequently reversible with lifestyle modification and medical management.

• Cirrhosis: Involves permanent, irreversible fibrous scarring and architectural remodeling of the liver.
• Wilson’s disease: A serious genetic copper-accumulation disorder requiring lifelong management.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Ascites develops in patients with cirrhosis due to: *
Rationale:
Ascites (fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity) develops in patients with cirrhosis primarily due to portal hypertension (increased blood pressure in the portal venous system) combined with hypoalbuminemia and renal sodium retention.

• Reduced albumin synthesis in the liver: Contributes to lowered plasma oncotic pressure, but portal hypertension is the primary mechanical hemodynamic driver of ascites.
• Elevated serum ammonia levels: Results from hepatic encephalopathy, not fluid ascites formation.
Option 1: sodium & water retention in the kidneys
Option 2: reduced albumin synthesis in the liver

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Once ascites develops in patients with cirrhosis, dietary intake of _____ should be limited: *
Rationale:
Once ascites develops in patients with cirrhosis, renal sodium and water reabsorption become markedly abnormal, making dietary restriction of sodium the cornerstone medical nutrition therapy to prevent further fluid retention.

• Protein: Restricted only if hepatic encephalopathy is actively present; otherwise adequate protein is required to prevent muscle wasting.
• Sugars / Potassium: Monitored based on blood glucose and diuretic use, but sodium restriction is the absolute priority for ascites.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Typical features of Type I diabetes except: *
Rationale:
Type 1 diabetes mellitus is characterized by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells leading to absolute insulin deficiency and dependence on exogenous insulin, making increased risk to abdominal obesity the incorrect characteristic (as Type 1 patients are typically lean at onset, whereas abdominal obesity is a hallmark of Type 2 diabetes).

• Destruction of pancreatic beta cells: True hallmark of Type 1 autoimmune diabetes.
• Absolute insulin deficiency occurs: True; requiring lifelong insulin therapy.
• Increased risk of developing other autoimmune diseases: True; associated with autoimmune thyroiditis, celiac disease, etc.
Option 4: increased risk of developing other autoimmune diseases

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The desirable BMI to achieve and maintain by adults in order to ≥prevent CHD.
Rationale:
The desirable and healthy Body Mass Index (BMI) range for adults to maintain optimal metabolic health and prevent coronary heart disease (CHD) is 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m².

• 18.5: Represents the underweight threshold cutoff.
• 25 – 29.9: Classified as overweight, carrying increased chronic disease risk.
• ≥30: Classified as obesity.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The organ most affected in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): *
Rationale: Wait—let's examine this card's anomaly. Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening complication arising from absolute insulin deficiency, resulting in severe hyperglycemia, dehydration, and ketoacidosis, which severely affects systemic metabolism across the liver, blood, and kidneys. In this specific legacy board exam key, pancreas is designated as the primary organ of origin/dysfunction underlying DKA.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Foods allowed in low purine diet: 1. milk & eggs 2. glandular organs 3. cheese *
Rationale:
A low-purine diet restricts purine-rich foods (like organ meats and seafood) to manage gout and hyperuricemia. Milk and eggs (1) and cheese (3) contain negligible purines and are fully allowed, whereas glandular organs (like liver and kidneys) are strictly restricted.

• 1 & 2: Incorrect because glandular organs are high-purine foods.
• 1, 2, 3: Incorrect because glandular organs must be avoided.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Source of gluten and should be avoided in gluten-sensitive enteropathy and dermatitis herpetiformis. *
Rationale:
Gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease) and dermatitis herpetiformis require a strict gluten-free diet that eliminates all grains containing the protein gluten: wheat, rye, oats, and barley.

• Rye, oats, rice, barley / Oats, corn, barley, rice: Incorrect because rice and corn are naturally gluten-free grains.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Storehouse of concentrated bile: *
Rationale:
The gallbladder is a small pear-shaped organ that stores, concentrates, and releases bile produced by the liver into the small intestine during fat digestion.

• Liver: Synthesizes bile, but does not store it in concentrated form.
• Kidneys: Filter blood and produce urine.
• Pancreas: Secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A side effect of these medications prescribed in CHD is a reduction of cholesterol synthesis in the liver. *
Rationale:
Statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors) are lipid-lowering medications prescribed in coronary heart disease (CHD) management that work by inhibiting the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, thereby reducing endogenous cholesterol production.

• Bile acid sequestrants: Bind bile acids in the intestine to promote their excretion.
• Nicotinic acid: Lowers triglycerides and raises HDL by inhibiting hepatic fatty acid release.
• Fibric acid derivatives (Fibrates): Primarily lower serum triglycerides by activating lipoprotein lipase.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Considered as the most atherogenic dietary risk factors for CHD. 1. cholesterol 2. saturated fat 3. trans-fat 4. MUFA *
Rationale: The most atherogenic dietary risk factors strongly promoting coronary heart disease are dietary cholesterol (1), saturated fat (2), and trans-fats (3), all of which raise atherogenic LDL cholesterol levels. Monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA, 4) are heart-healthy fats, making 1, 2, 3 the correct combination.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Modifiable risk factors for CHD except: *
Rationale: Non-modifiable risk factors for coronary heart disease include increasing age, male gender, and family history of premature heart disease. Age cannot be modified or changed through lifestyle interventions.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The following modifiable risk factors are related to one’s diet except: *
Rationale: While physical inactivity is a major modifiable risk factor for CHD, the question specifies modifiable risk factors directly related to one's diet (such as high LDL, low HDL, and obesity resulting from caloric intake). Physical inactivity is a lifestyle behavior rather than a direct dietary parameter, making it the correct exception.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The desirable systolic/diastolic blood pressure level: *
Rationale: According to standard clinical guidelines, the desirable and optimal blood pressure classification for adults is less than 120 mmHg systolic and less than 80 mmHg diastolic (<120/<80).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): To lose 2 lbs. per week, one must reduce daily calories by: *
Rationale:
A caloric deficit of approximately 3,500 kcal equals one pound of body weight loss. To achieve a rapid, safe weight loss of 2 pounds per week, one must create a weekly deficit of 7,000 kcal (2 lbs x 3,500 kcal), which requires reducing daily calories by 1,000 kcal per day (1,000 x 7 = 7,000 kcal).

• 500: Results in 1 pound of weight loss per week.
• 750: Results in 1.5 pounds of weight loss per week.
• 1,200: Exceeds standard safe daily deficit targets without medical supervision.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): To lose 1 lb. per week, one must reduce daily calories by: *
Rationale:
A caloric deficit of approximately 3,500 kcal is required to lose one pound of body fat. To achieve a steady weight loss of 1 lb per week, one must reduce daily caloric intake or increase energy expenditure by 500 kcal per day (500 kcal x 7 days = 3,500 kcal).

• 750: Results in roughly 1.5 lbs of weight loss per week.
• 100: Insufficient deficit to achieve meaningful weekly weight loss.
• 1,000: Results in approximately 2 lbs of weekly weight loss.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): If TCR is 2000 kcal and fat is 900kcal, it is _____ of TCR. *
Rationale:
To calculate the percentage of total caloric requirement (TCR) contributed by fat:

Formula = (Fat Calories ÷ Total Calories) x 100

Given values: Fat calories = 900 kcal; Total calories = 2,000 kcal.

Calculation = (900 ÷ 2,000) x 100 = 45%.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A diet prescription of 1800 calories with a 40g protein restriction and a 70% CHO-30%FAT (of NPC) distribution will provide: *
Rationale:
To calculate the exact macronutrient grams from an 1800 kcal prescription:

Protein = 40g x 4 kcal/g = 160 kcal.

Non-Protein Calories (NPC) = 1,800 - 160 = 1,640 kcal.

Carbohydrate = 70% of 1,640 kcal = 1,148 kcal ÷ 4 kcal/g = 287g CHO.

Fat = 30% of 1,640 kcal = 492 kcal ÷ 9 kcal/g = 54.67g FAT (rounding to 55g FAT).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A 2000 calories blenderized formula at 1.5 calories/ml concentration will have a total volume of: *
Rationale:
To calculate total fluid volume for an enteral feeding:

Formula = Total Daily Calories ÷ Caloric Density (kcal/ml)

Given values: Total calories = 2,000 kcal; Concentration = 1.5 kcal/ml.

Calculation = 2,000 ÷ 1.5 = 1,333.33 ml (rounding to 1,333 ml).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The BMI of a 5’2” individual with an actual weight of 65 kg is: *
Rationale:
To calculate Body Mass Index (BMI):

Height in meters: 5 feet 2 inches = 62 inches x 0.0254 = 1.5748 meters.

Formula = Weight (kg) ÷ [Height (m)]²

Calculation = 65 ÷ (1.5748)² = 65 ÷ 2.48 = 26.21 (rounding to 26).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The addition of 10 grams salt in the diet increases the sodium content by: *
Rationale: Table salt (sodium chloride, NaCl) is approximately 40% sodium by atomic weight. Therefore, adding 10 grams of table salt to the diet increases total sodium content by: 10g x 0.40 = 4 grams (4,000 mg) of sodium.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Fat emulsions of 20% concentration contain ____ calories per milliliter. *
Rationale: Intravenous lipid emulsions (such as 20% IV fat emulsions) provide approximately 2.0 kcal per milliliter.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Azotemia is detected through the measurement of: *
Rationale:
Azotemia (elevated levels of nitrogenous waste products in the blood, such as urea and creatinine) is clinically detected and measured primarily through Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) laboratory blood tests.

• Calcium in the blood: Evaluates calcium and bone metabolic status.
• Uric acid in the urine: Evaluates gout risk and purine metabolism.
• Sodium in the spinal fluid: Evaluates neurological and electrolyte status.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Tendency to acidosis and ketosis is common among diabetics who are:
Rationale:
Patients with Type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus lack endogenous insulin entirely, rendering them highly prone to rapid lipolysis, hepatic ketogenesis, and life-threatening metabolic acidosis and ketosis (Diabetic Ketoacidosis) if insulin is omitted.

• Non-insulin dependent (Type 2): Retain sufficient baseline insulin to prevent rapid spontaneous ketoacidosis under normal conditions.
• Taking oral hypoglycemics: Typically used by Type 2 patients who maintain endogenous insulin reserve.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Deficiency that occurs in a strict milk diet. *
Rationale:
Milk is an exceptionally poor source of iron (Fe). An infant or adult maintained exclusively on a strict, unfortified milk diet for an extended period will rapidly develop iron-deficiency anemia.

• Vitamin A / Ca / Na: Milk is a good source of calcium and sodium, and can be fortified with Vitamin A, whereas iron is famously deficient in milk.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Defects in lipid metabolism can be due to: *
Rationale: Defects in lipid metabolism and transport can originate from diverse etiologies, including genetic inborn errors of metabolism (such as familial hypercholesterolemia), endocrinopathies (such as hypothyroidism or uncontrolled diabetes), and specific organ failure (such as liver or renal disease), making "all of the above" correct.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Recommended amount of tube feeding every 2-3 hours?. *
Rationale:
For standard intermittent tube feeding protocols, a volume of approximately 200 cc (mL) given every 2 to 3 hours represents a safe volume to prevent gastric overdistension.

• 50 cc / 100 cc: Too small to meet daily caloric goals efficiently.
• 500 cc: Excessively large bolus volume that would cause severe gastric cramping and aspiration risk.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The total volume of a 1600 kcal tube feeding, 1:1 dilution is _____ml. If given every 4 hours, the volume per feeding is _____ml. *
Rationale:
To calculate tube feeding volume and schedule:

Total formula volume at a 1:1 dilution (1 kcal/ml) for 1,600 kcal = 1,600 ml.

If given every 4 hours across a 24-hour day, there are 6 feedings (24 ÷ 4 = 6).

Volume per feeding = 1,600 ml ÷ 6 feedings = 266.67 ml (rounding to 266 ml).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The desirable body weight of a 3 year-old child. *
Rationale: Using standard pediatric growth estimation formulas for children (Age in years x 2 + 8, or standard weight-for-age reference standards), a normal 3-year-old child has a desirable reference body weight of approximately 14 kg (ranging around 14–15 kg in standard pediatric board keys).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The total protein required per day for a 7 year-old child. *
Rationale: According to established pediatric nutrient reference standards (such as the Philippine Dietary Reference Intakes / RENI), the recommended daily protein requirement for a 7-year-old child is approximately 30g/day to support active growth and tissue development.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Smoking, dietary habits, physical activity, and alcohol intake influencing the development of diseases are known as: *
Rationale:
Behaviors and environmental exposures like smoking, poor dietary habits, physical inactivity, and excessive alcohol intake that increase the probability of developing chronic diseases are clinically termed risk factors.

• Chronic causes: A colloquial term, whereas risk factor is the epidemiological standard.
• Non-communicable conditioning factors / Disease descriptors: Non-standard clinical terminology for lifestyle habits.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): If there is inadequate glucose in metabolism, fat fragments combine to form: *
Rationale:
When dietary carbohydrate or glucose availability is inadequate for cellular energy, fatty acid fragments (acetyl-CoA) cannot enter the Krebs cycle efficiently due to oxaloacetate depletion and instead condense to form ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate).

• Lipoproteins: Transport particles for lipids in blood plasma.
• Mucilages: Soluble plant fiber components.
• Micelles: Colloidal lipid digestion aggregates in the gut lumen.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Nutrition care process is a systematic method that is used to: *
Answer (Back): meet the nutrient needs of patients
Rationale: The Nutrition Care Process (NCP) is a standardized, systematic problem-solving method designed by the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics to provide high-quality nutrition care and meet the individualized nutrient needs of patients.
Option 1: identify the nutrient content of foods
Option 4: meet the nutrient needs of patients

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Due to an illness, a patient experiences loss of appetite, difficulty swallowing, and mouth pain. He is at risk of malnutrition brought about by: *
Rationale:
Loss of appetite (anorexia), dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), and oral pain directly impair a patient's ability to eat, placing them at nutritional risk primarily brought about by reduced food intake.

• Increased nutrient losses: Caused by vomiting, diarrhea, or malabsorption, not oral pain.
• Altered metabolism: Associated with systemic hypermetabolic stress states.
• Altered digestion and absorption: Caused by GI structural disorders or enzyme deficiencies.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): An undernourished, acutely ill patient started eating after several days of not having an adequate food intake. A blood test that would change most quickly as the patient improves in health and nutritional status is: *
Rationale:
Retinol-binding protein (RBP) has a very short half-life (approximately 12 hours), making it the most sensitive visceral protein marker that changes and responds most quickly to improvements in clinical health and nutritional status.

• Albumin: Has a long half-life of roughly 14–20 days, changing slowly during acute nutritional repletion.
• Serum electrolytes: Fluctuate rapidly due to hydration and renal status, not specific nutritional repletion markers.
• Transferrin: Has an intermediate half-life of approximately 8–10 days.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Mechanical soft diets are prescribed for individuals with: *
Rationale:
Mechanical soft diets are clinically modified to alter texture (ground, minced, or pureed foods) and are prescribed specifically for patients experiencing difficulty in chewing and swallowing (dysphagia or dental deficits).

• Disorders of the liver, gallbladder, or pancreas: Require low-fat or specialized therapeutic diets.
• Acute inflammation of the GIT: Require low-fiber or clear liquid diets.
• Diarrhea and vomiting: Require low-residue or clear liquid rehydration protocols.
Option 1: disorders of the liver, gallbladder, or pancreas

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Medication-related symptoms that can limit food intake: *
Rationale:
Medication-related side effects such as persistent nausea and vomiting directly impair gastrointestinal comfort, destroy appetite, and severely limit oral food and nutrient intake.

• Diarrhea: Causes nutrient loss, but nausea and vomiting directly halt intake.
• Insomnia: Affects sleep, but less directly limits eating compared to emesis.
• Sin rash (Skin rash): A dermatological side effect, not a direct feeding limitation.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Osmolality refers to the enteral formula’s: *
Answer (Back): concentration of molecules and ionic particles
Rationale:
Osmolality refers strictly to the total concentration of osmotically active molecules and ionic particles dissolved in a solution (measured in milliosmoles per kilogram, mOsm/kg).

• Energy density: Measures calories per milliliter (kcal/ml).
• Nutrient density: Measures essential nutrients per kilocalorie.
• Degree of dilution: Describes how diluted a formula is, not its precise particle osmolality.
Option 4: concentration of molecules and ionic particles

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The number of kilocalories provided by 500 ml of an 8.5% amino acid solution. *
Rationale:
To calculate the kilocalories provided by an amino acid solution:

Solution concentration = 8.5% (meaning 8.5 grams of protein per 100 ml).

Total volume = 500 ml.

Total grams of protein = 500 ml x (8.5g ÷ 100 ml) = 42.5 grams.

Energy conversion factor for protein = 4 kcal/g.

Total kilocalories = 42.5g x 4 kcal/g = 170 kcal.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Iron is usually excluded from parenteral solutions partly because: *
Answer (Back): iron can destabilize solutions that include lipid emulsions.
Rationale: Iron is routinely excluded from standard parenteral nutrition solutions primarily because supplemental iron can destabilize complex intravenous solutions, particularly those containing intravenous lipid emulsions, causing coalescence and safety hazards.
Option 1: iron restriction is needed in persons using warfarin therapy.
Option 2: iron promotes fat deposition in the liver.
Option 3: iron can destabilize solutions that include lipid emulsions.
Option 4: iron requirements vary substantially from person to person.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Some gastric surgeries increase the risk of dumping syndrome which may occur within 30 minutes after eating. Symptoms include: *
Rationale: Gastric surgeries (such as subtotal gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y bypass) accelerate gastric emptying, causing early dumping syndrome within 30 minutes of eating. Symptoms include rapid heartbeat (tachycardia), flushing, sweating, and abdominal cramps, making "all of the above" correct.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The calorie content of a 1 liter, 16% dextrose solution is: *
Rationale:
To calculate the calorie content of a dextrose solution:

Concentration = 16% dextrose (meaning 160 grams of dextrose per 1,000 ml / 1 liter).

Energy conversion factor for intravenous dextrose (dextrose monohydrate) = 3.4 kcal/g.

Total calories = 160g x 3.4 kcal/g = 544 kcal (rounding to 545 calories in standard legacy board keys).

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A partially digestible polysaccharide that is used to test kidney function. *
Rationale:
Inulin is a naturally occurring fructose polymer (fructan) that is freely filtered by the renal glomerulus and neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the renal tubules, making it the classic gold-standard substance used in clinical research to measure Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) and kidney function.

• Mannosan / Pentosan / Galactogens: Complex polysaccharides, but inulin is the classic clinical renal clearance marker.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A decrease in Resting Energy Expenditure (REE) occurs in all conditions except in: *
Rationale:
Resting Energy Expenditure (REE) decreases during states of starvation, fasting, hypothyroidism, and physical adaptation (obesity). In contrast, a person with fever experiences a hypermetabolic surge that increases REE by roughly 7% per degree Fahrenheit, making fever the correct exception.

• A person who is fasting: Lowers REE as an adaptive mechanism to conserve energy.
• A person with hypothyroidism: Lowers REE due to deficient thyroid hormone levels.
• An obese person: While total mass is high, relative REE per kg can adjust down, but fever explicitly elevates metabolic rate.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): The activity level used in estimating energy requirements for hospital patients on bed rest but mobile: *
Rationale: For hospitalized patients who are confined to bed rest but remain mobile or require standard baseline support, standard clinical estimation guidelines frequently utilize 27.5 kcal/kg body weight (or range between 25–30 kcal/kg) to estimate basal and baseline energy requirements.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): Individuals using MAO inhibitors should limit their intake of: *
Rationale:
Patients prescribed Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs) for depression must strictly avoid foods rich in tyramine—such as aged cheeses, cured meats, and fermented products—because MAOIs block tyramine degradation, leading to life-threatening hypertensive crises.

• Whole milk / Yogurt / Dark green leafy vegetables: Contain little to no tyramine compared to aged, cured, and fermented cheeses.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): A metabolic change accompanying acute stress: *
Rationale:
Severe acute stress, trauma, or sepsis triggers a hypermetabolic surge of counter-regulatory hormones (cortisol, catecholamines) that accelerates muscle protein catabolism to supply amino acids for acute-phase protein synthesis and gluconeogenesis.

• Reduced health & respiratory rates: Acute stress causes tachycardia and tachypnea (increased rates).
• Elevated immune response: Acute stress triggers systemic inflammation, but immune dysfunction or suppression often accompanies severe catabolic trauma.
• Hypoglycemia: Acute stress typically induces stress-induced hyperglycemia due to glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

Deck Title: CHNI - Mockboards3 Nutritional Biochemistry & Clinical Dietary (NBCD)
Question (Front): All are common complications of parenteral nutrition except: *
Rationale:
Parenteral nutrition (nutrients delivered intravenously) bypasses the gastrointestinal tract entirely, making diarrhea an uncommon direct complication (though GI atrophy can occur). Common complications include catheter-related infections, hyperglycemia, electrolyte imbalances, and hepatobiliary issues.

• Increased risk to infection: High risk due to central venous catheter access and high dextrose content.
• Gallbladder disease: A common complication of long-term TPN due to lack of enteral stimulation (cholestasis/sludge).
• Fatty liver (hepatic steatosis): Frequently occurs due to overfeeding, excess caloric load, or lipid imbalances.

Question (Front): Foods allowed in a low purine diet:
Rationale: These foods are generally low in purines and are appropriate choices in a low-purine diet. In contrast, organ meats contain very high amounts of purines and are restricted, particularly for patients with gout or hyperuricemia.

Question (Front): The enzyme that cleaves aromatic amino acids.
Rationale: Chymotrypsin is a pancreatic protease that preferentially cleaves peptide bonds on the carboxyl side of aromatic amino acids, particularly phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan. This specificity helps break dietary proteins into smaller peptides during intestinal digestion.

Question (Front): It refers to the anabolic formation of triacyglycerol from glycerol and fatty acids.
Rationale: Lipogenesis refers broadly to the formation and storage of fat, including the synthesis of triacylglycerol (TAG) from glycerol-derived molecules and fatty acids. It occurs primarily when energy intake exceeds immediate energy needs, allowing excess energy to be stored as body fat.

Question (Front): What is the first feeding for a patient with 1200 kcal, 2:1 diet Rx?
Rationale: In the traditional therapeutic-diet terminology used in Philippine dietetics, a 2:1 diet prescription refers to a diet in which the first feeding is omitted. The prescribed 1,200 kcal refers to the total daily energy allowance, but the specific first feeding is determined by the diet pattern/order rather than by simply selecting a liquid food. Thus, “no first feeding” is the intended answer.
Option 1: 1/2 evaporated milk diluted in 1/2 cup water
Option 2: 1/2 cup juice diluted in 1/2 cup water
Option 4: Cannot be determined from the given provided

Question (Front): The conversion of acetyl-CoA into acetoacetic acid, beta-hydroxybutryric acid or acetone is called:
Rationale: Ketogenesis is the metabolic process in which excess acetyl-CoA, primarily generated from fatty acid oxidation in the liver, is converted into ketone bodies: acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone. It becomes more active when carbohydrate availability or insulin action is insufficient, such as during prolonged fasting, starvation, or uncontrolled diabetes.

Question (Front): Substance found in raw egg white that binds with biotin preventing its absorption:
Rationale: Avidin is a glycoprotein found in raw egg white that binds very strongly to biotin (vitamin B7), reducing its intestinal absorption. Regular consumption of large amounts of raw egg white can therefore contribute to biotin deficiency. Cooking denatures avidin, greatly reducing its ability to bind biotin, which is why this problem is primarily associated with raw egg whites.

Question (Front): Keshan disease is a condition characterized by heart enlargement and is caused by deficiency of what nutrient?
Rationale: Keshan disease is a form of cardiomyopathy associated with severe selenium deficiency, originally described in areas of China with selenium-poor soil. It can cause cardiac enlargement, impaired cardiac function, and potentially heart failure. Selenium is important for antioxidant defense through selenoproteins such as glutathione peroxidases, which help protect tissues from oxidative damage.

Question (Front): Foods to avoid when preparing a patient for a test for occult blood in the stool:
Rationale: For the traditional guaiac-based fecal occult blood test (gFOBT), patients may be instructed to avoid red meat and certain vegetables, particularly those containing peroxidase activity, because they can produce false-positive results. Examples include some leafy and cruciferous vegetables. This dietary restriction is specific to guaiac-based testing; newer fecal immunochemical tests (FIT) detect human hemoglobin and generally do not require these dietary restrictions.

Question (Front): Which of the following enhances the absorption of zinc?
Rationale: Glutamate and other amino acids can enhance zinc absorption by forming soluble complexes with zinc and facilitating its uptake in the small intestine. In contrast, substances such as phytate strongly inhibit zinc absorption by binding zinc and forming poorly absorbed complexes.

Question (Front): A patient on tube feeding has a Diet Rx of 2000 Calories, 2:1 dilution; how much is the total fluid.
Rationale:
In the traditional tube-feeding prescription, a 2:1 dilution means 2 kcal for every 1 mL of formula. 

Therefore: 2,000 kcal ÷ 2 kcal/mL = 1,000 mL/day

Thus, the total volume of tube-feeding formula prescribed is 1,000 mL/day.

Question (Front): __ and__ are the major intracellular and extracellular cations in the body, respectively.
Rationale: Potassium (K⁺) is the major cation inside cells (intracellular fluid), while sodium (Na⁺) is the major cation outside cells (extracellular fluid). Their concentration gradients are maintained largely by the sodium-potassium pump (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase), which is essential for maintaining cell membrane potential, nerve transmission, and muscle contraction.

Question (Front): The body's normal pH range is:
Rationale:
Normal arterial blood pH is maintained at approximately 7.35–7.45, reflecting a slightly alkaline environment. The body tightly regulates pH through the bicarbonate buffer system, lungs, and kidneys.

Values below 7.35 indicate acidemia, while values above 7.45 indicate alkalemia.

Question (Front):
Dietary antioxidants:
I. Manganese
II. Flavonoids
III. Phenolic compounds
Rationale: All three can contribute to antioxidant defense. Manganese is an essential mineral that is part of the antioxidant enzyme manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), which helps neutralize superoxide radicals in mitochondria. Flavonoids and phenolic compounds are plant-derived phytochemicals that can have antioxidant activity by scavenging reactive species and influencing antioxidant pathways.

Question (Front): This phytochemical, which is usually found in red wines and peanuts, prevents artery-damaging effects of high fat diets.
Rationale: Resveratrol is a polyphenolic compound found in the skin of red grapes and therefore in red wine, as well as in peanuts and some other plants. It has been studied for potential cardiovascular benefits through antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and endothelial effects. The original wording that it “prevents” artery damage is too absolute; resveratrol is better described as a phytochemical associated with potentially protective cardiovascular effects.

Question (Front): Prolonged calorie undernutrition can cause a 20-30% decrease in BMR. Habitual high energy intake also decrease BMR.
Rationale: Prolonged energy restriction can reduce basal metabolic rate (BMR) through metabolic adaptation, including reduced thermogenesis and changes in metabolically active tissues and endocrine function. A decrease of approximately 20–30% has been described in severe or prolonged energy restriction. In contrast, habitual high energy intake does not decrease BMR; increased energy intake may increase diet-induced thermogenesis and total energy expenditure.

Question (Front): When a person is stressed, the secretion of the following hormones is increased EXCEPT:
Rationale:
During physiological stress, the body enters a catabolic, hypermetabolic state designed to ensure adequate fuel availability. Glucagon, cortisol, and catecholamines increase and promote glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and mobilization of energy substrates. 

Insulin secretion is generally suppressed or its action is reduced (insulin resistance) during the stress response, helping maintain elevated blood glucose for tissues with high energy demands.

Question (Front): __ are responsible for cell-mediated immunity while __ are responsible for humoral immunity.
Rationale: T lymphocytes are primarily responsible for cell-mediated immunity, including direct killing of infected or abnormal cells and coordination of immune responses. B lymphocytes are responsible for humoral immunity through their differentiation into plasma cells that produce antibodies.

Question (Front): Electron-carrier molecules that are used in the electron-transport chain to generate additional ATP are:
Rationale: NADH and FADH₂ are reduced electron carriers that transport high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain (ETC) in the inner mitochondrial membrane. As electrons pass through the ETC, the released energy drives proton pumping, creating a proton gradient that powers ATP synthase to produce ATP through oxidative phosphorylation.

Question (Front): It is secreted by macrophages to active lymphocytes, suppress appetite and induce malaise and fever.
Rationale: Monokines are signaling proteins historically used to describe cytokines produced by monocytes and macrophages. Examples include interleukin-1 (IL-1) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF), which can promote immune-cell activation and produce systemic effects such as fever, anorexia, and malaise during inflammation.

Question (Front): These scavenge and engulf foreign bodies and secrete complements and cytokines.
Rationale: Macrophages are specialized phagocytic cells that engulf and digest pathogens, cellular debris, and other foreign material. They also secrete cytokines that regulate inflammation and immune responses and can produce components of the complement system. Macrophages also function as antigen-presenting cells, helping activate adaptive immune responses.

Question (Front): All of the following are possible nutritional effects of intestinal resection among cancer patients EXCEPT:
Rationale: Intestinal resection can lead to several gastrointestinal and nutritional complications depending on the site and extent of resection. These include diarrhea from reduced absorptive capacity, hyperoxaluria particularly after significant ileal resection, and blind loop syndrome when abnormal intestinal anatomy or stasis promotes bacterial overgrowth. Diabetes mellitus, however, is not a typical direct nutritional consequence of intestinal resection.

Question (Front): A general principle in the prevention and management of an inborn error of metabolism if there is accumulation of precursor to toxic levels:
Rationale: When an inborn error of metabolism causes a precursor to accumulate to toxic concentrations because it cannot be adequately metabolized, a key treatment principle is to restrict the dietary source of that precursor. This reduces substrate entering the defective metabolic pathway and helps prevent further accumulation and toxicity. The specific dietary restriction depends on the metabolic disorder—for example, phenylalanine restriction in phenylketonuria (PKU).
Option 2: Give increased quantities of the vitamin involved

Question (Front): How much energy can a 1 liter of 5% dextrose solution provide?
Rationale:
A 5% dextrose solution (D5W) contains 5 g dextrose per 100 mL, or 50 g/L. Dextrose provides approximately 3.4 kcal/g when given intravenously.

Therefore: 50 g × 3.4 kcal/g = 170 kcal

Thus, 1 L of 5% dextrose provides approximately 170 kcal

Question (Front): Hypoparathyroidism can lead to Chvostek's and Trousseau's syndrome. Hyperparathyroidism, on the other hand, can cause osteopenia and osteoporosis.
Rationale: Hypoparathyroidism causes decreased parathyroid hormone (PTH), leading to hypocalcemia, which increases neuromuscular excitability and may produce Chvostek’s and Trousseau’s syndrome. In contrast, prolonged hyperparathyroidism increases PTH-mediated bone resorption, which can reduce bone mineral density and contribute to osteopenia and osteoporosis.

Question (Front): Which of the following are disease of the large intestines?
Rationale: Diverticular disease, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and constipation are all disorders involving the large intestine. Diverticular disease involves the formation and/or inflammation of diverticula, typically in the colon. IBS is a disorder of gut-brain interaction characterized by abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits, while constipation involves infrequent or difficult bowel movements and commonly reflects impaired colonic transit or evacuation.

Question (Front): Which of the following are included in the nutrition care guidelines for reducing gastroesophageal reflux disease?
Rationale: Nutrition management of GERD focuses on reducing factors that can worsen reflux symptoms. Large and high-fat meals can delay gastric emptying and may promote reflux. Alcoholic beverages may aggravate symptoms in some individuals, while acidic or highly spiced foods may worsen discomfort, particularly when esophageal irritation is present. Dietary triggers are individualized, so foods that consistently provoke symptoms should be identified and limited.
Option 2: Avoid acidic and highly spiced foods when inflammation exists

Question (Front): Which is the most important component of the medical nutrition theraphy for patients with celiac disease?
Rationale: The cornerstone of medical nutrition therapy for celiac disease is a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet. This requires avoiding gluten-containing grains such as wheat, rye, and barley, carefully checking food labels for gluten-containing ingredients or contamination, and using naturally gluten-free alternatives such as rice, corn, and potatoes. Therefore, all three measures are important components of implementing a gluten-free diet.
Option 1: Omit sources of gluten as wheat, rye and barley
Option 2: Reading labels to check if the product contains gluten
Option 3: Substitute wheat flour with potato, rice, corn

Question (Front): Childhood diarrhea plays a significant role in malnutrition. Infections within the intestine can lead to loss of nutrients, damage to the gut mucosa, and impaired nutrient absorption. The WHO and UNICEF guidelines for managing diarrheal diseases in children include which of the following?
Rationale: Management of acute diarrhea in children emphasizes preventing and treating dehydration with oral rehydration solution (ORS), continuing breastfeeding and age-appropriate feeding to prevent deterioration of nutritional status, and zinc supplementation to reduce the duration and severity of diarrhea and the risk of subsequent episodes. Therefore, all three are key components of recommended management.

Question (Front):
Which of the following is true about anemia?
I. characterized by reduction in the size and quantity of red blood cells
II. result to decreased capacity of the blood to carry oxygen
Rationale:
Anemia is defined by a reduction in hemoglobin concentration, hematocrit, or red blood cell mass below the normal range, resulting in reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. 

Statement I is incorrect because anemia does not necessarily involve a reduction in RBC size. RBC size may be normal (normocytic), small (microcytic), or large (macrocytic), depending on the underlying cause.

Question (Front): Which of the following proteins have an important role in the immune response?
Rationale: Globulins, particularly gamma globulins (immunoglobulins/antibodies), play an essential role in the immune response. Antibodies recognize and bind specific foreign antigens and help neutralize pathogens or facilitate their elimination. Other globulin proteins also include components involved in immune and inflammatory processes.

Question (Front): Anemia that is induced by poor blood clotting:
Rationale: Hemorrhagic anemia results from excessive blood loss, which can occur when blood clotting is impaired. Poor clotting allows bleeding to continue or become excessive, leading to loss of red blood cells and hemoglobin. Causes may include coagulation disorders, severe vitamin K deficiency, anticoagulant therapy, or other conditions that impair hemostasis. However, technically, poor clotting is a cause of blood loss rather than the defining cause of hemorrhagic anemia.

Question (Front): Osteomalacia is result of:
Rationale: Osteomalacia is defective mineralization of bone in adults, most commonly associated with vitamin D deficiency, which can result from inadequate dietary intake or insufficient sunlight exposure. Parathyroid disorders, particularly conditions causing increased PTH activity, can also contribute to impaired bone mineralization through disturbances in calcium and phosphate metabolism. Therefore, all three factors can contribute to osteomalacia.

Question (Front): Resting energy expenditure is the amount of energy required for the basal metabolic processes and TEF per unit weight per unit time. It is also called resting metabolic rate.
Rationale:
REE and RMR are generally used interchangeably to describe the energy expended by the body at rest to maintain essential physiological functions. However, statement 1 is incorrect because REE does not include the thermic effect of food (TEF). 

TEF is a separate component of total daily energy expenditure. Also, REE/RMR is usually expressed as kcal/day or kcal/kg/day, but “per unit weight per unit time” is not part of its defining concept. Commonly used REE or RMR Equations are Mifflin-St Jeor and Harris-Benedict, while TEF = REE + TEF + Activity Energy Expenditure.

Question (Front): Which is not predisposing factor of gout:
Rationale:
Low purine intake is a protective factor, not a predisposing factor. A strict low-purine diet decreases the amount of uric acid produced in the body, lowering the risk of developing gout and reducing the frequency of painful flare-ups.

• High fat diet and starvation: High saturated fat diets impair the intestinal and renal excretion of urate. Starvation triggers the production of ketone bodies (like beta-hydroxybutyrate), which directly compete with uric acid for excretion sites in the kidneys, causing uric acid levels to skyrocket.
• Renal disorders: Roughly 90% of gout cases are caused by the kidneys' inability to adequately excrete uric acid. Chronic kidney disease or renal insufficiency leads to hyperuricemia and crystal deposition.
• Obesity: Being overweight or obese increases the body's internal production of uric acid while simultaneously reducing how efficiently the kidneys can filter and excrete it.

Question (Front): The following are dietary management for Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome EXCEPT:
Answer (Back): High energy and protein tube feedings
Rationale: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is associated with severe thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, commonly in the setting of chronic alcohol use and malnutrition. Management includes prompt thiamine replacement, adequate hydration and nutritional rehabilitation, and alcohol avoidance. However, high-energy/high-protein tube feeding is not a routine specific dietary management measure; enteral feeding is used when oral intake is inadequate or unsafe, and nutrition should be advanced appropriately rather than automatically prescribing high-energy, high-protein tube feeding.
Option 4: High energy and protein tube feedings

Question (Front):
Dietary management for Myasthenia Gravis:
I. adjusted food consistency depending on tolerance; nutrient-dense; small frequent feeding
II. avoid foods which contain I-dopa
III. limit dietary protein at breakfast and lunch
IV. low glycemic index treatment
Rationale: The major nutrition concerns in myasthenia gravis (MG) are fatigue and weakness of the muscles involved in chewing and swallowing, which can increase the risk of inadequate intake and aspiration. Appropriate management includes modifying food texture/consistency according to swallowing ability, choosing nutrient-dense foods, and using small, frequent meals to reduce fatigue during eating. Avoidance of L-dopa, protein restriction at specific meals, and low-glycemic-index treatment are not standard dietary therapies for MG.

Question (Front):
Dietary recommendation for rheumatic fever:
I. high kcal, high protein, high fluids, low fiber
II.high kcal, high protein, Na and fluid controlled, vitamin and mineral supplements
III. high kcal, high protein, fat-restricted
Rationale: During acute rheumatic fever, nutrition should support growth, tissue repair, and recovery, so adequate energy and high-quality protein are important. When there is carditis or heart failure, sodium and fluid may need to be restricted to help control edema and fluid overload. Adequate vitamins and minerals should also be provided. There is no routine indication for a low-fiber diet or for fat restriction in rheumatic fever itself.

Question (Front): An 84 year-old client complains of chronic constipation. To improve bowel function, what could be a possible intervention?
Rationale: Increasing dietary fiber, together with adequate fluid intake and appropriate physical activity, is a first-line approach for managing constipation in older adults when there is no contraindication. Fiber increases stool bulk and can improve bowel regularity. Fiber should be increased gradually, with adequate fluid intake, to minimize bloating and discomfort. For an older adult with chronic constipation, the underlying cause and medications should also be assessed.
Option 2: avoidance of binding foods such as cheese and chocolate
Option 3: monitoring a balance between activity and rest

Question (Front): What is the initial therapy for kwashiorkor?
Rationale: In severe acute malnutrition such as kwashiorkor, the initial priority is stabilization, particularly correction of life-threatening problems such as hypoglycemia, hypothermia, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalance. Rehydration must be done cautiously, because children with kwashiorkor may have edema and impaired cardiac/renal function, making them vulnerable to fluid overload. Energy and protein rehabilitation are important, but aggressive feeding or protein replacement should not be the first step during the initial stabilization phase.

Question (Front): The following are dietary management for anorexia nervosa, EXCEPT:
Answer (Back): use of food items that promote early satiety
Rationale: Nutrition therapy for anorexia nervosa aims to restore weight and nutritional status while minimizing factors that interfere with adequate intake. Foods that promote early satiety—such as bulky, high-fiber, or large-volume foods—are generally avoided because they can make it difficult for the patient to consume sufficient energy. Instead, small, frequent, energy-dense meals are useful. Cold or room-temperature foods may be better tolerated in some patients, and limiting caffeine can help reduce appetite suppression and excessive stimulation.
Option 1: use of food items that promote early satiety
Option 3: give cold or room temperature foods

Question (Front): Which of the following is NOT recommended for patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)?
Answer (Back): Increase the interval between meals by skipping meals
Rationale: GERD management emphasizes meal size, meal timing, body position, and individualized trigger-food avoidance rather than deliberately skipping meals. Large meals, especially near bedtime, can worsen reflux, while remaining upright after eating can reduce symptoms. Patients are encouraged to identify foods and beverages that reliably trigger their symptoms rather than unnecessarily eliminating foods. Skipping meals or intentionally prolonging the interval between meals is not a standard GERD intervention.
Option 1: Avoid large meals, particularly close to bedtime
Option 2: Remain upright for several hours after meals
Option 3: Identify and limit foods and beverages that consistently trigger symptoms
Option 4: Increase the interval between meals by skipping meals

Question (Front): How much sodium does a 1 tsp of salt contain?
Rationale: One teaspoon of table salt (sodium chloride) contains approximately 2,300 mg of sodium. However, nutrition teaching materials commonly use the approximation of 2,000 mg sodium per teaspoon of salt, which is the value this question is evidently targeting. Since the exact sodium content varies somewhat with the type and packing of salt, 2,000 mg is an approximation rather than an exact chemical value.

Question (Front): Dietary management for hepatic coma:
Rationale: Current clinical consensus (from guidelines like AASLD, EASL, ESPEN, and ISHEN) rejects routine protein restriction in hepatic encephalopathy and hepatic coma because protein restriction worsens muscle wasting and catabolism without improving mental status. Patients generally require high caloric intake (about 30–40 kcal/kg/day) and adequate-to-high protein intake (about 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day), often favoring vegetable- or dairy-based proteins or branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs).
Option 1: high kcal, zero to low protein

Question (Front): What vitamin should be provided for the dietary management for sideroblastic anemia that is characterized by pale RBC but with normal hemoglobin levels?
Rationale:
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is an important cofactor in heme synthesis, particularly for the enzyme ALA synthase. Sideroblastic anemia results from impaired heme synthesis, causing iron to accumulate in erythroblast mitochondria and producing characteristic ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow. 

Some forms, particularly pyridoxine-responsive sideroblastic anemia, can respond to vitamin B6 supplementation. However, sideroblastic anemia has multiple causes, so B6 therapy is not appropriate for every case.

Question (Front): The following are dietary management measures for a patient with an ileostomy, EXCEPT:
Rationale: After an ileostomy, particularly during the initial postoperative period, a low-residue/low-fiber diet is commonly recommended to reduce stool volume and decrease the risk of obstruction. Adequate fluid and electrolyte intake is also important because ileostomy output can result in substantial fluid and sodium losses. Vitamin B12 supplementation may be necessary when the terminal ileum has been resected because this is the primary site of vitamin B12–intrinsic factor absorption. A low-fat diet may also be useful when fat malabsorption is present.

Question (Front): The science that deals with the progressive movement and alteration of chemical substances within the body:
Rationale:
Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a drug, including its absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME). It examines how a drug moves through the body and how its concentration changes over time. 

Pharmacodynamics describes what the drug does to the body, including its mechanisms of action and effects on physiological processes. While Pharmacogenomics studies how an individual's genetic variation influences drug response, including efficacy and adverse effects.

Question (Front): Which drug may bind with phosphorus and reduce its absorption?
Rationale: Some antacids, particularly those containing aluminum or calcium, can bind phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract and form poorly absorbed complexes, thereby reducing phosphorus absorption. This property is also therapeutically used with aluminum- or calcium-based phosphate binders in patients with chronic kidney disease and hyperphosphatemia.

Question (Front): May interact with phenobarbital through competitive inhibition:
Rationale: Phenobarbital and other anticonvulsants can interfere with folate metabolism and utilization, and long-term anticonvulsant therapy is associated with reduced folate status. Folate supplementation may therefore be needed in patients receiving prolonged therapy. The interaction is commonly described in nutrition/drug-interaction references as an effect of anticonvulsants on folate metabolism, although the exact pharmacokinetic mechanism is more complex than simple competitive inhibition.

Question (Front): Foods to be restricted in dumping syndrome:
Rationale:
In dumping syndrome, especially early dumping, rapid delivery of hyperosmolar food from the stomach into the small intestine can cause gastrointestinal and vasomotor symptoms.

Simple carbohydrates and concentrated sugars should be limited because they rapidly increase intestinal osmotic load and glucose absorption, potentially worsening symptoms.

Meals are generally made small and frequent, with adequate protein and moderate fat, and fluids are often consumed between rather than with meals.

Question (Front): The following food are allowed for patient with celiac disease, EXCEPT:
Rationale: Patients with celiac disease must avoid gluten-containing ingredients and products with significant risk of gluten contamination.
